title: The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges
author: Venerable Yuanyin
excerpt: The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is a high-level practice in Buddhist tantra: cultivating yet cultivating nothing, cultivation itself being no-cultivation, where the path of words is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. In the place where not a single thought arises and yet all is vividly clear, and where all is vividly clear and yet not a single thought arises, one seeks a message there; then one awakens to the truth that affliction itself is bodhi, that deluded thoughts are wondrous function, that emptiness and existence are non-dual, that substance and function are one, and that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma.

rows.s: Chapter One: An Explanation of the Three Essentials of the Mahāmudrā
Chapter Two: The View of the Mahāmudrā
Chapter Three: The Meditation of the Mahāmudrā
Chapter Four: The Practice of the Mahāmudrā

inline.s: The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is a high-level practice in Buddhist tantra: cultivating yet cultivating nothing, cultivation itself being no-cultivation, where the path of words is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. In the place where not a single thought arises and yet all is vividly clear, and where all is vividly clear and yet not a single thought arises, seek a message there; then you will awaken to the truth that affliction itself is bodhi, that deluded thoughts are wondrous function, that emptiness and existence are non-dual, that substance and function are one, and that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma.

Venerable Yuanyin (the elder Mr. Li Zhongding), at the advanced age of ninety-four, taught the Dharma, expounded the scriptures, and wrote books without sparing himself. This book is another great work following The Essentials of Buddhist Practice and Realization: exhorting again and again, holding nothing back, vivid and lively, leading from one point to another, it is truly a precious raft for ferrying beings across and a key to becoming a Buddha. May the people of aspiration and benevolence who read this book open the eye of wisdom, enter the gate of no-marks, and bring forth great capacity and great function, with an endless vow of compassion, so as not to betray the old man’s earnest heart!
January 1999, respectfully prefaced by the student Xu Hengzhi

Here I will speak to everyone about the Mahāmudrā. The Mahāmudrā is the highest teaching of the tantras. The tantras are divided into nine vehicles, and this belongs to the highest of them; in Tibetan it is called Atiyoga, that is, the Heart Center Dharma of perfect union. We have all practiced the Heart Center Dharma for a long time now, and should have some results. Some of you have already broken open the original and seen the nature; others, perhaps, when the nature manifested before you while sitting, did not notice it and let it slip past.

So today I will speak with you about what Buddha-nature actually is, how one may come to see it, and how, after seeing it, one may go further upward, bringing forth wondrous function and perfecting the Buddha-fruit.
In this way I hope to remind and urge everyone to advance together.

Note: In the tantras it is determined that the Buddha-dharma is divided into nine vehicles — the outer three, the inner three, and the secret three. Let me explain the content of these nine vehicles a little: the outer three are the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle, referring to the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six perfections and ten thousand practices carried out by arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas — broadly speaking, the exoteric teachings. The inner three refer to the three classes of practice: the action class, the performance class, and the yoga class. The action class is also called the activity class, and includes such methods as increasing, pacifying, magnetizing, and subjugating. These are all dharmas that arise in response to the wishes of beings; they are also the expedient means of drawing beings in by first hooking them with desire and afterward leading them into Buddha-wisdom, and they are not ultimate. The purpose of the performance class is to end birth and death and escape the sea of suffering; only this counts as entering genuine practice. One begins from visualization and cultivates the winds, the channels, and the drops, as in the phowa method and so on. Yoga means “union”: in the yoga class, phenomena accord with principle, words accord with action, one is in union with all Buddhas above and with all beings below. From this there open out three levels, which are the secret three. The secret three are Mahāyoga, Anuyoga, and Atiyoga. Mahāyoga means “union with the great perfection”: the visualized winds, channels, and so on — things that have marks — are dissolved into emptiness, so as to be in union with the markless dharmakāya. Anuyoga means “union with the supreme perfection”: taking the wisdom of the sphere as the gate of entry, one further dissolves all appearances into a single true reality. Atiyoga means “union with the peerless perfection,” and one further joins the three vehicles into one great mantra vehicle.

The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is exactly the same as the Chan school: it too does not speak of any dharma to practice, but speaks of no cultivation, no attainment, no realization, directly pointing to the human mind so that one becomes a Buddha. But this no cultivation, no attainment, no realization is the natural wisdom of the true suchness of the nature; only when we have realized this state can we speak of no cultivation, no attainment, no realization — it is not something to be idly talked about. If one merely understands a few principles, and has not yet made mind and circumstance one, is not free in favorable and adverse conditions, and is not at ease in every direction, yet says there is no cultivation, no attainment, no realization, then it has lost all meaning! So we should speak about the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges with everyone.

What is called the Mahāmudrā is not a hand-seal (mudrā) that one uses in practice, as when we practice the Heart Center Dharma with its six mudrās and one mantra, which must be practiced by forming the seals and reciting the mantra. This dharma is a direct-pointing gate: it tells us directly what the true mind is, how to develop wisdom, and how to bring forth wondrous function. So this dharma is a straightforward, direct-pointing gate, and those who practice the Heart Center Dharma will find it very useful, since the Heart Center Dharma likewise does not go through marks but directly realizes the mind-ground. There are many kinds of Mahāmudrā; the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is the highest of them all, for it requires no visualization, winds, channels, drops, or deity yoga, and no recitation of any mantra; it directly points us to see the nature and become a Buddha, and so it is the highest teaching of all.

What is called the Mahāmudrā is the one true dharma-realm. What is the one true dharma-realm? It is our own true suchness, the wondrous substance of the nature, which is also the root of becoming a Buddha. Why is it called the great mudrā? Because our Buddha-nature is so great that nothing lies outside it, and so small that nothing lies within it. As it is said, “The greatest form has no shape; the greatest sound is scarcely heard.” The greatest mark is the mark of no-mark; what has no mark to be seen is the greatest form. Our nature is neither empty nor existent, neither blue nor yellow, neither great nor small — everything is negated. So to describe it as resembling anything at all misses the mark; there is nothing to which it can be compared, because it is formless, markless, and beyond comparison. It is inconceivably vast, filling all space and pervading the dharma-realm, excluding nothing and lacking no dharma. The hand is the mind, and the mind is the hand; the common saying “the hand responds to the mind” expresses just this principle. Were it not the mind, the hand would not move either. The seal means that we and the Buddha are mind-to-mind, sealed with one another: the Buddha-mind is my mind, my mind is the Buddha-mind. Hence the scripture says: “Mind, Buddha, and beings — these three are without distinction.” It also says: “A thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas share one body,” which is exactly this meaning. So the Mahāmudrā is our own great mind, our own nature. All things arise from it, appear through it, and change through it — this is called the Mahāmudrā. The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is just this good and this high; therefore below we shall openly explain this precious dharma to everyone.
All-embracing within the mind: view, meditation, and action

blocks.text: 1. Mind, Buddha, and Beings Are Without Distinction

inline.s: We Buddhists should know that our mind — the Buddha-nature — is no different from that of the patriarchs of every generation. Here the patriarchs of every generation stand in place of the Buddhas, because the Buddhas have already entered nirvāṇa and the Buddha-dharma is now transmitted by the patriarchs; taking the patriarchs to represent the Buddhas, Buddha and patriarchs become one body. Since our mind is no different from that of all the lineage gurus, it is therefore no different from the Buddha.

Here some people cannot help but raise doubts: we are ordinary beings and the Buddha is holy; ordinary and holy are not the same, so how can they be without distinction? Such a person does not know that the substance of the nature is neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; ordinary and holy are exactly alike. The reason the Buddha has vast spiritual powers and boundless wondrous function while we do not is that every stain and impurity on the Buddha’s nature has been washed clean. Because we cling to the false appearances of things and give rise to inverted deluded thoughts, we defile our own nature; it is like the sun covered by dark clouds, whose light cannot show through, and so we cannot manifest spiritual function. But however thick the clouds and however they cover it, the sun is still there, its light has not diminished by a single fraction, and when the clouds disperse the sun appears in all its glory. That is to say, however defiled our mind may be (because we cling to marks), as soon as we wash away the defilement and accumulated grime, we are as radiant as the Buddha. As it is said, “In the sage it does not increase; in the ordinary being it does not decrease” — we do not lose the radiant substance of the nature merely because we are ordinary beings. It is only that, because we cling and have inverted deluded thoughts, our habitual taints are deep and heavy and cover the nature, so its light cannot appear; the essence itself remains the same.

Why say this? This saying is extremely important, because now we wish to become Buddhas, to end birth and death, escape the round of rebirth, and deliver beings. First we must know how to practice; and in practicing, the first thing is to have a correct view. This view is the cause-ground: when we begin, we must first know what we practice with and how to practice, so that we may quickly and perfectly succeed; otherwise we take many detours. So first we must know that our own nature is originally the same as that of all the Buddhas, without difference, and that to cultivate and realize with it is like needing rice to cook a meal — there is absolutely no failure. Once we understand this, we are no longer in doubt about being able to cultivate and become a Buddha, and only then does our practice bring results quickly. Otherwise, the Buddha is highest and supreme, beyond all reach, and we are all ordinary beings — how could we become Buddhas? How could our practice succeed? As soon as doubt arises we hesitate and shrink back, and cannot succeed. For faith is the mother of success: to accomplish anything, the first requirement is abundant faith; without faith, nothing can be accomplished. Take those who practice the Pure Land school: first they must believe deeply and without doubt that the Western Pure Land truly exists, and that if they simply vow and recite the Buddha-name, then at the end of life Amitābha Buddha will certainly receive them and bring them to birth in the West. Then, reciting the Buddha-name diligently, they succeed at the end of life. But if their faith is not deep and they half believe and half doubt — “Oh dear, my karmic obstacles are heavy; can I be born in the West? I am afraid I cannot” — then it will not do, for because they doubt and waver, their effort has no strength and they cannot press forward single-mindedly, and so they cannot succeed. Therefore faith is first; it is so in everything, and so in worldly matters too. If I believe a thing can succeed, I am willing to work hard at it; though I meet failure I am not afraid, and I strive again and again, and in the end I certainly succeed. Otherwise, at the first setback I lose heart, and inevitably accomplish nothing.

The opening sentence is simply telling us to have firm faith that our nature is no different from the Buddha’s. Since all the lineage gurus represent the Buddha and are the same as the Buddha, and our nature is the same as the gurus’ nature, then it is no different from the Buddha-nature. In the path of cultivation, the view is of first importance; if the view is wrong, the result will certainly be roundabout and full of detours. If we can truly have firm faith that our nature is the same as the Buddha’s, without difference, and if we simply cultivate, knowing to cultivate upon the essence, transforming inverted deluded thoughts and recovering our original face — not cultivating on the physical body and not seeking outside — then we will certainly become Buddhas. With firm faith, we no longer seek outside. Otherwise we race about seeking outside: today we seek the Buddha here, tomorrow we seek the Buddha there, or we expend effort on the physical body, and after all our seeking we end up with nothing. For you do not know that the nature itself is Buddha; not seeking within, you turn to grasp outside, and so your energy is wasted. To succeed in cultivation, one should seek from one’s own true mind. Wake up your own master: do not be deluded, do not dream! All the forms of the world are false, all are flowers in the sky and moons in the water, ungraspable; do not be deluded by your wife and children, your wealth and status — all are a fleeting blossoming of the udumbara, ungraspable.

That is why the Lotus Sūtra says, “Only this one matter is true; the other two are not real.” The only true thing is our one true dharma-realm — the true nature. What is the dharma-realm? The dharma-realm is the dharma-nature, also called true reality. “Dharma” refers to all dharmas; “realm” means division. Gathering in all that exists, it is broadly divided into ten, namely the four holy and the six ordinary. The four holy are Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats; the six ordinary are the beings of the six paths — gods, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals — all manifested by this nature. So not only are we humans the same in nature as all the Buddhas, but the true mind of the beings of the six paths is also no different from the true mind of all the Buddhas; sadly, they are deluded by sights and sounds, and their karmic obstacles are so heavy that they do not know it themselves. Therefore the Buddha, in compassion for us, appeared in the world to wake us: cling no more and dream no more — you are all the same as me, the Buddha; awaken quickly and escape the suffering of birth, death, and the round of rebirth!

On the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month, when the Buddha saw the morning star and awakened to the Way, he said: “How wonderful! All beings are endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous marks. It is only because of deluded thoughts, inversion, and clinging that they cannot realize it.” This shows that we beings have not lost the Buddha-nature because of birth, death, and the round of rebirth; if we simply awaken, and are no longer deluded by sights and sounds, we can recover our original face.

The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is exceedingly profound and high, and at the very outset it reminds us: the mind of every lineage guru and our own mind are the same, without distinction; do not suppose that they are too high to reach. We and all the Buddhas are exactly alike in mind, with no second difference. Once this is affirmed, and we no longer doubt that we ourselves are Buddhas — that it is only because we are deluded and unawakened, clinging to marks and inverted, that we fall into the round of rebirth — then, now that we are awake and no longer deluded by marks, no longer grasping, we recover our original state. This is the first essential of becoming a Buddha. So at the outset this vital sentence is spoken, and below it is explained: how we are no different in mind from all the Buddhas, how we recover our original state, how we bring forth wondrous function. This sentence is a general outline, and extremely important.
“View, meditation, and action — all practices are gathered into the mind.”

The three essentials of view, meditation, and action are the three secret keys of the Mahāmudrā, and also the essentials of practice for every dharma-gate. Why is this said? Because in cultivation the first requirement is a correct view. What has been said above — that our mind is no different from the mind of all the Buddhas — is what is called a correct understanding or a correct view. When the view is correct, the cause-ground is correct. When the cause-ground is correct, the fruit-ground can be correct. Otherwise one will surely go astray, mistake the wrong road, and fail to realize the true fruit. Hence it is said: “When the cause-ground is not correct, the fruit is crooked.” A practitioner whose cause-ground is not correct will certainly take detours and in the end fail; therefore this “view” is extremely important.

We ordinary beings all have the view of the body, clinging to this physical body as “I,” and clinging desperately! We must keep the body well, eat well, dress well, have everything good — all for this husk. Look at the teeming multitude of beings: who is not busy for this husk? From morning to night they are busy for the husk’s enjoyments; all the great and small affairs of this world are busily done for the husk; they always want to live in comfort and keep this husk well. Because they want enjoyment, they are not afraid to commit every kind of outrage. What they do not have, they snatch from others. The wars in this world are fought to seize things: if you will not give it to me, I will strike you, wipe out your country, and everything you have becomes mine. These bandit acts are all for the enjoyment of the husk. Not one crime in this society is committed for anything but the husk: they want to eat well and play well — and with no money in hand, what then? So they kill, set fires, and rob. In truth, if you create evil causes you must receive evil fruits! By the law of cause and effect, plant melons and you get melons, plant beans and you get beans, without the slightest error! If you do evil in the cause, you must receive evil retribution in the fruit. But these pitiable ordinary beings are deluded and unawakened, caring only for the pleasure before their eyes and ignoring the evil fruit to come. You think of killing someone — you will be punished by the law and beheaded; you rob others — you will face a lawsuit and go to prison. Do you not think: can evildoers escape? Alas, it is all delusion! And being repaid before your eyes is not the end of it; in the future you must also endure the terrible retribution of hell — it is dreadful!

Some people do not understand this principle: you say there is terrible retribution, but how is it that we see some bad people enjoying great good fortune now? And conversely, some good people suffer instead — cause and effect do not match! They do not know that cause and effect must be seen across three lifetimes. In the Buddhist scriptures there are two lines: “If you would know the causes of your past life, look at what you receive in this life; if you would know the fruits of your next life, look at what you do in this life.” The blessings he enjoys in this life were obtained by doing good deeds in the past. If he now does evil, he will receive evil retribution in the future; and not only that, his present blessings also diminish and his lifespan is shortened. When you now see a good person suffering, it is because he did evil in the past and is only now receiving the bitter fruit; and since he now does good, his evil retribution is imperceptibly reduced — where he was to suffer a great deal, it has now been lightened. These retributions are transformed in the unseen, and everyone is unaware of it. The Buddha’s eye sees it clearly, and so he says: “If you would know the causes of your past life, look at what you receive in this life.”

The Buddha’s eye does not see things as our ordinary eyes do; what we cannot see, he sees. Several thousand years ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there were neither telescopes nor microscopes, yet he told us: “A man sees a cup of water; a Buddha sees ten thousand insects.” He sees tens of thousands of insects in a cup of water, seeing it clearly, while people cannot see them. Now with our fleshly eyes we see only one sun in this world; only with an astronomical telescope can we see stars billions of light-years away. Since there are other planets, suns, and fixed stars in space, there must also be living beings on other planets. But the Buddha knew this long ago and saw it clearly. He told us: in space there are many worlds — worlds facing upward, worlds turned over, worlds aslant, and so on — and there are also many suns, exactly as scientists now say, with no difference. So the Buddha was one who knew beforehand and saw clearly, while people are very muddled. We should follow the Buddha’s teaching and put it into practice — only that is right.

The view must be correct; if the view is not correct, one will “vaguely and wildly meet with disaster.” The Buddhist scriptures speak of delusion of view and delusion of thought, meaning that we have incorrect views and thoughts that fixate on objects. We have just spoken of the view of the body; this is the first delusion among delusions of view. Next comes the extreme view. Because of the view of the body, one holds that the body cannot remain forever in the world — it must die. And after death, where does it go? Some say that after death there is nothing, which is annihilationism; others say it still exists, which is eternalism. Either one clings to eternalism or one fixes on annihilationism; both fall to the two extremes, and not departing from the two extremes of annihilation and eternity is called the extreme view. There is also the wrong view, which denies cause and effect, saying there is no cause and effect in the world — this does great harm to people; in the future, when he suffers in hell, he will know. And not only in the future: even the retribution before his eyes is unfailing — if you do evil you will be shot or imprisoned. Can you escape? So the wrong view is the most destructive and harmful of all.

Below there are also the outsiders’ view of the supremacy of views and the view of the supremacy of ascetic precepts. The view of the supremacy of views is to be deludedly attached to false views — that is, to hold the first three views (the view of the body, the extreme view, and the wrong view) as right view. The view of the supremacy of ascetic precepts is to deludedly cling to mortifying the body — undertaking all kinds of false precepts and austerities as the cause of being reborn after death among humans and gods in pleasant realms. For example, some cult nowadays falsely claims that the end of the world has come and that everyone should quickly commit suicide and ascend to heaven, causing people to die in mass suicides.

The above five views — the view of the body, the extreme view, the wrong view, the view of the supremacy of views, and the view of the supremacy of ascetic precepts — are all incorrect views; when the view is incorrect, the fruit is certainly crooked. We know that mind is Buddha and Buddha is mind; that in cultivation one does not seek outside; and that not clinging to the view of the body is correct view. When we recite the Buddha-name, we recite the mind; when we recite the mind, we recite the Buddha. If by our practice we can make this mind level and straight, without crookedness, without clinging, removing its abiding nature and its grasping nature, and thereby recover the original — this is correct view. Only by practicing thus can one attain anything, and so a correct view is extremely important. Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi said: “Because of differences in their views, practitioners realize five different fruits. First, one who cultivates with a different calculation (seeking dharmas outside the mind), delighting in the higher and loathing the lower, practices outsider-dhyāna. Second, one who correctly believes in cause and effect, yet likewise cultivates with delight and loathing, practices ordinary-being dhyāna. Third, one who awakens to the principle of the partial truth of the emptiness of self and cultivates accordingly practices Hīnayāna dhyāna. Fourth, one who awakens to the truth revealed by the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas and cultivates accordingly practices Mahāyāna dhyāna. Fifth, one who awakens that this mind is originally pure, that it is without affliction and has the nature of undefiled wisdom, originally complete in itself, and that this mind is Buddha — this is the supreme vehicle dhyāna. The Chan transmitted under Bodhidharma’s gate is this Chan.” From this it can be seen how important the view — that is, the causal mind — is in the process of cultivation.

What is meditation? Practitioners all know that to become a Buddha and attain the Way, one must sit in meditation and enter samādhi before one can develop wisdom and perfectly realize bodhi. But there are many kinds of meditation. Tathāgata Chan teaches the four dhyānas and eight samādhis: the practitioner rises from the first dhyāna gradually to the second, the third, and up to the summit of the fourth dhyāna heaven, which are the four dhyānas. Above these, passing through the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and entering the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, these are the four formless-heaven samādhis. Together with the first four dhyānas, that makes eight samādhis — these are the samādhis realized by the gradual dharma-gates. Patriarch Chan is not like this: Patriarch Chan is sudden cultivation, sudden awakening, sudden realization. Its followers do not cultivate this kind of samādhi; rather, with the very highest wisdom they break open the original, personally realize the Buddha-nature, and their minds are intimately attuned to samādhi. They say: a samādhi with entering and exiting is not great samādhi; only not being deluded when facing circumstances is true samādhi. To remain unmoved by any state, not to be deluded or confused by it, is what is called great samādhi. It is not that one is moved by a beautiful sight, covetous at the sight of gold and silver, and yet able to enter samādhi while sitting. Some further think that to sit motionless for several days and nights, or for many years, is great samādhi; in fact this is wrong — that is not great samādhi, only the samādhi of the extinction of feeling and perception. Their seventh consciousness, the actualization of the delusion of dharmas, is not extinguished; they merely do not grasp the six outer dusts and falsely reckon that consciousness has ceased. Once they emerge from samādhi, their reaction to circumstances is stronger than before they entered; such a samādhi is not ultimate and is not great samādhi. Therefore the Chan school does not advocate cultivating this kind of samādhi.

Here is one example to prove it. Long ago the Sixth Patriarch met Chan Master Wolun. Chan Master Wolun said: “Wolun has a trick: he can cut off a hundred thoughts; facing circumstances the mind does not arise, and bodhi grows day by day.” Chan Master Wolun was boasting of the depth of his meditative power, saying that he could keep his thoughts unmoving from morning to night, that no circumstance could shake him, and that his bodhi wisdom grew day by day. At first glance such meditative power is truly remarkable, but in fact it is wrong. Why? Because you abide unmoving in samādhi — you are dead there. When we become Buddhas, we become living Buddhas, not dead Buddhas. There is a lively, vivid wondrous function; it is not sitting there dead and unmoving. So this is not right samādhi. Right samādhi has neither entering nor emerging and can bring forth wondrous function. If you hold to a “meditative achievement” and sit there unmoving, unable to function, what use is that samādhi? So the Sixth Patriarch came to his rescue, saying: “Huineng has no trick.” You have ability, I have none. Speaking of ability, many practitioners today cling to “ability”: I have spiritual powers, my “ability” is great; you have no spiritual powers, so you have no “ability” at all. They do not know that clinging to spiritual powers means they have long since fallen into the old rut and are dead there. Whatever a practitioner abides in, the thing he abides in and clings to obscures the original radiance of the nature, and he cannot see the nature or become a Buddha. So although you may have spiritual powers, not only can you not become a Buddha — you are a candidate for becoming a demon. To become a Buddha, the mind must be empty and pure, utterly without clinging. Therefore the Sixth Patriarch said, “Huineng has no trick” — I, Huineng, have no trick: that is to say, you have ability, I have none. Why say this? Because to say one has a trick is already to have a place to fall. The nature is naked and bare, utterly clean, with not one dharma established, not one speck of dust clinging; the moment you say there is something, you have already missed it. “Huineng has no trick” is precisely picking out Wolun’s place of falling. “I do not cut off a hundred thoughts” — why? Because I must bring forth wondrous function to deliver beings! The Buddha is lively and vivid, with boundless wondrous function, not sitting there dead and unmoving. When the Buddha appeared in the world to teach the Dharma, he too had to use thought; if his thoughts did not move, could he have spoken the Dharma to us? So he said, “I do not cut off a hundred thoughts.” No thought need be cut off at all, because we still have a use for it!

The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts,” and immediately continues: “Toward all deluded minds, likewise do not extinguish them.” If you extinguish the deluded mind, the right thought is gone too, and you are dead, because the deluded mind comes from the true mind, just as waves rise from water; if the waves are extinguished, the water is gone as well. If we extinguish the deluded mind, we become earth, wood, metal, and stone — could you still realize the Way then? You would become a great boulder, a great log, a great clod of mud. So do not be impressed when someone sits in samādhi for a week, for months, for years, even for a hundred or a thousand years — it is of no use. To realize the great Way, one must open the perfect and sudden understanding, practice in accordance with reality, train unremittingly amid circumstances, and keep far from the deluded, illusory realms manifested by one’s own mind; only then can one be in accord. The skill of sitting blankly will not do — that is dead samādhi, and one cannot realize the Way by it.

Let me give one more kōan to prove that this teaching is not false. Long ago, when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world, a woman sat down beside him and entered samādhi. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva came and saw this, and thought: how can this woman be so ignorant of propriety as to enter samādhi right beside Śākyamuni Buddha? She ought to have withdrawn far behind the Buddha. So he snapped his fingers in front of the woman and called her to come out of samādhi, but the woman did not stir at all and did not emerge. Seeing that she had not emerged, Mañjuśrī displayed spiritual powers and lifted her up to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, yet the woman still did not emerge. Seeing that this would not do either, he cast her down into the eighteen hells, and still could not make her emerge. Śākyamuni Buddha said: “You cannot make her emerge; below there is a Wangming Bodhisattva who can.” No sooner had he spoken than Wangming Bodhisattva arrived from below, and the Buddha said: “You have come at just the right time; make this woman emerge from samādhi.” Wangming Bodhisattva snapped his fingers once in front of the woman, and she emerged.

This kōan is very puzzling: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is the teacher of seven Buddhas, the master of seven Buddhas, with inconceivable wisdom — how could he not make this woman emerge from samādhi? And Wangming Bodhisattva is merely a bodhisattva from below — how could a single snap of his fingers make her emerge? This kōan must be seen in terms of its essential meaning. The woman grasped at marks and entered samādhi: that was already a great mistake. As we said just now, if you abide in the mark of samādhi, if there is something you abide in, that is wrong. To become a Buddha, one must be utterly unattached, bringing forth wondrous function with lively vividness, and must not abide dead in samādhi. The woman’s abiding in samādhi was her first mistake. Then what of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva? He represents great wisdom — and is great wisdom not very good? But what we call wisdom is worldly cleverness and discriminative intelligence, not the great wisdom of prajñā. To become a Buddha, one must remove this deluded intelligence completely. If you have cleverness and intelligence, that is the obstruction of the known, the delusion of the known, barring the gate of your awakening to the Way, so that you cannot awaken.

Long ago Confucius went to visit Laozi, and Laozi said to him: “Strike down your wisdom” — that is, he told him to abolish and demolish his cleverness and intelligence, so that his mind was empty, with nothing at all and nowhere to abide, and only then could he awaken to the Way. So we should not boast of being clever; playing with petty cleverness is a great obstruction. One must be “greatly wise as though foolish,” with a mind that does not waver and clings to nothing, and only then can one realize the great Way. The mind settled and unmoving, abiding in nothing, is not like wood and stone, unknowing and unaware; it is a mind unmoved, vividly clear and perfectly distinct, with no rejecting and no grasping, no love and no hatred. So we must understand that right samādhi is not being confused by circumstances and having neither emerging nor entering — it is not sitting dead and unmoving. Then why could Wangming Bodhisattva make the woman emerge from samādhi? Wangming means to abolish your worldly cleverness and discriminative intelligence; when it is gone, with no knowing and no clinging, the great wisdom of prajñā appears before you. So this kōan is a presentation of Dharma; it is not that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva truly could not make her emerge, and still less that Wangming is higher than Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.

So if we wish to realize the Way, we must remove this worldly cleverness and discriminative intelligence, keeping the mind empty as if washed clean at every moment, neither turning with thoughts within nor pulled by circumstances without, training diligently, reducing and again reducing — only then can we succeed. The Sixth Patriarch said: “How unexpected that the self-nature is originally pure! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally neither born nor extinguished! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally unmoving! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally complete in itself! How unexpected that the self-nature can produce all dharmas!” Since the self-nature is complete in everything, lacking nothing, and originally pure, no different from the Buddha, if we can truly make the mind empty and undefiled, what is there that cannot be accomplished? Later Dahui Zonggao wrote a verse in praise of this kōan of emerging from samādhi, saying: “Whether one can emerge or not, that is samādhi but not right samādhi.” If you are busy with entering and emerging from samādhi here, that is not right samādhi but dead samādhi. True samādhi has neither entering nor emerging: it is thus in movement and thus in stillness; it is not sitting there dead and unmoving, but has boundless wondrous function. It is not that one is not in samādhi when speaking or doing things, but that the mind abides nowhere and does not see movement even when moving. If you abide in the mark of stillness, that is not right samādhi. The two great bodhisattvas Wangming and Mañjuśrī still make a fuss over entering and emerging from samādhi, and so cannot avoid departing from their original position. In the school it is said: “Absent for a moment, one is the same as a dead man.” To depart from one’s original position is to lose one’s life. So Chan Master Dahui Zonggao’s verse concludes: “Wangming and Mañjuśrī both lost their poor lives.” These two great bodhisattvas, the Buddha, and the woman performed a play for us precisely so that we might know how to apply effort. This is extremely important: in our practice we must on no account take up dead samādhi; we must be lively and vivid and unhindered in all things. Chan Master Lanrong said: “Just when the mind is applied, just then there is no mind applied; no-mind just applies, and constant application is just no-mind.” That is to say, precisely when we are doing things and speaking, our mind is still unattached and peacefully unmoving; it is not that sitting there motionless counts as samādhi while the moment something comes up we are thrown into confusion. Only when movement and stillness are one is there true samādhi.
What then is action? It is all our practices — our cultivation, that is, our deeds and activities.

View, meditation, and action are of vital importance to us practitioners, and so they are the three essentials of the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges. The view spoken of above means that when we first begin to practice, we should first set our understanding straight, so that we do not take detours, and so that we know what to do, how to apply effort, and what to practice with. So view is the practice of the causal ground. When we speak of becoming a Buddha, it is the mind that becomes Buddha, not the body; if the cause-ground is mistaken, the fruit will be crooked. We know that whatever dharma-gate one practices, one is cultivating the mind, and that only when the mind is empty and pure, clinging to nothing, can one realize the Way. So one must have a correct view and choose a dharma-gate suited to one’s own faculties; this cultivation is action. Through practicing according to one’s capacity one enters deep samādhi and opens great wisdom, and only then can one realize the Buddha-fruit. What this Mahāmudrā teaches is the great dharma of no cultivation, no attainment, no realization, no adjusting, and no distraction; it points out that the very capacity to speak, to act, to know, and to be aware is the Buddha, and tells us to awaken directly and see the nature — an unsurpassed wondrous dharma that needs no gradual practice.

There are many dharma-gates for our practice: some partial, some perfect, some sudden, some gradual. The practice of the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is the direct-pointing dharma within the perfect and sudden, telling us to see the nature right now and not to cultivate any dharma at all. Yet whether or not you have a method of practice, all is held within our true mind; hence it is said that all practices are gathered into the mind, all are contained and embraced by our mind. So the scripture says: “Nothing does not flow forth from this dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this dharma-realm.” Although the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges directly points us to see the nature right now without practicing any dharma, after seeing the nature the deluded habits of many lives cannot be removed all at once; so it also teaches action — that is, after seeing the nature one must still protect and sustain it closely, exhaust the old habits, enter the position of the unconditioned, and further dissolve its traces, and only then can one become one piece, perfectly fused and unobstructed.

blocks.text: 2. The Right View of Suchness

inline.s: “The view is to know clearly the one true dharma-realm, the naturally abiding Tathāgatagarbha mind, which manifests immeasurably the dharmas of defilement and purity and is complete in the meaning of naturally abiding equality.”

The view — what does one view? Clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. That is, we must know that to become a Buddha one must first have a clear view, recognizing that this one true dharma-realm, the naturally abiding Tathāgatagarbha mind, is right here shining at the six sense-gates, and then diligently protect it, and only then can one perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit. The one true dharma-realm is our true mind, our own nature. What is called “one true” means that only this one nature is real and all else is illusory; the “dharma-realm” is the ten dharma-realms spoken of above, namely the four holy and the six ordinary. The one true dharma-realm spoken of here is the essence of the four holy and the six ordinary; it has no holy and no ordinary, and so it is called the one true dharma-realm. Our nature is neither ordinary nor holy, utterly naked, with not one dharma established. The naturally abiding Tathāgatagarbha mind is simply thus from the beginning, without any fabrication; as it is said, the Buddha-nature is a matter of innate truth, not something produced by later fabrication.
“Naturally abiding” means simply thus from the beginning. The Tathāgatagarbha mind has two meanings: first, in the position of an ordinary being it is the Tathāgatagarbha (
cang

, the “store” of storing), that is, the Tathāgata’s nature is stored within; second, after you awaken to the Way it is the Tathāgatagarbha, a treasury, complete within it with all wondrous functions, like a maṇi jewel that can rain down all treasures, containing every wondrous function. Complete in all wondrous functions is the Tathāgatagarbha; once the treasury is opened it is inexhaustible and infinitely usable. Such a great treasure is right beside us, and yet we do not know it — do you see how pitiable, how wronged we are! The Lotus Sūtra says: “There is a maṇi jewel sewn into the lining of a man’s own garment, yet people do not know it and go begging outside instead.” This is truly utter folly. Alas, this is what the beings of the six paths are! The round of rebirth in the six paths is begging: one who is originally a supremely noble and wealthy man, complete in everything, now falls to begging in the streets — is this not too unjust? Now you must be made to know and to see your own original true nature, and not become a ghost who dies wronged. So the Mahāmudrā tells us directly: not only humans, but all beings are complete in the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature; it is only obscured by ignorance, clinging, deluded thoughts, inversion, and affliction, so that they cannot see it. If we can truly not cling to outer marks and exhaust all deluded thoughts and inversions, we can recover the radiance of the original face, and the great treasure we had forgotten returns to our hands. This treasure is not outside; do not seek or search for it outside — it is shining at your own six sense-gates. You need only turn the light around and look back; when the present thought has ended and the next has not yet arisen, a cool glance and you will understand that you were originally a Buddha. So the Mahāmudrā is a direct-pointing gate, directly pointing us to see the nature; it does not tell you to investigate a huatou and raise doubt until you can awaken.

What is called the view is not seeing something with the eyes, but experiencing. But how does one see this one true dharma-realm? It is when you do not think of good, do not think of evil, and no deluded thought arises at all; turn the light around for one look — this one where not a single thought arises, vividly clear and perfectly distinct, and yet not the same as wood and stone — what is it? Right now everyone can test this on the spot: when not a single thought arises, is it not vividly clear? Is it as unknowing as wood and stone? Clearly not; it is still vividly clear (hearing distinctly, seeing clearly), illuminating like a mirror reflecting things, only without giving rise to discrimination (not the slightest thought of love or hate, of grasping or rejecting). This vivid awareness that does not discriminate is our own nature — the one true dharma-realm!

So the view is to know the one true dharma-realm, the naturally abiding Tathāgatagarbha mind; it is the treasure everyone possesses, and it is nowhere else — it shines at this very person’s six sense-gates. But all beings simply do not know this; they only know to grasp outer marks and so obscure their own radiance, sinking into the beings of the six paths — is this not lamentable? We need only turn the light around for one look, and recognize that this vividly clear, thought-free numinous knowing is precisely our own nature, the root of becoming a Buddha and the root of accomplishing all things and the world. So it is said: “It manifests immeasurably the dharmas of defilement and purity, and is complete in the meaning of naturally abiding equality.”

First let us speak of “manifests immeasurably the dharmas of defilement and purity.” That is, all the men and women, young and old, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, grasses, trees, and forests, and so on, are all manifested by this mind of mine (the true mind). “Defiled” means polluted, the things that are not good; “pure” means clean and beautiful things. For example, our Sahā world is a land of filth, defiled; the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is a pure land, clean. Whether pure land or filthy land, by what are they made, by what are they manifested? All are made and manifested by our one true dharma-realm. So the Buddhist scriptures say: “Nothing does not flow forth from this dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this dharma-realm.” From this we can see that the present mountains, rivers, and great earth, men and women, young and old, are also manifested by this one true dharma-realm. Without this one true dharma-realm, where would there be mountains, rivers, the great earth, men and women, young and old? Someone will raise a doubt: how can the mountains, rivers, the great earth, men and women, young and old be manifested by the one true dharma-realm?

This would take long to explain. Before the mountains, rivers, and great earth took shape, the ancient Chinese called it “the vast chaos of the cosmos,” and also “the undivided chaos”; in the Buddhist scriptures it is called “enlightened clarity and empty darkness.” “Enlightened” is our original enlightenment — every person, every being, has this awareness, this awareness-nature. The nature is the energy, the inherent capacity for awareness, the function of being able to be aware. Enlightenment itself is no fault, but the trouble lies in recognizing this enlightenment and deciding that one definitely is aware — this is called giving rise to clarity upon enlightenment; “clarity” means clearly being aware, clearly knowing that one is aware. This is adding knowing upon knowing, setting a head on top of a head, and so this clarity becomes ignorance. Enlightenment itself is clarity and clarity itself is enlightenment; but by giving rise to clarity upon enlightenment, one divides and opposes, thinking that since one has the capacity to be aware, there must be something to be aware of, and there must be things for me to be aware of. In that age of vast chaos and empty darkness the earth had not yet formed and there was nothing, so everyone stirred wildly, searching for something that could be the object of awareness. But in the age of the empty kalpa there was nothing — this is called “empty”; because nothing could be found, everyone grew confused in a mass — this is called “dark”; the more dark and confused, the more wildly they stirred. When stirring reached its extreme, wind arose, and so the great wind-wheel came into being and rubbed against the earth-element among the seven great elements — earth, water, fire, wind, space, root, and consciousness — that our one true dharma-realm inherently possesses. When earth and wind rub together, the fire-element forms; the fire-element blazes upward; the turbid sinks and the clear floats up; and thus arose the world composed of earth, water, fire, and wind. The earth we now live on came into being in just this way.

So this world — whether the earth, trees, sun, or moon — is formed by the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; and earth, water, fire, and wind are constituents inherent in our own nature, just like what chemists call elements. Look at this earth: the earth’s crust is the earth-element; there is water below and above the ground, which is the water-element; there is fire at the earth’s core, and so volcanoes erupt, which is the fire-element; the earth turns without cease, rotating and revolving, which is the wind-element. So the earth is entirely composed of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind. Even a great tree is inseparable from earth, water, fire, and wind: the trunk of the great tree is hard, which is the earth-element; there is moisture in the tree, which is the water-element; the tree’s body is wood, with the nature of fire and able to burn, which is the fire-element; the movement of the great tree’s absorption of nutrients and its swaying in the wind are the wind-element. So the great tree too is composed of the four great elements. A person is likewise: the skin, flesh, and bones of the body are the earth-element; the blood and fluids are the water-element; the fire-element is the heart — everyone has a body temperature of

; the wind-element is our breathing, blood circulation, digestion, and so on — turning without cease belongs to the wind-element. So everything without exception is manifested by our true mind; this is called manifesting immeasurably the dharmas of defilement and purity. All worlds, pure lands and filthy lands alike, are manifested by our mind.

Next it says: “complete in the meaning of naturally abiding equality.” What does it mean to be complete in the meaning of naturally abiding equality? It means that whether pure land or filthy land, all is manifested by the true mind, all is equal, equal, and again equal. One does not think that our filthy land is the response to beings’ karma while the pure land is the response to the pure minds of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and so feel inequality because of the difference between pure and filthy. At the same time one must know that all forms are illusions; whether good or bad, beautiful or ugly, none can be grasped — therefore they are equal. Though we have now fallen to the state of ordinary beings, the one true dharma-realm is equal; it is only because of ignorance that the original radiance of the nature is temporarily obscured. Yet the essence is still neither defiled nor pure, unmoving and unchanging; it is not that because its radiance is obscured the essence becomes defiled. Suppose a pearl is for a time buried in mud, its radiance covered so that it cannot be seen — has the radiance been lost? No! Dig it out and wipe off the mud, and the pearl is as radiant as before; the radiance of its essence cannot be lost by being wrapped in filth. So it is said that the nature does not increase in the sage and does not decrease in the ordinary being; it is equal, equal, and again equal. It is precisely because we do not know this meaning of equality that we have grasping and rejecting, love and anger. This is good and pure, that is filthy and bad — but in fact all is manifested by our true mind; therefore one who truly sees the Way has no grasping and no rejecting, no love and no hate.

When by our practice we remove ignorance and extinguish all defilement, clinging, affliction, and inversion, we can recover the radiance of the original nature and manifest the originally pure dharma-body; then the Pure Land is right here. The Pure Land has the Western of principle and the Western of phenomena. The Western of principle is our own pure mind, called the Pure Land of Mind-Only. In terms of phenomena, it is the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss that lies beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from our world. But although this Western world is far away, it is not separated from us, because our true mind fills all space and pervades the dharma-realm; however many the pure lands of the ten directions, none lies outside our true mind — it all depends on whether your mind is pure or not. If the mind is pure, the Pure Land is not separated from you; it is right before you. If the mind is impure, then it is inevitably separated, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands away from you. Our mind is complete in everything, and all practices are gathered into the mind. The scripture says: “The three realms are mind-only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only.” Apart from mind, nothing exists at all. So we said above that the deluded mind should not be extinguished — why should the deluded mind not be extinguished? Because the deluded mind is manifested by the true mind; without the true mind, where would the deluded mind be? Just as without water, where would waves be? Waves represent the deluded mind, water represents the true mind: if you abolish the waves, the water is gone too. So the deluded mind should not be extinguished; it need only be set down. Hence it is said that when the mad mind is set down, that is true suchness; all dharma-gates simply tell us to set the deluded mind down. Do not grasp at holiness; simply set the mind down, and when the deluded mind is set down, that is it.

The Mahāmudrā is a direct-pointing gate: it tells us that to see the one true dharma-realm, we must set the deluded mind down; when not a single thought arises, turn the light around for one look and see the radiance of the nature — this is one’s own original face. Do not go seeking other miraculous and mysterious things. As soon as there is seeking, as soon as there is attainment, one is clinging to marks; not only can one never realize the Way, one is a candidate for becoming a demon. Why? Because our nature is originally complete in everything and lacks nothing; therefore it is the Tathāgatagarbha, a treasury, and once you open it you can use it inexhaustibly, without needing to seek anything outside. As soon as there is seeking, the mind is not empty and pure but abides on marks, and so it becomes the aggregate-māra. Therefore after seeing the Way we must protect and sustain it closely, diligently removing the old habits of clinging — this is called cultivating the Way. Why must we do this? Because after seeing the Way one has only recognized one’s own original face; there are still the habitual tendencies of beginningless clinging that have not been dissolved. These habits, from beginningless kalpas, have grown used to clinging to marks and have accumulated; it is hardly possible to become utterly unattached and purely unconditioned all at once. For example, a dark room sealed for many years: once the windows and door are opened or the electric light switched on, the darkness is gone, and though there is light in the room, the musty smell of long enclosure cannot be removed all at once; it takes a long period of ventilation, sweeping, and washing before the musty smell accumulated over the years can gradually be dissolved.

Again, take a stinking night-soil bucket that has held dung for many years: once the dung is poured out, the stench still cannot be removed, because the stench has soaked deep into the wood and cannot be eliminated at once. It takes long soaking, steeping, washing, and scrubbing before the stench can slowly be exhausted. By the same principle, even though we may see the original face all at once and recognize our own true mind, and know that all things and immeasurable appearances are manifested by our true mind, yet to dissolve the habitual tendencies all at once and be utterly unattached amid circumstances, wholly unmoved, is still very hard to do. So after awakening, one is only at the stage of seeing the Way; one must still pass through the stage of cultivating the Way, diligently training and applying effort amid circumstances, until the habit of clinging to marks and abiding in circumstances is completely dissolved; only then can one perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit. Only then does one enter the stage of realizing the Way.

Seeing the Way is only equal to a tiny infant just born, a baby newly delivered, unable to walk, speak, or do things; it must slowly grow into an adult before it can gradually speak, walk, and work, and even become a hero, a great man, a person of greatness. So after seeing the Way we must still pass through cultivation of the Way, and only then can we realize the Way. But the first and most important thing is to see the Way. If one does not see the Way, one does not know what the original face is or what the true mind is; there is always doubt in the mind, always seeking outside, with no master within, and one cannot avoid inversion and clinging to marks, so in the end one cannot realize the Way. Therefore a practitioner must first see the nature, understand what the true original is, and only then can he set about sweeping away illusory deluded habits — just as when the electric light in a room is switched on, one sees clearly where the filth is, what place is dirty, where there is rubbish, and only then can one set about cleaning. If the light is not on and the room is pitch dark, not only is there no way to begin; even if one cleans by guesswork, one will bump east and west, until one’s nose is bruised and face swollen, and still cannot clean it properly. So to realize the Way, one must first open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and understand that this one true dharma-realm is inherent in all beings, not something produced by cultivation! In the school it is said: “The Way belongs to awakening, not to cultivation,” which is exactly this principle. Once we truly understand this principle, our practice is on the road.

As said above, although the truth may be suddenly awakened to, the old habits of many lives of clinging to marks cannot be eliminated at once; one must protect it at every moment. As soon as a deluded thought arises, be aware; being aware, dissolve it into emptiness; and do not abide even in emptiness. Only then can one be perfectly fused and unobstructed. The skill goes from shallow to deep, from unfamiliar to familiar, and only when it is utterly familiar can one forget it; after forgetting, one can transform, and then one can change without obstruction. So we must first be aware and illumine, and then gradually advance to quiescent illumination. “Awareness” is knowing: when a thought arises, know it and do not run after it — this is the function of effort. If you see a thought move and cannot let it go, and your concentration is insufficient to stop its continuation, that will not do; you must quickly borrow the power of the Buddha’s blessing to cut it off. One who recites the Buddha-name quickly raises the holy name of Amitābha Buddha, settles the deluded mind on the Buddha-name, and the deluded thought cannot continue; one who recites mantras raises the mantra, and the deluded thought is transformed; one who practices Chan attends to the huatou at all times, and deluded thoughts naturally do not arise. If a deluded thought arises and you do not even know it, running after the thought, then you are finished. So after seeing the Way, one must protect it closely. When the protection is ripe, one need not protect any more; one can go on from aware illumination to quiescent illumination. “Quiescent” means unmoving; one no longer uses awareness, and at the same time forgets illumination. Illuminating naturally without clinging to illumination — if there is still an illumination present, there is still abiding, still the function of effort; no illumination and no non-illumination, and only then does one enter the unconditioned. The function of no effort has immense merit. Only on reaching this can one enter the stage of non-regression.

Complete in the meaning of naturally abiding equality” means that all good and bad, defiled and pure, long and short are equal, equal, and again equal, without difference, because all beings are Buddhas. Do not look down on cattle, horses, and other animals; they too are Buddhas — it is only because they have done much evil and their karmic obstacles are heavy that they have fallen into the three lower paths. We must give rise to great compassion, vow to deliver all beings, and ascend together to the shore of awakening; only thus do we accord with the original intent of the Buddha’s appearing in the world to deliver beings. Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva adorns the hells within the hells and delivers the beings there, spreading the power of Dharma widely to wake them from their deluded dreams, so that they may know: for those who suffer here, the Buddha-nature is not diminished by a single fraction; it is only because they are unawakened, cling to marks, and create karma that they have fallen into the hells to suffer. If they quickly awaken and repent, and recover the original radiance of their nature, they will at once ascend and be freed.

From this it can be seen that a practitioner must first clarify the mind and see the nature; only after seeing the nature will one not create karma and receive retribution. Without seeing the nature, one cannot avoid blind practice; after seeing the nature, one’s practice is true. After truly seeing the nature, you will also understand that the Western Pure Land and the filthy land we dwell in are equally equal. The scripture says: “As the mind is purified, so the Buddha-land is purified.” If your mind is pure and undefiled, this very place is the Pure Land; for when the mind is pure there is no grasping and rejecting, so where would there be any distinction of good and bad, beautiful and ugly? When the mind gives rise to discrimination, that is the ruin of it: good and bad, beautiful and ugly arise accordingly, and with them people’s love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and so they cannot avoid creating karma and receiving retribution. Cultivation is for escaping the round of rebirth and transcending the three realms, so one must first rectify one’s understanding, recognize this equal mind that everyone inherently possesses, and understand the meaning of the equality of things; only then can one set about removing habits and transforming consciousness into wisdom. A practitioner who would perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit must transform consciousness into wisdom. Consciousness is knowing, the discriminative mind — the deluded mind of ordinary beings who cling to circumstances and create karma; only when it has been transformed by diligent effort into the perfect great wisdom of enlightenment is one’s wish fulfilled. In the process of transformation, one first transforms the sixth consciousness into the wisdom of wondrous observation, then transforms the seventh consciousness into the wisdom of equality, and only then can one transform the first five consciousnesses into the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, and transform the eighth consciousness into the great perfect mirror wisdom. It is not possible to transform the deluded consciousness into the perfect great wisdom all at once, which is why the Sixth Patriarch said: “The sixth and seventh are transformed in the cause; the eighth and fifth are perfected in the fruit” — this is exactly the meaning.

You should know that the lineage gurus are no different from my own mind.” One who has seen the Way deeply knows that my mind is the Buddha-mind and the Buddha-mind is my mind; then my mind is not only no different from the lineage gurus, but also no different from all things and circumstances. In such a state of mind, what love and hate, what grasping and rejecting could there still be? If there is still discrimination — this is beautiful, I will grasp it; that is ugly, I will reject it — then your mind is still not equal, and you have not yet truly seen the Way.

So we must understand that the one true dharma-realm is originally neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing, complete in everything. In other words, we are originally Buddhas; we need only not be deluded, not run after deluded thoughts, not cling to circumstances or chase after things, and we can return home along the road we came by and recover our original nature. Therefore the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges tells us: you need not cultivate — you are inherently complete in the true suchness of Buddha-nature; you need only turn the light around and look back, be unattached to everything, and when a thought arises be aware of it without following it: that is right cultivation and true practice. But first one must have a correct view — this is the practice of the causal ground; when the view is incorrect, the fruit is crooked. That is why the Mahāmudrā says at the very outset that the view must be correct. Only after seeing the nature can one be constantly in samādhi. Why? Because only after awakening does one know deeply that no mark whatsoever can be grasped, that all are flowers in the sky and moons in the water, with nothing to grasp or cling to; only the nature is real, and though one responds to capacities and follows conditions the mind does not move. The Diamond Sūtra says: “One should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.” Only thus is there a lively great samādhi with boundless wondrous function, and only practice of this kind is the true practice of a practitioner. Therefore the mind of a practitioner is surely equal, without partiality, and in dealing with people and things there is no distinction of close and distant; if there is still a view of difference, then you have not yet reached the state of true equality.

View, meditation, and action are all gathered in by the mind and all are complete within the mind; so in learning Buddhism we should learn the mind-ground dharma-gate. It is the born prince, like the emperor’s own son who will one day surely become emperor; one who practices it will surely become a Buddha. Practicing other dharma-gates belongs to the outer rank of merit and service: however good one’s skill, one can only be enfeoffed as a king or a marquis, and cannot become emperor — cannot become a Buddha. Especially do those who nowadays practice qigong cling to the physical body, working at small heavenly circuit, great heavenly circuit, or else dabbling in shamanic arts and illusions to show off and fool the ignorant. They think they have succeeded, but in fact they are only playing with the spirit-soul. However great your spiritual powers and however good your health, in the end it all decays and cannot last. Hence the school says: “Outsiders who train the body in the end must ruin it.”

So in our practice we must have a correct view, know what the root of becoming a Buddha is, and then cultivate it diligently, and only thus can we realize the true fruit. Master Hanshan, in his Direct Pointing to the Heart Sūtra, says: “The reason the cultivation of prajñā succeeds so quickly is that everyone is endowed with this true suchness, this wondrous nature. The Buddhas realize it and make of it wondrous spiritual function; beings are deluded about it and make of it deluded thoughts and worldly toil. Thus they use it daily without knowing it, benighted as to this original truth, suffering hardship to no purpose — is this not lamentable! If one can suddenly awaken to what one originally has, turn the light around and look back right now, and cultivate with a single thought, then the pass of birth-and-death and emotion suddenly collapses, like a room dark for a thousand years that a single lamp can light up, and there is no need to seek any other expedient!” From this we can see that if we simply awaken, are not deluded by forms, turn the light around and look back at every moment, and cultivate on the mind-ground dharma-gate, without using other dharma-gates, we will surely become Buddhas in the future.

blocks.text: 3. The Mind-Ground Dharma-Gate

inline.s: Speaking of the mind-ground dharma-gate, I am reminded of the kōan of Huanglong and Lü Chunyang. Lü Chunyang practiced the Daoist teaching. Daoism stresses refining essence, energy, and spirit, gathering the great medicine and refining it into the great elixir, the so-called golden elixir, which transforms into an infant and becomes the indestructible yang spirit. When he visited Patriarch Huanglong, he had already succeeded in refining the elixir and sending forth the yang spirit. Once the golden elixir is successfully refined in Daoism, one can roam the four directions and visit the good teachers of the great famous mountains. One day he passed by Mount Huanglong and saw purple clouds gathering like a canopy over the mountain; knowing that an extraordinary person was there, he went to pay a visit. It happened that Chan Master Huanglong had ascended the hall to teach the Dharma, so he mixed in with the crowd to hear what Chan Master Huanglong would say. Huanglong knew it was Master Lü and wanted to lure him into the Way, so he said sternly: “Today I will not teach the Dharma; there is a stealer of Dharma beside my seat!” Thereupon Lü Chunyang boldly came forward and asked Chan Master Huanglong: “A single grain of millet holds the world; within a half-pint cauldron rivers and mountains are boiled. What does this mean?” Huanglong pointed at him and said: “This corpse-guarding ghost!” Lü Chunyang said: “But there is in my bag the medicine of deathlessness.” Huanglong said: “Though you live through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end you fall into emptiness and death.” Lü Chunyang was greatly shocked at hearing this, and so sent his flying sword at Huanglong; Huanglong brushed it aside with his fly-whisk, and the flying sword fell to the ground. The sword is the view: the sword falling to the ground means the view was defeated. Lü Chunyang at once knelt and bowed, asking for instruction. Huanglong said: “I will not ask about boiling rivers and mountains within a half-pint cauldron; but what is it to hold the world within a single grain of millet?” At these words Lü Chunyang had a great awakening. What did he awaken to? He awakened to the markless mind. This markless mind is precisely the root of becoming a Buddha and the root of realizing the great Way. This great energy, formless and markless, that can manifest the yang spirit, is the eternally indestructible innate Buddha. In learning Buddhism and cultivating the Way, one must never grasp at forms; forms are the shadows of the true mind, and in the end they decay. So after his great awakening Lü Chunyang said: “I cast away gourd and bag, I smash the lute; from now on I refine no more the gold within the water. Only since I met Huanglong have I begun to feel that formerly I used my mind wrongly.” “Water” means mercury, the ingredient for refining the elixir. In Daoist elixir-refining one stresses taking kan to fill li: water is the yin, named kan, and the gold taken from it is the yang, named li; taking kan to fill li is the great way of the golden elixir that joins yin and yang to refine the yang spirit. “From now on I refine no more the gold within the water” means that now he no longer refines this thing, because Patriarch Chunyang had recognized the innate Buddha of the nature, this markless mind. It is simply thus from the beginning, naturally so, not produced by fabrication and cultivation; it is only that beings are deluded by outer circumstances and do not recognize it. Today he recognized it and knew it, and so no longer clings to outer circumstances.

In our practice we must first understand what the root of becoming a Buddha is. Otherwise, once the direction is wrong, we are a thousand miles off and there is no hope of realizing the Way. For example, to cook a meal you must use rice, and only then can it become a meal; if you cook sand and mud, you may cook for days or for ten thousand years and it still will not become a meal. So the view is extremely important. What is the root? It is our one true dharma-realm (the nature), and not anything else; it has nothing to do with refining energy or refining the elixir. After recognizing the nature, one has right view. After seeing the nature, one should in principle have no cultivation, no attainment, no realization; but if your habits are not yet finished and your mind still stirs when facing circumstances, then birth and death are not ended and you must still cultivate. Why is this said? Because after you become a Buddha, the Buddha too cannot be grasped — what then could there be to attain? So it is no attainment. Since there is no attainment, what is it that you realize? So it is no realization. With no attainment and no realization, you are originally a Buddha and not made by cultivation, so it is no cultivation. Yet because your habits are not finished, you must still cultivate. How does one cultivate? Cultivation that is no cultivation — that is, illumining at every moment, without needing any method. So the cultivation that is no cultivation is still necessary. After recognizing the nature, one understands that all forms in the world are manifested by this one true dharma-realm (the nature). So the nature is the mark and the mark is the nature; nature and mark are non-dual. Therefore our Buddhism speaks of the gate of non-duality. The Heart Sūtra says: “Form is emptiness; emptiness is form.” This form is manifested by our one true dharma-realm, the substance of wondrous existence and true emptiness — it does not mean that when we say “form is emptiness,” form is utterly nonexistent; that would be wrong. To be utterly nonexistent would be to fall into dumb emptiness and annihilation, which is incorrect. So we say that all forms have no self-substance, no self-nature, and are originally empty — that is, the emptiness in which nothing whatsoever can be grasped.

Emptiness is spoken of in several ways. Generally there is the emptiness of opposition, the emptiness of annihilation, and the true emptiness of analyzed dharmas. For ordinary beings there is the emptiness of opposition: a thing is existent when present, and when absent it is empty. Outsiders hold the emptiness of annihilation: they think that after death a person is utterly finished and gone — that is annihilating emptiness. What the two vehicles see as the Way is the true emptiness of analyzed dharmas: they separate the two dharmas of form and mind — form is form-dharma and mind is mind-dharma. Take the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The two vehicles say form is form-dharma, while feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are mind-dharma, and they separate them. They hold that in cultivating the Way the body is useless and must be abandoned. But in fact it is not so: form is emptiness and emptiness is form; all forms, including our body, are the true mind. For example, a mirror can reflect images; if a mirror could not reflect images it would not be a mirror. Because it can reflect images, it is called a mirror. Our essence is wondrous existence and true emptiness; “wondrous existence” is complete in all dharmas, it is not utterly nonexistent, and so it can manifest the reflected images of all things and bring forth wondrous function. If it could not manifest all things and bring forth wondrous function, it could not be called the nature of true emptiness. So when we say form is emptiness and emptiness is form, we mean that all forms are manifested by the true mind (the nature of true emptiness) and accomplished by the true mind. The nature of true emptiness (the true mind) has no marks; it cannot be seen or touched, and must be reflected and manifested through phenomenal marks (form). Put this way, it is more thoroughgoing; hence the saying, “Phenomena are perfected by principle, and principle is revealed through phenomena.” “Phenomena are perfected by principle” means that all things are accomplished by the principle-substance. This principle-substance — our formless, markless one true dharma-realm — where can it be seen? It is seen in phenomenal marks, revealed through phenomena; hence it is said that principle is revealed through phenomena. For example, if we want to build an airplane, we must first design the drawings, and then engineers lead the workers to manufacture it according to those drawings. Once it is built, the airplane goes up into the sky. The airplane is a thing: when the phenomenal thing is accomplished, it shows that the design, the drawings, are correct without error, and so the airplane flies up into the blue sky. If the design, drawings, data, and so on were incorrect, the airplane could not go up, or would fall out of the sky. This design, these drawings and data, are the principle-substance, and the airplane is the phenomenal mark. The airplane is the phenomenal mark accomplished by the design, drawings, and data — that is phenomena perfected by principle; and the successful building of the airplane proves that its design, drawings, and data are correct — that is principle revealed through phenomena. This is an analogy. Our true mind is markless, and the mark of no-mark is revealed in things: today’s mountains, rivers, and great earth, men and women, young and old, sun, moon, and stars, grasses, trees, and forests, and all the myriad transforming things, are manifested by our one true dharma-realm. So to see marks is to see the nature; nature and marks are non-dual.

The patriarchs of old said: “The green, green bamboo is all the dharma-body; the lush, lush yellow flowers are nothing but prajñā.” Bamboo is an elegant thing, and Su Dongpo wrote a very ingenious poem about bamboo: “Without bamboo one grows vulgar” — if a household plants no bamboo, it is very vulgar; “without meat one grows thin” — if one does not eat meat, one grows thin; “if you would be neither vulgar nor thin, then give me bamboo shoots fried with meat at every meal.” This bamboo shoots fried with meat tastes very good, and keeps one neither vulgar nor thin, which shows that bamboo is a very elegant thing. To see the green, green bamboo is to see our dharma-nature body; to see the lush, lush yellow flowers is to see our prajñā wisdom. Why is this said? Because principle is revealed through phenomena! But does this mean that these things are entirely us, and we are entirely these things? It cannot be put that way! Why not?
