Long ago Great Master Dazhu said that if the green bamboo is the dharma-nature body, then when we eat bamboo shoots, are we not eating up this dharma-body? For example, if a bowl is your dharma-body, then when you smash the bowl you smash the dharma-body too. That is not right either! So is this saying right or not? How should it be understood? It should be said to be “neither one nor two” — neither entirely one body, nor two utterly different things. To say “not one” is to say they are not the same: our dharma-nature body is formless and markless, while things have marks, and in terms of marks they are not one body. Yet the nature is not apart from marks, nor marks from the nature, and from the standpoint of inseparability they are “not two,” one body. A mirror holds an image, and the image is never apart from the mirror; can you take the image out of the mirror? You cannot. Wrap the mirror in cloth, and the weave of the cloth is reflected in it too — the image is still inside. Turn the mirror to the ground, and the things below are still reflected in it; turn it to the sky, and the clouds, stars, sun, and moon above are reflected in the mirror as well — there is always an image in the mirror. So from the standpoint of inseparability, the mirror is the image and the image is the mirror. Yet the image is still the image and the mirror is still the mirror; so in terms of marks, one has marks and the other is markless, and they are not one body. Hence “neither one nor two.” This principle must be thoroughly understood.

Long ago, when Patriarch Dongshan was crossing a river, he bowed his head to roll up his trouser legs, and just at that moment he saw his own reflection appear in the water and was suddenly greatly awakened. He wrote a verse, in which the wonderful lines occur: “He now is precisely me; I now am not him,” proving that he had truly awakened to the Way. This “he” is not the “channel” of a canal but means “he.” “He now is precisely me” means that the reflection in the water is precisely me; “I now am not him” means that I am now not him. Why say that he is now me, and I am not him? The myriad different reflections in the world are all manifested by our true mind, so all these reflections are my own nature; yet I am not these reflections. This is called “neither identical nor separate.” “Not separate” means that the dharma-nature body is manifested without being apart from these reflections; “not identical” means that these reflections are not just me. The Buddhist principle is very clear and at the same time very mysterious. When we have clarified these things and the Buddha-nature, we understand realizing the essence and bringing forth function; otherwise we are deluded. Long ago, when Chan Master Dahui Zonggao read Patriarch Dongshan’s verse, he thought: Patriarch Dongshan awakened to the Way — how is it that there is still a “he” and an “I”? Since he has awakened to the Way, there should be no he and no I; why then is there still he and I? So he doubted. Only after his own true and thorough awakening did he know that “I” and “other,” “other” and “I,” are all ungraspable, and that in this ungraspability it is not that no false mark remains at all; all marks are still undestroyed and are all the wondrous function of our true mind. So we must clarify all these questions thoroughly.

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form.” This nature is the substance of wondrous existence and true emptiness: utterly naked, undefiled by a single dust, without the slightest mark; to describe it as resembling anything at all misses the mark. This omnipotent substance of true emptiness is the principal agent that constructs and manifests everything. That is to say, this emptiness is not the emptiness of utter nothingness but the emptiness of wondrous existence and true emptiness. For all forms are without exception manifested by the substance of true emptiness and wondrous existence, and all are functions arising from our own nature; apart from the nature there are no forms. So all forms are the nature, and the nature is all forms. The nature is markless; it is the true emptiness that is existent yet not existent, empty yet not empty; while forms are the wondrous existence that is nonexistent yet existing, empty yet not empty. All forms and true emptiness and wondrous existence are originally without the slightest difference. Yet people in the world usually cling to forms with marks as truly existent, deluded to the very core of their hearts, hard as rock. The Buddha, in compassion for beings, taught us to see the truth clearly and stressed: “Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form.” What is meant by “not different” is that there is no difference at all. Why is it that “the nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form”? Because only because the nature is empty can forms be manifested. If the nature were not empty but had already become a solid entity with form and marks, it could not manifest any marks. Why? Take a very simple example: only if this room of ours is empty can tables, wardrobes, and so on be moved in. Conversely, if the room is packed full of things with no empty space left, then nothing more can be moved in. So the substance of the nature is true emptiness without marks, and only thus can it manifest all forms and transform into myriad wondrous marks.

Precisely because the self-nature is markless, it cannot be seen with the eyes, and so the nature is also called the wondrous substance. It cannot be found in any part of the body, inside or out. Open the skull and you will not find it; dissect the body, cut open the heart, and you will not find it. It is neither in the brain nor in the heart; it leaves no trace and cannot be grasped. This is to say that the nature leaves no trace of marks and cannot be seen with the eyes. Though all the things with marks before our eyes can be seen by borrowing this “seeing-nature,” who can see his own “seeing-nature”? Because the eyes can see only things with marks — that is the first point; second, the eyes can see only things that stand opposite them, and what does not stand opposite the eyes cannot be seen. For example: can our eyes see our own eyes? Because they do not stand opposite the eyes, they cannot be seen. The self-nature, however, is the absolute true mind, not something relative, and so it cannot be seen with the eyes. If there is a seeing, it is not true seeing.

The nature leaves no trace of marks and cannot be seen with the eyes. Therefore the nature is true emptiness. Yet although it is true emptiness, it can respond to conditions and bring forth function. That is, having met with circumstances, it can give rise to consciousness and discriminate what this is and what that is. So the nature is also wondrous existence, not dumb emptiness. Only when the “seeing-nature” discriminates all forms through the eyes do all forms appear. For example, when we see a person, how do you know it is a person and not something else? How do you know whether it is a man or a woman, whether it is Zhang San or Li Si? This depends entirely on the discrimination of consciousness for the mark of this person to appear. Since forms are manifested by the seeing-nature, forms are the nature. From this we can know that the six natures — seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and knowing — function through the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, thereby manifesting all forms, which are the six dusts. So all forms and all phenomena are manifestations of the nature. Form cannot be apart from the nature, nor the nature from form. Apart from the nature there is no form; apart from form there is no nature.

Someone asks: taking the “seeing-nature” as an example, is it form that comes first, or seeing? Let us analyze it a little. If seeing came first and form afterward, then seeing should be before and form after. But without form, what could you see? How could one speak of that as “seeing”? What is called seeing is seeing this or that only because there is form. Without form, from what would the function of “seeing” arise? So the “seeing-nature” can display its function of seeing only through form. Conversely, if form came first and seeing afterward, then form should be before and seeing after. But without seeing, how could form appear? Since you have not seen it, how could you know what form there is? That is, without the “seeing-nature,” from what would this form be manifested? If no one saw it, then although the form existed it would be as if it did not, and could not be manifested. Therefore nature and marks cannot be separated. So it is with the “seeing-nature,” and so it is with the functions of the other natures, such as hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and knowing. Hence it is said that form and nature cannot be separated from one another. If the essence of the nature is emptiness, how is the essence of form any different from emptiness? Therefore form and emptiness are utterly without distinction, that is, form is not different from emptiness and emptiness is not different from form.

We often say that Buddhism is the gate of non-duality, and this is exactly what it means: nothing is dual. For it is one and yet two, two and yet one. Say it is one, and it is also two; say it is two, and it is also one. It is originally one body and cannot be divided. If you insist on discriminating, you go astray. We have repeatedly used the example of water and waves. Water and waves are also one, because both water and waves have wetness as their substance. Water is the mark of stillness, while waves have movement as their mark; when wind stirs the water into waves, the mark changes from stillness to movement. The mark has changed and looks like two things, but it is one body. So it is one and yet two, two and yet one. The same principle holds for a mirror and its image. Whatever material it is made of and whatever style it takes, so long as it is a mirror it can reflect images. If it could not reflect images, it would not be a mirror. Because the mirror cannot be apart from the image and the image cannot be apart from the mirror, the mirror is the image and the image is the mirror, and this is called the gate of non-duality. As for us people: from birth, as soon as we have knowledge, we take the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all the images of the universe manifested by the nature as truly existent, and chase after wind and shadows. That is, we see only the image and know the image, but do not know that the image is manifested by the mirror’s light, and we do not recognize this mirror-light. If we could recognize this mirror-light, we would recognize the Buddha-nature. Why? Because images come and go, are born and die, while the mirror-light is always present. A mirror shows a cat when a cat comes and a dog when a dog comes; the images it manifests come and go, are born and die, but the mirror-light never changes. All the states and marks of the mountains, rivers, and great earth are likewise images in the eternal quiescent light. We often speak of “blue seas turning to mulberry fields”: what is now a blue sea may in the future become mulberry fields; what was mulberry fields in the past has now become a blue sea. For example, Yunnan in China was once a great sea and is now mountains and fields. Though these forms and the images in the mirror just spoken of are constantly changing, coming and going, being born and dying, the mirror-light, like the substance of the nature, is without birth and death, thus, thus, unmoving.

Without a mirror, no image can appear; without an image, it cannot be a mirror. That is to say, the nature cannot be apart from form, nor form from the nature. So the nature is form and form is the nature. This principle is the Buddhist gate of non-duality. To see through this point is to clarify the mind and see the nature. Do not think that clarifying the mind and seeing the nature is a matter harder than hard, realizable only by sages. Practitioners are often intimidated by the four words “clarify the mind and see the nature,” thinking it too high to reach and beyond what modern people can do. So at the mention of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature they turn pale, as if at the mention of a tiger, and dare not draw near. They think that we ordinary folk cannot reach this state, and that our only way out is to rely on the Pure Land school and the practice of Buddha-recitation to seek birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once we reach the Western Pure Land and hear the Buddha teach the Dharma, then we may clarify the mind and see the nature! For ordinary good men and women this is perfectly true. For we are now in an age of the Dharma’s decline, when beings’ faculties are dull and their obstacles heavy, and to practice in this Sahā world is truly hard to accomplish. But even in the age of the Dharma’s decline there is true Dharma, and there are still people of sharp faculties; one must never cut everything with a single stroke and treat all alike, pushing the clarifying of the mind and seeing the nature high up into the realm of sages while not daring to take it upon oneself. In fact, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature is nowhere else — it is right before your eyes, right where you can see, hear, act, and do. Turn the light around for a glance, recognize that this numinous knowing is your own Buddha-nature, and a lifetime of study and practice is finished. All beings can see and hear, and so all beings are Buddhas. This omnipotent wisdom-nature does not decrease in ordinary beings nor increase in sages. Since all beings can see and hear and are all endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom-nature, then do not push the clarifying of the mind and seeing the nature up into the realm of sages and think it too high to reach. You need only, at these eight great functions of seeing, hearing, and so on, turn the light around for one look and recognize who it is that sees and who it is that hears. Once you have seen and affirmed it here, never doubting again, and then protect and sustain it closely, not letting it be stained by the dust of circumstances, keeping it numinously empty at all times — no sooner does a thought arise than you awaken and break it; no sooner do you begin to cling to a circumstance than you pull yourself back — then, if within you do not turn with thoughts and without you are not moved by circumstances, why worry that you cannot perfectly realize bodhi!

The self-nature is the markless substance of true emptiness; the nature is empty and abides nowhere, and forms too are empty and ungraspable. So there is no need to scheme and calculate, no need to worry about gain and loss. The Diamond Sūtra says: “If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.” Once you understand the truth that the nature of form is true emptiness, you will not fall onto the dust of form or be swayed and shaken by it. If you can be your own master, not fooled and controlled by servants, not abiding in any state or mark, not clinging to any thing, and illumine closely at every moment, then you can enter the state of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.

All states and marks are manifestations of the self-nature; without the self-nature there would be no states and marks, nor any seeing of them. It is because of the “seeing-nature” that forms can be seen. Since seeing marks is seeing the nature, and marks are manifested by the seeing “seeing-nature,” then marks are the nature and the nature is marks. And if the nature is true and not false, then forms too are true and not false. The Lotus Sūtra says: “This dharma abides in the dharma-position; the marks of the world abide forever.” It means that all marks of the world are manifested by the nature; because the nature is true, marks too are not false but abide forever — this is “the nature of emptiness is true form.” Hence it is said: if one is true, all is true; if one is false, all is false.

Someone asks: is the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss after all true or false? The Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is neither true nor false, both true and false, immediately true and immediately false. For you to divide it into true and false here is still the discrimination of the deluded mind. Because the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is likewise manifested by the Buddha-nature; in terms of marks, whatever is manifested from the nature belongs to the nature, and since the nature is true, marks are also true, and the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is true. In terms of the substance of the nature, the nature is real and marks are shadows. The Diamond Sūtra says: “Whatever has marks is delusive.” All marks are delusive shadows, and so the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is false. Let us not engage in deluded discrimination! When one truly understands the principle that nature and marks are one and that form and emptiness are non-dual, then to see marks is to see the nature, and one can see through all forms to the self-nature. To see the nature is to see marks, and one can bring forth wondrous function from the nature, freely and abundantly, abundantly and freely, radiant and at ease, perfectly realizing bodhi. The Buddha-nature has boundless wondrous function, and so the Mahāmudrā says, “It manifests immeasurably the dharmas of defilement and purity, and is complete in the meaning of naturally abiding equality.” The Buddha-nature is complete in everything; it can immeasurably manifest pure and defiled states and marks. These states and marks are all without exception equal, because our own true mind is equal. Our mind and the mind of all the Buddhas are equal and without a second: it does not decrease because we are ordinary beings, nor increase because the Buddhas are sages. It is equal, equal, and again equal. So once you understand this principle, the mind has a master, and when we practice the Dharma we will not be deluded or confused. If you do not understand this principle of the true mind, you will seek outside, always doubting, and your mind will be unsettled, so that you do not obtain true benefit.

In learning the Buddha-dharma we seek true benefit; therefore the Buddha-dharma is a dharma that settles the mind and brings true benefit, and it is not like other outsider teachings that seek to gain something. Nowadays many who study Buddhism want to develop spiritual powers and show them off before the crowd to display themselves. Alas! They are mistaken. To cultivate the dharma of no attainment with a mind of attainment — is that not to run counter to the Way?

From the very first step in cultivating the Way, one must know that nothing whatsoever can be grasped, that only our true mind — the Buddha-nature — is real, and that all other dharmas are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, ungraspable and unseekable. Once you have recovered the radiance of your own Buddha-nature, the wondrous function of spiritual powers will appear completely, attained without seeking. But when it appears, you must not cling to it either; as soon as there is clinging, it becomes an old rut, and you fall in and cannot pull yourself out. If there is something your mind abides in, the demon-king will seize the chance and enter; then the Buddha-fruit cannot be attained, and you are a candidate for becoming a demon — take the greatest care! In learning Buddhism we are originally without cultivation, attainment, or realization; yet in this process of no cultivation, no attainment, and no realization there are always some traces. We said earlier that the first awakening is like a small child: it must grow into an adult before it can function. In this process of growth there are inevitably stages. The length of the process differs according to each person’s faculties, practice, and diligence or sloth. Just after awakening one has reached only the edge of the dharma-body, not yet its center; therefore one must train diligently amid things and circumstances, exhaust the habitual tendencies, and advance upward, and only then can one become a Buddha.

blocks.text: 4. Linji’s Three Mysteries and Three Essentials

inline.s: For us to go from ordinary being to Buddha, the teachings say it takes three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas; the school does not speak this way. The Chan school’s Patriarch Chan is a perfect and sudden dharma-gate; it speaks of no cultivation, no attainment, no realization, and does not speak of dhyāna and liberation. Even so, it is by no means without stages. The Linji school speaks of the three mysteries and three essentials.

Chan Master Linji said: within one phrase there are three mysteries, and within one mystery there are three essentials. “Three mysteries and three essentials” is the true purport attained in Chan Master Linji’s own mind; because he was meticulous and had personally passed through it, he explained the work from shallow to deep, from the first step to the last, clearly and thoroughly. He said: in general, when expounding the school’s teaching, one phrase must contain the three mysterious gates, and one mysterious gate must contain the three essentials. Patriarch Linji spoke three phrases, so by reckoning three times three makes nine, nine mysteries in all, and each mystery contains three essentials, which would make twenty-seven essentials. In fact it is not so: the three phrases are spoken at three levels. Only by penetrating them carefully do we come to know the mystery of progressing from first awakening to gradual perfection. But as to which three mysteries and three essentials these are, the various quarters since ancient times have each held their own view, arguing endlessly without resolution. Master Linji said: one phrase contains the three mysteries. Before clarifying the three mysteries, one must first understand which phrase this phrase is; without understanding this phrase, how can one penetrate the three mysteries? What Master Linji said was: “On the lump of red flesh there is one true person of no rank, who right now is speaking the Dharma and hearing the Dharma.” This phrase is of the utmost importance; it is the general outline of the three mysteries and three essentials. To understand this phrase and recognize the original face is to recognize the one true dharma-realm, and only then can one go on to discuss the mysteries and speak of the essentials — the process of practice. Otherwise it is like discussing warfare on paper, empty talk with no benefit. Our original face, namely the one true dharma-realm, is without cultivation, realization, or attainment. To comprehend this original face is only first awakening; the habits are not yet removed and one cannot save oneself, and one must still train the mind through circumstances and advance upward step by step, and only then can one walk hand in hand with the Buddhas and patriarchs. So Master Linji divided this process of advancing into the three mysteries and three essentials. The three mysteries and three essentials speak of the three steps: from first awakening and establishing the view of the school, through protecting and sustaining it and training the mind through circumstances to remove habits, to bringing forth great capacity and function and perfectly realizing the nature.
The first phrase, the mystery within the phrase: “Just look at the puppets playing on the stage; the pulling of the strings depends entirely on the man inside.”

This is our first seeing of the nature, when we recognize the original nature. Our body can move, our hands can work, our feet can walk, our eyes can see, our ears can hear, our mouths can speak — what is it that functions in all these things? If our breath stopped, could this body still do anything? Could it still move? It could not. Then what is it that moves? “The pulling of the strings depends entirely on the man inside.” When we watch a puppet show, someone below pulls the strings; if no one pulled the strings, the puppets would not move. Who is the string-puller? The string-puller is our one true dharma-realm, our own nature. To recognize the string-puller is our first awakening to the Way, our recognizing the original nature.

Does recognizing the original nature mean one has realized the Way? No! Master Linji said that one who understands this phrase cannot save himself, and cannot yet escape the six paths of rebirth. For first seeing the nature is only the edge of the dharma-body; one is still a small child. This is precisely where the Pure Land people criticize the Chan school: they say Chan is no good, that it cannot end birth, death, and the round of rebirth; the Pure Land is better, for in the West one is safe. Those in the Chan school still have delusions of thought, and birth and death within the round of rebirth with its segment-by-segment existence cannot be ended — indeed it is so.

But in practicing Chan or other schools, it is not that awakening to the original and seeing the nature is enough; one must still apply effort, protect and sustain it closely, and do the work of removing habitual tendencies! Hence the Chan school speaks of herding the ox: the ox-nature is very wild, so we must hold the nose-rope tightly and raise the whip high; as soon as its wild nature shows, we lash and beat it. That is, we must be aware and illumine at every moment, attend to the huatou, watch it, not let it sink into deluded thoughts or be turned by circumstances, applying effort at every moment and doing the work of protection and sustenance, and only then can we exhaust the habitual tendencies and end birth and death.

How does one apply effort after awakening? This phrase is divided into three essentials, and these are the three essentials of the first phrase: the beginning essential, the middle essential, and the highest essential.

What is the beginning essential? It is seeing the nature. After seeing the original, you understand it without error and accept it for yourself; it does not count if you begin to doubt just because someone talks about it. You must truly accept it for yourself, no longer doubting, and affirm that this is our own nature — that is the beginning essential. If you half believe and half doubt, it does not count. Once your feet are firmly planted, even if a Buddha or patriarch appeared in the world you would not waver — and this is not easy. Speaking of this, I am reminded of the kōan of Doctor Yu Xiu visiting Chan Master Ziyu. Doctor Yu Xiu asked Chan Master Ziyu: “What is Buddha?” The Chan master called to Doctor Yu Xiu: “Doctor!” Yu Xiu answered: “Yes!” Chan Master Ziyu said: “Just this is it; there is nothing else.” This is Buddha; what you answered with is Buddha, and there is nothing else. “Oh —” the doctor understood and awakened to the Way. But when Chan Master Yaoshan heard of it, he said: “Alas, what a pity — Doctor Yu Xiu has been buried by Mount Ziyu.” When this reached Doctor Yu Xiu, he thought: “Alas, perhaps what I awakened to is not it? Why does he say Mount Ziyu buried me? Am I not awakened to the Way? Was I wrong?” He doubted, his feet were not firmly planted, and Chan Master Yaoshan hooked him with a single cast. He hurried off to ask Chan Master Yaoshan: “Great monk, I hear you said that I was buried by Mount Ziyu and that my awakening is not it. Please, great monk, instruct me.” Seeing Doctor Yu Xiu say this, Yaoshan laughed heartily and thought: this man’s feet are indeed not firmly planted; one cast of mine hooked him in. So he said: “Very well, you ask and I will answer.” Doctor Yu Xiu asked his earlier question again: “What is Buddha?” Chan Master Yaoshan did not, like Chan Master Ziyu, call to Doctor Yu Xiu and after he answered point directly. Yaoshan, like Ziyu, summoned him: “Doctor!” Yu Xiu answered: “Yes!” Yaoshan at once asked him back: “What is it?” He turned the light around to see what it was. “Oh!” At this he awakened to the Way.

In fact both are direct-pointing methods; only the technique differs — one tells you directly, the other asks you back. Because when you ask what Buddha is, I must answer your question and cannot answer something off the point. In answering, one does not directly say what the Buddha-nature is like, but first calls to you, and then there are two ways of answering: one is to point directly at what you answered with, as in Chan Master Ziyu’s “Just this is it; there is nothing else”; the other is Chan Master Yaoshan’s question, “What is it?” — asking back, who is it that answered me? Oh! This is Buddha! And so he awakened to the Way. It looks very simple; it depends on whether your feet are firmly planted. If you are truly firmly planted, telling you directly will do as well. Thus when Damei visited Mazu, he too asked Mazu what Buddha is, and Mazu said: “This very mind is Buddha.” Your mind is Buddha. Damei awakened to the Way and went straight back. Mazu still wanted to test whether his awakening was true, so after some time he sent an attendant to examine Damei: tell Damei that Mazu’s Buddha-dharma has now changed — it is no longer “this mind is Buddha” but “neither mind nor Buddha”; see what he does. The attendant went as ordered to see Damei. When Damei saw Mazu’s attendant arrive, he asked him: how is Mazu now? The attendant said: ah, Mazu is very well! Damei asked: how is Mazu’s Buddha-dharma? The attendant said: Mazu’s Buddha-dharma is now “neither mind nor Buddha.” Damei said: hey! This old fellow confuses people’s minds; let him have his “neither mind nor Buddha,” I will just keep to “this mind is Buddha.” See how firmly his feet were planted, without the slightest doubt. So if we truly see the Way, our feet are firmly planted and we do not doubt. This is the first awakening and clarifying of the mind, the beginning essential of the first phrase.

What is the middle essential? Since one has awakened to the Way, one should protect and sustain it; it is not finished with a single awakening, because the habits remain, and one must attend to the huatou and protect it at every moment. As we said above, one who recites the Buddha-name, as soon as a thought stirs, immediately raises the Buddha-name; one who recites mantras immediately raises the mantra; one who practices Chan is simply aware at once that nothing whatsoever can be grasped. In the Mahāmudrā, when your mind moves, “Phat!” — a shout in its face to shout away the deluded thought: this is the highest oral instruction of the Mahāmudrā for the work of protection and sustenance. So all practitioners must do the work of protection and sustenance; to know how to protect and sustain is the middle essential.

What is the highest essential? We attend at every moment, protect at every moment — protect, protect, protect — until the protection is ripe; yet one must not cling to the protection. To hold it without letting go is the function of effort, and we must advance further upward and remove this “protection,” entering the function of no effort. But when the work of protection has been done for a long time, removing it is not easy either; one wants to remove it and cannot — this is the highest essential of the first phrase. This speaks of the process of the work, so in our practice we must understand that it is not finished with a single awakening. Of course there is also sudden awakening, sudden cultivation, and sudden realization — a thorough completion upon a single awakening — but that is a great bodhisattva come again, not something ordinary beings can do. When a great bodhisattva comes again, he can awaken, cultivate, and realize suddenly; but in former lives he too progressed gradually in this way, and did not succeed all at once. We must understand its sweetness and bitterness and work diligently. So I often tell people to work diligently, that it is not finished with a single awakening; one must go from the edge of the dharma-body into the true position of the dharma-body and advance further upward, and only then succeed.
The second phrase, the mystery within the meaning: “How could wondrous understanding allow Wuzhuo to question it? How could bubbles and foam bear the mechanism of cutting off the stream!”

The Buddha-nature is markless; it is the root of all dharmas, and can be illumined and personally recognized only by the light of wisdom, not beheld with the eyes. To understand that all the myriad different things of the world are shadows manifested and accomplished by our wondrous nature — that the nature is the mark and the mark is the nature, that nature and mark are non-dual, and that wondrous function is boundless — is truly wondrous to understand, but there are still marks to be seen and words to be spoken, and it is not yet truly wondrous. One must realize that all radiance and spiritual powers are gathered back into one’s own mind, utterly without abiding, with not one dharma established, utterly naked, with nothing to be said — only then is it truly wondrous. So the scripture says: “Whatever is spoken has no true meaning.” One must understand to the point where it cannot be understood in words, and be wondrous to the point where it cannot be spoken as wondrous — only then is it truly wondrous. So Master Linji said, “How could wondrous understanding allow Wuzhuo to question it?” Having realized this, even Wuzhuo Bodhisattva, the most skilled of all at raising questions, could not open his mouth to ask. “How could bubbles and foam bear the mechanism of cutting off the stream!” “Bubbles and foam” are water bubbles rising one after another, in mutual response — meaning question and answer. However you question a hundred times and answer a thousand, however you speak of mysteries and expound wonders, there is always an explanation, and it is nothing but water bubbles. For none of it is true, none of it is the real subject, and so it is compared to water bubbles. However many hundreds of thousands of millions of words of question and answer you have, like water bubbles gathered into one great mass, how can they bear the great capacity and great function of cutting off the multitude of streams? So “one step above, not one of a thousand sages transmits it” — it cannot be reached by words or grasped by thought. One must let everything go, work earnestly oneself, and truly realize this state, and only then can one illumine and recognize it with the light of wisdom. Hence it is said: “How could wondrous understanding allow Wuzhuo to question it? How could bubbles and foam bear the mechanism of cutting off the stream!”

Here too there are three essentials: beginning, middle, and highest. This shows the advance of the work. The highest essential of the first phrase we spoke of above is the work of protection and sustenance: when the protection is ripe, one should not protect again — to protect again is to make extra trouble; one must forget it. But if one’s power is insufficient, it is not easy to forget all at once. So the above phrase is the “mystery within the phrase.” We say the three mysteries are the mystery within the phrase, the mystery within the meaning, and the mystery within the substance. A phrase is a spoken phrase; the “meaning” is the great purport that issues from the substance in us — the great purport of the coming from the West. From the meaning arise spoken phrases; through spoken phrases — that is, speaking and writing — one can teach everyone. So this first phrase, “Just look at the puppets playing on the stage; the pulling of the strings depends entirely on the man inside,” is the mystery within the phrase, and the mystery within the phrase has its three essentials. Next, the second phrase, “How could wondrous understanding allow Wuzhuo to question it? How could bubbles and foam bear the mechanism of cutting off the stream!” is the mystery within the meaning: it refers to the great purport issuing from this radiant substance of ours, the one true dharma-realm. For only with meaning can it become a spoken phrase; spoken phrases are infinitely various, but without meaning how could speech be issued? So at a meeting, when someone asks what opinion you have, what do you mean? From the meaning one issues spoken phrases — this is the mystery within the meaning. What is the beginning essential? The highest essential of the mystery within the phrase above is that even when one would forget the protection and sustenance, one still cannot. Here, when the work has been done for a long time, one can forget it, forget the protection, and no longer protect it; so when the work reaches this point and one no longer protects, it is lighter and happier than when one was protecting. For while there is still protection, one carries a burden; though ninety-nine of a hundred catties are gone, one catty still remains. So when even the protection is gone and one is truly about to enter the unconditioned, it is of course light and happy. But though one has forgotten it, sometimes it still turns up again, and it is not yet thorough.

And the middle essential? Then one truly enters the unconditioned, and not one dharma can be grasped. At this time there is no inside and no outside, no long and no short, no blue and no yellow, nothing at all; one has entered the true position of the unconditioned. When the work reaches this, it is very good, very fine — like a full harvest moon shining above your head, which cannot be pushed away or pulled near. This is the sign that the work has advanced to this level. Everyone has a radiant substance; it is only because of inverted deluded thoughts and clinging that they do not see it! Now that these vain things have all been cleared away and are gone, when delusion is purified the radiance naturally appears — the light is discovered. So when one reaches this middle essential, one is naturally blissful beyond measure, with radiance shining all around.

And the highest essential of the mystery within the meaning? Even the unconditioned can no longer be grasped. At the middle essential there is still an unconditioned present; this is why, when our work reaches the stage of the seventh-ground bodhisattva, to enter the unconditioned there is still an unconditioned present, and the unconditioned still cannot be forgotten. At the stage of the eighth-ground bodhisattva, even the unconditioned is gone, and that is better still; so the work advances level by level. At this point there is no such thing as work at all. What is work? Alas! It is all gone. This merit of no merit is immense merit: all traces of doing work and of the unconditioned are dissolved and gone, all dispelled at once, and there is no such thing as the unconditioned. At this time one does not seek spiritual powers and transformations, yet they come of themselves. When the work reaches this stage, one has understood the two mysteries and six essentials and can teach humans and gods; hence Master Linji said that one who has verified this phrase can be a teacher of humans and gods. This is the highest essential.

So in practice there are levels; one cannot ascend to heaven in a single step. It depends on how each person strives, never forgetting at any moment, protecting at every moment, until the protection is long and ripe, and when ripe, forgotten, and when forgotten, transformed, entering the realm of transformation. At this point, has one completely arrived home? Not yet: there is still the mystery within the substance — “The three essentials’ seal opens; the vermilion dot is narrow; before one can deliberate, host and guest are distinguished.” This is the last phrase. Originally there is only one phrase, namely our quiescent single mind, the one true dharma-realm. This one true dharma-realm is divided into three levels to subtly indicate the progress of practice, lest one be vague about true suchness and muddled about the Buddha-nature and take the unrealized for realized. So one phrase is divided into three.
The last phrase, the mystery within the substance: “The three essentials’ seal opens; the vermilion dot is narrow; before one can deliberate, host and guest are distinguished.”

What is the vermilion dot? The vermilion dot is our true mind. “Narrow” means cramped, not broad. That is, at this time your vermilion dot (the true mind) is not yet broad and its wondrous function is not yet great; you must still train at three important links.

What are these three essentials? They are not the beginning, middle, and highest essentials spoken of above, but the three essentials of body, mouth, and mind. It is like our practice of the Heart Center tantra, using the three mysteries to bless body, mouth, and mind. All dharma-gates and all worldly matters whatsoever require body, mouth, and mind for the work; whatever school you practice or whatever you do, you cannot depart from body, mouth, and mind. The body displays dignity: when your practice reaches a certain level, your appearance and even your physical frame change; body and mind are dignified, and you lead by example as a model for everyone. You are not droopy-eyed and dispirited, but dignified and full of spirit. A practitioner must lead by example, especially in all his conduct being a model for all people; he cannot live, eat, drink, and rest like an ordinary worldly person, but must strictly observe the precepts and be endowed with dignified bearing and the bearing of a great person. So do not look at whether someone’s words are fine and his tone lofty; look at the level of his conduct. If his conduct is low and he cannot do what he says, that will not do; to speak a yard and walk a foot is even worse. So not only must a practitioner do what he says, but worldly people too must match words with deeds. This is our dharma-realm of unimpeded principle and phenomena; when one reaches the later dharma-realm of unimpeded mutual interpenetration, then everywhere and at every moment the body displays dignity. “Mind” is the great purport issued from the substance, how to teach certain beings — this is mind. “Mouth” is speaking, teaching the Dharma, responding according to the occasion; the Dharma has no fixed dharma, the medicine is prescribed for the illness. At first one is of course unfamiliar; gradually, over time, as one becomes familiar with observing capacities, one can clearly see the capacities of all beings as they come and teach according to the occasion — these are the three essentials of body, mouth, and mind. Through such training your vermilion dot, that is, the true mind, is sealed open, and from it arises vast and boundless wondrous function. “Seal” is like the seal of an official: whatever it is stamped on is carried out. The seal spoken of here is our mind; our mind is the seal. When our mind reaches this time, it brings forth great capacity and great function — nothing whatsoever is unknown, nothing is not known, all can be accomplished. This is “the three essentials’ seal opens; the vermilion dot is narrow.”

Before one can deliberate, host and guest are distinguished”: whatever matter comes before you, you need not ponder or consider it — you are utterly clear about everything. If we can reach this level of skill, we can be teachers of Buddhas and patriarchs. But not teachers of Amitābha Buddha and Śākyamuni Buddha (since Amitābha Buddha and Śākyamuni Buddha have already become Buddhas), but teachers of those who vow to become Buddhas and patriarchs in the future, guiding them onto the right road, to realize the great Way and accomplish the Buddha-fruit; hence it is said to be a teacher of Buddhas and patriarchs. That is to say, if a great man of great stature vows to become a Buddha and to deliver beings, you can be his model and teacher. So do not mistake this.

This phrase too must be divided into beginning, middle, and highest essentials. What then is the beginning essential? The highest essential of the mystery within the meaning above has already dissolved the mechanism of the unconditioned; it is the great function of no effort. What work is there still to speak of? None. When there is none, one returns to the root and reverts to the source, and from the wondrous one returns to the plain. Originally all was inconceivably wondrous, because when one reaches the point where radiance shines overhead, the position of the eighth-ground bodhisattva, one brings forth all spiritual powers and wondrous functions. Only if we do not abide in spiritual powers and wondrous functions can we return from the wondrous to the plain; if you abide in spiritual powers and wondrous functions, you cannot return, and will enter the demonic. So in practice one must not cling; nothing whatsoever can be grasped, and one must return to non-attainment. Hence the Heart Sūtra says: “Because of non-attainment, one attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Only by non-attainment does one realize supreme perfect enlightenment; attainment ruins it. Here one returns from the wondrous to the plain: ungraspable, ungraspable, utterly ungraspable. This plainness is not a plainness in which there is nothing at all, but like water — plain, plain, plain, and within the plainness there is a supreme flavor, an inexpressible, supreme flavor. This is only an analogy; there is no way to speak of it.

And when one reaches the middle essential? One is muddled and dazed from morning to night, as if foolish and stupid, merely dressing and eating. So Layman Pang’s daughter said: “It is not hard, nor is it easy: when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep.” The talk of this whole family concerns the three passes. Layman Pang spoke of breaking through the first pass: “Hard, hard, hard — spread ten loads of sesame oil on the tree.” His wife spoke of breaking through the heavy pass: “Easy, easy, easy — on the tips of a hundred grasses is the meaning of the coming from the West.” His daughter spoke of breaking through the last pass: “It is not hard, nor is it easy: when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep.” So when one reaches this middle essential, one merely dresses and eats. Many people, hearing these principles, feel they bring little benefit: how is it that there is not a trace of spiritual power — has one become an idiot, a fool? So when people hear this, they do not want to listen. What they most love to hear is what spiritual powers one develops, what transformations one has, how great and vast the wondrous function is. When they hear that it is merely dressing and eating, they say: “Alas, there is nothing at all to it! It is like being an idiot or a fool; there is no meaning in it.” They find it lonely and dull. So only people of great wisdom can understand it; they can know it intimately without doubt, know it intimately and delight in it. So in practice one must be a great man of great stature; this is not something people of small wisdom and petty cleverness can do. When our practice reaches this middle essential of the mystery within the substance, it has long been plain, plain, plain, so plain that there is nothing to say. Then how is it spoken of? It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in movement and stillness, in dealings and comings and goings, there is always the vividly solitary radiance! Vividly solitary radiance, like radiance shining above the head, which cannot be pushed away or pulled near, without the slightest trace of interruption or continuation. When the radiance of which the mystery within the meaning spoke above shines, the moon is there, but it is not yet very bright; now the radiance shines inconceivably, having changed from the light of the moon into the radiance of the sun — hence “radiance shining above the head.”

And the highest essential? Alas! It is even more beyond words; here one can hardly open one’s mouth or find words. The World-Honored One, when Mañjuśrī and Kāśyapa had struck the gavel, straightway descended from the seat; and the great Chan masters of old, at this point, straightway shook out their robes and returned to the abbot’s quarters. For at this time even your shining sunlight is gone.

Long ago a monk asked Great Master Caoshan: “What is it like when the bright moon is overhead?” That is, what is it like when a moon shines above your head? His work had already reached the mystery within the meaning, but not yet the mystery within the substance. When one reaches the mystery within the substance, the moon has changed into the sun and is brighter still. But in the school’s phrases only the moon is used to express it; the sun is not mentioned. What is it like when the bright moon is overhead? Caoshan said: “You are still a fellow at the bottom of the steps.” You are still below the steps of the reception room; not only have you not ascended the hall and entered the room, you are still below the reception room — that is, your work is still far from enough. But this monk was a man of spirit too, and would not let Caoshan off: he said: “Master, please receive me and lead me up the steps.” That is, please lend me a hand and pull me up, receive me so that I may ascend the hall and enter the room! Caoshan said: “We shall meet when the moon has set.” When the moon above your head has set and is gone, then I will meet you again. When the work reaches its very end, one is wholly dissolved and forgotten, and nothing at all remains. Is that annihilating emptiness? We said above that within the tasteless there is a supreme flavor! It is not that the radiance is gone, but that one is unaware of it, does not see it, does not cling to it — wholly dissolved and forgotten, without the slightest trace.

blocks.text: 5. The Three Essentials of the Mahāmudrā

inline.s: When we first see the light we find it very bright, but once we are used to it we no longer feel that we are in the light. For example, we now live in the air — do you feel the air? You do not. But shut yourself in a room cut off from air, and at once you feel stifled, as if about to die; then you want to get some air, and only then do you feel that the air exists. When one has lived in the air a long time and grown used to it, one no longer feels it. What is meant by “we shall meet when the moon has set” is that you should not cling to the radiance; if you still have this, it is an old rut. The slightest clinging prevents the accomplishment of the Buddha-fruit. So we say that no spiritual power or transformation whatsoever may be clung to; one must be as if there were nothing at all, like a fool or an idiot. In fact it is not that the radiance is gone or that the spiritual powers are gone; it is that they exist without one being aware of them. For example, we can all put on clothes and eat — do you still find that strange? Dressing and eating are so ordinary that they are not worth mentioning, and so people generally do not cling to them. Now when the work reaches this point, one is so utterly familiar with it that there is not the slightest trace, and one is wholly dissolved and forgotten.

It is the same in our study of tantra: cultivation reaches its end like the moon of the thirtieth day of the twelfth month. Does a moon still appear on the night of the thirtieth of the twelfth month? It means that at that time you forget it, abide in no radiance at all, and have truly arrived home. At this time only the perfectly round great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone, and nothing else remains; nothing at all remains.

The great wisdom of perfect enlightenment is no enlightenment at all; it has no counterpart. If there is an enlightenment and something enlightened, it is ruined. Only when practice reaches this point has one truly arrived home! At this time one can gather all the myriad things of the universe back into oneself; these things are all oneself. So Great Master Sengzhao said: “He who can gather all things back into himself — is he not a sage alone?” Is it only sages who can do this? Yes. What ordinary being can do it? What ordinary being can know that all these myriad things are himself? So only a sage can do it.

Speaking of this, I recall a kōan. A monk asked Chan Master Dasui: “When the great chiliocosm is destroyed, is the dharma-body destroyed or not?” We know the great chiliocosm has four stages — formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness — and in the end it must be destroyed. When the great chiliocosm is destroyed, is this dharma-body destroyed or not? We all know that the Buddha said the dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking, neither changing nor altering, ever green through the ages — the wondrous substance. The visitor raised the question of whether the dharma-body is destroyed when the great chiliocosm is destroyed. If it were we, we would answer at once: “The dharma-body is not destroyed.” But to answer without regard to the visitor’s capacity would be wrong. Why? Because in answering one must follow the visitor’s line of speech, drive the point home into his question, so that he knows pain and itch, and at the place where thought cannot proceed he suddenly turns his head and sees the nature. If one does not drive it home into him, he cannot awaken. Do not reason with him; at such a time reasoning is useless. So the words of the Chan school are not the expounding of principles; they are a two-edged blade — one edge kills you, the other brings you to life, letting you come to life out of death. So Dasui answered him: “The dharma-body is destroyed too.” Alas! Do these words not greatly contradict what the Buddha said? Is this not a mistaken saying that deludes the world, deserving a fall into the vajra hell? But if this answer were truly wrong, why did Chan Master Touzi Qing, a great Chan worthy, burn incense and bow in reverence and praise him as an ancient Buddha come again? The reason is that what is called the world, whatever thing it may be, is all transformed and manifested by the Buddha-nature of us vast multitudes of beings (that is, the dharma-body); apart from the dharma-body there is nothing at all. So the Lotus Sūtra says: “This dharma abides in the dharma-position; the marks of the world abide forever.” That is, no thing in the world is not established in dependence on the dharma-body. “This dharma” refers to whatever thing it may be, and the “dharma-position” is the one true dharma-realm (that is, our dharma-body). “This dharma abides in the dharma-position” means that all the myriad things of the world are manifestations of the dharma-body, established in dependence on the dharma-body; therefore the marks of the world are the dharma-body, and the dharma-body is the marks of the world.

We know that phenomena are perfected by principle and principle is revealed through phenomena, and that principle and phenomena cannot be separated. So the scripture says: “Nature and marks are non-dual; mind and realm are one body.” The marks of the world are precisely the manifestation of our dharma-body. The ancients said: “Amid the tangled myriad forms, the body alone stands revealed.” Since the mind-dharma-body is eternal and indestructible, the marks of the world are naturally eternal as well.

On the surface the marks of the world seem to be blue seas turning to mulberry fields, changing in the twinkling of an eye and never lasting — how can they be said to abide forever? In fact the essence of things is truly without destruction; it is only that when one side is destroyed, another side is born — it has merely moved to another place. Su Dongpo put this principle very well in his Rhapsody on the Red Cliff: “Do you too know of the water and the moon? What passes is like this, yet it has never gone; what waxes and wanes is like that, yet in the end it neither increases nor decreases. For if you look at it from the side of change, then heaven and earth could not last even for a single instant; but if you look at it from the side of changelessness, then things and I are both endless.” The water flows on and on; though it flows, it is not that once it has flowed past it is gone — the water still flows in an unbroken torrent. The moon waxes and wanes, is hidden and full; when hidden and waning nothing is lost, and when bright and full nothing is added; despite fullness and waning, the moon’s body remains as it is. Layman Dongpo used water and the moon to explain that the false marks of all things change while the true essence does not alter. At the same time he further explains that those whose hearts are not open and who cling to false marks see the world as blue seas turning to mulberry fields, changing in the twinkling of an eye, while those of open and wise mind who recognize the one true essence of things and beings know that everything in heaven and earth abides forever unchanging.

One who has truly awakened to the Way is just this free and at ease: grasping horizontally and pointing vertically, all becomes wondrous truth; speaking inverted or upright, nothing is not a rare flower. How could such a wondrous savor be described with brush and ink! Therefore in our practice we must be diligent and strenuous and must not slacken or procrastinate; in this life of ours let us realize the great Way and broadly deliver beings, and only then will we not be ashamed of this life!

In practicing the Dharma the first thing is a correct view. As was said above, when the cause is right the fruit is right; when the cause is not right, the fruit is crooked. The view is the cause-ground at the beginning of practice, and so it must be rectified. Especially at the present stage, in the age of the Dharma’s decline, when fish and dragons are mixed together and false dharmas flourish, and all kinds of crooked ways and false paths run rampant without restraint, we who practice the Dharma must all the more possess the eye that chooses the Dharma and recognize a true teacher, so as to avoid mistakenly entering a wrong path and taking a wasted road.

Speaking of views, we said above that because students’ faculties differ and their knowledge varies, there are many kinds of views. Some people are generous and bold, full of spirit, able to sacrifice themselves for the benefit of others, yet unwilling to study Buddhism, thinking that to be an upright person who delights in goodness and gives generously is to be the noblest person in the world. This is the view of the human-and-heavenly vehicle.

Some think only of themselves and are indifferent to the birth and death of others; as it is said, each sweeps the snow from his own doorstep and does not bother about the frost on his neighbor’s tiles. This is the Hīnayāna view of partial emptiness.
Some see others’ suffering as their own and strive to cultivate the Way in order to save them. This is the Mahāyāna bodhisattva view.

Others, steeped in Buddhist learning, know that all beings are endowed with the same undefiled wisdom-nature as the Buddha, and that it is only because they are deluded by outer circumstances that they are unaware; they need only turn the light around and look back to recover the original radiance of the nature and bring forth all wondrous functions. This is the supreme vehicle’s Buddha-view.
Others seek dharmas outside the mind and abide in spiritual powers: this is the outsider view

Generally speaking, whatever the view, only one that proceeds from great compassion and self-sacrifice for others is a right view; otherwise it is a wrong view. For if it does not proceed from great compassion, then whatever way you cultivate, you either fall into partial emptiness or abide in clinging to spiritual powers, and you can never realize the right samādhi in which emptiness and compassion are fused as one, and so you cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha-fruit.

From this it can be seen that to choose a correct cause-ground view for studying Buddhism, one must carefully discriminate with the great wisdom of prajñā, and only then will there be no error. Sadly, people who study Buddhism nowadays do not know what is right; they all tend toward spiritual powers, thinking that spiritual powers mean a great dharma, and go off to learn this or that exercise or way, not knowing that those exercises and dharmas that hang up the signboard of Buddhism are all false dharmas cultivated apart from the mind and nature, and that the so-called spiritual powers are all the possession of ghosts, spirits, demons, and monsters, not true spiritual powers issuing from the mind of the self-nature. To learn them is not only useless but carries the danger of entering the demonic. There are also some fellow students of Buddhism of many years who should know that only cultivation from the mind-ground — the root — is the right path, yet because their greed is not yet extinguished and they cling to spiritual powers, they too, as if driven by ghosts, turn their backs on the true Dharma and follow those counterfeit ox-ghosts and snake-spirits to do the tiger’s work. All this is the wronged suffering brought on by lacking the wisdom of prajñā and having an incorrect view.

On the road of cultivation and realization there is a fork that must also be known, or one will mistakenly enter the partial emptiness of the “samādhi of extinction.” There are people who, in practicing, take suppressing thoughts so that they do not arise and sitting there unmoving as the ultimate. Sitting in a dead pool of water, they become earth, wood, metal, and stone, and fall into yet another kind of withered and silent birth and death; this too is the fault of lacking great compassion and not thinking to bring forth function to deliver beings. As the verse of Chan Master Wolun quoted in the Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch shows: “Wolun has a trick: he can cut off a hundred thoughts; facing circumstances the mind does not arise, and bodhi grows day by day.” That is to say, such people go the wrong way in practice and cannot realize the Way.

You must know that although our dharma-body is empty and markless, it has boundless wondrous function; it is not a dead silence unable to bring forth function. If you suppress the nature to death so that not a single thought arises, you not only fall into the samādhi of extinction but can never thoroughly see the whole of the dharma-realm. For the reason the nature is empty is that emptiness can contain all existence; it is not a markless dead emptiness or dumb emptiness. So it does not depart from great compassion in bringing forth all kinds of wondrous function to deliver beings. Only when substance, mark, and function are all complete is it the whole of the dharma-realm; otherwise, dead and unmoving, how could one perfect both merit and wisdom and realize the Buddha-fruit!

Therefore in cultivating the Way one must fuse emptiness and wisdom, and neither may be lacking. What is called emptiness is wisdom: to recognize that all is the image of one’s own mind, ungraspable and unseizable, to let go completely and make the mind empty as if washed clean. What is called compassion is merit: to bring forth from great compassion the great vow to deliver beings widely, tirelessly doing all kinds of good deeds that benefit beings without abiding in them, accumulating merit, and only then can one realize the fruit-ground Buddha in whom wisdom and merit are both perfect and complete. Otherwise, cultivating wisdom without cultivating merit, one falls into the “arhat’s meager offerings”; cultivating merit without cultivating wisdom, one falls into the incomplete retribution of “the great elephant adorned with a necklace of jewels.”

If in cultivating the Way we can truly establish a right view, recognize that the nature is the root of realizing the Way, begin from the path of the twin operation of emptiness and compassion, and apply ourselves diligently, then before long we can break open the original and personally see the Buddha-nature; then we know that every single thing and every single heading is the manifestation of our own nature, and that at every time and in every place there is nothing but the wondrous function of prajñā. All is one and one is all: what distinction could there be between self, others, things, and beings!

If there is the slightest clinging, the least partition or barrier, one cannot avoid being deceived by things and marks or by the old master’s tongue, and one will suffer defeat in speech and action and lose one’s freedom.

Once there was a layman who went to visit the old Master Xuyun. The old Master Xuyun asked: what practice do you do? The layman answered: I contemplate the mind. The old Master Xuyun asked: ah, have you seen your mind? The layman could not answer. Master Xuyun said: you must still work hard! In fact it is very easy to answer. If he asks whether you have seen it, answer that you have. One should not really answer in this way, since the true mind is markless and cannot be seen with the eyes, and the mind is utterly free of faculties and dusts, shining alone in isolation, with no opposing subject that contemplates and object contemplated. But in speaking with the old master, one may as well place oneself crosswise in the tiger’s mouth and see how he opens his jaws to bite! Master Xuyun would certainly not let you off; he would press the question: you have seen it — where then is the mind? And he would stretch out his palm and say: here it is, laid out completely. That would display your true mind completely. The true mind is nowhere else; it shines before you at every moment, so what is so hard to answer? The ancients said: “The Way cannot be departed from even for a moment; what can be departed from is not the Way.” The true mind has no mark of interruption or continuation, and so cannot be departed from; and because it cannot be departed from, one is constantly in samādhi without entering or emerging. If this samādhi has entering and emerging, it is not right samādhi. A samādhi of partial emptiness, a samādhi without great compassion, is of course not right samādhi; likewise, a samādhi with entering and emerging is not right samādhi. Right samādhi is neither partial emptiness nor with entering and emerging. What is great samādhi? It is not being deluded by circumstances: whatever state appears before you, you are utterly unmoved — as the Confucians say, “Though Mount Tai collapse before him, his countenance does not change; though a deer start up at his left, his eyes do not blink.” So we must practice in just this way at every moment, training amid confusion and movement, training in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down and in the comings and goings of human affairs. Do not learn that samādhi of partial emptiness and with entering and emerging; you must learn the right samādhi in which emptiness and compassion are fused. Cultivating right samādhi is the essential point of the Way.

Once we possess the right view and right samādhi for cultivating the Way, our practice will not go astray and success will come easily. So in cultivating the Way there must be right view and right samādhi; without right view and right samādhi, it is all cooking sand and hoping for rice — there is no such thing, and one cannot realize the Way. What accords with the sprout that gives birth to all Buddhas is precisely our possessing right view and right samādhi: the sprout of bodhi has come forth, and in the future it will surely grow strong and bear the fruit-ground Buddha. When the cause is right the fruit is right; when the cause-ground is not right, the fruit is crooked. This is the “course of the bodhisattva’s practice,” the correct road of a bodhisattva’s practice (course means road). Only by doing this do we walk the bodhisattva path and only thus can we become Buddhas in the future.

For us Mahāyāna people the starting point of practice is to benefit others, not to benefit ourselves — like the lifeguard at a swimming pool. In order to save those who fall into the water, the lifeguard must first learn to swim and master lifesaving skills. If he has not first learned the skill of saving people and jumps into the water, not only can he not save anyone, he will drown first himself. So in learning Buddhism we must learn the Mahāyāna, studying Buddhism in order to deliver beings, not only for ourselves. To seek only our own escape from birth and death and a comfortable rebirth in the West is not our aim. Those who seek birth in the Western Pure Land must also cultivate the great Way there and then return to deliver beings; only that accords with the heart of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. So in learning Buddhism we must never for a moment be apart from beings!

To return to what was said: if we are apart from beings, we cannot become Buddhas. Why? Because apart from beings, your wisdom and merit cannot be perfected either. Did we not say that we must break the four kinds of delusion — delusion of view, delusion of thought, delusion as numerous as dust and sand, and ignorance? The delusion as numerous as dust and sand is the subtle delusion that follows the first two; it means that the seeds of our subtle afflictions and habits are as numerous as silt and as fine as dust. To break through it and sweep it clean, one must train in the work of delivering beings. Why? Because beings’ habits and tendencies are all different; to deliver them you must sacrifice yourself and follow others, accommodating and drawing close to them, and only then can you lead them in. To do this, you must first sweep your own habits clean. Otherwise, with your own habits still present and with pride and arrogance, how can you accommodate others? Hence one of the bodhisattva’s four means of gathering is the means of acting together with others — accommodating others. Only by undertaking things together with beings can you draw them over. Every being’s character and temper differ, and only when you can adapt to all and suit every capacity do your own subtle habits of subjectivity dissolve, your mind become broad, the delusion as numerous as dust and sand be cut off, and your wisdom be perfected. So this delusion can be ended only in the midst of delivering beings, and wisdom cannot be perfected unless it is applied to delivering beings. And merit? If you do not act for the sake of the great mass of people, where will merit be accumulated? You must serve the great mass, you must sacrifice yourself for them! Śākyamuni Buddha, for instance, sacrificed himself for the masses more than once. When beings, because of their shared karma, met with famine and had no food, Śākyamuni Buddha transformed into an inconceivably vast creature and descended from the heavens to feed everyone; when they had eaten their fill, he taught them the Dharma. Thus they received the gift of food and the gift of Dharma and escaped the bitter sea of hunger, birth, and death — what a magnificent model of learning Buddhism and delivering beings! Since we study Buddhism, we too must sacrifice ourselves for beings and serve them, and only thus can we accumulate merit. The Buddha is the honored one among the two-footed; to become a Buddha one must be complete in both wisdom and merit. So it is in reliance on beings that one becomes a Buddha: without beings you could never become a Buddha; without beings you could at best become an arhat, with the delusion of dharmas still unremoved. For the habits as numerous as dust and sand cannot be changed, wisdom is not perfected, and merit is even less complete. Therefore, if you can become a Buddha, you should also thank beings: it is beings who help you realize the Way. Without beings, your habits cannot be changed, merit cannot be accumulated, and you can never become a Buddha. Hence it is said: “Only all the six perfections and ten thousand practices that benefit others constitute the good capacity for the practice.”

The six perfections and ten thousand practices are giving, precepts, patience, diligence, dhyāna, and wisdom. First, giving: giving to the great mass, including the giving of wealth, the giving of Dharma, and the giving of fearlessness. Second, observing precepts: keeping the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the most basic are the five precepts — not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking alcohol — and the purpose of keeping precepts is to purify the mind. Third, patience: everyone misunderstands patience, thinking it means that when others scold or strike me I hold it in and do not move — that will not do. Carry on that way for long and you will fall ill. What is patience? There is no insult to be patient about. Patience is not endurance but acceptance, agreeing — truly submitting in one’s heart. The Diamond Sūtra says: “No mark of self, no mark of others.” With no mark of self, who scolds whom? With no mark of others, who scolds me? Who scolds whom and who scolds me: neither can be grasped, both are empty. If he insults me in this way or that, I accept it. With no self, his scolding is like the wind blowing through a tree — it passes and is finished. No mark of others, no mark of self, empty and ungraspable — this is the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas! The acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is truly accepting the truth of the universe and human life, understanding that the so-called great chiliocosm is a false mark, with fundamentally no arising and no ceasing. All things are the manifestation of the wondrous function of our own nature, and all arise from causes and conditions: “Whatever dharmas arise from causes and conditions, I say is emptiness.” Being empty, not one dharma is obtainable — where is there arising? Without arising, where is there ceasing? With nothing at all, what is there for you to be patient about? To say it again: patience means not endurance. To be patient is to accept, to have made the mind truly empty, to have truly submitted, to be without contention — that is the practice of patience! Fourth, diligence: to deliver beings one must realize the Way — without realizing the Way, how can one deliver beings? To realize the Way one must be diligent. One is diligent and unremitting in order to deliver beings, not for oneself. Fifth, dhyāna: cultivate dhyāna at every moment, not wavering when facing circumstances, not turning with deluded thoughts. Sixth, great wisdom: only with great wisdom can one, according to different occasions, use skillful means to deliver beings. All these good practices that benefit others are the bodhisattva’s practice; otherwise one is not a bodhisattva. The Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is a great tantric dharma and does not speak of those lesser dharmas, and so it comes straight to the essential point.

blocks.text: 6. The Weight of Genuine Practice

inline.s: A practitioner who recognizes the self-nature and can also adapt within a noisy environment and is fully at ease need not cultivate any dharma; he simply turns amid the dust of circumstances and trains his own habits. But some cannot adapt, their faculties being rather weak — what then? There is a way: one can “again, in a quiet place, put down all affairs and conditions” and find a pure place, such as a quiet mountain forest or a relatively quiet household; that is very good. But having found a good place, one must put down all affairs and conditions. If you have a quiet place but your body is in the quiet place while your mind is not quiet, it is all in vain! Cultivating the Way and realizing it depends on the mind: if your mind is in a jumble and full of random thoughts, you might as well be in a busy market — so it will not do! To realize the Way one must put down all affairs and conditions; everything must be set down when one sits to practice, and only then can practice get on the road. So I often urge everyone: when you sit, be as if you had died, caring for nothing, no longer thinking wildly. On no account think about how to do this or arrange that, how to discipline your sons and daughters, and so on. If you keep thinking of these things when you sit, that is terrible! We must be unconcerned with everything. The worst is to sit on the cushion worrying about one’s children: oh, A-mao and A-gou, it is time, get up or you will be late, get up, get up! Alas! With the mind thus divided and the mental power scattered, how can one sit well? I have seen many such cases — this is not fabricated, but truly seen and heard! Ah — with that, how can one sit well in meditation? So when we sit we must be unable to attend to anything, as if we had died and could not care about so much. I stress again: when you sit, put down all affairs and conditions and be as if you had died, unmoving; only then can you obtain benefit and right samādhi. Otherwise how will you attain samādhi? You cannot! So in practicing the Dharma one must put down all affairs and conditions. If you cannot put them down, then even if there is a quiet place to go to, do not go — going is useless; with your mind in a jumble, staying in a quiet place is as bustling as Nanjing Road. So the key to practice lies in truly being able to put things down; only by putting them down can one press forward single-mindedly.

If you can truly put things down and cultivate single-mindedly, then whatever dharma you practice will at once accord with your own mind, like a pole set up in the sun casting its shadow. I often hear people say: ah, so-and-so is so quick! He hardly sat at all, and yet he realized the original face! Why is it that I have sat for so long and still have not reached that state? Ha ha! His mind could be put down and became pure, so he realized it quickly; your mind cannot be put down and is in a jumble, unable to be pure, so how could you have the state of personal realization? Of course you would not. So the time spent in practice does not lie in length but in whether your mind is pure or not, whether your mind has died or not. To speak frankly: if your mind has truly died, then after sitting only a short while you will peacefully enter samādhi, and naturally there will be the meditative state of ease and serene joy, and naturally great radiance will shine forth. If your mind is impure, where would the state you seek come from? Of course it would not. Therefore in practicing the Dharma, do not discuss whether the time is long or short; look instead at whether your mind is pure, whether your mind has died — this is where the key lies.

If one can truly put down all conditions and press forward single-mindedly, “then, born upon the originally pure substance of mind, one will surely attain right liberation and ascend to wondrous enlightenment.” “Born upon” refers to this present life. Tantra teaches becoming a Buddha in this very life, that is, becoming a Buddha in this life. Some also take it as the body — that this body becomes a Buddha; there is such a saying in tantra. Last time we spoke of the Great Perfection and the Great Perfection of Sublime Wisdom; those dharmas teach that the body can attain accomplishment. This Mahāmudrā is the forerunner of the Great Perfection. The Great Perfection has two stages: one is Trekchö and the other is Tögal; one is cutting through, the other leaping over. Cutting through is cutting off decisively on the spot: at once cutting off all affliction, deluded thought, and clinging, so that the nature shines forth clearly. Leaping over is leaping beyond the three realms all at once and becoming a Buddha. This Mahāmudrā is the Trekchö dharma, directly pointing you to cut off deluded thought and see the nature right now without any method of practice; later it also speaks of the union of the three emptinesses, which we will discuss later and not now. So the Mahāmudrā is a most profound tantric dharma that directly points you to realize the Way.
