If in this life we can put things down, we will surely attain true great liberation upon the originally pure substance of the nature. The “originally pure substance of the nature” means that our inherent wondrous nature is originally pure and undefiled. Why is it defiled now? Because we cling to marks and run after circumstances, deluded by outer objects and unaware of the original. People of old had thick faculties and light clinging; at a single point from the master they understood, could accept it on the spot, no longer deluded, put circumstances down, protected and sustained their own nature, removed deluded habits, and soon realized the Way. And people now? Their faculties are dull and their obstacles heavy; though you talk your throat hoarse, they still cannot recognize it but cling to circumstances, and so they take many detours.

My master, Mr. Wang Xianglu, once said: “One who practices Chan must investigate the phrase ‘Who is reciting the Buddha-name?’ for thirty years without straying before he breaks open the original and personally sees the Buddha-nature. Practicing tantra, we can break open and see the nature in three years.” In terms of time, that is ten times shorter than Chan, and already very fast. Yet in terms of the nature itself, there is no need for Chan investigation at all. Three years or thirty years — either way it is a wasted road! For everyone is originally a Buddha; there is no need to investigate Chan here, nor to recite anything: “
ong bala...”

Sitting here applying effort — is that not putting on fetters and shackles, making trouble where there is none, and merely trapping yourself? Put everything down, recover the original true Buddha of your own nature, sleep when you want to sleep, sit when you want to sit — how good it is to be lively and innocent! As Layman Pang’s daughter Lingzhao said: “It is not hard, nor is it easy: when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep.” The nature is just this free and blissful; why take pains to cut flesh to patch a sore and seek trouble for yourself! Yet we must know that what Lingzhao spoke of was passing through the last barrier; without first passing through the first two barriers spoken of by Layman Pang and his wife, it cannot be done. For though we are endowed with the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature, the habits of many lives are deep, and without a period of bitter training the habits will not be removed and one cannot obtain true benefit. So one must still practice Chan and sit in meditation, taking a wasted road to pass through the first two barriers. Layman Pang said: “Hard, hard, hard — spread ten loads of sesame oil on the tree.” Breaking through the first barrier is the hardest; when we first begin, deluded thoughts fly in confusion and we cannot settle, and it is hard to see the nature — as hard as spreading sesame oil on a tree. Layman Pang’s wife said: “Easy, easy, easy — on the tips of a hundred grasses is the meaning of the coming from the West.” This speaks of breaking through the heavy barrier: once by our practice we recognize the original face, then it is easy, easy, very easy — on the tips of a hundred grasses there is nothing but the original face! “On the tips of a hundred grasses” means on the tips of every single thing and matter; what is there on the tips? On the tips of a hundred grasses there is nothing at all! Is this not all empty and pure? There are many such kōans!

In ancient times Chan Master Chuanzi studied under Chan Master Yaoshan together with Yunyan and Daowu and had his awakening confirmed. When he left Yaoshan he said to his two senior brothers, Daowu and Yunyan: “In the future you should each take charge of a region and establish Yaoshan’s teaching. I am by nature free and rustic, fond only of mountains and waters, delighting myself in my own way; I cannot bear the great task of teaching beings. If later you learn where I am staying, and meet a sharp and able master of the seat, send one to me, and I will transmit to him all that I have gained in my life, in repayment of our master’s kindness.” So he went to the bank at Huating in Xiuzhou, where he floated a small boat and ferried travelers back and forth, living as conditions came and awaiting the visit of one ripe for the occasion; hence people called him “the Boat Monk.” Once Daowu went to Jingkou and encountered Jiashan ascending the hall to teach the Dharma. A monk asked: “What is the dharma-body?” Jiashan said: “The dharma-body is markless.” Again he asked: “What is the dharma-eye?” Jiashan said: “The dharma-eye is without flaw.” Daowu could not help laughing. Jiashan then descended from the seat and bowed, asking for instruction. See how earnest the ancients were! Nowadays you would be served with a stick and driven out. He humbly asked Daowu: “Great master, my answer just now must have been at fault, to make you laugh. Where did I speak wrongly? Please, in your compassion, point it out.” Daowu said: “I will not say. But you can go to Huating and find the Boat Monk.” Jiashan asked: “What sort of man is he?” Daowu said: “He has not a tile above his head nor a foot of ground beneath his feet. If you go, you had best change your clothes.” So Jiashan dismissed his assembly and changed his dress, and went to Huating to visit the Boat Monk. As soon as the Boat Monk saw him he asked: “Master of the seat, what temple do you dwell in?” Jiashan answered: “A temple I do not dwell in; dwelling is not like it!” The Boat Monk asked: “If not like it, what is it like?” Jiashan said: “Before my eyes there is nothing like it.” The Boat Monk asked: “Where did you learn this?” Jiashan said: “It is not reached by ear or eye.” The Boat Monk said: “A single apt phrase — a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.” Then he asked again: “A thousand feet of line let down, the intent is in the deep pool. Three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?” Jiashan was just about to open his mouth, when — smack! — the Boat Monk knocked him into the water with a boat pole. Jiashan had just climbed back into the boat when the Boat Monk said again: “Speak! Speak!” Jiashan was just about to open his mouth when — smack! — he was knocked into the water again. At that moment Jiashan was suddenly greatly awakened, and he nodded three times. The Boat Monk said: “Good, good, good, come aboard!” Why? Because by then there was nothing in his mind; everything was empty and pure. Empty and pure indeed, yet not dumb emptiness but numinously aware and vividly clear — and so he could only nod. Hence Layman Pang’s wife said, “On the tips of a hundred grasses is the meaning of the coming from the West” — it is very easy, if you are free of marks! Only be unattached to marks and it is very easy! So we say that seeing the nature and awakening to the Way is not hard — not hard at all! Do not cling to marks, do not cling to great spiritual powers!

But I often hear people say: “If this is awakening to the Way, why do I not develop great spiritual powers? Awakening to the Way should come with spiritual powers; without them it is not awakening.” Alas! In practicing the Dharma we must know the order of things: first recognize the nature, affirm it, protect it, protect it closely until the skin sloughs off clean, abiding in nothing at all, unmoved by whatever state appears, and then naturally great radiance is released. That radiance is not merely like one or two suns but like the radiance of a hundred thousand suns; then of course the divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds, knowledge of past lives, and the power of travel are all penetrated. In fact the great radiance is inherent in everyone, as the Amitābha Sūtra says: “The light of that Buddha is measureless and shines upon the lands of the ten directions without obstruction.” The two words “that Buddha” have a very broad scope; do not narrow them, thinking that “that Buddha” means only Amitābha Buddha. Amitābha Buddha’s light is measureless and shines upon the lands of the ten directions, but the scope of “that Buddha” is not so small. “That Buddha” means all the great mass of beings. “That Buddha” is that Buddha, not our physical body; the body is not the Buddha — do not mistake this! Within the body there is a Buddha, just as within a house there dwells a person. That Buddha is “that Buddha,” which is the great mass. The original radiance of the nature of all beings is incomparably measureless, shining brightly upon the lands of the ten directions without obstruction. Do you not believe it? Then apply effort yourselves and try!

In hearing this explanation of the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges, you must recognize that the numinous knowing at the point where a thought is cut off is the Buddha-nature; only this is real, and all other marks are false, shadows of the true nature. Put everything down; with a settled and unwavering heart recite the Buddha-name, recite mantras, apply effort, and when the mind is truly empty, great radiance will be released, and in this very life you can truly be liberated and ascend to the stages of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment. Tantra teaches becoming a Buddha in this life and ascending to the stages of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment. Whether we reach those stages depends on how we apply effort. If we apply effort deeply and closely, we can do it in this life; if we apply effort shallowly and loosely, lazily putting things off from today to tomorrow and tomorrow to the day after, then even by the time Maitreya Buddha descends we shall not realize the Way. Even if we rely on the power of Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, we must still apply effort! If you want to be reborn in the Western Pure Land while your mind is always clinging to the wife, wealth, children, and emoluments of this Sahā world — what the ancients called “hugging the post while working the oar” — you cannot even move, so how can you resonate with Amitābha and become one piece and be reborn in the Western Pure Land? So first put everything down; if you do not put things down, how can it be done? National Master Yulin once said: “Those who wish to be born in the Western Pure Land but cannot put things down will not be born there.” If you cling to the Sahā world and cannot let go, then do not recite the Amitābha Sūtra; better to recite the Medicine Buddha Sūtra and make offerings to Medicine Buddha! Medicine Buddha made great vows to bless people with success in all things and to satisfy people’s private desires. If in this world you wish for wealth, he gives you wealth; if you wish for children, he gives you children; if you wish for high office, he gives you high office — satisfying all people’s desires. When your private wishes are satisfied, he causes the bodhi-mind to arise in you naturally: oh, all that I have obtained is the Buddha’s blessing, and the Buddha-dharma is truly inconceivable. In deeply thanking the Buddha, you should then vow to study Buddhism and practice the Dharma to realize the Way. So reciting and making offerings to Medicine Buddha brings great benefit!

If you truly wish to be born in the Western Pure Land, you must put everything down; to cultivate while clinging to this Sahā world is to run counter to the Way and is utterly useless. Yet merely to speak of putting things down with the mouth while the mind cannot let go, and refusing to strive in practice, lazily and loosely, while hoping to be born in the Western Pure Land, is like wanting to row a boat to the opposite shore while refusing to pull hard on the oar — utterly useless. So whatever dharma we practice, we must still apply effort; without effort, relying on the Buddha’s power to receive us alone will not do. In fact, to be born in the West, not only Buddha-recitation can bring rebirth: Chan practice, mantra recitation, and sūtra recitation with the vow for rebirth can also get you there. For the Buddhas and bodhisattvas are not like the narrow-minded worldly people of the Sahā world, who will not receive you if you have not recited the Buddha-name; they arouse unconditional great compassion, receiving everyone and saving every being. Whatever being it may be, at the end of life the Buddhas and bodhisattvas regard all alike, release radiance universally, and receive them into the West. It is only that beings’ obstacles are heavy, so they cannot connect with it; some even fear the intensity of the Buddha’s light and run away from it, bolting into the evil paths — how lamentable and pitiable! If one does not apply effort oneself, relying only on the Buddha’s power to receive one, one cannot be reborn, for the Buddha cannot pull us to the West. If he could, the Buddha would long ago have pulled us all there — why then should we still be suffering in the round of rebirth in this evil world of the five turbidities! The Buddha has three things he cannot do: he cannot transfer karma for another, he cannot make another become a Buddha, and he cannot save those without affinity. If you wish to be born in the West and to realize the Way yet do not wish to apply effort, then truly there is nothing to be said. So the ancients said: “You cannot drag him along by the arm; only when he himself consents is there accord.” You must be willing to apply effort yourselves, everyone!

This stresses that among the three of view, meditation, and action, the most important is to make the body abide as unmoving as Mount Sumeru. If you can sit steadily, the mind settles; if the mind is unsettled, you cannot sit steadily. When the mind is unsettled it jumps about like a monkey, and you certainly cannot sit steadily. When your mind has truly settled and your body abides as unmoving as Mount Sumeru, that is the most important point in sitting meditation. So we often ask: when you sit, can you remain unmoving? Not yet! Then pay attention, train slowly, and do not be impatient; just sit with perseverance and gradually you will become unmoving. So we stress again and again: the hand-seal must not come apart! Only when your legs are truly numb beyond bearing may you move a little, but not at random — this is for beginners. Gradually the legs too will not move, and as soon as you sit you are utterly still; only by being still is it easy to enter samādhi. If you shift about on the cushion, how can you enter samādhi? Hence those who hold recitation beads in their hands while reciting the Buddha-name will never attain samādhi however much they recite. They recite Amitābha with the mouth and finger the beads with the hand; shifting about like this, however much they recite they cannot enter samādhi. And if to that they add discussing others’ faults while reciting, they are even less able to attain the samādhi of Buddha-recitation! Could reciting the Buddha-name in such a way bring rebirth in the Western Pure Land? That would be too easy! So Master Lianchi sighed: “Many recite the Buddha-name, few are born in the West. Why? Because their reciting mind is not keen; though the mouth recites the Buddha-name, the mind wanders in random thought, and so they cannot be reborn.” Master Hanshan also said: “The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered; though the throat be shouted hoarse, it is all in vain.”

Making the mind quiescent and clear, not drawn along by outer circumstances, one can practice anywhere.” The body abides as unmoving as Mount Sumeru, and the mind is made quiescent and clear like a cup of clear water without a speck of silt; only thus is one not drawn about by outer circumstances. When the mind is truly quiescent and clear, no outer state can shake you, and you can apply effort and practice anywhere and at any time. One who truly attains great samādhi, whose mind is truly quiescent and clear, can practice on Nanjing Road; though traffic streams and horses neigh, the mind does not waver in the least. But beginners cannot do this, and so they must find a quiet place to practice. Hence it was said above: find a relatively quiet place, put down all conditions, and practice there, and later on one can practice anywhere and at any time. This skill of practicing anywhere requires time; it is not demanded that everyone do it at once. For now, everyone is asked to be able, in a quiet place, to put the mind down at once. If you cannot put the mind down in a quiet place, what will you do in a noisy one?

Whatever dharma you practice — Chan, tantra, or Pure Land — the mind must be put down. How can one realize the Way otherwise? Do not be like some people nowadays who practice the Pure Land method and say: I do not want this; at any rate I rely on the other-power of Amitābha Buddha’s reception and do not need self-power; I need only recite Amitābha, Amitābha ten times in one breath, and Amitābha will pull me up to the Western Pure Land. Alas! This is to misunderstand the method of ten recitations. The method of ten recitations uses the breath to gather the mind: breathe in and recite “Amitābha, Amitābha...”; breathe in again without letting the mind stir, and recite “Amitābha, Amitābha...”; recite ten times in this way as training, to gather the mind and make it still, to remove emotion and craving and be reborn in the Western Pure Land. They do not know that the method of ten recitations was devised specifically for people busy with worldly affairs who have no time to sit in meditation, using the breath to gather the mind. Once the mind is gathered and still, one must sustain and illumine this state, training amid affairs so that nothing moves one, and not forget it the moment one steps out the door. So one must apply effort; without effort it is hard to be born in the Pure Land! One cannot be born in the West carelessly and lazily!

If a practitioner’s faculties are weak and he cannot manage to devote himself single-mindedly to the three gates of view, meditation, and action, he should still not give rise to greed, anger, and delusion and commit all kinds of evil karma.

Greed, anger, and delusion are the three poisons; all the evil karma we create comes from them. If you have no greed and are content and happy, you will not do bad things; if you are discontent and insatiably greedy, wanting more when you have much and better when you have good, your mind will never be pure, and it is impossible that you should not create evil karma. For you are always insatiably greedy, bent on making others’ things your own. To achieve your ends you will stop at nothing, murdering for wealth. Anger is the mind of hatred: when people or things do not go as you wish or as you intend, you hate others, and affliction comes. And both greed and anger come from delusion, because without wisdom one does not recognize the true substance of the nature but takes the false marks and shadows as real — hence “delusion.” Because of delusion one does not know that everything in the world is false, does not know that all things and matters are empty and ungraspable, all arising from causes and conditions with no self-substance; therefore one has greed and has anger, and so delusion is the root. Without wisdom there is ignorance, and ignorance is the absence of wisdom and radiance, a state of darkness.

The three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion are the worst of things, the poisons and evil karma in our minds. The three evil karmas of the body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the evil karma of the mouth is divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and false speech. Among the ten evil karmas, greed, anger, and delusion are the worst; they are the root of our suffering. Overcome greed, anger, and delusion and the other seven no longer matter — they will naturally change for the better. So if one cannot do as was said above and devote oneself single-mindedly to the three gates of view, meditation, and action, one should still not give rise to greed, anger, and delusion.

Greed, anger, and delusion are the great poisons and the great obstacles to becoming a Buddha; if we wish to end birth and death and become Buddhas to deliver beings, we must remove them. If these three evil things cannot be removed, then you are finished and cannot become a Buddha. If we can remove the three poisons, being neither greedy, angry, nor deluded, then even if we cannot devote ourselves single-mindedly to view, meditation, and action and realize the great Way, in future lives we can turn suffering into happiness and will not fall to evil places. That is, in the future we can be born in the three good paths and will not fall into the three evil paths. Those who practice Chan must make great vows to preserve their human body, to become Buddhas and deliver beings, to attain accomplishment. When this vow is made great, it protects oneself so that one never loses the human body, is a human being life after life, and moreover with deep faculties, so that in the next rebirth one can take up practice where one left off, understanding a thousand things upon hearing one — such is the advantage of practicing Chan. This Mahāmudrā is the same as Chan: even if our mind inclines to the three gates yet we do not practice view, meditation, and action well, still we should not give rise to greed, anger, and delusion or commit all kinds of evil karma; then in the next life we can turn suffering into happiness and will not fall into the three evil paths.

blocks.text: 7. Directly Pointing to the Reality of One’s Own Mind

inline.s: The three essentials of view, meditation, and action are the very root of life for cutting off delusion and falsehood. We ordinary beings have the delusions of view, of thought, and of dust and sand. The delusion of view is to be deluded by outer marks for want of right knowledge and right view. Many who study Buddhism nowadays are very confused in their views and do not recognize what the Buddha-nature is, and their feet are not firmly planted. For example, someone who has already vowed to study the Buddha-dharma hears that a certain outsider who practices qigong has great spiritual powers and ability, and thinks: ah, I had better go and practice qigong! He no longer practices the Buddha-dharma but goes off to learn outsider ways — this is to be deluded by spiritual powers. What is called delusion arises because our study of Buddhism is not earnest and our view, meditation, and action are not correct. View is the first and most important matter in studying Buddhism and cultivating the Way; if the view is not correct, one will inevitably be deluded and take detours in practice.

Confusion of view is the great enemy of practice, so in studying Buddhism one must first have a correct view, break the delusion of view, and then break the delusion of thought. What is the delusion of thought? It is giving rise to mind when facing circumstances, producing all kinds of clinging thoughts. The reason we have all kinds of delusion is that our view is incorrect. When the view is correct and the delusion of view is cut off, the delusion of thought can be cut off, and one can stand firm and not follow outsiders. However great an outsider’s spiritual powers, without the penetration of the exhaustion of outflows and without recognizing the Buddha-nature, he certainly cannot end birth and death. We belong to the mind-ground dharma-gate: we recognize what the Buddha-nature is and can end birth and death. Take Patriarch Lü Chunyang, who met Patriarch Huanglong. At that time Lü Chunyang had already accomplished the yang spirit, but Huanglong said: “You corpse-guarding ghost.” Lü Chunyang said: “Ha ha, there is in my bag the medicine of deathlessness.” The medicine in the bag has two interpretations: one is outer medicine, the golden elixir refined in the pouch, which is outer elixir; the other is the stinking skin-bag, the body, in which the golden elixir has been successfully refined, and once the golden elixir is refined it is the medicine of deathlessness — but do not guard this husk. Patriarch Huanglong said: hey! “Though you live through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end you fall into emptiness and death.” Even if you could live eighty thousand great kalpas, in the end you would still fall into emptiness. Because you do not recognize what the Buddha-nature is, what use are spiritual powers? You cling to marks, thinking the yang spirit is real; in fact the yang spirit is also false, also a dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow, merely an illusory body displayed by the wondrous function of our true mind. For example, the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and the body manifested by Amitābha Buddha are both Amitābha Buddha’s mind-born body. The so-called mind-born body is not only the body; all states and things are mind-born bodies. So the mountains, rivers, and great earth are also our mind-born body; it is only that we do not recognize this and so cut ourselves off from it, acknowledging only this body as myself and not the mountains, rivers, and great earth. The mountains, rivers, and great earth are composed of earth, water, fire, and wind, and our body too is composed of earth, water, fire, and wind. And our Buddha-nature can be great or small: “Great, and nothing is outside it; small, and nothing is inside it”; “Released, it fills the six directions; gathered, it withdraws and hides in secrecy.” It is only ignorance that has shrunk it and confined it within the cavity of your body, so that you do not recognize that the mountains, rivers, and great earth are also our mind-born body.

But this mind-born body is also false; Amitābha Buddha too will retire, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss will change. When Amitābha Buddha retires, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will take his place, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s world will not be called the Land of Ultimate Bliss but another world, even more beautiful and majestic than Amitābha Buddha’s present world. Why? Because Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva turns the ship of compassion around — he is an ancient Buddha come again, becoming a Buddha once more. This is a conjuring trick performed for you to see; do not take it as literal, for to take it literally is wrong. If one is true, all is true; if one is false, all is false. If you say this Sahā world is false, then the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is false too; if you say the Land of Ultimate Bliss is true, then the Sahā world is true too. In fact it is neither true nor false, both true and false, immediately true and immediately false. To divide true from false is your discriminative mind, your deluded mind; in fact there is no discrimination. So once you understand this principle, your mind will not abide in marks; if you do not understand it, you always abide in marks and are always discriminating there: the Western world is beautiful and true, the Sahā world is foul and false. In fact this is all the fault of lacking right view and being deluded by circumstances!

We ordinary beings are all deluded by circumstances. So when Śākyamuni Buddha, on the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month, saw the morning star and awakened to the Way, he said: all beings are endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous marks — why do they not know it themselves? Because they are covered by deluded thoughts, inversion, and clinging; they do not know, they are deluded. So to realize the Way we must cut off the root of delusion. To cut off the very root of life of delusion, one must first have a correct view — this is of first importance. After the view is correct, one applies effort to cultivate right samādhi, training at every moment, the body unmoving as Mount Sumeru, the mind quiescent like sunken water unruffled, entering deep samādhi, opening wisdom, and realizing and seeing the nature. After recognizing the nature one must be diligent in illumining, protect and sustain it closely, not be drawn by circumstances without nor turned by thoughts within, not cling to marks nor abide in states, train the mind through circumstances, exhaust the habitual tendencies, and then the true mind will release great radiance, shining brightly upon the ten directions, and all deluded minds, deluded thoughts, and deluded notions will be transformed into the wondrous function of the Buddha-nature. At every place and every time it is the manifestation of our Buddha-nature, the function of our Buddha-nature; and all that we do at every time and in every place is for the great mass, not for ourselves — this is the wondrous practice of prajñā.

So it is said that the three essentials of view, meditation, and action are the three secret keys of the Mahāmudrā and the essentials of practice for every dharma-gate; they are the very root of life for cutting off delusion and falsehood, the dharma-gate that directly points to the reality of one’s own mind. The practice of the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges is the direct-pointing dharma within the perfect and sudden; it directly points us to see right now the wondrous luminous essence — no cultivation, no adjusting, no distraction — the wondrous luminous true mind, and is the dharma-gate of the fundamental reality by which the great Way is accomplished. In practicing the Heart Center Dharma we must still form seals and recite mantras single-mindedly; in practicing Chan we must still raise a great mass of doubt; in reciting the Buddha-name we must still gather all six faculties and keep the pure thought continuous — only then can we realize the Way. Put this way, to realize the Way we must all pass through a period of cultivation and realization, and this is not as lofty as the Mahāmudrā. You must know that although the fundamental teaching of the Mahāmudrā is that nothing at all need be cultivated, but only that you be pointed to recognize your own wondrous luminous true mind, yet because the Buddha-nature is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing — what would you cultivate? The Buddha-nature is without distraction — what would you adjust? So it is no cultivation, no adjusting, no distraction. Therefore all doing of work is taking a wasted road! But without doing work, can one recognize this thought-free numinous knowing as one’s own nature and realize the Way? You must know that the Mahāmudrā is the White School’s final consummate technique; at the beginning one must also pass through a period of bitter training before one can enter the state of the Mahāmudrā. So if we wish to break open the original, realize and see the nature, and accomplish the great Way, we must still recite the Buddha-name single-mindedly, raise a great mass of doubt, and recite mantras closely, doing the work without the least slackness! Although we are explaining the tantric Mahāmudrā, we do not divide the schools; we explain Chan, Pure Land, and tantra together. In fact the Mahāmudrā and the Chan school breathe through the same nostril: they are the perfect and sudden dharma-gate that directly points to the mind-nature and tells people to become Buddhas right now, sparing everyone a wasted road. But after several talks, everyone still does not quite understand “form” and “emptiness.” Last time someone asked me: is this “emptiness” an emptiness apart from form? For example, now there is a house, and so many men and women, young and old, gathered in one hall — is it only when one leaves the house and leaves the men and women, young and old, and there are no marks, that there is “emptiness”? No, that is not it; he does not understand the meaning of form and emptiness! So it is necessary for us to understand the doctrine of form and emptiness and grasp the purport of the Mahāmudrā, so that practice may go more smoothly; otherwise one cannot avoid taking a wasted road.
Then what exactly is form and what is emptiness?

I once gave the kōan of Chan Master Qinbatuo questioning Master Senggong; I may as well bring it up and speak of it again. Master Senggong was then famous throughout the land, enjoying the reputation that “when Senggong preached, even the stubborn stones nodded.” Qinbatuo came to see Senggong and asked him: “Great master, at so advanced an age you still expound sūtras — what sūtra do you expound?” Senggong said: “I expound the Prajñā Sūtra.” We know that the Great Prajñā Sūtra in six hundred fascicles is devoted to form and emptiness; its abridgment is the Diamond Sūtra, and the abridgment of the Diamond Sūtra is the Heart Sūtra. The Heart Sūtra says, “Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form” — this is the meaning of form and emptiness.

Chan Master Qinbatuo asked: “Oh! Then may I ask what is called form?” (What is form?) Senggong answered: “The gathering of many minute particles is called form.” The many minute particles are what the Buddha spoke of when he asked Subhūti in the Diamond Sūtra: “all the minute dust-motes of a great trichiliocosm” — this great world is all gathered from minute dust-motes. The houses we see now are likewise gathered from minute dust-motes. Why? Bricks, tiles, timber, steel bars, and cement are all minute dust-motes. Are bricks and tiles not clay? Clay is made into shapes, put into a kiln, and fired. And timber? It is a great tree. Where does a great tree come from? The seed of the tree draws nourishment from the soil, is warmed by sunlight, and slowly grows and accumulates. All are compounded, gathered from many minute particles. It is not that some particular thing exists on its own; originally none of them has a self-substance — all are “the gathering of many minute particles.”

Chan Master Qinbatuo asked again: “Then what is called emptiness?” Senggong answered: “The many minute particles have no self-nature; that is called emptiness.” That is, the minute dust-mote itself does not exist; it is compounded from other things. Scientists now say that all matter is compounded of chemical elements (for example, water is compounded of the two elements oxygen and hydrogen); chemical elements are composed of atoms; atoms are composed of nuclei and electrons; nuclei and electrons are compounded of even smaller fundamental particles. Fundamental particles are not “fundamental” either; they are compounded of still finer things, until analysis reaches “wave-particle duality” — like a wave and yet like a particle; neither wave nor particle. In fact the Buddhist scriptures long ago spoke of the “neighboring-emptiness dust-mote” — the dust-mote neighboring on emptiness. At this point everyone may understand it this way: before the compounding of anything, there is nothing at all, and that is emptiness — that is, “the gathering of many minute particles is form, the non-gathering of many minute particles is emptiness.” In fact the “emptiness” spoken of in Buddhism does not mean this. Senggong did not say, “The gathering of many minute particles is form, the non-gathering of many minute particles is emptiness”; he put it very well: “The many minute particles have no self-nature; that is emptiness.” The many minute particles also have no essence — no self-nature. Form is emptiness and emptiness is form; it is not the emptiness of “utter nothingness.” The emptiness of “utter nothingness” is annihilating emptiness. The “emptiness” Senggong spoke of is the emptiness of self-nature, which is our own nature. All forms are manifested by our own nature. Our own nature is the Buddha-nature, the root of all forms.
Why is it called “Buddha-nature” and not “dharma-nature”? What is the difference here?

The dharma-nature is the root of all dharmas. All things and matters, including our thoughts, are called dharmas. In the Buddhist scriptures the scope of “dharma” is very, very broad. All things, all matters, and even our thoughts are produced by our numinous luminous true nature and are the wondrous function manifested by our numinous luminous true nature. Our numinous luminous true nature is the root of all dharmas, and so it is called “dharma-nature.”

The Buddha-nature is the root of becoming a Buddha. When we have removed all deluded thoughts, cut off ignorance entirely, and recovered the original face, the wondrous function of our numinous luminous true nature is complete. When the three bodies and four wisdoms are complete, that is becoming a Buddha; there is no other Buddha to become. Our numinous luminous true nature is the root of becoming a Buddha, and so it is called “Buddha-nature.” Buddha-nature and dharma-nature both refer to the “one true dharma-realm,” which is our numinous luminous true nature. So this numinous luminous true nature is the root of all Buddhas and the source of all dharmas.

Form” is “emptiness”: all form is manifested by our numinous luminous true mind, and all forms are our numinous luminous true mind, and our numinous luminous true mind is all forms. It is not that one leaves all forms to seek emptiness, for that would be the emptiness of utter nothingness, and that is wrong. Hence Senggong said, “The gathering of many minute particles is form, the many minute particles have no self-nature and that is emptiness,” and did not say, “The non-gathering of many minute particles is emptiness.”

At this point Qinbatuo questioned him further: “What is it when the many minute particles are not gathered?” For Senggong had said the gathering of many minute particles is form — is that form? He had not gone to the root. In fact this form is our own nature, because without the nature nothing can manifest form. Senggong said, “The gathering of many minute particles is form.” Then what about when the many minute particles are not gathered? What is it before they are gathered? Senggong was at a loss — here he could not answer. It is clear that Senggong had not fully penetrated the meaning of form and emptiness. In fact this question could be answered quite easily: asked what it is when the many minute particles are not gathered, answer him, “At midnight the sun shines red!” Midnight is the third watch of the night. In the night of the third watch the sun shines bright red — at midnight the sun shines red. There is another way of answering, such as the ready-made phrase in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: “The nature of form is true emptiness.” The nature of form is the form of our true mind, which is wondrous existence and true emptiness; this true emptiness is not dumb emptiness. “The nature of form” — does the nature have form? I am afraid that is a mistake. We know that the exoteric teachings say that this “wondrous existence true mind,” the Buddha-nature, has not the slightest mark — it is markless. But the tantric teachings say there is a subtle mark, a refined form. Just as it is also incorrect to say that the “four formless heavens” (the formless realm) have not the slightest form; a refined form is still present. So tantra and the exoteric teachings differ slightly. But this form is not coarse; it is refined, subtle, exceedingly subtle form. “The nature of form is true emptiness” — why is it true emptiness? Because it fills all space and pervades the dharma-realm, being everywhere. So space is it, and it is space; they are not two things.

Senggong did not truly understand the meaning of form and emptiness, but when he said, “The gathering of many minute particles is called form, the many minute particles have no self-nature and that is called emptiness,” he went a step further than our understanding of “leaving forms and being empty.” He did not say utter nothingness; he said the many minute particles have no self-nature, just as a house has no essence of its own and does not exist in itself but is successfully compounded of steel bars, cement, bricks, and tiles; a sofa chair too has no essence of its own but is put together from springs, boards, leather, and so on. No thing has an essence of its own, and so having no self-nature is called emptiness — it is not that having no marks is called emptiness. Some say that if it is empty there should be no marks, and if there are marks it is not empty. That is to misunderstand: the emptiness we speak of is “wondrous existence and true emptiness.” That is, all forms are manifested by our own nature; if there were no such nature (that is, if there were not this numinous luminous true mind of ours), there would be no mountains, rivers, and great earth, no sun, moon, and stars, no men and women, young and old; that there are today is precisely the manifestation of this numinous luminous true mind.

Why speak of this principle? The purpose is to let everyone understand that these forms are originally our own true mind. Do not leave marks to seek the true mind; seeking the true mind apart from marks, you will not find it. The reason it is said that the Buddha-nature has boundless wondrous function is that the marks it manifests are infinitely various and its wondrous function is boundless. Once one understands this truth, one no longer grasps marks or clings to marks, and lets all marks appear before one without obstruction, and so it is easy to see the true mind and perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit. If one does not know where the mind is, one’s practice has no place to land. For example, when you recite the Buddha-name, if you do not know where the Buddha-name lands, then reciting “Amitābha, Amitābha...” is seeking a Buddha outside the mind, seeking the Buddha of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands beyond the Sahā world, not knowing that your mind is the Buddha and the Buddha is your mind. The Buddha is nowhere else; he is right at your mind, and you need not seek elsewhere. So when Qinbatuo asked Senggong about the meaning of form and emptiness, Senggong’s answer was wrong.

Chan Master Qinbatuo questioned Senggong further: “Apart from this Prajñā Sūtra, what other sūtras do you expound?” Senggong answered: “I also expound the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.” Qin asked: “May I ask what the meaning of nirvāṇa is?” He answered: “Ni means not born; vana means not extinguished.” Qin asked: “Is not being born and not being extinguished nirvāṇa?” He answered: “Yes!” Qin said: “That is the nirvāṇa of the Buddha’s fruit; where is the nirvāṇa of the cause?” Senggong could not answer, and asked: “Does nirvāṇa have two meanings?” Nirvāṇa is all the same — does it have two meanings? Seeing that Senggong did not grasp his meaning, Qinbatuo picked up his ruyi scepter and asked him: “Do you see it?” He answered: “I see it.” Qin asked: “What do you see?” He answered: “I see the Chan master holding a ruyi in his hand.” Qinbatuo threw the ruyi to the ground with a bang and asked: “Do you still see it?” He answered: “I see it.” Qin asked: “What do you see?” He answered: “I see the Chan master’s ruyi fallen to the ground.” Qinbatuo laughed heartily: “Looking at your understanding, it does not rise above the common run — how then is your fame to fill the universe?” That is, your understanding does not rise above the common run; like an ordinary person you cling to marks and turn with the thing in my hand. (At this point Master Yuanyin picked up a book and asked: what is this thing? Everyone answered: a book, a Buddhist sūtra. The master laughed and said: oh! You are stuck on it, ha ha!) Yes — throw the thing on the ground and you still turn with the state. You do not know that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. Why then is your fame so great? This is truly a wrong and undeserved reputation! He turned and walked away.

Senggong had many disciples, and they were bewildered: oh, what is the reason for this? Could our master have spoken wrongly? So they ran after him and asked Qinbatuo: “Dharma master, dharma master, how do you explain this form and emptiness?” Qinbatuo answered: “What your master said cannot be called wrong; it is only that he does not understand the form and emptiness of the cause, only the form and emptiness of the fruit.” The disciple asked: “What is form and emptiness of the cause?” Chan Master Qinbatuo said: “Because one minute particle is empty, the many minute particles are empty; because the many minute particles are empty, one minute particle is empty. In the one minute particle’s emptiness there are no many minute particles; in the many minute particles’ emptiness there is no one minute particle.” One minute particle is empty: a single dust-mote is fundamentally empty, having no self-substance — that is, no self-nature. If one dust-mote is empty, the other dust-motes are of course empty too. And so by analogy all the many minute particles are empty. Because the many minute particles are empty, one minute particle is empty — the many minute particles are all empty, that is, all dust-motes are empty, and so one dust-mote is empty too. Because one minute particle is empty there are no many minute particles — if even one dust-mote is empty, what many minute particles are there? Because the many minute particles are empty there is no one minute particle — since all the many minute particles are empty, can one dust-mote still be found? What he taught by “the many minute particles empty, one minute particle empty; one minute particle empty, the many minute particles empty” is that all things whatsoever are ungraspable.

All forms are the wondrous function of our true mind, so we must understand this meaning of form and emptiness. If we can truly understand it, we see the nature upon circumstances and need not leave circumstances to see the nature. For example, if someone points at a tree and asks what this is: to say it is a tree is to be stuck on it; to say it is not a tree is to contradict and leave the circumstance. What exactly is it then? To put it another way: “Hard to deceive the monk” — a single phrase that touches neither side displays this undeceivable numinous knowing and so slips free. The Chan school uses the method of slipping free, not being bound by that form or state. When he asks you, he is seeing whether you are stuck on existence or on emptiness. If you are stuck on neither side, a single phrase slips you free. But you cannot say, “I am neither empty nor existent” — that is still talking principle, and still will not do. You must say a wondrous phrase whose words touch neither emptiness nor existence yet which secretly contains both, and only then does it accord with the wonder of the Way. To realize this state one must illumine at every moment and understand that all marks are manifested by the self-nature, neither clinging to marks nor leaving marks. This is what the school calls “neither identical nor separate,” and only when this is clear can one’s wondrous function be perfect and fused. Worldly dharmas too are inseparable from principle and phenomena: phenomena are accomplished through principle — one accomplishes a thing according to the principle of emptiness; and principle is revealed through phenomena — only when the thing is accomplished is the principle revealed. Without principle one cannot accomplish a thing, and without a thing one cannot reveal principle; hence it is said that principle and phenomena are perfectly fused.

What is principle? Take an example: when scientists design something and want to build it, they must first set out formulas and work out the data; these formulas and data are the principle. Constructing according to the formulas and data, the thing is made. For example, if we build a house — how many stories, what style — we first draw the plans and then calculate how much steel, how much cement, how much material is needed, and so on. Then the workers build according to the plans, and the house is completed. If it is well built, it proves the plans were right, that the principle was correct; if it is poorly built, the plans were wrong, the principle was not correct. So phenomena are accomplished through principle, and principle is revealed through phenomena.

Principle and phenomena cannot be separated; phenomena are principle and principle is phenomena. We must understand this truth and train ourselves upon circumstances at every moment, training our true mind. So we must understand the meaning of form and emptiness, and on no account explain emptiness as the emptiness of utter nothingness. This emptiness is wondrous existence and true emptiness, which is our wondrous mind, our true mind. Where is the true mind? Right upon things and marks, not apart from them; yet to be stuck on things and marks is also wrong, for to be stuck on things and marks is to cling to things, and that too is a mistake. In our Chan school there are two lines: “The lush, lush yellow flowers are nothing but prajñā; the green, green bamboo is all the dharma-body.” Great Master Dazhu said: if the green bamboo is the dharma-body, then when people eat bamboo shoots they are eating the dharma-body! Bamboo grows from bamboo shoots; if we take the shoots and fry them, are we not eating up the dharma-body? So to be stuck on the dharma-body, to be stuck on things and marks, is wrong. And leaving things and marks? To leave things and marks is to fall into emptiness, which is also wrong. So one must be neither identical nor separate, must see through things and marks to the nature, and must abide in nothing. Hence the Diamond Sūtra says: “One should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere” — do not be stuck on it, and the wondrous function of the true mind is ever present. “Giving rise” means manifesting: your wondrous existence true mind appears. So we must be without abiding at every moment and must train this non-abiding true mind.

blocks.text: 8. The Dharma Values Suiting the Capacity

inline.s: In practicing the Dharma, whether we practice the Pure Land school, the Chan school, or tantra, we must all do the work in this way. For instance, when we recite the Buddha-name, should we cultivate contemplation? What is contemplation? Contemplation is Chan contemplation, which is cultivating samādhi! When you recite the Buddha-name you must recite with the mind and hear with the ear, quietly listening to the sound of the recitation, and only then can you gather the mind and enter samādhi; this is called the contemplation of Buddha-recitation. Reciting the Buddha-name is not singing a mountain song, and still less may you recite “Amitābha, Amitābha” while talking with others — that will not do! You must cultivate the “contemplation of Buddha-recitation”; contemplation is cultivating Chan! There are many kinds of Chan: ordinary-being Chan, Hīnayāna Chan, Mahāyāna Chan, supreme-vehicle Chan, and outsider Chan. What is called ordinary-being Chan and Hīnayāna Chan is having a different calculation in the mind. What is a different calculation? It is discrimination in the mind. Mistakenly thinking that mind and dharma are not one road, that emptiness and form are not one thing, clinging to marks in seeking the health of the physical body, or thinking that mind-dharma is not form-dharma and form-dharma is not mind-dharma, cultivating Chan by the principle of partial emptiness, and so on — all are different calculations. And outsider Chan? It too carries a different calculation in the mind; it either falls into emptiness — leaning toward annihilation — or clings to existence, clinging to the “yang spirit, the divine self.” None of the above is the true way of Chan. In cultivating Chan we must first clarify the correct cause and set our views straight, and then choose a correct dharma that suits our own faculties and practice it, and only then will we not go astray.

To make this clearer for everyone, let me speak again of outsider Chan, Hīnayāna Chan, and Mahāyāna Chan. To admire the Buddha-way and loathe the Sahā world is called “the mind of delight and loathing.” In the Pure Land school this is very good: with a single Amitābha, delight and loathing are both complete — that is, hoping to go to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and escape this Sahā world. But in terms of Chan practice, any mind that delights in the higher and loathes the lower is ordinary-being Chan; one has not entered the sage’s realm but is still at the ordinary-being level. Outsiders too delight in the higher and loathe the lower: they want to become immortals and leave this ordinary world. They do not understand that the immortal is an ordinary being and the ordinary being is the immortal; that the Buddha is an ordinary being and the ordinary being is a Buddha, originally one body. So delighting in the higher and loathing the lower and seeking outside the mind, not knowing that the self-nature is real, is what makes them outsiders.

One who awakens to the principle of the partial truth of the emptiness of self and cultivates accordingly practices Hīnayāna Chan. He already knows that body and mind are compounded of the four great elements and the five aggregates: the body is earth, water, fire, and wind. The mind is thought, thought is mind, and mind is feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, which together with the form-body composed of the four great elements are called the five aggregates. The Hīnayāna practitioner of Chan knows that what is compounded of the four great elements and the five aggregates is false and unreal. Unlike us ordinary beings, who cling to this body, take it as “I,” want to protect it, dress well, eat well, live well, wanting everything to be good, and so create karma and receive retribution. The Hīnayāna sage knows the four great elements and five aggregates are false; he knows that this “person-self” (the body) is empty and unreal. But he leans toward emptiness. Toward what emptiness does he lean? He says: after I escape the six paths of rebirth I will dwell in a pure land outside the realms (that is, a pure land beyond the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm), and abide there unmoving. He clings to the four great elements — earth, water, fire, and wind — as self; his “clinging to dharmas” is not yet ended, and he does not yet know or understand that all false marks are the wondrous function manifested by our true mind. So he is said to have awakened to the “emptiness of self” but only to “partial truth”: he leans toward this true and unfalse true mind and does not understand that “the false is the true and the true is the false; the wholly false is the true, the wholly true is the false.”

Without the false, where is the true? Without the true, where is the false? So the false is the true and the true is the false. To divide true from false here is still the deluded mind, still discrimination! Take the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss: everyone thinks the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is true and the Sahā world is false, and so wishes to loathe the Sahā world and delight in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is a division of true and false.

In fact the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is true, and our Sahā world is also true. Why? Because the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is manifested by the Buddha-nature of Amitābha Buddha and all the good people there, and so it is a pure land, manifested by a pure mind; while our Sahā world is manifested by the karmically obstructed minds of beings, and so it is an evil world of the five turbidities. But the karmically obstructed mind — what is the ālaya-consciousness? It is our Buddha-nature, our true mind. For this eighth consciousness, the ālaya-consciousness, is the true mind; if it were not the true mind, where would the ālaya-consciousness come from? The reason it is called the ālaya-consciousness is that it is a mixture of the born-and-dying and the not-born-and-not-dying; remove the born-and-dying part and it is the pure essence. Therefore the ālaya-consciousness is not apart from the pure essence; though it is a defiled substance, it is also the true mind!

What is the true mind like? It is unmoving; it is thus when pure and thus when defiled. It is like when we sleep and dream: now we are frightened, now delighted, now we are emperor, now a beggar, yet our body has not left the bed but still lies there unmoving. Our true mind is unmoving: it is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor still, neither defiled nor pure; it has never moved. Everything is manifested by it, and apart from it there is nothing. So if you say true, the Sahā world is true too; if you say false, the Western world is false too.

Why? Because whatever has marks is delusive! One must not cling to marks. What are marks? Marks are the shadows of the true mind, images appearing in a mirror; do not take the shadow for the mirror! We need only be free of the shadows and images within the true mind — why insist on grasping the true? So to speak of true and false is the discrimination of our deluded mind; it is “neither true nor false, both true and false, immediately true and immediately false.” Just remove the discriminative mind and it is done. The Hīnayāna sages do not understand this truth; they think there is a true, that their realization of sagehood is true and the ordinary beings of the six paths are all false. So this is still not the supreme-vehicle Chan; this is Hīnayāna Chan.

One who awakens to the truth revealed by the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas and cultivates accordingly practices Mahāyāna Chan. We have spoken of ordinary-being Chan, outsider Chan, and Hīnayāna Chan; by Mahāyāna Chan one has already awakened: neither I nor dharmas can be grasped. As was said just now, the Hīnayāna sages — arhats and pratyekabuddhas — awaken only to the emptiness of the person-self, not to the emptiness of the dharma-self. The dharma-self is that beyond the person-self there are the four great elements as self, and beyond the person-self there is a dharma-body to cultivate, a Buddha-dharma to attain, a nirvāṇa to realize, a birth-and-death to end — dharmas still exist. So the dharma-self is not empty. Then advancing further, the person-self too is gone and the dharma-self too is gone; everything without exception is manifested by our wondrous existence true mind, and the wondrous existence true mind is the emptiness of nature, all ungraspable. But to awaken to the principle that person-self and dharma-self are both empty is still not ultimate, still not the best.

What is the best? The best is what we are explaining now: if one suddenly awakens that the self-nature is originally pure, with no affliction apart from it, and that the undefiled wisdom-nature is originally complete in oneself, and that this mind is Buddha, and believes it with firm conviction — that is a step further, and this is the supreme-vehicle Chan. That is, if we understand that our own mind is originally pure and undefiled, originally without affliction, and that the undefiled wisdom-nature is originally complete (defiled means having thought and fabrication, the conditioned; undefiled means all fabrication is absent, naturally thus, with no affliction at all and great wisdom originally complete), and that this mind is Buddha, no different from the Buddha — this is the best.

Since we are Buddhas, no different from the Buddha, why do we not know it? Since the mind is originally pure and originally without affliction, why do we now have so much affliction and are not pure in the least? What is the reason? It is ignorance making trouble! Because of ignorance we have deluded thoughts and discrimination, are deluded by outer circumstances without being aware, run after circumstances, and flow along with deluded thoughts. The reason we create karma and receive retribution, and revolve in the six paths without end, is precisely that we are deluded and unawakened. So I have explained the truth in tiresome detail to awaken everyone.

All beings are complete in this wondrous existence true mind. When Śākyamuni Buddha on the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month saw the morning star and awakened to the Way, he said: “Wonderful, wonderful! All beings on the great earth are endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous marks.” Why are they not aware of it themselves? Because of deluded thoughts, inversion, clinging, and affliction, they do not know it. So our expounding of the sūtras is to point out the ford and explain the wondrous luminous true mind that we originally possess in full. The Buddha-nature is nowhere else; it shines at our own faces. How does it shine? Who is it that sees things? Who is it that hears sounds? Who is it that smells fragrances and odors with the nose? Who is it that speaks with the tongue? Who is it that knows sour, sweet, bitter, and hot? Who is it that contacts outer circumstances? Who is it that walks? Who is it that works? All these are the wondrous function of our own nature’s radiance — you must recognize it! If we awaken to the Way right now, that is sudden awakening. Our mind is originally this pure, originally without a trace of affliction, originally complete in the Tathāgata’s wisdom. This mind is Buddha! Do not seek the Buddha outside. One who understands this truth and cultivates accordingly practices the supreme-vehicle Chan.

One who does not understand this truth practices blindly, takes detours, goes in circles, and circling round and round cannot get out. So the cause-ground must be correct; one must understand this truth and know at every moment that we ourselves are Buddhas and the Buddha is nowhere else. Perhaps you will ask: am I a Buddha right now? Then why do I not manifest spiritual powers? The Buddha has the three insights and six superknowledges! The ancients said: “Recognize the icy pond as all water, and rely on the yang warmth to melt it.” This is an analogy. In the cold of winter the water in the pond freezes into ice, yet this ice is water! “Recognize” means to know. “Recognize the icy pond as all water” is to recognize that this frozen pond is entirely water (an analogy for beings being originally Buddhas). “Rely on the yang warmth to melt it” means one must borrow the sunlight to melt the ice. Only after it has melted can it perform the work of irrigation. Ice is solid and cannot flow (an analogy for beings lacking the three insights and six superknowledges). After melting it can flow and can irrigate the fields (an analogy for the Buddha’s possession of the three insights and six superknowledges). Next: “Awaken that the ordinary being is the Buddha, and rely on the power of Dharma to permeate and cultivate.” “Awaken that the ordinary being is the Buddha” means we awaken and know that this ordinary mind is the Buddha-mind. “Rely on the power of Dharma to permeate and cultivate”: to rely is to borrow aid. What do we use as aid? The power of the Buddha-dharma — we must borrow the power of the Buddha-dharma to help our practice. For though we have awakened, it is only an awakening in principle, only initial enlightenment — we have just begun to awaken. The habits are still heavy and cannot be ended at once. So we must borrow the power of Dharma to help us, permeating it at every moment: that is, using the methods of reciting the Buddha-name, forming seals, reciting mantras, attending to the huatou, and raising doubt to permeate and cultivate, transforming the deluded seeds and defiled seeds in our eight-consciousness field into pure seeds, and turning habits into wondrous function.

After understanding the principle, one must still borrow the power of the Buddha-dharma to cultivate! Without cultivating, it does not land in reality and is useless. It is by no means enough merely to say it and understand it. That will not do! Perhaps right now you awaken: everything is false, put everything down, cling to nothing. But perhaps the moment you leave here and stroll in the street it is gone. Several friends have told me: alas! Today I went to the crematorium and my heart turned to ashes. Once a person’s breath stops and he is burned to ashes, nothing remains. What is there to cling to? No clinging, no clinging! The mind died and became empty. But before they had gone far, they wanted everything again — the habits are heavy! So we can only speak of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation. In fact “sudden awakening and gradual cultivation” does not hold together logically: if gradual cultivation is still needed, then there was no sudden awakening — this is what the Prajñā Sūtra says. But to speak too loftily will not do; we do not have that power. So the Śūraṅgama Sūtra teaches two kinds of dharma: “Principle belongs to sudden awakening, and with the awakening all is dissolved; phenomena must be removed gradually, and are exhausted by stages.” As soon as the principle is explained, one awakens at once; after awakening, all habits dissolve, one wants nothing, and at once all is empty and pure. Such people certainly exist, but they are only a few, an extremely small number — people of the very highest faculties, returners. If one is not a returner, one cannot, upon a single awakening, be thoroughly clear. Yet today’s suddenness is the gradualness of former days. It has been accumulated through practice in the past, and the past, and further past, slowly, slowly, and so today it drops off at a single “crack.” The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says, “Principle belongs to sudden awakening, and with the awakening all is dissolved; phenomena must be removed gradually, and are exhausted by stages.” This originally teaches two dharma-gates: one the perfect and sudden dharma, one the gradual dharma. The very few of the highest faculties, returners, hear the principle and awaken at once, and all habits are destroyed in the instant of awakening, so that spiritual powers and wondrous function can appear. Most people of middling and lower faculties must, after awakening, train amid affairs and gradually remove their habits before they can slowly bring their function into play. Now we may as well join the two dharma-gates into one: “principle belongs to sudden awakening, phenomena must be removed gradually” — cultivating the sudden and the gradual gates together. Why say this? Because we are now in the age of the Dharma’s decline, when beings’ faculties are dull and their obstacles heavy, and they cannot awaken suddenly, cultivate suddenly, and realize suddenly; so we must join the two gates into one, protecting and sustaining after awakening the principle, diligently removing habits, and gradually developing penetration and realizing the fruit. To join sudden awakening and gradual cultivation and speak of them together does not hold together logically, but it accords with the present actual situation and so may be borrowed. This principle is not easy to explain clearly; we may as well use a story from the time when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world to illustrate. Two disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha were discussing a sentence the Buddha had spoken; each had his own reasons, and neither would yield, so they went to ask the Buddha: Buddha, which of us speaks in accord with your meaning? The Buddha said: neither of you accords with my meaning, but both of your meanings can be used. Why? Because they accord with the actual situation! So now we can only speak of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation.

Then how does one cultivate? Pure Land people recite the Buddha-name: “Amitābha, Amitābha” — using this Buddha-name to sweep clean the defilement in our minds, sweep clean the habits in our minds, sweep clean our afflictions. The moment affliction emerges, recite “Amitābha” aloud and turn the mind to emptiness, dissolve it into emptiness. And Chan people? They attend to the huatou at every moment. The moment affliction stirs, ask: “Who are you?” — a blow straight to the head: “Who stirred this affliction? Who is it that stirs affliction?” A blow straight to the head — this is attending to the huatou. Tantric practitioners, the moment affliction arises, immediately recite a mantra to transform it. The methods differ, but the principle is the same. Do not say: my Pure Land is good and your Chan is wrong; my Chan is good and your Pure Land is wrong; my tantra is good and your Chan and Pure Land are both wrong. That is dividing into sects and households, and shows that you have not yet understood. When you understand and bring forth wondrous function, you will say: Chan is good, Pure Land is good, tantra is good — all are means; the expedient gates are many, but the return to the source is one road. Borrowing the power of the Buddha-dharma, we apply effort in practice, sweep clean our habits, and dissolve our afflictions into emptiness, and so “when the ice melts the water flows and moistens, and only then does the work of irrigation appear; when delusion is exhausted the mind is empty and penetrating, and the function of penetrating radiance responds and appears.” When the mind-flower is penetrating and bright, spiritual powers are revealed and wondrous function is boundless. All this is realized by practice; if you say there is no need to cultivate, will that do? It will not! So one must cultivate.
Someone asks: for one who has awakened, when the end of life comes, where does the spirit-nature go?

This is a great question! After awakening to the Way, where does one go? Many people ask this. A man from Hong Kong wrote to ask me whether one who has awakened should know in advance, at the end of life, where he is going — that is, foreknow the place. If he does not foreknow the place, then he has not awakened. Is this right? No! Why not? If one has truly awakened, there is no birth and no death, no coming and no going — what place is there? As I said just now, this wondrous existence true mind is subtle form, and subtle form is space; what place does space have? If you want a place, then there is still coming and going, still birth and death, and you have not yet awakened. The writer did not understand this principle, and so asked where one goes when the span of life ends and one dies. This is not only his question but everyone’s question. So today, borrowing a passage from Chan Master Guifeng, let us speak of this again. Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi said:

All beings are without exception endowed with the nature of enlightenment — numinous, luminous, empty, and still — no different from the Buddha. But because from beginningless kalpas they have never understood or awakened, they falsely cling to the body as the mark of self, and so give rise to love and hate and other emotions. Following emotion they create karma, and following karma they receive retribution. Birth, old age, sickness, and death, and long kalpas of rebirth. Yet the nature of enlightenment within the body has never been born or died: like one driven about in a dream while the body itself lies at ease; like water turning to ice while its wet nature does not change. If one can awaken to this nature, it is the dharma-body, originally unborn — what reliance would it have? Numinously undimmed, vividly ever aware, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Yet through many lives of false clinging, habit has become nature, and joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness flow on subtly. Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these emotions are hard to remove at once. One must constantly be aware, reducing and again reducing, like wind suddenly ceasing while the waves gradually subside. How could the cultivation of one lifetime equal the powers and functions of all the Buddhas? One need only take empty stillness as one’s own essence and not acknowledge the form-body; take numinous knowing as one’s own mind and not acknowledge deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them. Then at the end of life karma naturally cannot bind one. Though there is an intermediate state, one goes where one will, and may lodge at will among the heavens or among humans. If the thoughts of love and hate are already extinguished, one does not receive a body of segment-by-segment birth and death, and can of oneself change the short into the long, the coarse into the subtle. If the subtle flowing is utterly stilled and extinguished, and only the great perfect wisdom of enlightenment shines alone, then one responds to capacities and manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation-bodies to deliver beings with affinity — this is called a Buddha.
Now let me explain this passage of Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi:

All beings are without exception endowed with the nature of enlightenment — numinous, luminous, empty, and still — no different from the Buddha.” All beings — not only we humans, but ants, insects, flies, lions, apes, and so on — are without exception endowed with the nature of enlightenment. Which being would you say lacks the nature of enlightenment? Look at a mosquito: if you have blood here, it flies over at once to bite you. A fly: set out a piece of steamed cake, and it can fly from far away to land on it. They have the nature of enlightenment. Of humans there is no need to speak. The nature of enlightenment is the nature of knowing and awareness: do you know that your belly is hungry? Do you know that the weather is warm today? These are all the nature of knowing and awareness! So all beings possess the nature of enlightenment. “Numinous, luminous, empty, and still” means numinous yet luminous, radiant and transparent, vividly clear. It is radiance, and its numinous knowing is vivid and unmoving, thus, thus. This “luminous” has two explanations: “empty” — utterly nothing, with not one thing established; “still” — unmoving and unshaking, neither coming nor going. “No different from the Buddha” means no distinction whatsoever, no second difference, from Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Maitreya Buddha, and all other Buddhas.

But because from beginningless kalpas they have never understood or awakened, they falsely cling to the body as the mark of self, and so give rise to love and hate and other emotions.” “Beginningless” means having no beginning, and in the future no end either, going round and round, always like this. “Never understood or awakened” means never having awakened, never having known that one is oneself a great treasure. The Lotus Sūtra uses the analogy: a man has a maṇi jewel sewn into his clothing and does not know it. This maṇi jewel can rain down all treasures, and so you are not poor. You are complete in everything; whatever you want, it has. Yet you do not know it, and go begging outside. Just as our present revolving in the six paths and wandering in birth and death is begging. We have a great treasure and do not know it; we have never understood or awakened. “Falsely cling to the body as the mark of self”: through false clinging one does not recognize the true but takes the false as real. This body is fundamentally not “I,” yet it is taken as “I.” The body is like the house we live in, and within it there is a person. What is the person? The person is our numinous luminous true mind. Not knowing this, one takes the “house” as “I”: this body is me, this body is me! “And so give rise to love and hate and other emotions.” Thus love and hate and other emotions arise. I like this and dislike that; this person is friendly to me and that person is unfriendly. There is much discrimination, all of it deluded thought. What one likes one takes as one’s own; what one dislikes one strikes down — and so one creates karma and receives retribution.

Following emotion they create karma, and following karma they receive retribution. Birth, old age, sickness, and death, and long kalpas of rebirth.” Birth and death fundamentally do not exist; they arise because, after we have love and hate and other emotions, we create karma according to the mind. We want something and cannot get it, and it belongs to another, so we rob him or kill him — this creates the karma of killing. Creating karma means receiving retribution and revolving in the six paths. Creating good karma one ascends to the heavens; creating evil karma one falls into the hells; birth, old age, sickness, and death, and long kalpas of rebirth. Alas! There was fundamentally no birth and death, yet we have fallen into birth and death. Appearing and disappearing in the six paths, born and dying again and again, without liberation.

Yet the nature of enlightenment within the body has never been born or died: like one driven about in a dream while the body itself lies at ease; like water turning to ice while its wet nature does not change.” Though we revolve in birth and death again and again within the six paths, our nature of enlightenment has never been born or died; it is not born because you are born, nor extinguished because your flesh dies. If you fall into hell it is not pained; if you ascend to heaven it is not glad. It is originally neither born nor extinguished, empty, numinous, and abiding nowhere, never having been born or died, never having moved. It is like being in a dream, chased by villains, terrified beyond measure, running madly on, while in fact the body still lies peacefully in bed, unmoving. It is also like water turning to ice while its wet nature does not change. This is an analogy for the fact that although we revolve in the six paths, the Buddha-nature does not change.

If one can awaken to this nature, it is the dharma-body, originally unborn — what reliance would it have?” If we can awaken to this nature of enlightenment as the dharma-body and understand that our nature of enlightenment is the root of all things and matters, that it was originally never born and never extinguished, why should it still have a place to rely on? If you have truly awakened, you should have no reliance and no place to go. I remember a man from Wenzhou who said something very funny. He claimed to have awakened, and someone asked him: “We are not people who practice the Pure Land method seeking birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; we practice the Chan school — after we pass away, where do we go?” See how he answered: he said, “One may lean on grass and attach to trees, or on a rock, or on a great tree, or on withered grass — anywhere will do.” Oh no, that is bad — he has become a spirit clinging to grass and trees! How can that do? To lean on grass and attach to trees is to be a ghost clinging to a body. In Shanghai’s Fuxing Park there is a thousand-year-old bodhi tree said to be inconceivably efficacious, and everyone goes to worship it; in fact it is a ghost, a spirit-ghost attached to it. After death, to lean on grass and attach to trees is to become a ghost — what kind of Way would you say he has awakened to? In fact it has nothing to do with the Way; it is all false. Our nature of enlightenment is “originally unborn — what reliance would it have?” There should be no reliance. One who leans on grass and attaches to trees has never caught a glimpse of even half a thread of the nature of enlightenment.

Long ago there was a broken stove abandoned for many years, and a spirit attached itself to the stove and sent people a dream: come and make offerings to me on this stove, and whatever you want I will give you. Everyone said, there is a spirit on this stove, let us all go and make offerings! Many people came to make offerings to him, and the spirit satisfied their wishes. Word spread from one to ten and from ten to a hundred, and this broken stove became extraordinarily famous. There was a Chan master in that region (a disciple of National Master Hui’an), who saw that this spirit attached to the broken stove was causing everyone to kill living beings to make offerings to him and so create karma, and so he went and taught it the Dharma. Striking the stove with his staff — thump, thump, thump — he said: I ask you, you are compounded of bricks, tiles, and mud; where does the spirit come from? Where does the god come from? Bricks, tiles, and mud have no spirit and no god; the consciousness that has spirit is your own mind — why do you attach yourself to this stove of brick and mud?
