At a single pointer from the Chan master the stove spirit awakened: right, the spirit is not on the bricks, tiles, and mud — the spirit is in my own mind! He hurriedly abandoned the broken stove. That night he came to thank the Chan master and then ascended to heaven. Afterwards everyone called this Chan master “the Monk Who Abandoned the Broken Stove,” and his real name was forgotten. Even Chan knows not to cling to the body; can we manage it while clinging to grasses and trees? So there must be no reliance! We are originally unborn, originally without reliance!

Numinously undimmed, vividly ever aware, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.” If you have truly awakened to the Way, you are vividly ever aware and numinously undimmed, and everywhere is you. Wherever there is affinity, there you manifest a body. Hence it is called “the nirvāṇa of no abode.” There is no fixed place; you can manifest a body anywhere, and wherever there is affinity you can manifest. If one has truly and thoroughly awakened, how could there still be a fixed place? To have a fixed place is to be unawakened. “Numinously undimmed” means not the slightest mark of dimness. “Vividly ever aware” means utterly clear and bright. This knowing has no interruption, and so it is called ever aware. It is not that one knows now and after a while does not know — that would be useless. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere: if it does not come, how can it go? If there is coming there is going, and if there is going there is coming; all are relative, and all that is relative is false. It is the absolute true mind, and so it has no coming or going, no entering or emerging.

blocks.text: 9. Knowing One’s Own Mind as It Really Is

inline.s: Next we are shown how to apply effort and realize the Way, and thereby become Buddhas.

Yet through many lives of false clinging, habit has become nature, and joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness flow on subtly.” What we are now explaining is the supreme-vehicle Chan: “One’s own mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is one’s own mind.” That you can hear this dharma and believe it without doubt means that your good roots were not planted with one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas, but were planted over many lives and kalpas.

But through many lives and kalpas we have grown used to false clinging; we cling to outer states as real, cling to the body as “I,” and habit has become second nature. Oh, this body is me, most precious, do not touch me! In fact it is a stinking night-soil bucket — what is there to prize? A Qing dynasty emperor fell in love with a concubine whose body had a fragrance; this Fragrant Concubine was from Xinjiang and was said to have a rare fragrance about her. What fragrance was it? The stench of fox! Yet the old emperor called it fragrance. It is clear that whether anything is beautiful or not has no fixed standard: what you like is good, and otherwise it is hateful. Or having grown used to it, what is not good is also not bad. As the saying goes: stay long in a shop of salted fish and you no longer smell the stench. Once a habit is formed it is hard to turn back. This is an unshakable truth. Hearing this, someone may think: “This body is me. And everyone thinks so; you say the body is not me — who will believe you?” Alas! Through many lives and kalpas we have falsely clung to outer states, grown used to it, and made it a habit. Thus we have produced all kinds of views about states and things, judging and measuring everything by our own likes and dislikes: what suits my mind I grasp, and otherwise I reject. Hence “joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness flow on subtly.” Joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, fear, alarm, and grief — everyone has them. When things accord with my mind I am all smiles; when they offend my mind I am furious; when I lose something I am sullen; when something pleases me I beam. These are all the subtle flowing.

The subtle flowing is extremely subtle deluded thought moving without cease. The most fundamental deluded mind consists of the five omnipresent mental factors: intention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition. These five omnipresent dharmas are in fact a single thought arising in the mind, good or evil; they exist within the eight consciousnesses and constantly stir up all the good and evil seeds in the eight consciousnesses. They are extremely, extremely subtle, and so are called the arising and ceasing of the flowing. What is called flowing is like a ceaseless stream of water — but this water is not like the towering waves of the great ocean, nor the rolling billows of rivers, but like a small brook flowing softly, faintly, and finely. In fact it flows extremely fast, so fast that it does not show its movement; ordinarily you cannot see it and think it is unmoving — this is subtle, extremely subtle deluded thought. We spoke earlier of coarse delusion, which is deluded thought arising when facing circumstances. If you know that circumstances are your mind and your mind is circumstances, then you do not cling. Without clinging, coarse deluded thoughts do not arise. But the subtle deluded seeds are still there. They are subtle and extremely subtle; you see them as if unmoving, yet in fact they move very fast. How can the subtle flowing be cut off? Only by entering deeply into the samādhi of Vajrasattva can one see it and destroy it; without the samādhi of Vajrasattva it is useless. So one must enter deep samādhi. One who recites the Buddha-name must attain the samādhi of Buddha-recitation; without it, it will not do. One who practices Chan must raise a great mass of doubt; once the great doubt is raised, deluded thoughts do not move and the mass of doubt envelops the whole body, and when the time and conditions arrive, with a “crack” it bursts open, and only then can one personally see the nature. Tantric practitioners are the same: with the blessing of the three mysteries of body, mouth, and mind, borrowing the Buddha’s power to empower us and push us forward, until conditions ripen and — crack! — it explodes and cuts off the subtle flowing! This subtle flowing is extremely subtle; you cannot see it, and only by doing the work and settling down can you see it. For example, in a cup of turbid water you cannot see the silt within; once it settles and the water above is clear, you see how much silt there is below. While it is stirred and turbid, you cannot see it. You must first settle, and only then can you see the subtle flowing.

Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these emotions are hard to remove at once.” We say the mind is Buddha and the Buddha is the mind. This is the truth; you awaken to it at once: yes, yes! We are originally Buddhas — if not Buddhas, how could we speak? Could we still ask who is reciting the Buddha-name? If not Buddhas, how could we recite the Buddha-name? If not Buddhas, how could we write? If not Buddhas, how could we walk? When this body’s breath stops it does not move; movement is the wondrous function of the Buddha-nature. The truth is suddenly awakened to and understood, but “these emotions are hard to remove at once.” Emotion is deluded emotion, the emotion of love. The emotion of love is hard to remove! The ancients said: “If reciting the Buddha-name were like thinking of love, we would long ago have realized the Way!” If reciting the Buddha-name were like thinking of love, we would long ago have realized the Way.

We ordinary beings find it hard to give up the emotion of love, and the scope of love is very broad: the love of men and women, of mother and child, of husband and wife, the love of music, beauty, dogs, and horses, and many other attachments, such as fondness for antiques, stamp collecting, calligraphy and painting, growing flowers, keeping birds, and so on. There are truly far too many things people love. For a woman the hardest to cut off is the love of mother and child: once she has a child it is forever in her heart and can never be forgotten, and even at death she cannot let go: I cannot bear to leave my child! There was an old woman who recited the Buddha-name; at the end of her life we urged her: “Let go, and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.” She said: “I am not going; I cannot bear to leave my children and grandchildren!” With such delusion, how could she be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Ordinary beings all find “these emotions hard to remove at once.” “At once” means immediately. Our emotions are very hard to remove immediately, and so we can only awaken suddenly and cultivate gradually. Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation is a matter of necessity, yet it suits the habits of beings in this Sahā world at the present stage. Do not sing lofty tunes and say that you are one of sudden awakening, sudden cultivation, and sudden realization, needing no cultivation, no cultivation no attainment no realization. It is very easy to say with the mouth, but can you truly do it? Boasting is useless; you must truly do it. If you boast, King Yama will not let you off; he will still send you an invitation. Only if you truly do it can King Yama’s invitation be cancelled.

One must constantly be aware, reducing and again reducing, like wind suddenly ceasing while the waves gradually subside.” One must be aware for a long time — this is doing the work. For example, one who practices the Pure Land school simply raises the Buddha-name: the moment a thought stirs, quickly raise the Buddha-name high and recite it aloud: “Amitābha, Amitābha, Amitābha...” and so dissolve the deluded emotion. If the deluded emotion is not dissolved, it will not do! “Reducing and again reducing” means reducing the deluded emotion day by day, reducing your habits, afflictions, and clinging day by day — reducing, reducing, and reducing still further. Deluded emotion cannot be removed in a single day: “like wind suddenly ceasing while the waves gradually subside.” As soon as the wind blows, waves arise, and after the wind stops the waves still surge, and only slowly do they come to rest. So the ancients said: “The wind stops but the waves still surge; principle appears but thoughts still invade.” “Principle appears” — the truth appears and one awakens; yet “thoughts still invade,” deluded thoughts still intrude, and so one must remove them slowly.

How could the cultivation of one lifetime equal the powers and functions of all the Buddhas?” To cultivate for a single lifetime and expect at once to have the three insights and six superknowledges of all the Buddhas, and the same powers as all the Buddhas — that cannot be done. Though we have not yet developed the three insights and six superknowledges, we must believe deeply and without doubt: our mind is the Buddha-mind, and apart from this there is no Buddha-mind.

Speaking of this, I want to discuss an important question with everyone. I have heard people say: the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is not awakening; only when both subject and object are forgotten is there awakening. In fact they do not understand what the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is, do not recognize the original, and yet pretend to be of great faculties; they have not read the books of the teachings, yet they chatter irresponsibly.

Long ago, when Dharma Master Chengguan was expounding the Avataṃsaka Sūtra to Empress Wu Zetian (do not think Empress Wu Zetian was bad! Empress Wu Zetian was an awakened emperor. The present sūtra-opening verse, “The unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma, in a hundred thousand million kalpas hard to encounter; now that I see and hear it and can receive and uphold it, may I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning,” was composed by Wu Zetian in praise of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and is now used as the sūtra-opening verse for all scriptures), he said to her: “When not a single thought arises and the preceding and following intervals are cut off, the illuminating substance shines brightly — this is the thus, thus Buddha.” When not a single thought arises, the preceding and following intervals are cut off. The preceding interval is the preceding thought; the following interval is the following thought. The preceding and following intervals are cut off with a “crack.” The illuminating substance is the essence that can illumine all things and bring forth all wondrous function — the nature. “Brightly” means not clinging to any mark. “The thus, thus Buddha” — this is the Buddha! See how clearly he put it. Yet some do not understand and say that the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is not awakening. They do not know what the cutting off of the preceding and following intervals is, and still pretend to be good teachers — are they not harming people! Not knowing themselves yet deluding others, they will fall into hell as swiftly as an arrow flies!

When for an instant our thought comes to rest and is yet clearly aware — what is this? Apart from this, to seek Buddha-nature anywhere else is to find nothing. Do not suppose that because one lacks the three insights and the six superknowledges, and lacks the same spiritual powers and functions as all the Buddhas, one is therefore not awakened, not a Buddha. It is not that in a single lifetime one can be endowed with the Buddhas’ great powers and functions. To awaken to the Way for the first time is only like a newborn babe: though the babe lacks the strength of a grown man, cannot work, cannot walk, cannot eat, and must be fed and carried, you cannot say it is not a person. One newly awakened to the Way is a Buddha in the cause-ground. You must be aware at every moment and guard it at every moment. Maintain it closely and continuously, and let it diminish again and again, letting your habitual tendencies and afflictions lessen day by day; then this babe grows up, becomes a grown man, and is complete in all powers and functions. To apply effort once the original self is understood is what is called true cultivation after enlightenment. If one has not realized it, then it is blind practice and wild striving. For instance, if you recite the Buddha-name without awakening to the original self, you are reciting a Buddha outside the mind. We who recite the Buddha-name must understand that reciting Amitabha is to rouse our own true master, to call our own master to wake again and again — not to sink into forms and colors, not to be swept along by circumstances, not to cherish the common feelings of grasping and clinging. Only by doing so can you succeed. This is of the utmost importance!

But one may take emptiness-and-stillness as the self-substance, not acknowledging the physical body; take the numinous knowing as self-mind, not acknowledging delusive thoughts.” We must understand that this physical body, this flesh, this husk, is not ourselves. Our true essence is that which is empty and still — an unmoving, unshaking, neither coming nor going, neither being born nor dying thing — not this husk. This husk changes slowly, from youth to age, from age to death. Do not acknowledge this body; the body is the form-body, and this form-body is not oneself. By no means should we acknowledge this form-body as self; rather, acknowledge emptiness-and-stillness as self. That Buddha-nature which is empty and yet still, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking, is our very self! “Take the numinous knowing as self-mind, not acknowledging delusive thoughts.” What is a delusive thought? To have attachment is a delusive thought. A thought arises and the mind is fixed upon it; with abiding, with clinging, this is a delusive thought. When a thought arises without abiding and without clinging, that is the true mind’s wondrous function. This clear, luminous knowing is the true mind; it is not dead. To sit motionless, to suppress thought so hard that not a single thought arises, is to turn into a great boulder, a great log. Therefore the luminous knowing, unattached, ungrasping, without love or aversion, is the true mind’s wondrous functioning. To abide, to discriminate — that is deluded feeling. But one point must be made clear: it is not that one may not discriminate, but that one discriminates without abiding. That this man is good I know; that that man is bad I too am clear — it is not that one fails to distinguish good and bad and becomes a muddlehead. Is a muddlehead the true mind? Not at all. One should know good and bad, and yet remain without aversion or attachment, without grasping or discarding. It is not that seeing a good person one delights, and seeing a bad person one recoils. The bad person too we do not abandon — why? We should teach him, pity him, help him, and turn him around; only that is right. The true mind is just this. Therefore the true mind and the deluded mind are quite easy to distinguish. At every moment let us not acknowledge the deluded mind as self; we must know that the numinous knowing, clear and unattached to form, is the true mind; the moment there is attachment, a nest is formed, and one falls into form.

If delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them. Then at the very time of death, karma can no longer bind you.” This speaks of the moment of death — what happens at death? To be able to take rebirth self-masterfully at the end of life, one must have done the practice in daily life of “if delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them.” If our delusive thoughts are not yet entirely eradicated, and in an instant a delusive thought arises again, we must be aware at once and not chase after it. If a delusive thought is strong, and awareness alone cannot cut it off, then quickly recite the Buddha-name, or hold a mantra; or raise the huatou (head-word) and ask where this delusive thought comes from, thereby dissolving it. If you have followed the delusive thought far gone before you realize it, then it is already too late. The speed of awareness and the quickness of removal are matters of the strength of one’s practice. It is like the difference between a candle flame and an electric light. At first it illuminates, but further on the light is dim; a delusive thought arises and only much later do we become aware of it — this is the candle flame. When the practice has become fully mature, the moment a thought arises we see it — like a strong light shining before us, so that every pit and hollow is clearly visible, and one walking the night road does not fall into a pit or a trench — this is the electric light. This reaches the stage of stillness that constantly illumines, and illumination that is constantly still; one no longer deliberately attends to the illumination, but it illumines of itself. In this matter there is a great depth of difference in the levels of practice.

In doing our practice we must be aware at every moment, practicing closely and continuously. If in a single day of twenty-four hours we practice for only an hour or two and are lax for the other twenty-two, that is far too lazy, and it is difficult for the practice to advance. Therefore we must practice constantly, always aware, within the four deportments of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; only then can the practice advance.

Again, if delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them along. It is not that because a certain delusive thought seems good one runs after it. Someone has a fine dream, and when he wakes cannot bear to let it go, still thinking of it. The dream scene is originally false — why cling to it? If in a dream you were emperor, are you truly an emperor? If in a dream you gained a great treasure, did you truly gain a treasure? To cling to it, is that not folly! How foolish people are!

Master Guifeng, with bitter heart and kind words, tells us: if delusive thoughts arise, do not follow them, do not run after them. If we truly accomplish this, then “at the very time of death, karma cannot bind you.” To bind is to tie up. All beings run along with karma! Those with good karma rise to heaven; those with evil karma fall into hell. If one can truly accomplish that when a delusive thought arises one does not follow it, then at that time karma cannot tie you, and you are free.

Though there is an intermediate state, where one goes is free; in heaven or among humans, one may dwell as one wishes.” One who has truly awakened to the Way has no intermediate body, and one who is born in the Western Pure Land likewise has no intermediate body. What is the intermediate state? It is when the former body has perished and the later body has not yet arisen: the former husk has broken, and one has not yet been conceived into the later husk; the body of that intermediate state between the two is the intermediate body. This intermediate body is dominated by the wind element, so it possesses the five superknowledges. Of the six superknowledges it lacks the knowledge of the extinction of defilements; it possesses only a small measure of the five superknowledges, not the five great superknowledges of a Buddha. The intermediate body has a portion of the five superknowledges, so it has the superknowledge of magical powers: wherever the parents are who have affinity with it, a thousand li or ten thousand li away, it drifts there in an instant. It has the heavenly eye, so it can see even a thousand li or ten thousand li away. Those born in the Western Pure Land have gone there and have no intermediate body. Those who fall into hell likewise have no intermediate body. Once fallen into hell, where would there be an intermediate body? The other realms all have an intermediate body. “Though there is an intermediate state, where one goes is free” — if one truly accomplishes that when a thought arises one does not follow it, then karmic hindrances cannot grasp you, cannot tie you, cannot obstruct you. Wherever you wish to go, you go there, free and self-masterful. “In heaven or among humans, one may dwell as one wishes” — either in heaven or in the human world, one may dwell as one wishes. This is the most elementary level of practice: before one can cut off delusive thoughts, when a delusive thought arises, one is able not to follow it. When practice reaches this point, even though one still has an intermediate body, one can still be free and self-masterful. But if a delusive thought arises and one runs after it, then it is ruined, and one cannot be free. So this is the most elementary step, the lowest grade.

If the thoughts of love and aversion are already extinguished, one no longer receives a body subject to birth-and-death in stages.” Love is affection, liking; aversion is hatred, dislike. The mind of love and hatred is gone. It is not that this being good I take, that being bad I discard. For all things are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows — what ground is there for good and bad? What is there to love or hate? This must truly be accomplished. If someone merely explains it to you and you can do it for a while, but when you are alone you still have feelings of love and aversion, then it still does not count. When the thoughts of love and aversion are extinguished — “extinguish” means to destroy, to make vanish — the thoughts of love and aversion are done away with, and one no longer receives birth-and-death in stages; one leaves the round of birth and death. Of course, there remains still the attachment to dharmas that must be removed.

Then of oneself one can turn the short into the long, the coarse into the subtle.” This speaks of function. Such a person can transform self-masterfully: the short can become long, the coarse and poor can become subtle and exquisite. He can transform; even the six realms of transmigration can be transformed into spiritual wonders; all things are transformed. Do you not often ask: “Where has my practice reached?” You may inspect and verify it for yourself. First, is it that delusive thoughts arise and you no longer follow them? If you can do this, then wherever you go you are free. Further, if you can extinguish the mind of love and aversion, without liking, without disliking, all equal, equal, and equal again, then birth-and-death in stages is eliminated, and you can transform self-masterfully.

To advance still further: “If the subtle streaming is all extinguished, and only the perfect-enlightened great wisdom alone stands luminous, then one can respond to conditions and manifest hundreds of thousands of koṭis of transformation-bodies, delivering beings with affinity — this is called a Buddha.” This is the supreme vehicle. In our practice we must bring it about that the subtle streaming is wholly extinguished, that the seeds of the subtle delusive thoughts are all eliminated, and thoroughly realize the state of “only the perfect-enlightened great wisdom, standing luminous and alone,” thereby perfecting the fruit of Buddhahood. If in this life, having seen the nature, we break through the first barrier, and then train ourselves amid the affairs of the world, diligently eliminating our habitual tendencies, until we are free whether in favorable or adverse circumstances, unhindered in all directions; after breaking the second barrier, then advance further upward, and eliminating the subtle streaming entirely, we emit a great radiance that illumines all ten directions without obstruction. You need not seek supernatural powers; supernatural powers will of themselves come to you. Thus one can respond to conditions and manifest hundreds of thousands of koṭis of transformation-bodies, delivering beings with affinity. Buddhas and bodhisattvas respond to conditions in this way, appearing according to the occasion, to deliver beings.

There are three kinds of mind-born bodies: first, the mind-born body of the bliss of samādhi; second, the mind-born body of the awareness of the nature of dharmas; third, the mind-born body of all kinds complete, without doing. Sitting in meditation, entering deeply into samādhi and deep chan concentration, one can bring forth the mind-born body of the bliss of samādhi. The mind-root is the seventh consciousness; the body that the seventh consciousness, the mind-root, manifests is called the mind-born body. It transforms from few to many, and finally all hundreds of thousands of koṭis of transformation-bodies are complete. “All kinds complete, without doing” — mountains, rivers, the great earth, towers, pavilions, and so forth can all be manifested and transformed. To what extent must the practice reach before the subtle streaming can be cut off? What is called subtle is that we cannot see it now; only after practicing deeply and entering the samādhi of Vajrasattva can we see it: ah, so many subtle delusive seeds, moving so violently! Knowing that these are moving, we dissolve them until they no longer move; but to have still a “not moving” is itself not enough — that “not moving” too must be eliminated. Break through it, and the realm of consciousness is broken. Consciousness is the last of the five aggregates; when the aggregate of consciousness is broken, one is accomplished. So in our practice and cultivation, we must truly cultivate after enlightenment. But if you have not awakened to the true mind and understood the principle, how can you cultivate? Therefore knowing the true mind and understanding the principle is most important, that is, the mind-born body of the awareness of the nature of dharmas is most important.

Today I have again explained the meaning of form and emptiness, and once more reaffirmed the importance of recognizing the true mind (correct view): why it is necessary to recognize the true mind, and I have spoken of where a practitioner finally goes at the moment of death. You should practice in this way at every moment — just “always be aware, and let it diminish again and again.” At every moment we should be aware and observe: oh, a thought has come. Oh, I have again attached to a form. Oh, a delusive thought has arisen. Quickly do not move, do not follow it — this is called “letting it diminish again and again.” Do not speak of sudden enlightenment complete in one go; that is probably not easily accomplished, is it? Do we not often hear people say, “Oh, how is it I still have so many thoughts?” You see, to wipe away thoughts completely in one stroke is no easy matter; therefore one must always be aware and let it diminish again and again. How then do we examine whether we are making progress? One should look back and compare with the past: how formerly one grasped and fretted; now somewhat less than before, and the heart much more calm and even — that is progress. Having progress is good, for knowing there is progress strengthens faith. In the course of our practice, when the body grows warm and radiance appears, these are good phenomena. But we must not chase after them; the moment we do, it is finished — that is attachment, that is deluded thought and feeling.

After enlightenment, in our practice we should let things be natural, like a flowing stream passing by, gush, gush, gush — not lingering, not attaching, not running after states, not following the flow of delusive thoughts; letting our idle thoughts and habitual tendencies diminish again and again until they are utterly wiped away, then we can accomplish the great Way. This is the secret of the practice; therefore, without recognizing the true mind, cultivation is of no avail; recognizing the true mind but not knowing the secret, one cannot accomplish.

blocks.text: 10. The Essential Meaning of the Pure Land

inline.s: When we recite Amitabha Buddha, we are awakening our own mind, not beseeching a Western Amitabha Buddha. When we make the vow to be born in the Western Pure Land, we are of one mind with Amitabha Buddha; it is both self-power and other-power. We should understand that the function of reciting the Buddha-name is to use the Buddha’s sacred name to wash away the defilement and affliction in our hearts, to use the Buddha’s radiance to illumine us and dispel our karmic hindrances. Then, when we make the vow to be born in the West, we can be born in the Western Pure Land. How is one born there? It is to sever the root of love. If one can do this, success is certain. If you still cling to this world, however much you insist “I have other-power, I have other-power, I have other-power,” in the end you cannot be born in the Western Pure Land. Because your root of love is not severed and you are still attached to this Saha world, how can you depart? In fact, other-power is self-power, and self-power is other-power; self and other are not two. To split self and other into two is wrong. In our practice we must cultivate both — that is, to combine self-power with other-power. Relying only on other-power, self-power does not rise, and it is useless. For your delusive thoughts are not eliminated and you cling to this Saha world, so other-power cannot pull you along. If Buddhas and bodhisattvas could pull, they would have pulled everyone long ago. How do the Buddhas and bodhisattvas receive and guide beings to the West? They shine a light upon you. If you do not open your eyes, they shine on you, but you cannot see their light — what use is it? Therefore Master Yongming Yanshou says: our mind is like a basin of water, and Buddhas and bodhisattvas are like the moon in the sky. When Amitabha Buddha shines his light upon us, if our mind-water is clear, then the reflection of the moon can appear — this is the mutual response of feelings and the Way, other-power and self-power combined in one. If our mind-water is a basin of filthy water, then the moon cannot be reflected. It is not that the Buddha does not shine upon you; the Buddha has no such unequal heart, the Buddha illumines universally. It is your mind that is defiled. Therefore the blind do not see light, and filthy water does not reflect the moon. This is entirely our own misunderstanding; it is not that the Buddha does not illumine us. Therefore we must cultivate both — there is other-power and there is self-power.

To be born in the Western Pure Land, one must let go of everything and recite the Buddha-name earnestly and sincerely: “Amitabha Buddha, Amitabha Buddha…,” awakening the self-mind. The other mind is the self-mind, and the self-mind is the other mind, fused into one, so that mind and Buddha interpenetrate. At the moment of death, that Buddha appears before you. This “moment of death” not only refers to the time when one is dying, but also to the time when the root of birth and death is cut off. What is the time when the root of birth and death is cut off? It is when our deluded feelings and deluded thoughts and deluded mind die down and are cut off — this is the moment of death. For the root of our birth and death is deluded feeling, deluded thought, deluded mind. Where did we originally have birth and death? It is all these deluded feelings, deluded thoughts, and deluded mind clinging to forms, creating karma and receiving retribution, thus transmigrating through the six realms in false birth and death. When we single-mindedly recite the Buddha-name, and practice matures, when the season and conditions arrive, “pa” — in an instant the deluded feeling, deluded thought, and deluded mind are cut off, and this root of birth and death comes to an end. “At the moment of death, that Buddha appears before you” — “that Buddha” is that Buddha, is Amitabha Buddha, is our self-nature Buddha; the self-nature Buddha is Amitabha Buddha. “Appears before you” means the original nature manifests — this is called “when the flower opens, one sees the Buddha and realizes non-birth.” When the heart-flower opens and one sees the self-nature Buddha, this is enlightenment. “Realizing non-birth”: when enlightened, one sees the unborn, undying original nature! This is the Pure Land school — the true Pure Land school! We must never push the great matter of birth and death onto Amitabha Buddha alone. Do not say this is other-power, and if you, Amitabha Buddha, do not save me, it is your fault, not mine. That is wrong. If your own deluded feeling, deluded thought, and deluded mind are not cut off, how can that Buddha appear before you, and how can you realize non-birth? This is entirely your own fault; how can you blame Amitabha Buddha?

The Pure Land school is the Chan school, and the Chan school is the Pure Land school. This is what the great sages of old taught: “Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land; the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan.” Chan is the Pure Land, and the Pure Land is Chan. They cannot be split into two, cannot be seen as two matters; they truly are one matter. For instance, Master Yongming Shou was a Chan master — how did he become a great patriarch of the Pure Land school? Master Lianchi too was a Chan master; Master Chewu also was a Chan master — how did they all become great patriarchs of the Pure Land school? Chan and the Pure Land originally breathe through one nostril; it is only people of later times, not understanding the principle, who forcibly divide Chan from the Pure Land. When we make the vow to be born in the West, our mind must be sincere, free of doubt. The vow must be earnest — not a mere mouthing of words, but with real action. If mind has flights and practice is scattered, it cannot be saved. Morning in this, evening in this, wandering in this, distressed in this, never forgetting at any moment — then you are near attaining the Way. So too with the Chan practitioner: he must always be aware, always protect, tending the huatou. So too with us who cultivate the esoteric path: I say again and again that in practicing the Heart-Mind method one cannot rely solely on the two hours of seated meditation; the contemplation after meditation is most important, and the post-meditation is even more important than the meditation itself. In the post-meditation, we train our mind amid circumstances: see whether your mind is empty or not — this is the most important move.

I often hear people say: Oh, today I was angry to death, so-and-so is this, so-and-so is that. Let me ask you — are you a person of Buddhist faith? What is there still to be angry about? Having taken up Buddhism, you should have no anger. All things are empty; no person, no self, no self, no other — what is there to be angry about? If you still have anger, then you have not practiced Buddhism, have not been aware at every moment, have not trained your mind amid circumstances. The more adverse the circumstances and the more infuriating the affairs, the more they train you — see whether you are still angry! If you are still angry, you have not trained, and without training how can you accomplish Buddhahood? Adverse circumstances are in fact good situations, training you to see whether you are awakened. Do not say that adverse circumstances are bad; bad or not depends on whether you are awakened, on whether you can use this situation to train yourself. We who study Buddhism, whether we practice Chan, the Pure Land, or the esoteric path, must at every moment train our mind amid circumstances. Failing this, there is absolutely no achievement.

Our wondrous, luminous true mind belongs neither to being nor to non-being. Say it exists, and yet there is no form to see, no sound to hear; say it does not exist, and in speech and silence, movement and stillness, walking, standing, sitting, and lying — there is not one thing that is not its functioning. The ancients compared it to “the taste of salt in the sea,” “the azure pigment in paint” — though it cannot be seen directly, its substance truly is not absent. Śākyamuni Buddha tells us that it is a great storehouse of true emptiness and wondrous being, of wondrous being and true emptiness. What is called true emptiness is distinct from callow emptiness and annihilating emptiness; because of wondrous being, it is empty and yet not empty. What is called wondrous being is distinct from false being or substantial being; because of true emptiness, it is being and yet not being, not being and yet being. Next, from the standpoint of form and function, it too is neither being nor non-being, neither non-being nor being. Say it does not exist, and yet forms and colors stand arrayed before us, and its wondrous functions are as many as the sands of the Ganges; say it exists, and yet all forms are born of causes and conditions, have no self-substance, and the functions that arise, like moon-in-water or flower-in-air, cannot be grasped. The Heart Sūtra says: “Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.” This says that form and emptiness are not two, neither being nor non-being. For all phenomenal situations are manifestations of the true-emptiness wondrous-substance, and the true-emptiness wondrous-substance likewise cannot exist apart from forms. For example, water raises waves; apart from the waves one cannot obtain water. In our practice, we must neither grasp forms as substantial and cling to them without letting go, nor be able to deviate from forms, discarding being to attach to emptiness. Therefore, whether we sit in meditation to establish concentration, or function in the post-meditation, we must be without grasping or discarding, so as to accord with the principle of the Middle Way and enter the great Way of true emptiness and wondrous being.

But because we still do not understand the principle of form and emptiness very well, I have above further set forth the meaning of form and emptiness, and quoted the recorded sayings of Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi, reaffirming the importance of recognizing the true mind; and I have spoken on the question of where a practitioner finally goes at the moment of death, so that everyone may enter into the gist of the Mahāmudrā, not take a detour in the practice, and go directly to the great Way of true emptiness and wondrous being.
Recognizing the Dharmakāya

blocks.text: 1. Clarifying the Coarse Delusions — Neither Grasping Nor Letting Loose

inline.s: Let us now return to the Mahāmudrā of the Ganges. Earlier we spoke of how the Mahāmudrā is an actual method that directly points us to the true mind. The Mahāmudrā is the one-real dharma-realm, is our true mind, is the substance that is without cultivation, without correction, without distraction. But to enter the experiential ground of the Mahāmudrā, at first one must also pass through a period of arduous cultivation. Without practice, you cannot recognize that the awareness apart from thought is the person’s own nature and accomplish the great Way. Why? The Mahāmudrā says:

What are the coarse delusions that turn with circumstances? When we give rise to mind on encountering objects and ceaselessly cling, seeing this and thinking of this, seeing that and thinking of that, unable to let go, in a jumble, topsy-turvy, idle brooding — this is called coarse delusion. The coarse delusion is like dark clouds covering the sun, covering the luminous original face of our mind; therefore it must be cut off. If the coarse delusion is not cut off, the practice does not get on the road. Why? When you are on the seat, all you have is topsy-turvy delusive thinking, thinking of this and that; off the seat you turn with circumstances, clinging ceaselessly; you absolutely cannot see the original face of the self-mind — this is wandering in birth and death! How can the practice ascend the road, how can it accomplish?

Where the true mind is, and what the true mind looks like, has been pointed out directly many times. If, after being directly pointed out, we still cannot see it, that shows our deluded mind is very heavy; then we should do the practice of cutting off the coarse delusion.

Enlightenment and realization of the Way have an order, and therefore the practice too has an order. How is it divided? At the beginning of the practice one must sever the coarse delusion that turns with circumstances. What is the coarse delusion? Seeing this and thinking of this, seeing that and thinking of that, giving rise to mind upon objects and clinging ceaselessly — that is called the coarse delusion. In our practice we pay no attention to it and let everything go — that is severing the coarse delusion. When the coarse delusion is severed, there still remains the subtle delusion, that is, certain thoughts in our mind. All of you who have practiced know that when we stop the coarse delusive thoughts, then the subtle thoughts, one after another, without our knowing, spring forth; this that springs forth is called the subtle delusion. In the Dharma-character school this is called “manas.” The five all-pervading mental factors that the Dharma-character school teaches, which everyone has, which all beings have — namely attention, contact, feeling, perception, and thought — these are the most fundamental deluded mind. The mind (manas) is the mind-root. It is always moving, like a submerged fish moving in the depths, and it moves very swiftly; on its surface you cannot see it moving, but it flows ceaselessly, without pause — this is the subtle, the extremely subtle delusive thought. This extremely subtle delusive thought is also called the subtle streaming. It is most subtle; in the place of utmost stillness, it is like water flowing at high speed — it looks as though it is not moving at all, but in fact it moves very swiftly, beyond what the eye can see. Only by entering the samādhi of Vajrasattva can one see it. Therefore after the coarse delusion is severed, there still remain the subtle, the fine, and the extremely fine delusions. How much less — when we first begin to practice, we have only achieved a motionless body. How can one see this extremely subtle delusive thought? Only by calming the mind and sitting in meditation, first clarifying the coarse delusions, can we see the subtle and extremely subtle delusive thoughts, and then sever them, realizing the original face of the self-mind. Therefore one must first break the coarse delusion.

How do we practice? The Mahāmudrā instructs us thus: “At first, let the mind abide in evenness, neither grasping nor letting loose.” At the outset of the practice, first let our mind be very even and calm, without attachment, without affliction, without constraint, without bondage — open, vast, and let it go. Confucianism says: “The gentleman is open and calm; the petty person is always anxious.” The petty person has profit and loss, gain and harm in his mind and turns in circles within it, anxious about loss, anxious about gain, and is therefore always anxious. The gentleman does not fret over gain or loss, regards everything indifferently, and is therefore open and calm. We who cultivate the Way are great gentlemen, great heroes, and all the more should be open and calm, letting everything go, even and without attachment. “Open and calm” means even and smooth, straight and straight, without any bending; the mind unbending — the straight mind is the place of practice. “Calm and vast” means sweeping everything entirely empty, without attachment; therefore it is free and at ease. The Mahāmudrā tells us to begin by doing this.

If one cannot do this, and there is some attachment, a turning ceaselessly in the mind, then we must apply a remedy according to the Dharma. How to remedy it? It is “neither grasping nor letting loose.” To grasp is to seize it, to hold it down; to let loose is to indulge it. We should neither seize it nor indulge it, but let it be natural. In our practice, if we seize the thought too tightly, afraid to move at all, then little by little it dies. But neither should we let a thought arise freely; otherwise we fall into indulgence, which is also wrong. When a thought comes, I pay it no attention — this is neither grasping nor letting loose.

In fact, in cultivating all dharmas we are simply training the practice of “paying no attention.” Thoughts do not fail to come; they do not fail to arise. Let them come, let them arise; pay them no attention, and they naturally dissolve. Whether reciting the Buddha-name, holding a mantra, or investigating chan, one must, when a thought comes, neither grasp nor let loose. In truth a thought cannot be seized or suppressed; it will come, just as the ancients said: when the wind stops the waves still surge. For one who recites the Buddha-name, when a thought comes, pay no attention to it, and raise the Buddha-name. For one who investigates chan, when a thought comes, pay no attention to it, and raise the huatou. For one who cultivates the esoteric path, when a thought comes, pay no attention to it, and raise the mantra. Single-mindedly tending the Buddha-name, single-mindedly tending the huatou, single-mindedly tending the mantra, the delusive thoughts are naturally transformed away. As for thoughts, it is not that one forbids them to rise, nor that one lets them run free; rather, one transforms them away — this is living, not dead. Earlier I mentioned the verse of Chan Master Wolun: “Wolun has a skill, he can cut off all thought; when mind meets objects it does not arise, and bodhi grows day by day.” That was suppressing thought so it does not arise — that is dead, and won’t do! It must be neither grasping nor letting loose — paying it no attention.

When a delusive thought comes, that is admittedly not good, but if you crush it to death, all is lost. For the delusive thought is born of the true mind, as waves arise from water. If you crush the delusive thought, just as when you eliminate the waves the water too is gone, then the true mind is no longer alive. We know the true mind is lively and vibrant, able to contain all things, able to produce all dharmas, able to rise to wondrous functions. If you truly crush the delusive thought, the true mind becomes wood, earth, metal, and stone, and can no longer perform wondrous functions.

Wood, earth, metal, and stone form one of the twelve classes of beings. Wood, earth, metal, and stone are without feeling. At first glance they seem unrelated to us, since we humans and all beings of the six realms of transmutation — devas, humans, asuras, hungry ghosts, animals, hells — all have feeling, all have sentient views and love. People are beings of feeling, while wood, earth, metal, and stone are dull and unfeeling, dead and motionless; they seem unrelated to us. But in fact this is not so. Though the twelve classes of beings are of various kinds, they are all one spiritual nature, all manifested from the one-real dharma-realm, of the same root and source as we humans; not a different class. The Buddha-nature is originally real and not false, able to produce all dharmas, and is the spiritual root complete with all wondrous functions. But because we cling to outer forms and are enveloped by ignorance, abiding in objects and cleaving to feelings, creating karma and receiving retribution, we lose the true mind, and the one-real is divided into inner and outer. The inner true is our own body and mind; the outer true is the mountains, rivers, great earth, sun, moon, stars, grasses and forests and other things outside — called things outside the body. In fact, all of these are ourselves! Because of ignorance, we take a small portion of the four elements — earth, water, fire, wind — and bind it within this fleshy husk as “self,” while ignoring the greater part of the four elements, regarding them as things outside the body. Thus there come to be the twelve classes of beings. In fact, with or without feeling, all share the one root. Therefore the scripture says: “Sentient and insentient alike are wholly the seed of wisdom.” The insentient too are ourselves! “Wholly the seed of wisdom” is the Buddha’s wisdom, is the wisdom of all kinds, is, on the one hand, knowing all the functions of all the Buddhas (that is, the Dharma of all the Buddhas, all of which one can completely know), and on the other hand, knowing the causal seeds of all beings.

Now, some people practicing have a little experience: a voice by the ear tells them what is about to happen, that someone is coming, and what he looks like — this is told by a “reporting spirit.” But some people think they have wisdom and supernatural powers, able to foresee who is coming and what will happen, and so preen themselves: Ah! How fine this is, I have foreknowledge. In fact it is not at all good! For this is a “transmitting ghost” at work. If you associate with it for a long time, you will be exploited by it and harmed by it. How does this ghost come to be? This person, while alive in the world, specialized in forming cliques for selfish ends, in abetting evil and stirring up litigation — that is, helping people do evil, helping people file lawsuits, plotting for wealth and harming life, and so on. He created hellish karma and therefore fell into hell to suffer. After the suffering of hell was over and he came out, his habitual tendency to form cliques and do evil throughout his former life still remained, and was moreover very heavy. Therefore he attaches to a person as his own body and tells people of future events. Hence he is called a transmitting ghost; he is no good thing.

In our practice, when we hear a voice by the ear telling us this or that, we must not suppose we have supernatural powers. That is not a good thing; that is a ghost! The scriptures speak of several kinds of ghosts. For example, greed for wealth: one who in life loved money and gold, the more the better, and because of greed did evil and fell into hell. After the suffering was over, his greedy habit remained: whatever he sees he wants, and when he meets grass and trees, he thinks they are very good, thinking they are himself. So he attaches to grass and trees to manifest spirits and do mischief. It is said that in Shanghai’s Fuxing Park there was a bodhi tree said to be very — how shall I say — efficacious, and everyone flocked to it, praying and worshiping, and all sorts of problems were solved; very efficacious. This was the mischief of a “strange ghost” attaching to grass and wood. There are also lecherous men and women; because lust is the fire of desire, when they fell into hell they were burned by the fire of desire. After the suffering ended and they came out, because lust is frivolous, they met the wind and took form, using the wind as their body — this is the “drought ghost,” that is, the female demon. There are also those who use great mountains and great water as their body — what ghost is this? It is called the “mountain-fiend,” that is, the ghost of wrong views. Because in their former lives their views were not correct; they were arrogant and self-important, thought themselves right, and when others held differing opinions, they resorted to secret schemes and cunning plots to harm others. Therefore they fell into hell. After the suffering ended, because of their arrogance and self-importance, they used the essence of sun and moon as their body, seizing the light of sun and moon, and attaching to mountains and water to manifest spirits. So everyone says this place is extremely efficacious. For instance, until recently there was far-flung talk of a “water-sprinkled Avalokiteshvara” in Hangzhou: on Ziyang Mountain there was a stone, ordinarily a smooth bare rock with nothing on it; but when water was poured on it, the image of Avalokiteshvara appeared, hence people called it the water-sprinkled Avalokiteshvara. People told one another that this place was incredibly efficacious, and everyone came from all directions to get water to drink, to cure all diseases. In fact this is a ghost that uses the essence of sun and moon as its body.

Thus it can be seen that all these ghosts, spirits, and even wood, earth, metal, and stone, are ourselves! For this reason it is said, “Sentient and insentient alike are wholly the seed of wisdom.” Our Buddha-nature is originally able to know the causal seeds of all beings, and also able to know the wondrous Dharma of all the Buddhas, the perfect, complete substance of great prajñā.

blocks.text: 2. The Insentient Preach the Dharma

inline.s: Last time someone asked: that sentient beings can perfect the wisdom of the Buddha, that much can be allowed; but how can the insentient do so? How can bricks and tiles, wood and stone perfect the wisdom of the Buddha? How can they become Buddhas? Today I shall speak of this again. Bricks and tiles, wood and stone are all our own intrinsic nature. Who is it that discovers bricks and tiles, wood and stone? Is it not our numinous light shining upon them that discovers them? And what is this numinous light? It is our Buddha-nature! Wherever the numinous light of our Buddha-nature shines, all sentient and insentient things, mountains and rivers, the great earth, sun, moon and stars, men and women, young and old, birds and beasts, are all shadows of Buddha-nature, all manifestations of Buddha-nature. You are a Buddha; then everything your numinous light shines upon is Buddha! Take a country: I am its king, and there is nothing in the land that is not mine. By the same token, you are a Buddha; the light of your Buddha-nature shines brilliantly through the ten directions, filling all space and the whole Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that is not illuminated by the numinous light of Buddha-nature. Therefore all things are Buddha, not one of them is not Buddha. But if our practice is not well done, if we do not know its lively and wondrous functioning and instead crush our thoughts to death, then we turn into earth, wood, metal and stone. Long ago two men practicing on a mountainside sat there without moving, and grass grew from their heads and out of their ears: they had turned into wood and stone. That was the result of the practice of crushing thought to death. So everything is ourselves, everything is our Buddha-nature, and every form we see is Buddha. For this reason stools, chairs, tables, desks and the rest are all Buddha, not one of them is not Buddha. Hence it is said: luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than prajñā; green green bamboo is all the dharmakāya. Flowers and bamboo alike are transformations of Buddha-nature; they are all Buddha! This question looks very hard to understand, but once the principle is clear it is not hard at all. Let me now tell a public case to discuss this question.

Long ago Chan Master Dongshan Liangjia could not understand this question either. He went to Patriarch Guishan to inquire, and asked: “I have heard that National Master Zhong of Nanyang had words on the insentient preaching the Dharma; I have not yet fathomed their subtlety.” Guishan asked: “Do you remember them?” Dongshan answered: “I remember.” Guishan said: “Try reciting them once for me.” So Dongshan recounted the matter.

A monk asked: ‘What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas?’ The National Master answered: ‘Walls and tiles are.’ The monk asked: ‘Are not walls and tiles insentient?’ (Walls and tiles are dull and dull-witted, without awareness, whereas the Buddha is the Awakened One, knowing all and capable of all. Walls and tiles have no awareness, are dull and dull-witted; how could they be the mind of the ancient Buddhas? By your account, walls and tiles would not be insentient either? This was the monk's rejoinder.) The National Master answered: ‘They are.’ (These words hold a profound meaning. Because sentient and insentient alike perfect the wisdom of the Buddha, it is only because of discrimination that the difference between sentient and insentient arises. If one does not discriminate, then all sounds and forms, mountains and rivers, the great earth, and even food and drink, men and women, are all perfected within the mind-nature, and not a single dharma is obtainable; what sentient or insentient could there then be? Because dharmas are held to be obtainable, one goes on to sort them into categories, to love and hate, to accept and reject, and so afflictions spring up in clusters and the wheel turns without cease. As said before, our body is originally a false union of the four great elements, just like the insentient. Only because the true mind is wrapped about by ignorance does it become the deluded mind, bound inside this shell of the four great elements and clung to as the self, and only thus does deluded knowing arise. Otherwise, would our bodies not be just the same as walls and tiles? But this monk did not understand this principle, and so had the following doubts.) The monk asked: ‘Does it also expound the Dharma?’ (Because the Buddha expounds the Dharma to save beings, and the ancient Buddhas did expound the Dharma; since the insentient is the mind of the ancient Buddhas, it must surely expound the Dharma too. This monk was like us ordinary beings, always falling into the sights and sounds of the dust-realms, never seeing the nature that can see and can hear.) The National Master answered: ‘It speaks constantly, it speaks blazingly. Without interruption.’ (The insentient preaching the Dharma is not intermittent, speaking at one time and not at another; it speaks at every hour and every moment, and the sound of its preaching is very loud, like a fiercely blazing great fire, and its preaching never pauses. We for our part always fix on what is seen and heard, not knowing that non-speaking is the true speaking. When a sound is heard, that is hearing; when no sound is heard, that is not hearing. In fact, not hearing a sound is also hearing! You hear a no-sound! Therefore non-speaking is true speaking: because the great sound is rare in its sound, the greatest sound is no sound. To say that there is a sound that can be heard is never true hearing, for you have fixed on what is heard. The nature of hearing does not lie in sound or in no-sound. Sound has arising and ceasing, and so is false; the nature has no place of cutting off, and so is true.) The monk asked: ‘Why do I not hear it?’ The National Master answered: ‘You yourself do not hear it; you cannot hinder another's hearing of it.’ (This is your own not hearing: because you are muddled about Buddha-nature and fix on there being a sound to be heard, you do not know that no-hearing is true hearing. Look further: who is it that hears the unheard? Who is it that hears no sound? You say you do not hear, yet it is shining at your ear-faculty — why do you not know it? You hear a no-sound; is that not hearing? To hear a no-sound, is that not true hearing? When you hear a sound, you follow the sound into discrimination and run off after it. But in this no-sound and no-discrimination, it is precisely when your hearing-nature is present before you; therefore it is true hearing. You yourself do not hear, but you cannot hinder that which can hear! Here the National Master rebuked, pointed out to, and reminded that monk. At this time when no sound is heard and the hearing-nature is truly hearing, you say you do not hear: it is you yourself who are not alert, not clear — yet the hearing-nature is still vividly and distinctly there!) The monk asked: ‘I wonder who can hear it.’ (In all the great earth there is not one person who does not hear. Who does not hear? Who lacks the hearing-nature? Only if one does not cling to sound, who then is not luminous with the hearing-nature? A pity that one's own eye-light does not so much as glance at it!) The National Master answered: ‘The sages hear it.’ (Buddhas, bodhisattvas, arhats, pratyekabuddhas and other sages can hear it; ordinary beings cannot. This answer of the National Master has a flaw, for everyone is originally a Buddha, the dharmakāya is without marks, ordinary and sage are not established — what sage or non-sage could there still be? Pressed hard by this, the National Master used these words to cover his eyes for the moment, yet the monk saw through him and questioned him further.) The monk asked: ‘Does the Master hear it or not?’ (Can you yourself hear it? Because the National Master had said the sages hear it, this question pressed him until he had no words. If he said he heard, that would be praising himself; if he said he did not hear, then the National Master would be no sage and no master.) The National Master answered: ‘I do not hear it.’ (He could only confess and plead guilty.) The monk asked: ‘Since the Master does not hear it, how do you know the insentient expounds the Dharma?’ (A good question, full of power: using the National Master's own spear to jab the National Master, leaving him nowhere to flee.) The National Master answered: ‘It is lucky that I do not hear it. If I heard it, I would be equal to the sages, and you would not hear me expound the Dharma.’ (Luckily I cannot hear it: if I heard it, I would be a sage, and you would not hear me expound the Dharma. This question was hard to evade, but the National Master was an adept in Chan and had his own place to turn. ‘It is lucky that I do not hear it’ — a clever flick, turning danger into safety. Yet whatever is spoken has no true meaning. Originally there is no dharma to speak and originally no one hears the Dharma. If there is still a dharma to speak and someone to hear it, that is precisely clinging to the mark of person and the mark of self. Hence when the National Master says, ‘You would not hear me expound the Dharma,’ he too is slandering himself.) The monk pressed him hard: ‘Then sentient beings have no part in it.’ (If so, sentient beings cannot hear the insentient preach the Dharma, and attainment of the Way is hopeless?) The National Master answered: ‘I speak for sentient beings, not for the sages.’ (The National Master turned the point of his words.) The monk asked: ‘After sentient beings hear it, what then?’ (This monk kept the National Master pinned fast: after sentient beings hear you speak, what happens?) The National Master answered: ‘Then they are not sentient beings.’ (The National Master pushed the boat with the current and turned the monk's sharp point aside. If sentient beings can hear the insentient preach the Dharma and take up this unborn, undying hearing-nature, then they transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, and so he says, ‘then they are not sentient beings.’ The Diamond Sutra says: ‘Sentient beings, sentient beings — the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings, therefore they are called sentient beings.’ Sentient beings? Where are there sentient beings? All sentient beings are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, none of them real. The reason sentient beings are sentient beings is simply that they do not awaken; if they awaken in this very moment, they are not sentient beings. Yet while in the dream they do not awaken, they cannot but be sentient beings, and so it is said they are called sentient beings. Therefore awaken quickly from the dream! Someone once said: you say everything is nothing? Suppose my ear is struck deaf and cannot hear sounds — still, this is there! That my ear is deaf is still a phenomenon, it cannot be emptied. This is clinging to marks with a sticky mind, not awakening! Wake up quickly! Do not dream on. For example, in a dream we are beaten, or our head is cut off, but on waking we have not been beaten nor killed, and our head is quite well. Your ear struck deaf: in fact this deafness is an illusory false appearance, just like being beaten and killed in a dream, unobtainable. So do not cling to the dream; empty it quickly! Awaken quickly! After waking, nothing is left! When Lord Guan had his head cut off by Lü Meng, he cried out in agony: ‘Give me back my head, give me back my head!’ When he learned of it, Great Master Zhiyi went to save him. The Master sat cross-legged and blocked Lord Guan's path. Lord Guan thought: this monk is very bold, daring to block my way — I shall teach him a lesson. Thereupon, whuo — a wild wind arose, flying sand and stones struck at his face, but Great Master Zhiyi did not move a hair. Lord Guan thought: you do not fear wild wind and flying sand; then I shall bring a great mountain to frighten you. Thereupon a great mountain came pressing down, covering sky and earth, and still Great Master Zhiyi did not move a hair. Now Lord Guan was filled with admiration: this monk has true skill! He quickly stepped forward and bowed. Then Great Master Zhiyi expounded the Dharma for Lord Guan: ‘Here you cry, Give me back my head, give me back my head. Someone cut off one of your heads and you demand it back — how many heads did you cut off in your life? Can you give them back? Besides, though your head is gone, you lack nothing at all! Why? Because you have only lost this illusory form-body; your numinous knowing, your true mind, lacks not the least bit.’ We have said that one should take emptiness-and-stillness as the substance and not acknowledge the form-body as the substance; space alone is my true body, the husk is not the true body but only a house. Take the numinous knowing as mind, and do not acknowledge delusive thoughts and delusive notions as mind; delusive notions and delusive thoughts are not real but are things that cling to marks and climb after objects. The nature of numinous knowing is the knowing-nature that knows cold and heat, knows pain and itch; it does not abide in marks, and this thing has no head and no tail, no name and no word. Long ago the Sixth Patriarch, Great Master Huineng, asked the assembly: ‘I have one thing: no head, no tail, no name, no word, no back, no front. Do you all know it?’ Shenhui came forward and said: ‘It is the source of all Buddhas, Shenhui's Buddha-nature.’ The Sixth Patriarch said: ‘I told you it has no name and no word, and you call it the source, Buddha-nature. Later on you will set up a hut over your head and be no more than a doctrinal adherent of intellectual understanding.’ The nature of numinous knowing — its intrinsic nature is without marks and without name; to say it resembles a thing misses it at once. Shenhui added a name to it, and that was already delusive thought. Therefore we should not acknowledge delusive thought as mind, but should acknowledge the nature of numinous knowing. This is the Dharma that Great Master Zhiyi expounded for Lord Guan: that you feel your head ache is the deluded-thought mind's clinging; your husk is already ruined, already gone — what pain is left? Once the mind is empty, you shine with great light, Buddha-nature is luminous, and what pain or no-pain is there! After Lord Guan was thus pointed out to by Zhiyi, he awakened, and thereupon vowed to become a Dharma-protecting spirit. So sentient beings need only wake from the dream and take up the unborn, undying intrinsic nature, and then they transcend the ordinary and enter the sage and are not sentient beings. Therefore, when National Master Zhong of Nanyang said that after sentient beings hear the insentient preach the Dharma they are not sentient beings, that is what he meant.) The monk asked again: ‘The insentient preaching the Dharma — on what scripture is it based?’ (That the insentient can preach the Dharma — I have never heard of it; is there a basis? From what scripture does it come? Surely you did not invent it yourself? This monk stuck fast to the National Master and would not let go.) The National Master answered: ‘Indeed. If one's words do not accord with the scriptures, they are not what a gentleman speaks of. Have you not seen what the Avataṃsaka Sutra says: lands speak, sentient beings speak, all three times speak.’ (The National Master is saying that of course you are quite right: if the insentient preaching the Dharma had no basis, no scriptural authority, it would have no meaning at all and would not be a gentleman's words either. Then he brought out scripture: the Avataṃsaka Sutra says, lands speak, sentient beings speak, all three times speak. That is, every mote of dust, every land is speaking the Dharma; every sentient being contains all; whether the sentient world or the insentient world, there is nowhere that is not speaking the Dharma; past, present and future — the dharmas of the three times are nowhere not speaking the Dharma!)” This was National Master Zhong of Nanyang's instruction to that monk. Chan Master Dongshan did not understand it, and so he recounted this public case to Patriarch Guishan.

After hearing it, Guishan said: “I too have this here; only I seldom meet the right person.” This insentient preaching of the Dharma — I too have it here. Only when one meets a person of comparable capacity can the opportunity meet the opportunity, and so he says, “seldom meet the right person.” Dongshan Liangjia earnestly requested: “I am not clear; I beg the Master to instruct me.” Guishan raised his fly-whisk and said: “Do you understand?” This is the insentient preaching the Dharma — can you comprehend it? The insentient preaching the Dharma has no sound, yet it is not that it does not speak. When flowers bloom and fall, that too is the insentient speaking the Dharma. Flowers are insentient; a flower opens, tender and beautiful, but before long it withers and scatters — what Dharma is this speaking? It speaks the Dharma of impermanence. The river flows on with a hua, hua — the flowing water does not abide, it does not stay; it flows past today like this and tomorrow like this, never resting. This flowing water tells us: the false marks of the ten thousand things change, but the true substance never alters. Su Dongpo understood this principle and said: “What passes is like this, and yet it never goes.” Flowing water is insentient, yet it too speaks the Dharma. So the insentient is speaking the Dharma at every moment; it is not that it does not speak, only that you yourself do not know it. Thus Guishan's raising of the fly-whisk means to ask: who is it that raises the fly-whisk? It is not only by opening the mouth that one speaks the Dharma; this one raising is itself speaking the Dharma.

But Dongshan Liangjia still did not understand and did not comprehend, so he said: “I do not understand.” Dongshan honestly admitted that he did not understand and had not grasped it. In truth, at such a moment one is closest to it. For if you understand and comprehend it, that is emotional view and there is a principle to be had. On the contrary, when you do not understand, that is precisely the time when not one thought arises; turn the light around at once — what is this? In that instant you see the nature. A pity that Dongshan always supposed there was still a principle to be had, mistook the meaning, and let the opportunity slip. Dongshan went on: “I beg the Master to speak.” Guishan said: “A mouth born of parents will never speak it for you.” This flesh mouth born of father and mother can never tell it to you. Why? Because no matter how much you say, it is never said. This is what words cannot reach and thought cannot arrive at: “the path of language is cut off, the place of mental activity is extinguished.” Say it and you miss it; know it and it is not it. Here Guishan was hinting to Dongshan that non-speaking is true speaking and non-hearing is true hearing; this is the insentient preaching the Dharma. Sadly, at this moment Dongshan was still muddled and did not understand. People always cling to the six dust-objects — form, sound, smell, taste, touch, dharmas — which the seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing confront, that is, they cling to what is seen and heard; and then what is unseen and unheard is not it. They do not know that this true nature which can see and can hear in the absence of the seen and heard is never interrupted, leaves no trace of continuity, and is thus, thus unmoving. Hence Buddha-nature is also called “thusness.” From this we can see how thick and heavy people's habit of delusive thought and clinging is!

Moreover, Chan Master Guishan's “A mouth born of parents will never speak it for you” has another layer of meaning: the work must be done by oneself alone, and Buddha-nature must be awakened to by oneself. The ancients said: “What enters by the door is not the family treasure.” What you hear in through the ear enters by the door, for the gates of the six faculties all face outward. The principle heard in through the ear is not your own treasure. Only what you awaken to yourself is true. For me to explain it to you does you not the least good, and in the future you will resent me for it.

Speaking of this, I am reminded of Patriarch Xiangyan, who met this same question. Patriarch Xiangyan and Patriarch Guishan were both disciples of Patriarch Baizhang. Xiangyan was thoroughly familiar with the Buddhist scriptures; if someone asked him about the Dharma, he would often answer ten times over for one question, and he thought himself quite extraordinary, privately reckoning: my wisdom is like the sea! Yet while Baizhang was alive he did not attain in Chan. After Baizhang passed into nirvāṇa, he had no choice but to go to his senior brother Guishan to practice Chan. Guishan said to him: “Junior brother! I hear that with our late master Baizhang you answered ten for one question and a hundred for ten.” He quickly said: “Not at all, not at all.” Guishan said: “That is your cleverness and sharpness, your conceptual understanding and intellectual reckoning — the root of birth and death. Now I have a question to ask you; give me an answer and let me see.” On the surface he asked lightly: “What question is it?” But in his heart he was saying: “What question could there be that I cannot answer? Hmph!” Guishan said: “I will not ask you about anything else, only this: before your parents gave birth to you, what was your original face? Try and say one phrase.” When Xiangyan heard this, his mind went utterly blank. So he returned to his quarters and read through all the scriptures and commentaries he had studied, from beginning to end, seeking one phrase with which to answer — and in the end he got nothing at all. He sighed: “A painted cake cannot fill hunger.” Then he begged Guishan again and again to explain it. Guishan said: “If I explained it to you, you would curse me later on. What I say is mine and in the end has nothing to do with you. You had better go and look into it yourself!” Thereupon Xiangyan burned all the writings he had studied, took leave of Guishan, and went off to look into it on his own. He looked into it morning and evening, looked into it at all times, walking, standing, sitting and lying down. One day he was weeding in the field; as his hoe came down it struck a stone. He picked the stone up and tossed it away at random; it hit a bamboo — “crack!” — and he suddenly awakened and saw his original face. Then he went back, bathed and burned incense, and bowed from afar to his senior brother Guishan, praising him: “Great is the Master's compassion, a kindness surpassing that of my parents. Had you explained it to me then, how would today's matter have come about?”

So the work must be done by oneself. Therefore Patriarch Guishan said to Dongshan: “A mouth born of parents will never speak it for you. If I told you, it would be of no use; you must look into it yourself!” Chan Master Dongshan Liangjia could not awaken, and feeling that the opportunity did not match, he asked again: “Is there anyone else who seeks the Way at the same time as the Master?” Thereupon Guishan directed him to go and study under Chan Master Yunyao.

We have said before that a person has two bad things: one is emotion, the other is thought. If deluded emotion and love were cut off, all would be well. Why? Because emotion is born of love, and love can produce water; the nature of water is to flow downward and it cannot rise to heaven, and so it must be cut off. For example, when we meet something we love to eat, saliva comes; if someone dear to us is about to leave, or to set out on a long journey, tears flow out unbidden; and if a dear one dies, we weep all the more bitterly; as for men and women in love, there is no need even to speak of it. The nature of water is moisture, and whatever water it is, it is moist and it flows downward. So the “emotion” in love-emotion sinks downward; but if we wish to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, we must rise and fly — sinking down leaves no hope. Therefore emotional views must be cut off completely. If love-emotion is not cut off completely, one cannot be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so emotion is a bad thing. Thought is somewhat better, but this thought is not random thinking — random thinking is still emotion. Only because we have emotion do we think randomly. For example, if we love someone, we think up every way to get that person into our hands; if that person has a partner, we think up some way to get rid of the partner and then get the person. You see, plays and novels are all written like that — without it there would be no plays or novels. This is creating karma! Creating karma means undergoing its retribution. Random thinking is in fact love-emotion, and it still will not do.

Then what is this thought? It is secretly thinking about the method of practice: thinking how we may escape this realm of the sentient, and realize our original face; or thinking of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, tying the mind to the West and reciting the Buddha-name with effort — that is better. But speaking from the ultimate point, thought and emotion are equally unworkable. Why? Without emotion how could there be thought, and without thought how could there be emotion? Emotion and thought are not separate. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says that if we truly cultivate contemplative visualization in secret, and the seventh consciousness can leave our bodily form, or transform into whatever is visualized, this is called “pure thought, therefore flying” — but it is not yet truly pure. When truly pure, even thought is gone. If there is still a Buddha to be mindful of, that is not yet truly pure; when truly pure there is nothing at all, and that alone is the Pure Land of Eternal Stillness and Light.
