It is like buying a piece of plain cloth with no pattern on it. The mind that can abide in non-doing is the bare dharmakāya, is the light of wisdom. Some say this bare dharmakāya has no superknowledges or wondrous function and its light is not great. That is because you still have a place of abiding: you cling to “abiding in non-doing” and are not truly non-abiding — this is precisely the deluded emotion that covers your intrinsic nature! When deluded emotion is removed and thought after thought does not cling to marks, the light of wisdom can appear. You must not stir your mind to seek it, because it is originally bright. For example, a precious pearl has light, but if there is a layer of mud on the pearl, it covers it and the light cannot appear. Once the mud is removed, the light comes forth of itself — do you need to seek another light? So do not have anything to seek; only remove delusive thoughts, and the light of wisdom appears of itself.
Conversely, if we practice with doing and have something abiding in the mind, then something blocks it, and it is hard to attain the Way.

Doing” means having something to seek. To take having something to seek as the “Way” is the deluded mind, is having a place of abiding, and it is a hundred and eight thousand miles from the empty, numinous, non-abiding true mind; thus one absolutely cannot awaken to the original face. Not knowing the true mind and not recognizing the original is blind practice and wild refinement; to want to attain the Way thereby is like “boiling sand to make rice” — it has no such possibility. For example, those who cultivate the Pure Land pray to Amitābha in the West: “Come and pull me, come and pull me!” This is practicing with a mind of doing, and it is very hard to be in accord with Amitābha. Because they do not know what the mind is or what the Buddha is, they split mind and Buddha into two sides, with something to pursue, something to long for, something to abide in; their minds are impure, and they absolutely cannot be born in the Western Pure Land. Nowadays many who study Buddhism want to get rich, especially lay practitioners among compatriots in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan and overseas Chinese; when they come to study the Dharma they all ask: is there some way to make my business prosper? They study Buddhism not to end birth and death but to get rich. And students of the Dharma on the mainland mostly want superknowledges. All this is practicing with doing. People who practice thus will certainly not awaken to the original source; they absolutely cannot awaken or realize the original face. Because their use of mind is not upright: they still cling to marks and have something to seek. One must wash the mind empty and pure: wanting nothing, clinging to nothing, practicing non-doing — only then is one in accord with the original truth; as soon as there is something sought, one turns one's back on the Way and diverges, and cannot awaken to the Way. If you say you want only superknowledges, that is even worse. If you want superknowledges, the demon king takes the opportunity to make mischief, transforming into a Buddha to confuse you; you take it for the true Buddha, your mind blossoms in chaos, and the demon takes the opportunity to enter your mind and make you a demon, and even the Buddha cannot save you. Therefore those who practice taking “doing” as the “Way” “certainly cannot awaken to the original source”: they absolutely will not awaken, absolutely will not recognize the root, absolutely will not know what the root, Buddha-nature, is, and absolutely cannot attain the Way! Abiding in something, how could one attain the Way? Becoming a demon, on the other hand, is quite likely!

Therefore in practicing the Dharma we must recognize the root, must have nothing to seek, must know that we are originally Buddha and need only dissolve our deluded emotions, not seek anything. As soon as there is something sought, one will become a demon. Demons have superknowledges: they know when your mind moves, and then they come. So when the mind-demon moves, the outer demon arrives. What is the mind-demon? Abiding in something is the mind-demon. Once the mind clings to marks, the outer demon takes the opportunity to enter; if the mind does not cling to marks and does not move, the outer demon finds no door to enter by. When a demon comes, pay it no heed: “Whatever has marks is false”; a Buddha coming, cut down the Buddha; a demon coming, cut down the demon — all is unobtainable, so how could it get in? Do not fear demons; demons are manifested by the mind. If your mind is not demonic, then however great the outer demon's powers, it cannot enter.

In learning the Buddhadharma and practicing the Dharma, the cause-ground must be right; first make this question clear: our vividly ever-knowing, numinous, luminous true mind is the Buddha, and apart from this there is no Buddha. A thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas are one body and one and the same as this vividly ever-knowing true mind; though the Buddha's form appears before us, we pay it no heed. Knowing that all marks are false and all is unobtainable, and that this wondrous luminous true mind alone is the true Buddha, you will not fall into demonic states and can attain the great Way. Otherwise, with an impure mind, abiding in something and seeking something, you will surely summon demons, enter demons and become a demon, having not the slightest connection with the Way. Hence the Mahāmudrā stresses that cultivators who take “doing” as the “Way” certainly cannot awaken to see the intrinsic nature and cannot attain the great Way.

This light of wisdom that is free of knowing is not obtained from outside; it is a capacity inherent in the self-mind. But even a beginner who very much wants the mind to abide naturally in the pure original source cannot do it, because he does not understand the original face and still falls into practicing with doing; and the place he abides in does not go beyond bliss, clarity, non-thought (that is, emptiness) and other such states of the work. Do these states exist? They do. Bliss, for instance: when your practice reaches the blissful state of the third dhyāna, no happiness in the world can compare with it. But do not greedily abide on it; though it exists, it must be as if it did not — do not be greedy for it. If you greedily abide in bliss, clarity and non-thought, you are ruined; and if you greedily abide in non-thought, you are ruined even more, because this non-thought is dead. Sitting there without moving, without a single thought — you turn into earth, wood, metal and stone and press your own mind to death. Greed for bliss is the demon of joy arriving; greed for clarity is the demon of brightness arriving; greed for non-thought is the demon of emptiness arriving. But our intrinsic light is the great light: though it brightly illumines the ten directions without obstruction, it does not itself say that it is light and does not abide in the mark of light. If you abide in the mark of light, you are covered by the mark of light and the boundless spiritual function of your wondrous substance is covered over; therefore you must not abide in light. Hence when we sit in meditation we do not permit seeing light or seeing Buddhas: to have light visible still will not do. It is not that you are not even allowed to look, but that you are not allowed to abide greedily on it: seeing it must be as if not seeing it. Why? Because the light that first arises is faint; a slight stir of your mind and the light is gone. When the light comes, if you pay it no heed and do not move, the light grows greater and greater; if you pay heed and your mind stirs, the light is covered over. So if you practice with ulterior designs, on the good side you merely abide in bliss, clarity and non-thought; on the bad side, you will be possessed by demons, because you have something to seek and the demon takes the opportunity to enter. Therefore do not practice with ulterior designs!

In our practice we should cast off the states of power just described — bliss, clarity, non-thought and the rest. Why? Because these are only the shadow-marks of a preliminary state of samādhi; the naked original substance of the self-nature has not yet appeared, and one has only a little shadow-state more than a beginner. The work is not awakening! Take Patriarch Gaofeng: his master asked him, “In the busy daytime, can you be master?” A cultivator must be master in all the states of daily activity, not dragged along by circumstances, not following circumstances — only then does he have a little samādhi-power and is somewhat in accord with the original substance. So his master asked whether in daily activity he could see through all circumstances, not delighted by delight, not pleased by pleasure, not grieved by grief, not pained by pain, not emptied by emptiness and purity, not disturbed by circumstances — could he be master? Patriarch Gaofeng said: “I can be master.” The master asked again: “In sleep and dreams, can you be master?” To be asleep and dreaming, to know it is a dream and not be moved, to fear nothing that comes — a tiger coming, no fear, it is false; an enemy coming, no fear, it is false; great wealth coming, wanting none of it, all is false — this is being master in sleep and dreams. To be master in sleep and dreams is ten times the strength of the daytime. For when awake we are only deluded, but asleep we are comatose. If in comatose sleep you can still clearly and freshly know this is an illusion, a dream, and your mind does not move, that is great strength. For us to be master at death requires being master in dreams, because at death there is great coma and in sleep there is small coma; if you cannot be master in small coma, how much less in great coma. Patriarch Gaofeng's work was good and his ability great; he answered: “I can be master.”

Patriarch Gaofeng answered twice, “I can be master.” Truly good work — a model and example for us latecomers in doing the work. We study Buddhism and cultivate the Way precisely in order to be master at the brink of birth and death, not to be dragged down by karmic obstacles and sink into the sea of suffering. To do this, we must all first practice being master amid daily affairs: not turned by favorable or adverse conditions, not moved by the delusive emotions of joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure, not delighted by prosperity nor worried by adversity, all things like flowers in the sky and illusions, unobtainable, unstuck and non-abiding — and only then can we be master in sleep and dreams. If we cannot even do this, what is the use of speaking of ending birth and death? For the root of birth and death is precisely that delusive thoughts never cease and the mind climbs after circumstances!

In Ningbo there was a lay woman who, while sitting in meditation and working hard, was suddenly told that her son had fallen into the water; she sat there without moving at all. Someone scolded her: “How can you be so heartless? Your own flesh and blood has fallen into the water, and you will not even go to save him?” She remained unmoved and went on with her practice. Her samādhi-power was good, but not saving one who is dying is not good — it is rather cruel. What should she have done? She should still have saved him, but with a mind that did not move, saving as if not having saved — not sitting there without the least movement. Yet on the other hand, her practice was not bad; we would long ago have been thrown into confusion. There was a man whose house caught fire; the mistress of the house remembered that her child was still inside, panicked, rushed into the house, grabbed at the bed and came out: oh! Wrong — she had carried out a pillow. She fainted on the spot, and the child was burned to death. You see, that is the result of a mind thrown into confusion!

So whether you move or not amid circumstances is a great test, and this too is the work. Patriarch Gaofeng, amid daily affairs, whatever came up, could be master and not move — his work was very good; and he could be master in sleep and dreams too, which is even more remarkable. His master, seeing that his work was indeed good, wanted to examine his awakening, and so asked him further: “When there are no dreams and no thoughts, where is the master of the house?” Gaofeng was startled: no dreams and no thoughts — where is the master of the house? He thought it over and over and in the end could not answer, and his master told him to go and investigate. (Master Yuanyin said: “You all, answer on behalf of Patriarch Gaofeng — with no dreams and no thoughts, where is the master of the house?” The assembly was silent. The Master said: “Shall I try to answer on your behalf?” And immediately he cried out sternly: “Precisely there!”) Patriarch Gaofeng investigated further and later awakened. After his awakening Patriarch Gaofeng shut himself in a death-closure at Lion Cliff on Mount Tianmu. So the work is the work and awakening is awakening! If in our practice we can cast off the states of power such as bliss, clarity and non-thought, and cultivate until subject and object both perish, faculties and dusts drop away, and the former and latter limits are cut off, then with a “crack” it suddenly bursts open: within, body and mind; without, the world, and even space, are shattered at once and reduced to nothing, and one suddenly abides unmoving. At this time, though there is nothing at all and one abides unmoving, one is not like wood or stone but is numinously aware and distinct, and our “naked, thoroughly penetrating original substance of the self-nature” appears.

Therefore, whatever school we practice, we must cultivate until subject and object both perish and mind and dharma both vanish; then with a “crack —” “the great earth sinks level and space is shattered,” and only when there is nothing at all and yet vivid distinctness can the original substance of the self-nature appear! Take the method of Buddha-recitation: with one Buddha-name, “Amitābha...,” one gathers in all six faculties, seizing eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind altogether, and recites until one is truly unified; when there is no mind to be mind and no thought to be thought, the recitation is gone too and the Buddha is gone too — “crack —” and in that instant one personally sees the true Buddha and is born in the Buddha-land. So too with those of us who practice the Heart Center method: with one Buddha-mind mantra, “Om, bhara bhara...,” one gathers in the six faculties, mind reciting and ear hearing, the mind not wandering outward, and when the time and conditions arrive, “crack —” the reciting and the recited fall away at once, and the thoroughly penetrating, non-abiding original self-nature clearly and distinctly appears. The work must be done; otherwise there is no way to break open the original and see one's own nature. To talk emptily of theory is to paint a cake to satisfy hunger — it has no such possibility. We must be master amid daily affairs; if the moment something comes up you cannot do it and cannot be master, then you are quicksilver, which flies off at a touch of fire, and you cannot withstand birth and death. Do the work, break open the original, wake from the dream, and know that all is a dream-scene — what mind would you stir? All gratitude and resentment, all right and wrong, are extinguished — hence it is called “vanishing together with the awakening.” All things are a dream-scene; if you do not awaken, you cling to them as really existing; once you awaken, like hot water melting ice, all karmic obstacles are emptied. This is what is commonly called “when it is understood, karmic obstacles are originally empty”! So the work must be done; if it is not done, how could the time and conditions for awakening come? How could the original be broken open?

Someone asked me how long the work takes. That depends on whether your work is close and continuous or not; if it is fitful, it will not do. If our work is close and continuous — sitting today, sitting tomorrow, going on without pause, and after sitting, never forgetting to watch over, never running after circumstances — then within three to five years you will see the intrinsic nature thoroughly. Why do we say that in practicing the Heart Center method one must do a thousand sittings? It means that three years of earnest practice will do it. If you do not practice closely and continuously, practicing and stopping, stopping and practicing, three days fishing and two days drying nets, then not to speak of three or five years — even thirty or fifty years will not do.

Someone else asked what happens after a thousand sittings. On this question I have spoken many times; let me repeat it once more. A thousand sittings means that this Heart Center method relies on the empowering blessing of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and its practice is supremely effective: if one practices earnestly and solidly for three years, one can certainly break open the original and personally see the intrinsic nature. But if one practices sluggishly, fitfully, with one day of effort and ten of idleness, then not to speak of a thousand sittings — even three or five thousand sittings will not let you see the nature.

Someone else asked: after a thousand sittings, does one stop practicing? We said last time: even if you are of sharp capacity and awaken suddenly, the habits of many lives and kalpas cannot be exhausted at once; you must still watch over at every moment, temper yourself amid affairs and circumstances, reduce and reduce again, and only when the habits are exhausted is it done. After awakening, the work is the no-work of non-doing as true practice; it is not that one does not practice, but that one should not cling to sitting and fall into a blissful state, making it an obstruction of dharma-clinging. Conversely, if your samādhi-power is insufficient and you still waver when circumstances appear, then you must add more sitting to strengthen your samādhi-power, and only thus can you pass the heavy barrier. If your samādhi-power is adequate, you need only be alert at every moment, without spending the least effort — very relaxed and easy — and not go on cultivating this dharma and accumulating that merit, busily tangled in dharma-marks. Whether you are awakened or not, working on dharma-marks is a waste of energy and self-made trouble; it has no such possibility. So in doing the work, the more effortless the better, the more relaxed the better; the more effort it costs, the worse.

blocks.text: 5. Cutting Off Delusive Thought at Once, and the Self-nature Appears

inline.s: When a delusive thought stirs, cry out sharply, “Pei!” — this is the Mahāmudrā's key to cutting off delusive thought. Those who recite the Buddha-name do not need this method; they need only raise the Buddha-thought and recite “Amitābha” once. Other practitioners, the moment a delusive thought stirs, cry out sharply, “Pei!”, and at once become alert, and the stream of delusive thinking is cut off with a “crack.” For example, if we think of getting rich, “Pei!” — get rich how? Daydreaming! And so the delusive thought is cut off. If the delusive thought is strong, that is, if greed is heavy, and “pei” will not cut it off, then one must hold a mantra and use the Buddha's power to dissolve it.

Put to rest the coarse deluded mental factors (our mind-king and mental factors: there are eight mind-kings and fifty-one mental factors. The worst of the mental factors are the five omnipresent ones, namely attention, contact, feeling, conception and volition. “Attention” is the mind-faculty, whose surging power is so great that it has never stopped; do not suppose it stops when you sleep — it is proliferating dreams and still has not stopped, and only at the final vajra-sattva samādhi can it be settled), that is, put to rest the coarse delusion of giving rise to mind toward objects, and only then can one abide in the state of samādhi without moving. If in practice one can face objects without giving rise to mind, one has considerable power. We people at every moment give rise to deluded mind toward objects and moreover climb on without cease, from this thinking of that and from that thinking of this, without pause. If the climbing mind can stop, one can peacefully enter samādhi, leave all states of delusive thought and climbing, and our self-nature is clearly and thoroughly, nakedly and without remainder, manifested (that is, luminously appearing before us), and thereby one opens the great prajñā-wisdom that is free of birth and death, existence and non-existence, and is empty, numinous, non-abiding and thus unmoving. That is, the first step of our practice is to put to rest the coarse delusion of giving rise to mind toward objects; going further, to leave the states of climbing and not let the mind stir randomly — then our original self-nature clearly, purely and nakedly appears, and the unmoving great light of wisdom that is free of deluded mind appears as well.

So the Buddhadharma is wonderful: it teaches us to know the truth and not to run after false marks. If we are deluded by false marks, we turn in the six realms; if we leave false marks and recognize the true mind, we transcend and can realize great superknowledges and attain great benefit.

Therefore if we truly want to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is not something to be had by casually reciting a couple of Buddha-names and a couple of lines of scripture; we must use Amitābha Buddha's sword of wisdom to cut off our clinging love for this false mark, the Sahā world, and only then can we be born in the West. Hence “pure thought, therefore flying” — that is, what we ordinarily call the first samādhi: our practice can reach the point where, even if the true Buddha really came, we would only recite, “Amitābha, Amitābha...,” with nothing else at all; this thought alone is Buddha, my whole thought is Buddha, the Buddha is my whole thought, all Buddha is thought, all thought is Buddha — then you will certainly be born in the West. But if you are not like this? Reciting “Amitābha” a few times with thoughts and without, while your mind is on this matter and that — that will not do. Someone asked why, in practicing the Buddha-recitation method, one should recite scriptures. Reciting scriptures is to make you know the truth. The scriptures say that for the highest grade of the highest birth one must read and recite the great vehicle scriptures. Why? Because reading and reciting the great vehicle scriptures makes one understand the principle: to understand that all is originally Buddha, that sentient beings are Buddha, and that it is only because we are deluded and cling to marks that we forget the self-nature. We must not be deluded and cling to marks, must not greedily cling to merit and virtue: merit and virtue are our own mind, and the self-mind is the mother of great merit; when the great work is accomplished, that is Buddhahood. Whether we turn in the six realms or are born in the Western Pure Land is brought about by the mind. The root of all virtue is the mind; all virtue comes forth from the mind — “nothing does not flow forth from this Dharma-realm, nothing does not return to this Dharma-realm.” So the mind is the root, the root of all dharmas! Ordinarily I tell everyone to read and recite the great vehicle scriptures precisely so that we understand this principle. The Pure Land teaching spoken of here is the great vehicle Pure Land teaching, breathing through the same nostril as the principles of Chan. The Pure Land school is a great vehicle Buddhadharma that gathers in all three capacities; it saves not only those of middling and lesser capacity but gathers all three capacities, for all are one and the same mind: the Pure Land is the mind and the mind is the Pure Land. The Amitābha Sutra says, “West of here, past a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss.” A hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands are the ten pāramitās and ten thousand practices — that is, using giving, precepts, patience, energy, dhyāna, wisdom, method, vow, power and knowledge to cultivate the mind empty and open great wisdom. When the mind is empty, one crosses the hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands and arrives in the West. So the West is not far away; it is right before you. To put it simply: if your mind abides nowhere and all is empty, your mind is Buddha and Buddha is your mind; here is the West and the West is here, and in that instant you are born in the West. Do not wait until after death; to be born in the West while alive is truly to be born in the West. If you cannot be born in the West while alive, then to be born in the West only after death will, I fear, be difficult.

The meaning is that we should clearly and distinctly know that the relative views of birth and death, existence and non-existence and so on are false, and should leave these extreme views and transcend the relative state of linguistic and mental discrimination; then we naturally abide in the original self-nature of the illumining great wisdom, in which there are no words to speak and no thoughts to stir.

Thoroughly penetrating” means clearly understanding and completely penetrating. To leave the extremes of birth and death, existence and non-existence is to leave birth and death, existence and non-existence and all such extreme views. Views of birth and death, existence and non-existence and the rest are all relative deluded knowing and deluded seeing; like a mirage they are false and unreal and do not accord with the meaning of the middle way, and so they are extreme views. Yet we are buried at every moment and in every place, living amid relative deluded states, distinguishing good and bad, right and wrong, long and short, never leaving the extremes of birth and death, existence and non-existence. For example, to think that a person exists while alive and that after death there is nothing at all — this is an extreme view. If one can know that whatever exists relatively is a false shadow and does not pursue it, then at the place where the deluded mind rests one can thoroughly penetrate the originally existent absolute true mind. The true mind is Buddha-nature: not existent, not non-existent, not long, not short, not born, not extinguished, not good, not bad, not beautiful, not ugly... all is not; language cannot describe it and thought cannot reason it out, and there is originally no discrimination at all. This is “the state beyond the reach of language and mental discrimination.”

The state of linguistic and mental discrimination is the state in which language and consciousness discriminate; it means that when we speak, the mind-faculty in the brain stirs without cease, and so right and wrong, good and bad, long and short are discriminated without end, and relative views blaze up. For example, some people recite the Buddha-name while talking: “Amitābha — how bad my daughter-in-law is; Amitābha — how good my daughter is.” This is the state of linguistic and mental discrimination — how can that do? If this could bring about birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, then those born there would be very many. We must cut off deluded emotion and extreme views, abide in nothing, and single-mindedly recite “Amitābha, Amitābha...,” with the whole thought being Buddha, the Buddha being my mind and my mind being the Buddha, mind and Buddha meeting on the Way and becoming one piece; only then can we be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore we must transcend the state of linguistic and mental discrimination, understand that these states are false and unobtainable, not follow them, not be turned by them, and let go of everything, and let go again. Thus the Brahmin ascetic held mandārava flowers in both hands as an offering to the Buddha, and the Buddha instructed him: “Let it down.” The ascetic put down the flowers in one hand. The Buddha said again: “Let it down.” The ascetic put down the flowers in the other hand. The Buddha said again: “Let it down.” The ascetic was bewildered and quickly asked the Buddha: “My hands are empty of flowers now — what is there left to let down?” The Buddha said: “I tell you to let down the outer six dusts, the middle six consciousnesses and the inner six faculties — let it all down.” That is, when inner, middle and outer are all let go, all is unobtainable, and the ascetic awakened upon hearing it. So we must transcend the state of linguistic and mental discrimination, let go of everything and let go again, let it all go, and naturally abide in the state of the wisdom-nature beyond words and thought.

“Beyond words and thought” is transcending language and thinking. The state of the wisdom-nature beyond words and thought is the great wisdom inherent in the self-nature, which transcends language and thinking. If you transcend the state of linguistic and mental discrimination, you will naturally abide in this great wisdom and enjoy inexhaustible benefit.

To be natural and spontaneous at every moment, without the least trace of deliberate practice, is very hard: we all practice with effort! From the first ground to the seventh ground the bodhisattva still practices with effort; only from the eighth ground to the tenth is it practice without effort. It is not easy for us ordinary beings to reach practice without effort all at once, so we must go up step by step from practice with effort to practice without effort.

What is practice with effort? It is being aware and illumining at every moment, watching over oneself and caring for oneself. The moment a thought stirs, immediately warn yourself: “Hey, don't move — I see you.” If you are not aware, you cannot illumine it, and you will run off a hundred and eight thousand miles after the thought without even knowing it! So being always aware and illumining is practice with effort. When the illumining has become familiar, you no longer need awareness: it illumines of itself and does not move of itself — still and yet constantly illumining, illumining and yet constantly still — and that is practice without effort. In the end even stillness is unobtainable and illumining is unobtainable, and only that is truly arriving home. Only by doing the work thus at every moment can we go from practice with effort to practice without effort; we cannot leap to heaven in a single step.

How is this work done? Be awake at every moment and abide in the illumining great wisdom in which there are no words to speak and no thoughts to stir — that is, what the school calls “the path of language is cut off, the place of mental activity is extinguished.” When our mind does not move, it illumines of itself and responds with extraordinary speed; if the mind moves, abides in something, or is afflicted, the response is very slow. Because you have been dragged off by circumstances, the mind's light is covered by circumstances and cannot illumine, and so the response is slow. If you can abide at every moment in the state of the wisdom-nature beyond words and thought, where speaking is unobtainable, thinking is unobtainable, and all is unobtainable, then you are naturally vivid and distinct, and all superknowledges and wondrous functions come. If you do not do this, do you want superknowledges? They are unobtainable; you cannot get them. Ordinary beings are at every moment calculating and discriminating, anxious about gain and loss, and so they have no peace or freedom. We cultivate the Way precisely in order to leave delusive thought, remove clinging, restore the intrinsic light, and bring forth the great functioning of the great opportunity. Our Buddha-nature is like the sun, with immeasurable light, but covered by delusive discrimination it cannot send forth great light or produce great spiritual function. When the dark clouds disperse, the sun sends forth great light; when delusive clinging is left, all superknowledges and wondrous functions come without seeking. The Mahāvairocana Sutra says: “The bodhisattva abiding in this and cultivating will before long, with diligence, obtain the samādhi that removes all obscuring veils. Having obtained it, he dwells on an equal footing with all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and will develop the five superknowledges and obtain immeasurable dhāraṇīs of language and sound.”

The bodhisattva abiding in this” — abiding where? “Abiding in the state of the wisdom-nature beyond words and thought.” In this state, cultivating diligently to remove old habits, before long the five superknowledges all arise and eloquence is unobstructed. The five superknowledges are the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives and the superknowledge of travel. The Buddha has six: beyond the five there is the superknowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, which is the complete purification of all delusive thoughts, clingings, discriminations and afflictions and other places of outflow. That is “the state of the wisdom-nature beyond words and thought”! In our practice we first obtain the superknowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and naturally abide in the state of the wisdom-nature beyond words and thought; this is also called “the wisdom of the essential nature of the dharmakāya,” also called “yoga,” also called “the view as the school.” The dharmakāya is without marks, and without marks yet without non-marks; it does not increase in the Buddha nor decrease in sentient beings. The wisdom of the essential nature of the dharmakāya is the great wisdom that transcends all relativity and all worldly wisdom. “Yoga” means correspondence. Corresponding to what? Corresponding to the dharmakāya Buddha. That is “the view as the school”!

All things that arise are the manifestation of the functioning of the self-nature. Therefore to recognize the wisdom of the liberated essence is of the utmost importance. Master Guifeng, whose mind was set on the Way, said: “What arises in the mind is the functioning of the self-nature; what is not arisen is also the functioning of the self-nature.” What does this mean? Whether rising or ceasing, all is the functioning of the self-nature.

Now, although we have learned the Buddhadharma, so long as the seventh consciousness has not been transformed we cannot avoid inequality. For example, those who practice the Pure Land school say the Pure Land school is best of all and other dharmas will not do; those who study Chan say Chan is highest and the rest are not good; those who study tantra say tantra is most perfect and the rest are not so good. Alas! To affirm oneself and deny others is all because one has not truly realized the wisdom of equality and one's mind is not equal. In fact all Dharma-gates are the same: they are tools and means, not the goal; our goal is Buddhahood. If you succeed by this means and I succeed by that means, and both of us succeed, are we not the same? Hence it is said: “Expedient means are many, but the return to the source is not two.” All dharmas are the same; hence “this Dharma is equal, without high or low.” The reason there is inequality is the mischief of the seventh consciousness. So when our seventh consciousness is transformed, there is equality. All right and wrong, self and other, are equal; all oppositions are equal. Equal, equal, all things equal — and one awakens thoroughly to the great Way. When the sixth consciousness is transformed into the wisdom of wondrous observation, it changes from using delusive discrimination to make right and wrong, gain and loss, into the wisdom that observes all things wondrously and handles them correctly. For example, how best to do this matter, how to arrange that person reasonably, how to transform a bad person and turn him from bad to good, from ordinary to sage, and so on. The wisdom of wondrous observation is clear and unmoved, direct perception and inference, inference and direct perception. Direct perception is to manifest the form according to its measure, without adding discrimination; inference is to compare whether it is good or bad, long or short, right or wrong. Having realized this wisdom, though one clearly discerns right and wrong, gain and loss, one has no love or hate, no grasping or rejecting; though one handles all things equally, one is not ignorant of right and wrong, long and short — hence it is the functioning of great wisdom. When the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the wisdom of accomplished action, the eye seeing form, the ear hearing sound, the nose smelling fragrance, the tongue tasting flavor, the body experiencing objects — these are the functions of the wisdom of accomplished action.

Now, although we have learned the Buddhadharma, so long as the seventh consciousness has not been transformed we cannot avoid inequality. For example, those who practice the Pure Land school say the Pure Land school is best of all and other dharmas will not do; those who study Chan say Chan is highest and the rest are not good; those who study tantra say tantra is most perfect and the rest are not so good. Alas! To affirm oneself and deny others is all because one has not truly realized the wisdom of equality and one's mind is not equal. In fact all Dharma-gates are the same: they are tools and means, not the goal; our goal is Buddhahood. If you succeed by this means and I succeed by that means, and both of us succeed, are we not the same? Hence it is said: “Expedient means are many, but the return to the source is not two.” All dharmas are the same; hence “this Dharma is equal, without high or low.” The reason there is inequality is the mischief of the seventh consciousness. So when our seventh consciousness is transformed, there is equality. All right and wrong, self and other, are equal; all oppositions are equal. Equal, equal, all things equal — and one awakens thoroughly to the great Way. When the sixth consciousness is transformed into the wisdom of wondrous observation, it changes from using delusive discrimination to make right and wrong, gain and loss, into the wisdom that observes all things wondrously and handles them correctly. For example, how best to do this matter, how to arrange that person reasonably, how to transform a bad person and turn him from bad to good, from ordinary to sage, and so on. The wisdom of wondrous observation is clear and unmoved, direct perception and inference, inference and direct perception. Direct perception is to manifest the form according to its measure, without adding discrimination; inference is to compare whether it is good or bad, long or short, right or wrong. Having realized this wisdom, though one clearly discerns right and wrong, gain and loss, one has no love or hate, no grasping or rejecting; though one handles all things equally, one is not ignorant of right and wrong, long and short — hence it is the functioning of great wisdom. When the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the wisdom of accomplished action, the eye seeing form, the ear hearing sound, the nose smelling fragrance, the tongue tasting flavor, the body experiencing objects — these are the functions of the wisdom of accomplished action.

blocks.text: 6. Not Knowing the Self-nature, Practice Is of No Benefit

inline.s: If you do not know your own wondrous mind, do not have right knowing and seeing, and do not know to cultivate from Buddha-nature but cling to marks and seek outward, then you have not left the functioning of the deluded mind; that is a wrong view of doing, and it is as far from the “Way of the self-nature’s great perfection” as the wind from the ox, and you will not obtain the “uncreated wheel of light.” The self-nature’s great perfection means that Buddha-nature is inherently complete and originally perfect, not obtained by grasping nor produced by cultivation. The uncreated wheel of light means that Buddha-nature is originally infinite in light, illumining the lands of the ten directions, complete in all wondrous functions, able to produce ten thousand transformations. The wheel of light is not produced by cultivation but is inherent in the self-mind. Hence it is said: “The Way is not a matter of cultivation but of awakening.” To awaken to the Way is to wake up, to understand, to enter the true mind, and to restore the original. That is, in practice, at the place where a thought is cut off, with a “ho” — you realize the original truth. After awakening, is cultivation needed? It is! Because the two clingings to self and dharma since beginningless time are still there, and one cannot yet develop great spiritual function; these two clingings must be exhausted before one can thoroughly realize the source. Then how shall one cultivate? That depends on the weight of each person’s habits, and different methods are used; but the best is the no-cultivation of non-doing, using the method of watching over. The Mahāmudrā method is: when a delusive thought arises, cry “Pei!”, cut it off, and thereby protect the true mind. But we may also use other methods, such as reciting the Buddha-name or holding mantras. When a delusive thought arises, recite Amitābha, or hold a mantra, do not follow the delusive thought, transform it, and you can equally protect the true mind. Or again, when a delusive thought arises, become alert and let all dissolve into emptiness, and the delusive thought subsides. So to obtain the “uncreated wheel of light,” one must first clearly realize this wondrous luminous true mind. If one does not understand what the true mind is, one cannot obtain it.

The view as the school is right knowing and right seeing: under the influence of right knowing and seeing, one recognizes the intrinsic nature. If you do not yet recognize the intrinsic nature, then “though you cultivate, you have no ground of preservation”; even if you practice diligently, you will not obtain the “uncreated wheel of light,” because you have no ground of preservation — you do not know what to preserve! That is, if you are still uncertain about the right knowing and seeing spoken of above, do not recognize the intrinsic nature, cannot stand firm on your feet, and are still in doubt, then what are you preserving? For example, if we have a small child, we must carefully look after him, protect him, not let him go hungry or cold, not let him fall, caring for him in every detail and bringing him up. If you have no child at all, then whom are you protecting?

Preservation is two stages of work: first preserving, then letting be. It is like a small child: first you must protect him, and when the child has grown up you let him be, let him stand on his own, do his own work, manage his own affairs, and you need not look after him. Preservation looks like only two words, but in practice it is a long road to walk! To do the work of preservation, one must first see the intrinsic nature; if you do not see the intrinsic nature, what are you preserving? And what is the intrinsic nature? Much has been said above: it is the nature that can now see and now hear; recognize it, do not doubt it, and care for it well. How to care for it? “It is not that one does not see, not that one does not hear,” but that “one is vividly aware of it, without clinging to seeing and hearing.” In daily life it is not that one does not look at things or listen to sounds, but that one does not discriminate good and bad, beautiful and ugly, and does not give rise to love and hate, acceptance and rejection. Though you look and though you listen, there is nothing in the mind — “vast and non-abiding”; that is “preserving.” When preservation has ripened, you no longer preserve: let it go, you may go anywhere, do anything at all, with not the slightest abiding — and so you reach the state of non-obstruction in all things and free and easy functioning. Concerning “non-obstruction in all things,” Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen has a verse: “Non-obstruction in all things, / Sovereign and free; / A pig’s head in the hand, / Pure precepts on the lips, / Thrown out of the brothel, / The wine debt unpaid, / At the crossroads, / Opening the cloth bag.” Holding a pig’s head in your hand, gnawing pig’s head meat, and reciting the precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct... I am a vegetarian — I have just come out of the brothel, ha ha ha! “Thrown out” means being driven out. A brothel is a house of prostitutes. When the money is spent in the brothel, the madam drives you out. Drunk and in debt, the tavern comes to dun you for the wine money, and you are too poor to pay. Just so slovenly, just so down and out, and thereby free and easy, without care or worry. Someone may ask: pig’s head in hand, pure precepts on the lips... not eating vegetarian — is that not breaking the precepts? Not at all! He has not eaten meat; he is a vegetarian. Why? His mind is empty, he does not cling to marks, and he has never felt that meat tastes good and so eaten more, or that vegetables taste bad and so eaten less. To be without love and hate, without grasping and rejecting, is to be a vegetarian. By contrast, some who eat vegetarian food cling to flavors: this dish tastes good, delicious; that dish tastes bad, unpalatable! Picking and choosing — that is as good as not being a vegetarian. If our mind is truly empty and pure, eating is as if not eating, and holding a pig’s head in the hand does not matter.

But then again, if you have not realized to this degree and you let yourself go like this, then you will “fall into hell as swift as an arrow”! Your mind has not truly become empty and pure, and “karma” sticks to you, entangles you, and will not let you pass. Here is such a public case: long ago there was a Chan master who loved beef, and he said, “Eating is not eating!” Was his mind empty and pure? No! It was only talk; his mind could not be emptied, and karmic obstacles stuck to him and demanded repayment. When this Chan master’s last breath did not come, he entered a cow’s womb and became a cow to repay the debt. One day a farmer led the cow out and met Chan Master Baozhigong. Zhigong looked: oh! Is this not Chan Master So-and-so? Did you not say, “Eating is not eating”? You should not have become a cow — how is it that you became a cow to repay a debt? The cow, tears streaming down its face, dashed itself to death. So unless one has truly reached the stage of emptiness and purity, to talk wild and big is to fall into hell. We are determined to realize the great Way; we should speak only according to the stage we have realized — no wild talk! To realize the stage of “non-obstruction in all things,” one must first have pure and correct views, clearly see the true mind, and then further remove deluded habits and enter non-doing. To cultivate while clinging to marks, to cultivate with doing — neither can realize “non-obstruction in all things.” Nowadays some people, with minds not empty and pure, vainly seek superknowledges — ruined! Not only can they not become Buddhas, they are in line to become demons! If you want superknowledges, the demon manifests superknowledges in your mind, changes into a Buddha’s form to show you, and you think it is the true Buddha, happily hold on to it, and the demon takes up residence in your mind. The demon king will even expand his influence, making you expound the Dharma and gather a host of demon sons and demon grandchildren. All this is because of clinging to marks; therefore we must not cling to marks, must not cultivate with doing.
“Therefore to verify and confirm the view as the school is foremost.”

This is the weightiest sentence. The view as the school is clearly seeing the intrinsic nature. The Ganges Mahāmudrā places the view as the school in the foremost position, and the Caodong house’s “five positions of lord and minister” highlights this too. The Linji house has the “three mysteries and three essentials,” and among them the first essential of the “mystery within the phrase” is to know one’s own mind and see one’s own nature, which highlights this as well.

One must first realize and see the intrinsic nature; only then can one manifest the “wisdom of self-abiding.” After awakening, preserve the intrinsic nature without losing it, practice diligently, and sweep away deluded habits. If in any favorable or adverse circumstance the mind is like still water, without the least deviation, then all superknowledges and wondrous functions come without seeking. “Abiding in one’s own intrinsic nature” means that it is inherent in the self-mind and naturally issues from the original mind. “Not sought from another” means it is not obtained by cultivating some dharma, nor given to us by Buddhas and bodhisattvas, still less manifested by some ghost or spirit possessing one. “Nor is it absent before and present now”: it is not that it did not exist before and exists only now, but that it has always existed. Someone asks: “You say it has always existed, so why do I not have it now?” Because your delusive thoughts and delusive habits are not yet exhausted! First you must recognize Buddha-nature and clearly awaken to the fact that this capacity to see and to hear is the intrinsic nature. Then care for it at every moment, do not cling to marks, do not run after circumstances. When preservation is complete and ripe and the mind is truly empty and pure, superknowledges will appear of themselves.

If it is not “abiding in one’s own mind” and not developed by oneself, then it has nothing to do with you: when the last breath does not come, none of the functions remain, and you do not even know where you are going. If you have done bad things, you will fall into hell — very dangerous! In Shanghai there were several so-called “possessors of superknowledges”; as death approached, the spirits attached to them left and went away, and then they not only had no superknowledges but suffered greatly in the body and, in mind, were tormented by guilt and the reproaches of conscience, crying only, “Pain! Suffering!” and falling into the three lower realms. We who practice the true Dharma should take warning!
Becoming familiar with the dharmakāya

blocks.text: 1. Affliction Is Bodhi

inline.s: In our practice we must let the mind be like a river, bending and turning as it goes. Have no subjective abiding at all; let all follow conditions and be free, without self-view and without obstruction. At all times flow on peacefully and freely like flowing water — this is how the work should be done. We ordinary beings are heavy with selfishness and full of delusive thoughts, and want everything to accord with our own wishes: “I want it this way, so it must be this way,” and otherwise the mind is afflicted; hence karmic obstacles are heavy and we cannot see the Way. Now that we practice the Way, we must change this habit of abiding and be able to follow conditions and things: bend where it bends, turn where it turns, and not stubbornly hold to our own views. For example, in our work, if we are promoted, we are promoted; if demoted, demoted — it does not matter. We must not be delighted by promotion or angered by demotion. Because everything is service to the people, not to oneself, one must be able to go up and to go down. Having learned the Buddhadharma, we know that all sounds, forms, goods and profits are like flowers in the sky and moons in water, not to be sought and not to be obtained, and the mind abides always in emptiness and stillness, without affliction; so every problem can be discussed, and every task can be taken up selflessly and pressed forward with courage. If everyone acted thus, giving up self for others, society would be at peace, the nation would flourish, and the country would be strong and prosperous. So learning Buddhism is of great benefit to the world and to people’s minds, and should truly be vigorously promoted.

When we do things, we should not care whether we succeed or fail, but only do our utmost: not delighted by success, not angered by failure, summing up experience, correcting mistakes, and pressing on with renewed effort. If one can make one’s thinking broad and open, without crookedness or selfishness, unmoved and unshaken, then one naturally realizes the original face of the dharmakāya. Likewise, one should not, merely because a thought arises, give rise to the notion that “the mind’s light is covered by dark clouds”; nor, when delusive thoughts subside, give rise to the notion of “having removed them.” For as soon as the thought of “leaving” and “emerging” arises, that is delusion upon delusion, and one is still clinging to something and cannot be liberated. The Mahāmudrā teaches action in non-doing, with no defilement at all, following conditions and being free at every moment; its work is a level higher and harder to do. If for the moment you cannot do it, you must do other work; this will be explained later.

Therefore we must be thus at every moment: when a thought comes, pay it no heed, do not press it down, do not run after it; follow conditions and be free, respond to the ten thousand opportunities without abiding — this is our dharmakāya’s own mark. Our own Dharma-nature is originally thus: it can produce wondrous function according to the opportunity, it is not dead and motionless. It responds with extraordinary speed, faster than light. The reason ordinary beings respond slowly is that they have many delusive thoughts; it is like the sun covered by dark clouds, so that its light cannot come forth and its function is thereby reduced. To develop superknowledges is simply that when delusive thoughts are exhausted the mind’s function comes fully into play. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is inherently complete with infinite superknowledges and wondrous functions. If only we can be mindless like a flowing river and let it be natural — as it is said, the fallen flower has intent, the flowing water has none — and thus at every moment be free and unconstrained, we can restore the dharmakāya’s own mark and greatly manifest superknowledges. The dharmakāya’s own mark is not the absence of a single thought, rigidly knowing nothing. It is lively, arising in function according to conditions, with boundless wondrous function. What is called no-thought does not mean that not one thought arises; it means that thoughts arise without abiding. Emptiness is existence and existence is emptiness!

Speaking of emptiness and existence: this matters greatly for studying Buddhism. Only when the relation of emptiness and existence is fully understood can one advance swiftly. Those who practice always say all is empty and one should not cling to existence, while ordinary beings in their affairs all cling to existence, so that emptiness and existence seem irreconcilable opposites. This is because people understand “emptiness” and “existence” differently. What ordinary beings call emptiness is that everything is nothing; what the Buddhadharma calls emptiness is only the absence of self-substance, not the absence of false marks. Hence “form itself is emptiness,” and it is not that one speaks of emptiness apart from false marks. The emptiness we speak of is not the ordinary being’s emptiness of total nothingness but the emptiness of not abiding in false marks, the emptiness in which “emptiness is existence, existence is emptiness, emptiness and existence are non-dual.” So no-thought is not the non-arising of a single thought but the arising of thoughts without following or abiding; this principle must be understood. Buddha-nature is truly empty, but it is not that it does not manifest, for when it functions it must manifest. If it were empty and had no marks, it would not be the self-nature. For where there is mind there must be marks; mind is marks and marks are mind, mind and marks being non-dual. As I said last time, there must be a shadow in a mirror, and without a shadow it is not a mirror; so Buddha-nature can certainly manifest form and mark, and without form and mark it could not be called Buddha-nature, for without wondrous function Buddha-nature would become dead emptiness, barren emptiness. But Buddha-nature is not barren emptiness: it is numinously clear and all-pervading, able to produce all wondrous functions and to manifest all kinds of form and mark; hence “the myriad phenomena are perfected within the mind.”

Speaking of this, let me tell you a story. In Zhenjiang there is a Jinshan Temple, and in the temple there is a treasure that guards the mountain. The treasure is Su Dongpo’s jade belt, made of square jades strung on gold thread. How did this jade belt remain in Jinshan Temple? Su Dongpo and the abbot of Jinshan Temple, Chan Master Foyin, were close friends. Su Dongpo wrote excellent poetry and was also a Buddhist practitioner, and he prided himself that his practice had reached the point of being unmoved by the eight winds. Chan Master Foyin wanted to test the depth of his practice, and deliberately belittled him: “Su Dongpo’s poems are not worth a dog’s fart.” Hearing this, Su Dongpo could not help but be greatly angered, and raising a punitive expedition, he crossed the river in a rage to confront Chan Master Foyin. Chan Master Foyin laughed: “A fine ‘unmoved by the eight winds’ — one fart blew you across the river.” This is a joke.

Once Su Dongpo came to Jinshan Temple to visit Chan Master Foyin. The Master was at that time in the Chan hall leading the assembly in sitting meditation, and it was the time of stillness when idlers should not enter. Su Dongpo knew the rule and sat waiting in the guest hall for Chan Master Foyin to come out. When that stick of incense was finished another was added, so he came out very late. Su Dongpo had waited a long time and was very impatient. When the incense was finished and the stillness ended, Chan Master Foyin came out: “Ah! Great Scholar Su, please sit, please sit.” Su Dongpo said: “Hey, you still tell me to sit! I want to sit on the head of you bald donkey!” They were good friends joking, calling the Master a “bald donkey.” Hearing this, the Master said: “Oh, you want to sit on this old monk’s head? Good, good, good. I have a question to ask you. If you can answer it, this old monk’s head is yours to sit on; if you cannot, then untie the jade belt from your waist and give it to us as a treasure to guard the mountain.” Su Dongpo laughed heartily: “Whatever question you like, I can answer ten for one; I have many wondrous interpretations and broad explanations.” Chan Master Foyin said: “Good. I ask you: the four great elements are originally empty, the five aggregates are not existent — where do you sit?” The meaning was: you want to sit on my head; my body is the four great elements and five aggregates, empty and non-existent — how will you sit? Su Dongpo thought: the four great elements are empty, the five aggregates originally do not exist, everything is nothing — then I fall into emptiness; where shall I sit? I cannot sit in empty space... He thought and thought, walked back and forth three times, and for the moment could not answer. Chan Master Foyin seized the chance and called the novice monk: “Come, untie his jade belt — he cannot answer.” And so Su Dongpo’s jade belt remained in Jinshan Temple as a treasure to guard the mountain. This is the public case of “empty yet existent, existent yet empty.” In fact this question is not hard to answer, for emptiness is not barren emptiness and existence is not real existence; emptiness does not obstruct existence and existence does not obstruct emptiness; emptiness is existence and existence is emptiness, mind is mark and mark is mind. So one may answer him: “True emptiness does not obstruct wondrous existence — I sit right on your false-mark head!” Or simply sit down on the chair and say: “Thus I sit!” Or raise one finger and say: “I sit right here!” Or again raise a finger and ask him: “Where do you sit?” These answers are picked up at random and need no racking of brains.

Someone asked the lecturer on the Diamond Sutra: “No mark of person, no mark of self — then who speaks and who hears?” This question looks very hard: with no person and no self, there is no speaking and no hearing — can one still expound and listen to the sutra here? In fact the Diamond Sutra is about breaking marks to see the nature; it does not belong to barren emptiness. Though things and marks are absent, Buddha-nature is not absent. One may answer him: “It speaks only of no marks, not of no person.” Our Buddha-nature is wondrous existence that is not existence, true emptiness that is not emptiness. If everyone makes clear the principle of emptiness and existence, existence and emptiness, and then goes further to preserve it closely and continuously at all times, not abiding in marks and not falling into emptiness, one can perfectly realize the great Way. Otherwise, as soon as we meet a circumstance or mark we stick to it and are not free — when will it ever end?

In the school there are many such public cases. In the time of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, a prime minister invited the elders of all schools and sects to hold an unveiling assembly — with nothing covered, each stating his own view, directly and revealing the intrinsic nature and perfectly realizing the great Way. A lecturer on the Avataṃsaka Sutra said: “In our teaching, becoming a Buddha requires three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. But the school says that one shout or one blow can make one a Buddha, which does not accord at all with the Buddha’s teaching. Now I ask the great Chan masters present: if one shout of yours can penetrate the five teachings spoken of by the Avataṃsaka school, I will acknowledge that one blow or one shout can make one a Buddha; if it cannot penetrate the five teachings, then it is a demon’s teaching. Will one of you come forward and explain?” The Avataṃsaka school divides the Buddhadharma into five teachings: the Hīnayāna teaching, the elementary Mahāyāna teaching, the final Mahāyāna teaching, the sudden Mahāyāna teaching, and the perfect Mahāyāna teaching, with doctrines from shallow to deep and practice advancing step by step. Among the great Chan worthies present was Patriarch Yuanwu Keqin, over eighty years old, the master of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao. He looked with his eyes at the young Chan master Jingyin Cheng, over forty, and Chan Master Jingyin Cheng understood; he stepped forward and said to the Avataṃsaka lecturer: “Your question is not hard to answer; it is not worth the great patriarchs present explaining it to you — let me, a junior elder, explain it to you. Let us first settle the doctrines of the five teachings: the Hīnayāna teaching holds to existence — there is a Way to attain, a nirvāṇa to realize, a birth and death to end; the elementary Mahāyāna teaching speaks of emptiness; the final Mahāyāna teaching speaks of neither emptiness nor existence — neither empty nor existent; the sudden Mahāyāna teaching speaks of both emptiness and existence; the perfect Mahāyāna teaching speaks of neither emptiness nor existence, neither existence nor emptiness, perfectly interfused and unobstructed. Is that the meaning?” The Avataṃsaka lecturer said: “Yes!” Chan Master Jingyin Cheng gave a great shout, and asked the assembly: “Did you hear it?” The assembly said: “We heard it!” Cheng said: “If you heard it, that is existence! You have penetrated the Hīnayāna.” Emperor Huizong was at that time sitting among the assembly in plain clothes and a small cap; he had told the prime minister not to reveal him, so that he might listen well to how it was explained. After a while the sound died away, and Cheng asked again: “Now that you listen, is there still a sound?” The assembly said: “There is none!” Cheng said: “No sound is emptiness — you have penetrated the elementary teaching.” He said further: “Now there is none and just now there was — that is not emptiness; just now there was and now there is none — that is not existence. Is this not neither empty nor existent? You have penetrated the final teaching. Moreover, if there were not the existence of just now, what emptiness could be spoken of now? If there were not the emptiness of now, what existence of just now could be spoken of? When existence is spoken of, emptiness is within existence; when emptiness is spoken of, existence is within emptiness — is this not both empty and existent? You have penetrated the sudden teaching. And the perfect Mahāyāna teaching? My one shout is not used as one shout: though I shout, I have never shouted, and at every moment and in every place I do not cling to marks. Eating, I have not bitten a single grain of rice; wearing clothes, I have not hung on a single thread. Though work is busy, it is as if I had never worked. This is the essential meaning of the Diamond Sutra’s ‘give rise to the mind that abides nowhere’: when existence is spoken of, not a hair is established; when emptiness is spoken of, it pervades the sand-grain worlds; not abiding in emptiness or existence, perfectly interfused and unobstructed — this is the supreme perfect Mahāyāna teaching, the highest state spoken of in the Avataṃsaka Sutra, the Dharma-realm of non-obstruction in all things. This is also the essence of the Chan school.” When the assembly heard this, all were convinced and praised, and Emperor Huizong nodded without cease. The Buddhadharma is truly the most sublime religion and the best philosophy of life. If we can believe, accept and practice it, what affliction of success and failure, gain and loss can remain? The Ganges Mahāmudrā teaches the supreme Buddhadharma; since we have most fortunately heard this Dharma, we should practice according to the teaching, making the mind at every moment like a river, functioning freely without abiding, and only then can we realize the dharmakāya’s own mark.

When a thought arises in the mind, one should know that this is the functioning of wisdom, the wondrous function of Dharma-nature. This is so not only when watching over but at all times. Therefore when one is lax and does not practice, Dharma-nature does not decrease; when one diligently accumulates practice, Dharma-nature does not increase. Dharma-nature itself neither increases nor decreases.

Many of us, in studying Buddhism and doing the work, tend to press thoughts down so they do not arise, thinking that to sit for ten days or half a month, or even ten or eight years, without a single thought arising is good practice. They do not know that cultivating dead samādhi thus brings no true benefit and cannot leave the three realms; it only suppresses for a time, and once it stirs and delusive thoughts arise they are worse than before. And even if it does not stir, what use is sitting there dead? After long dead samādhi one turns into earth, wood, metal and stone. True practice must be lively, tempering oneself amid affairs and circumstances, knowing that where a thought arises is the wondrous function of the intrinsic nature, and not clinging to marks — then wisdom grows daily. We must practice to become living Buddhas, not dead Buddhas; we must produce all kinds of wondrous function and benefit sentient beings — only thus is there value. Not sitting there dead and motionless — would that not make one a clay bodhisattva?

As said before, after seeing the intrinsic nature one must diligently remove habits amid affairs and circumstances. Watching over is the best method for removing habits. Watching over is the wondrous function of Buddha-nature! It is wondrous function not only when watching over but at all times. For example, wandering in mountains and playing in water, visiting relatives and friends, watching plays and dancing are all wondrous function. It is not that one may not watch a play, but one must not be watched by the play, nor turned by its plot. If while watching you repeatedly give rise to joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure along with the play’s partings and reunions, and afterwards cannot forget it and brood over it, your mind always turning with the plot — this person so good, that person so bad — that is called being watched by the play; how can that do? Watching a play can also be used to train the mind, to see whether this mind can be turned. If you can reach “like a wooden man watching flowers and birds,” that is good practice. But this is not to say that one does not know the good and bad people in the play, or does not know the plot. If one knew nothing at all, would that not be a pool of dead water? It is not that one does not know, but that one does not discriminate and choose, and is not moved by the play’s plot. Watching yet not watching, not watching yet watching, without the least abiding. “The affairs of the world are after all only a play”: we cannot let go of this or that, yet all of it is as false as a play! When the last breath does not come, the play is over — why cling to it?

In our practice, if we work diligently, the dharmakāya does not increase by a fraction; if we are lax, the dharmakāya does not decrease by a fraction. In other words, when we become Buddhas the dharmakāya does not increase a fraction, and as sentient beings it does not decrease a fraction; ascending to heaven it does not increase, descending to hell it does not decrease. It has no birth or death, no coming or going, and endures through all ages unchanging. In America a “living Buddha” named Lu Sheng-yen said: “By practice, Buddha-nature (the heavenly mind) ascends to heaven, and the bad, evil mind descends to the earth.” One ascends and one descends, one true mind split into two — that is truly terrible! Some Dharma masters say in expounding the sutras: “If we do bad things, the deluded mind that does bad things falls into hell, and the true mind ascends to heaven.” This too splits true and deluded into two minds. They do not know that the true mind (Buddha-nature) and the deluded mind are originally one body: the deluded mind is the true mind and the true mind is the deluded mind. For example, water (the true mind) gives rise to waves (the deluded mind): the waves are water and the water is the waves — how can there be two? Someone asks: “If there are not two, why do people speak of three souls and seven spirits? Are there not ten?” If it were really so, would a person not become ten? Not at all! What is called “soul” belongs to yang and is the bright, selfless, upright qi; what is called “spirit” belongs to yin and is the dark, defiled, evil thought. “Three souls and seven spirits” means that a person’s bright element is small, only three parts, while the dark, unseemly things are many, seven parts. It is not that a person is divided into ten things. If we drive out all seven parts of dark, evil mind and turn them all into light, we attain the Way. Thus Patriarch Lü Chunyang was called “pure yang” because his “spirits” were all transformed, the darkness all turned to light, and he attained the immortal Way. Therefore the true mind and the deluded mind are not two things. When you fall into hell, the true mind falls into hell with you, but its light does not decrease, nor is it defiled, nor does it suffer. It is like a pearl wrapped in mud: the pearl’s light does not decrease. When you ascend to heaven, it is not glad, and its light does not increase. Our self-nature at every moment is neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking, neither arising nor ceasing.

The reason we have feelings of greed, anger, affliction, suffering and pleasure is that they are all the natural wondrous function of the dharmakāya. If there were no dharmakāya, these feelings could not arise. But this changing of different emotions — now joy, now sorrow and affliction — is all the mischief of the three poisons of greed, anger and delusion. Meeting with what we dislike we are afflicted; seeking and not obtaining we are angry; unable to fulfill our wishes we are grieved and resentful; fulfilling our desires we are delighted and happy. These feelings are all empty and without self-nature, all delusive thoughts arising toward objects. As it is said, “The ten thousand dharmas are originally at leisure; only people make trouble for themselves” — and this is because of fundamental ignorance. Speaking of ignorance, all who practice fear it: it is this thing that harms people and makes us turn in the six realms! If it were not there, we would long ago have become Buddhas! But do not fear it: ignorance is not really existent, it is only a delusive thought, an illusion, and as soon as we awaken we illumine through it. Because it is not a really existent thing, it cannot be broken with any object. One need only awaken to the fact that greed, anger, delusion, pride and doubt are all deluded feelings arising from clinging to objects and sticking to the mind, all ignorance and delusive thought, inherently just so and utterly non-existent. “Just so” means “originally thus, not deliberately contrived.” When we understand this wondrous principle, all suffering, pleasure and affliction dissolve as soon as we awaken. As the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Know the illusory and at once you are free, without using any device; freedom from the illusory is awakening, and there are no stages.” We commonly say “karmic obstacles are deep and heavy” — what are karmic obstacles? Karmic obstacles are your clinging to marks. If you do not cling to marks, there is no affliction at all, and where would karmic obstacles come from? All feelings of suffering and pleasure are like dreams in sleep: in the dream, bad dreams and good dreams are perfectly there, but once you wake there is nothing. So if we can wake up sharply, let everything go, and not cling to marks, we obtain the dharmakāya’s wondrous function. The dharmakāya’s wondrous function is not hard: we need only be clear and awake at every moment and not abide in marks at every moment.

Someone says: “Ah! Chan practice and tantra are hard; reciting the Buddha-name and seeking birth in the West is easy!” In fact he is mistaken: Buddha-recitation, Chan practice and tantra are all the same, with no distinction of hard and easy; one simply chooses a method suited to oneself according to one’s differing capacities. Buddha-recitation uses the Buddha-name to sweep the accumulated dirt from one’s mind-ground and, by holding the name, to wake oneself up. Master Lianchi said that Buddha-recitation is “calling the master of the house to wake, sound by sound.” That is, with each sound one devoutly recites the holy name and wakes one’s own intrinsic nature, not abiding in marks and not sticking to objects, thereby personally seeing Buddha-nature and, at the end of life, being born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Chan practice is the same: at every moment tend the huatou, watching where delusive thoughts come from. As soon as a thought arises, ask it: where do you come from? A blow straight to the head. This delusive thought originally does not exist; it is a false illusion, and one blow and it is gone. This is the same as Buddha-recitation: both are to exhaust delusive thought and thereby personally realize the original. But some say they are different: they say Buddha-recitation has Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva and all the bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pool assembly to receive one, so that one is born in the West and transcends the three realms horizontally, while Chan practice cannot. In fact they are also mistaken: receiving and horizontal transcendence do exist, but receiving and horizontal transcendence do not mean pulling you away. Chan Master Yongming Shou said very clearly: the Buddha is like the moon in the sky and the mind is like a basin of water; only when the mind is pure can the moon’s shadow appear; if the mind is impure — foul water — then though the moon is in the sky (though the Buddha shines light on you, you cannot see it), the shadow cannot appear, and you cannot be born in the West. Great Master Hanshan said that in reciting the Buddha-name one must recite to the point of power, cutting off the root of love, and only then is there hope of birth in the West. The root of love is the love-emotion of ignorance and deluded movement; it is the root of birth and death, and if it is not cut off the mind is like foul water in which the moon’s shadow cannot appear. It is not that the Buddha does not come to receive you and does not shine light on you; it is only that you yourself cannot see, like a blind person who cannot see the sun. Moreover, for one who practices Chan, when the mind-ground is empty and pure, that is the Pure Land. For mind is the land and the land is the mind. The Buddha said: “If you wish to purify the land, first purify the mind; as the mind is purified, the Buddha-land is purified.” Only when the mind is pure is the Buddha-land pure, and then if you vow to be born in the West, you will certainly receive Amitābha Buddha’s compassionate reception and be born there. Amitābha is not like us ordinary beings, who have feelings of love and hate: if you have formed a good connection with me, I receive you; if you have not, I pay you no heed. Buddhas and bodhisattvas practice great loving-kindness without conditions and have no such inferior view: if you have not formed a connection with me, then I will form one with you and compassionately receive you. In tantric terms, whether you recite the Buddha-name or practice other methods, at the end of your life Amitābha shines light on you and receives you to birth in the West. And not only practitioners: even non-practitioners and evildoers he also shines on and receives. Only these evildoers, heavy with karmic obstacles, cannot see the Buddha-light, or seeing it so intense are frightened and flee, and have no fortune to be born in the West. The Amitābha Sutra says: “One cannot be born in that land with few roots of goodness, blessings, and causes.” Roots of goodness, blessings, and causes — not one of the three may be lacking. To be born in the West one must be complete in roots of goodness, blessings and causes; it is not something to be had by casually reciting a couple of “Amitābha.”

All you bodhisattvas, we must truly apply effort and completely settle the deluded mind before we can attain the Way! The Mahāmudrā teaches the mind-ground Dharma-gate. The one true Dharma-realm — the Lotus Treasury world — is the Mahāmudrā. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is within this Mahāmudrā and does not go outside it. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss’s “land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings” is on the thirteenth level of this Mahāmudrā, and the “land of real reward and adornment” is the twentieth level of the Lotus Treasury world. Our Sahā world is also the thirteenth level, parallel to the West’s “land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings.” The Buddha said: “West of here, past a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss.” That is, going west from here is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss’s “land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings.” If only we believe deeply without doubt, do all good deeds, and vow and transfer the merit toward birth there, we can all go, and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas will not refuse us. It is not that one cannot go without reciting Amitābha’s holy name. Someone says: “I recite the Buddha-name only a little; I fear I cannot go.” That is wrong! Whether one is born in the West does not depend on how much one recites — this is not a business transaction — but on the quality of your recitation, whether your mind-ground is devout, whether your mind is pure.
