If your mind is truly pure, then at the end of life even one thought can bring birth in the West. If we can reflect that all form, sound, smell, taste, touch and dharmas are flowers in the sky and moons in water, not to be sought and not to be obtained, and let go of everything at once, and with a pure, undefiled mind recite one “Amitābha,” this one pure thought can be in accord with the Buddha and bring birth in the West — no need for ten thoughts, a hundred thoughts, a thousand or ten thousand thoughts. It depends on whether at the end of life you can be single-minded without confusion and clear in right thought. At the end of life, to be unconfused in mind, undistracted in intent, and clear in right thought — this is the practice of deeply attaining the Buddha-recitation samādhi! To bring the practice to this point depends on the diligent sweeping away of deluded habits now. So we must now apply effort, devoutly letting go, letting go, and letting go again, making the mind pure and undefiled, so that in the future we may surely win and be born in the West — this too is the dharmakāya’s wondrous function! We blend Chan, Pure Land and tantra into one furnace because they are originally one body. Do not divide them into tantra, Chan, Pure Land — they are originally one Buddha school!

blocks.text: 2. The Great Natural Abiding of Non-cultivation

inline.s: In all our actions at all times and in all places, there is the wondrous function of the true mind, and all forms are our own transformation bodies. We should follow all kinds of conditions in responding and acting, doing our utmost to benefit the people — this is called “natural free functioning.” If one does not understand and does not penetrate the principle of “natural free functioning,” one will certainly cling to objects and stick to the mind, and with insatiable greed, to satisfy one’s desires, delusive thoughts will fly in confusion, and one will bury a great living Buddha as an ordinary man or foolish woman. We practice the Dharma originally to see the nature and realize the Way, clinging to nothing. If one wants superknowledges, wants to obtain something, or prays to Buddhas and bodhisattvas for promotion and wealth, that runs counter to studying Buddhism. Now we need only be free and non-abiding at every moment, not adding knowing to any delusive state, and yet not like wood or stone, but vividly and distinctly responding to opportunities and following conditions — this is Buddha-work. We have said before: do not acknowledge this form-body as self, but take emptiness-and-stillness as the substance; do not acknowledge delusive thoughts, but take numinous knowing as the mind. Cultivating by the mind-ground Dharma-gate is like using rice to cook a meal: it will certainly become a meal. If one does not practice thus, it is like boiling sand to make a meal: however much effort is spent, no meal is made. Once we understand that this pure, undefiled, vividly distinct numinous knowing mind is the Buddha, we no longer cling to marks but freely and naturally serve the people, tempering ourselves amid affairs and circumstances, exhausting deluded habits, and perfecting the fruition of Buddhahood. Otherwise delusive thoughts will fly in confusion, one falls of oneself into the ordinary and foolish, and birth and death are not ended. We ordinary beings have been accustomed to clinging to marks for many lives and kalpas, and cannot change all at once: not only do we pick and choose in food, drink and daily life, but in practicing the Dharma too we pick and choose without cease. One says: “The Pure Land school is good and reliable; Chan is dangerous and unreliable.” Another says: “Tantra is good.” Another says: “Tantra is not good either — tantra is full of demonic air.” Oh, this is good, that is bad — all blind men feeling an elephant, falsely discriminating and talking nonsense. They do not know that the Dharma spoken by the Buddha is equal, equal, and again equal; it is only that different Dharma-gates are taught according to people’s differing capacities — this is called “giving medicine according to the illness.” It is like eating: if you like sweet food, take sweet food; if you like sour food, take sour food. If one who loves sour says sweet food is bad, and one who loves sweet says sour food is bad; if those who recite the Buddha-name say Chan is dangerous (in fact Chan is not dangerous), and those who practice Chan say tantra has demonic air (in fact tantra has no demonic air) — all this is over-weighting one’s own preference, falsely discriminating, and not only brings affliction on oneself but invisibly incurs the offense of slandering the Dharma. Whichever school you like, practice that school; do not say other schools are bad — any one school is the same. You say Chan is hard, but practicing other schools is not easy either; you say Buddha-recitation is easy, but practicing other schools is not hard either.

Pang the layman said: “Hard, hard, hard — ten loads of sesame oil spread on a tree.” This speaks of the beginner who does not understand the key to practice, and so it is very hard, like “a slippery fish climbing a slick pole”: the fish’s scales are slimy and slippery — to climb that oiled bamboo pole, how easy is that! But once it is pointed out, it turns out that this which can speak, can act, can weep, can laugh is our own self-nature; it shines at our face all day long, hiding nothing, needing no seeking and no praying — only let everything go and that is it. As it is said, “Wearing out iron shoes you search in vain; what you get costs not a bit of effort.” So Mother Pang took up the words: “Easy, easy, easy — on the tips of the hundred grasses is the meaning of the coming from the West.” Not hard at all — awakening to Chan is very easy. “On the tips of the hundred grasses” means on the tip of anything at all; “on the tip” means looking apart from marks, not looking downward and clinging to marks. The capacity to see things apart from marks is the wondrous function of the self-nature! Is that not very easy? So in our practice we should not divide into schools and sects, saying this is hard and that is easy; we need only recognize at every moment this true mind that is apart from marks and vividly distinct, and not acknowledge shadows — shadows cannot be grasped. At this point, though the principle is clear, the habit of abiding in marks from many lives and kalpas will still intrude. Master Guifeng said: “Deluded clinging from many lives, habit become nature; joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure flow in subtle streams. Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these feelings are hard to remove at once. One must constantly be aware, reducing and reducing again.” So we must be aware at every moment: as soon as a thought arises, be aware and remove it. If the delusive thought is strong and cannot be transformed for the moment, then recite the Buddha-name or hold a mantra to transform it. The Buddha-name and mantras are the sword of wisdom, used to cut off the mark-clinging deluded mind and emotional thinking; they have infinite power. If we only recite devoutly, we will certainly receive the empowerment of Buddhas and bodhisattvas; hence there is no difficulty in attaining the Way. Likewise, to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, any school will do if one makes the vow. We often say that Buddha-recitation has a very broad scope: it is not only reciting one “Amitābha” that counts as Buddha-recitation; reciting sutras is also Buddha-recitation, doing good deeds without clinging to marks is also Buddha-recitation, being alert in awakening is also Buddha-recitation. Why? Because Buddha means awakening: if you are never deluded at any moment and transfer the merit toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, is that not Buddha-recitation? The Pure Land school says that to attain the highest grade of the highest birth one must “read and recite the great vehicle.” Why read and recite the great vehicle? To make you understand the principle! To make you understand where birth and death and other such phenomena come from, and how to end birth and escape death. Only when you understand these principles clearly, empty the deluded mind completely, and abide nowhere, can you attain the highest grade of the highest birth. If you abide in marks and cling rigidly, thinking this world is bad and you want to go to the West to enjoy blessings, that is ruinous. Even if you can go, it will only be the lowest grade of the lowest birth. Because your mind is not empty and pure, you can only be born in the land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings, not in the land of expedient remainder or the land of real reward and adornment.

What is Chan? It is the original, sovereign, pure mind, which the school calls “the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa.” Is this wondrous mind of nirvāṇa not the Pure Land? Is it not also the secret treasury of tantra? So Chan, Pure Land and tantra appear as three schools but are in fact one body. Tantra has many methods for birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, such as the phowa method, the great Amitābha method, and the method of transferring consciousness, all for birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Reciting Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva also brings birth in the West, because Avalokiteśvara is in the West and also shines light on you and receives you to birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The reason there are nine grades of birth lies precisely in the distinction between clinging to marks and not clinging to marks! If you understand that mind is the land and the land is the mind, that birth is no-birth and no-birth is birth, and abide in no mark at all, then within no-birth there is no hindrance to being born. Such birth is wondrous function! No-birth is not dead immobility: unceasing generation is no-birth, and no-birth is unceasing generation — only thus is the wondrous truth of no-birth attained.

Therefore one should always not depart from the great natural abiding of non-cultivation.” What is called non-cultivation is “the cultivation of non-cultivation, which is true cultivation.” The Mahāmudrā is the supreme tantric method: it does not ask you to recite mantras, does not ask you to form hand-seals, does not ask you to cultivate any dharma; all is free and natural, with not the least abiding — that is it. This cultivation is the great natural abiding. After awakening in the Chan school it is the same: cultivating without cultivation, without antidotes. Antidote methods are the delusion-removing practices specially cultivated according to each person’s habits. For example, one with strong lust cultivates the contemplation of impurity and the contemplation of white bones; one who loves to talk cultivates silence, and so on — these are expedient methods for settling delusion and returning to the truth. The Mahāmudrā does not use such antidotes; it tells us that all forms are the manifestation of the self-nature, the wondrous function of the true mind, and that to be non-abiding at every moment is the great cultivation of cultivating without cultivation. For one who recites the Buddha-name, when a thought arises and as soon as one is aware it is empty, that is Buddha-recitation; it is not that one must recite one “Amitābha” to count as Buddha-recitation. But one’s practice must fit one’s own capacity and must not be forced into one mold. There are several ways of reciting the Buddha-name: to be aware as soon as a thought arises is Buddha-recitation of true mark; to contemplate oneself as Amitābha is Buddha-recitation by contemplation; to contemplate the Buddha’s marks and excellences is Buddha-recitation of marks; to be never apart from one “Amitābha” is Buddha-recitation by holding the name. In our practice we must choose a method suited to our own habits, so as to achieve twice the result with half the effort. If you cannot be empty as soon as a thought arises and you are aware, then recite the name-Buddha. If silent recitation still does not work and thoughts still stir, then recite aloud, “Amitābha...,” for you must always cut off your delusive thoughts and turn them into no-thought. It is the same Buddha-recitation, but whether one understands this principle or not makes a great difference in power. Not understanding, one clings to marks at every moment and clings to Amitābha in the West; understanding, one knows that Buddha-recitation uses Amitābha’s holy name to sweep clean the filth in our minds and to turn around the afflictions and delusions of mark-clinging, so as to realize the pure Buddha-nature that is the same as Amitābha’s. Because the methods of practice differ, the grade of one’s future birth in the West differs accordingly. This cultivation without clinging to marks is “the great natural abiding of non-cultivation”; the abiding that is no-abiding is called natural abiding.

The Chan master’s instruction says: “Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, pass quickly by.” Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, hurry past. This means that one may neither cling to existence nor lean toward emptiness; neither side of existence and nothingness is established, and the middle is not there either — that is the meaning of the middle way, which is the Tiantai school’s “empty, provisional, middle” threefold contemplation of the one mind. Therefore marks are not absent; they are illusorily manifested in function. If the true nature could not manifest illusory marks and function, it would be a stagnant pool — what value would Buddha-nature have? We practice in order to exhaust the deluded habit of clinging to illusory marks, not to sit there dead and motionless. If one can awaken and at every moment not abide in marks, and not cling to dharmas in practice, one is on the right road and enters “the great natural abiding of non-cultivation.”

At whatever time and in whatever place, take only the recognition of the intrinsic nature pointed out by the direct pointing as right knowing and seeing, and truly realize that this mind of ours is the one true Dharma-realm. The one true Dharma-realm encompasses all, including the myriad phenomena; any form is the wondrous function manifested by the self-mind, so do not cling to marks. Whether the circumstance is good or bad, whether it accords with my mind or goes against my wish, pay it no heed — then you see the nature at every moment. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “One who has seen the nature must see it in the words; if one is like this, then even wheeling a blade into battle, one can still see it.” Going into battle with thoughts of birth and death, of coming and going — that will not do. If I am killed, it does not matter: “I meet the white blade with my head as if cutting the spring wind,” ha ha! Cut it off and it is cut off; cut off this husk, and our true mind neither increases nor decreases, neither arises nor ceases — it still cannot be cut off. This is the conduct of one who has seen the nature.

Long ago, when Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song was sitting in meditation, he saw an emperor standing before him with many attendants, awe-inspiring. The emperor, seeing that the Chan master did not rise to greet him, was much displeased, and asked him: “Do you know me?” The master said: “I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; how could I look on you differently?” The emperor said: “I am the mountain god, holding the power of life and death; I can make people live and make people die — how can you look at me with ordinary eyes?” The master laughed and said: “I am originally unborn; can you make an unborn person die? In my view body and space are non-dual, and you and I are non-dual; can you destroy space and yourself? Even if you could, my true mind neither arises nor ceases. What you can destroy is only my body; you cannot destroy my true mind! You have not yet realized this true mind — how can you speak of making me live or die?” The mountain god was stunned by his words: “Ah, I have never heard such words; is there still a deathless true mind?” The master continued: “For example, you are now a great god, but you were once a human being too! Only because you were upright and unswervingly just and did many good deeds have you now become a great god wielding the power of life and death. But who became the mountain god? The husk of your human life is gone; it is the consciousness-spirit that became the mountain god. That consciousness-spirit of yours is not the same as our Buddha-nature; it differs by just a little. What is the difference? With ignorance present, Buddha-nature becomes the consciousness-spirit; when ignorance is removed, the consciousness-spirit is restored to Buddha-nature. Even if ignorance remains, Buddha-nature does not decrease by a fraction, for it neither increases nor decreases. Who is it that is now the mountain god? It is this unborn, undying Buddha-nature — and you do not know it at all!” When the mountain god heard the master’s instruction, he woke as from a dream and at once took Chan Master Yuangui as his teacher and took refuge in the Buddhist order.

And those who depend on grass and cling to trees to manifest spirits — what gods are they? They are ghosts! In life they were insatiably greedy and committed offenses and fell into hell; when the punishment in hell was complete and they left it, because the habit of greed remained, they attached themselves to grass and trees, and the grass and trees became efficacious. This is truly a greedy ghost making mischief, not any god. A god is a great ghost king whose superknowledges exceed other ghosts’, but they all cling to marks. Therefore at all times, take only the recognition of the true mind indicated by the “direct pointing to the view as the school” as essential, with a mind as vast as space, so that the myriad phenomena, not one of them, are not included within our mind-nature. To restore our original capacity we must begin now: let everything go, recognize this Buddha-nature at every moment, and not abide in marks. As soon as there is abiding, recite the Buddha-name quickly, hold a mantra quickly, and best of all be empty as soon as you are aware. Understand this principle and practice — whether Pure Land, Chan or tantra — and all are easy to accomplish swiftly; without understanding this principle, all are hard to bring to fruition.

Here it is said that in subduing and countering deluded thoughts we must not set to work on each rising and falling deluded thought; we must work on the root from which deluded thoughts arise. Ordinary people have so many deluded thoughts! Some are terribly fond of lust, some terribly greedy for wealth, some terribly eager for fame; each person's deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies differ, and if one counteracts them one by one, using delusion to cure delusion, the delusion only grows worse. But if you work at the place where the deluded mind stirs, then one stroke settles everything, and you sit securely at home. The doctrinal schools also have antidote methods; for instance, the “perfection of giving” among the “six pāramitās and ten thousand practices” is a vital method for countering our small-mindedness and stinginess. Again, the five precepts — “no killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, or alcohol” — are the Dharma-gate that counters the restless stirring of our deluded mind. The two hundred and more precepts of the bhikṣu are no more than this: guard against the mind's moving, and so the greatest precept is the mind-precept. When the mind moves, that is already a transgression; it is not that only when the deed is done does it count as a transgression. Once a disciple asked his master, “Master, what is breaking the precepts?” The master said, “When the woman next door washes her face and wipes it, if you hear the sound of her hairpins and ornaments, that is breaking the precepts.” Why is hearing such sounds breaking the precepts? Because as soon as you hear the sound you cling to marks; hairpins and ornaments are a woman's adornments, and once you cling to the mark of a woman, other thoughts arise.

The Mahāmudrā cultivates from the root and does not speak of countering each deluded thought one by one. Once you have seen the intrinsic nature, you look after it at every moment, never letting this mind cling to objects, and at every moment you shine upon emptiness. With the true mind you gather and hold all things: the myriad phenomena, phenomena myriad — all are things within the wondrous luminous true mind. The mind is the root; if you do not move your mind when you meet any circumstance, if you pay no heed to anything at all, then what difficulty is there in attaining realization in this very life? But if you cultivate on the branch-tips, countering each deluded thought one by one, you will be overwhelmed by endless trouble — that is truly, truly too hard! Not speaking of antidotes is the way of cultivating the Mahāmudrā. If this does not suit some of you, you may also cultivate antidote methods: for example, if lust is strong, cultivate the contemplation of impurity or the contemplation of white bones, and so on, choosing a different practice according to each person's differing situation.

blocks.text: 3. The Meeting of Mother and Son Luminosity

inline.s: Deluded thoughts and afflictions are both the intrinsic-awareness wisdom-mark of the dharmakāya. The dharmakāya is without marks, and yet it is not without any mark. To say it is without marks means that the substance of the dharmakāya has no concrete form that can be seen; to say it is not without any mark means that the myriad phenomena, phenomena myriad — every thing that has marks — is a manifestation of the dharmakāya, and there is not one thing with marks that lies outside the dharmakāya. Deluded thoughts and afflictions are things with marks, so of course they are not outside the dharmakāya. Where do deluded thoughts and afflictions come from? Their place of origin is the Dharma-nature, and the Dharma-nature is the root from which all dharmas arise. The Buddha-nature is the root of becoming Buddha. Spoken of as two things, the Dharma-nature and the Buddha-nature are in fact one thing; neither is apart from the dharmakāya. Intrinsic awareness is the originally perfect, complete awareness-nature; it is the numinous luminous true mind that everyone possesses from the start. This true mind can give rise to vast wisdom, can bring forth all wondrous functions, and can manifest forms of a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. Therefore, whether deluded thoughts or afflictions, all are the wondrous function of the dharmakāya substance. The dharmakāya is the root; without this root, where would deluded thoughts and afflictions come from? Only when there is water are there waves: water is the root, and waves are water's mark of stirring. Only when there is a mirror is there a reflection: the mirror is the root, and the ability to show reflections is the mirror's wondrous function. Only when there is the dharmakāya are there deluded thoughts and afflictions: the dharmakāya is the root, and deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the intrinsic-awareness wisdom-mark of the dharmakāya. If there were no dharmakāya, deluded thoughts and afflictions would have no way to arise either.

The intrinsic nature of deluded thoughts and afflictions is itself the true and undeceiving manifestation of the luminous substance of the dharmakāya. Here luminosity is mentioned: the substance of the dharmakāya is perfect in immeasurable light; it is a “great treasury of light.” In the course of practice, some people have seen red light, some have seen yellow light, some have seen blue light, some have seen green light… every kind of color is there. If you practice the Dzogchen practice of tögal, you must look at light; when the light is magnified, you will see luminous spheres. These spheres are first white, and as you go on looking they become colored; five colors, six colors, seven colors all appear. This is the light of our own nature, drawn out by sunlight, moonlight, lamplight and the like. It works by the same principle as modern laser technology: put a ruby inside a laser, use a pulsed xenon lamp to emit intense light upon it, and stimulated by that light the ruby's own light of a particular frequency comes bursting out — wham! As the saying goes, the eyes are the windows of the soul. According to tantric theory, the eighth consciousness — the ālaya-consciousness — is located in the heart-sheath, and two channels run from behind to connect the heart-sheath with the eyes. In tantric light-contemplation practice the outer light enters through the eyes and draws out the Dharma-nature light that our own mind possesses, by exactly the same principle as laser technology; hence tantra is quite scientific.

According to traditional Chinese medical theory, the five viscera and six bowels are connected through the channels and network-vessels to the whole body, and each finger corresponds to a particular viscus or bowel. Forming a hand-seal is arranging the positions of the viscera and bowels; reciting a mantra is using the mantra's sound to stir the mechanism of the vital energy. Mantra-sounds are not shot at random; it is not that reciting just anything at all will do. They are symbols that Buddhas and bodhisattvas, in meditative concentration, have transformed from their own minds. If you recite a mantra with your mind, and it matches the symbols emitted by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, you can connect with them responsively and receive their blessing power. This accords with the scientific principle of “resonance,” so tantra is very scientific and not at all superstition.

The Ganges Mahāmudrā we are now discussing is cultivation without cultivation: at all times and in all places, free and natural. This most easily connects one responsively with the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, because the Buddhas and bodhisattvas are all free and natural. We must first recognize our own true mind; we must first understand that all things, including deluded thoughts and afflictions, are the wondrous function manifested by our own true mind. This is the “view as the school” spoken of earlier, which in the Chan school is called “understanding the mind and seeing the nature.” Then, at all times and in all places, protect it, and at every moment and in every place do not cling to marks. When protection is perfected, the Way is attained. This Dharma is very direct and very refreshing; it is not a Dharma of countering things one by one. Cultivation without cultivation is true cultivation — hence it is said that the Mahāmudrā is the supreme vehicle's way of cultivation. Do not fear deluded thoughts; do not fear afflictions: deluded thoughts and afflictions are the wondrous function arising from the dharmakāya. Simply settle these deluded thoughts and afflictions down, and that is all. Settle the mad mind down, and that is bodhi; you need not get rid of it. To get rid of deluded thoughts and afflictions would be like getting rid of the waves and having no water left — would you not then have got rid of the dharmakāya too? And how could the dharmakāya ever be got rid of? Simply settle deluded thoughts and afflictions down; do not get rid of them. Do not think that deluded thoughts and afflictions are bad: they are precisely the manifestation of the true mind, and precisely the display of superknowledges and the arising of wondrous function. The Ganges Mahāmudrā tells us to recognize this wondrous principle, and in doing all our work not to cling to the marks of things, but to turn the deluded mind and deluded thoughts into the wondrous function of the true mind.

Knowing this principle is called “the luminosity of the abiding of the substance.” Abiding means not moving. If you can know that deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the wondrous function of the substance, and can settle them down so that they do not move — that is, when doing things, not clinging and not abiding, applying yourself according to conditions — then such “knowing” is the light of the substance's abiding emitted by the dharmakāya! Abiding carries the sense of “dwelling securely,” that is, planting the heels firmly, which in the Chan school is called “the heel touching the ground.” To recognize that the place where the deluded mind arises is the true mind, and no longer to look for it elsewhere — that is to stand with heels firmly planted. Then what master do you still seek to open your crown and transmit a Dharma to you? Can a master open your crown and make you attain the Way? To speak honestly: there is no such thing! If a master could open your crown and make you attain the Way, then the Buddha, being so compassionate, would long ago have opened everyone's crown and made everyone attain the Way — how would there still be so many ordinary people? To speak of opening your crown is a symbolic comfort, to make your mood cheerful and steady and so make it easier for you to enter the Way. Once we understand this principle, we should rouse ourselves and work hard, open our own crown, and not depend on others. Clearly and distinctly recognize that the true mind is not elsewhere: the place where deluded thoughts and afflictions arise is our true mind. Protect it at every moment and do not follow deluded thoughts. As soon as there is any straying, recite the Buddha-name quickly, or hold a mantra quickly, and turn the deluded thoughts away; this turning of the light back to shine within is the wondrous method of protecting the true mind. In doing the work you must shine inward, not outward. There are too many things outside: good things to eat, good things to wear, good things to play with… all of these are mere shadows, wholly unobtainable; follow them and you are finished. You must abide unmoving, plant your heels firmly, and wear away the old habit of clinging to marks; then naturally you will radiate great light. In fact we are all radiating light all the time: as soon as a thought moves, light is radiated — but this is deluded light. What the deluded mind emits is deluded light; only the light emitted by the true mind is true light. What is deluded light? Clinging to marks and so giving rise to deluded thoughts is deluded light, and deluded light is light too. Scientists of the former Soviet Union invented a machine that could photograph the light emitted by the human body; according to their account, that halo of light was seven or eight centimeters thick. Deluded light is limited in measure, but true light has no limit. If we can protect this original segment of true light at every moment, it will shine ever more widely, until it illumines Buddha-lands in the ten directions with nothing to obstruct it. This is the great treasury of light that our own mind possesses. We should abide thus: this is abiding in no-abiding, not abiding on anything, but only making your mind steady, unshakable and free of doubt.

Above we spoke of intrinsic-awareness luminosity: deluded thoughts and afflictions are the mark of intrinsic-awareness luminosity. Now we speak of initial-awareness luminosity. What is initial-awareness luminosity? It is the luminosity of the “direct pointing to the intrinsic nature.” It is directly indicated to you: that numinous knowing mind — in which not one thought arises yet all is perfectly clear — is the Buddha-nature, is the one true Dharma-realm, is the Mahāmudrā. To recognize it thus is to have the view as the school, is initial-awareness luminosity. But through immeasurable kalpas we have grown used to clinging to marks; “giving rise to mind toward objects” is a familiar road, while “vast and utterly non-abiding” is very unfamiliar, and so there must be a process of “turning the familiar into the unfamiliar and the unfamiliar into the familiar.” This is the process called “protection,” which is also the process of “contemplative illumination.”

To become thoroughly familiar with its own mark — this is called the initial-awareness luminosity of one who walks the Way.” To become familiar is to mature — not to mature in clinging to marks, but to mature in contemplative illumination, to mature in understanding the mind and seeing the nature: at every moment not abiding in marks, with not the least doubt. This is called “becoming familiar with its own mark.” Suppose that after hearing this we half believe and half doubt: Is this the Buddha-nature? Is this the root of becoming Buddha? I am afraid not! If it were, there should be great superknowledges — why is there no superknowledge? That is because you are not yet familiar; you are still unfamiliar with it! But if we have not the least doubt, and can look after it at every moment, then this is the initial-awareness luminosity of one who walks the Way. This is true practice; it need not have any particular appearance, need not have the appearance of sitting in meditation, the appearance of reciting the Buddha-name, or the appearance of holding a mantra. Rather, as soon as a deluded thought arises, you see it, do not run after it and pay it no heed, and it immediately turns empty and is wholly unobtainable. So it is in walking, standing, sitting and lying down; you cannot tell that such a person is doing the work, and yet he is doing the work at every moment and in every place. This is work of the mind-ground, and it is called “the initial-awareness luminosity of one who walks the Way.” Why is it called “luminosity”? Because as soon as a thought arises you can see it — if it were not luminosity, how could you illumine it? Someone says, “I do not recite the Buddha-name well; I have recited for a long time and still have many deluded thoughts.” I would say: you recite quite well! A deluded thought arises and you can illumine it — that is initial-awareness luminosity! Deluded thoughts are like the dust flying about a room: without light you cannot see it. But if a ray of sunlight comes in, you will discover how much dust there was! So when sitting in meditation or reciting the Buddha-name, to illumine deluded thoughts is a good thing, not a bad thing; this is initial-awareness luminosity, the beginning of awakening. Going further, you do not run after deluded thoughts but pay them no heed at all, and with whole-hearted attention recite the Buddha-name or hold the mantra, mind reciting and ear hearing, hearing perfectly clearly, and deluded thoughts naturally settle down. This is “the initial-awareness luminosity of one who walks the Way.”

Deluded thoughts and afflictions are intrinsic-awareness luminosity; the view as the school and walking the Way are initial-awareness luminosity. Intrinsic-awareness luminosity is “substance-luminosity,” and initial-awareness luminosity is “path-luminosity.” The own mark of these “two luminosities of substance and path” — although the two luminosities have different individual appearances, in substance they are one, and are without discrimination. To be free and natural in this, free and natural in the undiscriminated substance of these two luminosities, is what is called “the meeting of mother and son luminosity”! The mother is intrinsic-awareness luminosity, the son is initial-awareness luminosity. The meeting of mother and son is intrinsic awareness joining initial awareness, the two luminosities becoming one. The method of liberating the intermediate state is based on this very principle. The intermediate state, also called the between-state, is this: after a person dies there is a state of “swooning” lasting from three and a half to four days, after which the “intermediate body” arises, like a three-year-old child, and within forty-nine days passes through seven rounds of birth and death, with all kinds of scenes appearing. What is called “swooning” is a great faint; while fainting, deluded thoughts do not move, because the body — the four great elements of earth, water, fire and wind — has dispersed, and the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue and body have lost the power to take in outer objects. When deluded thoughts do not move, the luminosity of the intrinsic nature is about to appear. This luminosity, however, is called the light of death, the light emitted after death, and it appears twice within three or four days. Each appearance of this death-light does not last long, no more than the time of a meal, and — whoosh — it is gone. The death-light is also the light of the intrinsic nature, and if one can “seize it in one grab” as it appears, recognizing it in time, one attains the Way at once. The death-light is the mother light; to be able to perceive it is the son light. To recognize it in time is the meeting of mother and son, and joining with it in time brings sudden realization of the saṃbhogakāya Buddha. This is the first stage of “liberation in the intermediate state” — the intermediate state at the moment of death. If one cannot recognize it in time, the opportunity is missed. Then the intermediate body arises and manifests all kinds of karmic marks: good deeds done in life bring good marks, bad deeds bring evil marks, and beautiful marks and terrifying marks all appear. At the same time, during the first fourteen days, Buddhas and bodhisattvas each day emit intense lights of various colors and appear in embracing pairs to draw one in. If at that time one does not fear the intense light, does not give rise to mad and deluded discrimination, and joins with it in time, one can likewise be born in a Buddha-land Pure Land. On the fourth day after the intermediate body arises, the Buddha of Immeasurable Light of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss emits an intense red light and appears in an embracing pair with the White-Robed Buddha Mother. If at this moment you can be free of discrimination, astonishment and fear, and resolutely join with them, you will immediately be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. These first fourteen days of drawing in by Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the second stage of “liberation in the intermediate state” — the intermediate state of the Dharma-nature. Immediately following is the third stage — the intermediate state of rebirth — which the book The Esoteric Method of Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State sets out in great detail, so I will not say more about it here.

When we sit in meditation and cultivate, to be able to illumine deluded thoughts is a good thing; do not give rise to doubt, but continue to practice diligently. When the work matures, crack! — it comes apart all at once, son light and mother light merge into one, one great treasury of light! And then the Way is attained. It is the same for those who recite the Buddha-name: a single recitation of the Buddha-name at every moment and in every place, and after long, long practice the work matures, and the mind that recites and the Buddha recited fall away at once, with no one who recites and no Buddha recited, yet bright and distinct, perfectly clear. This too is son and mother joining, this too is “the meeting of mother and son luminosity”!

Do not forget the “own mark luminosity of the view as the school” that you have already recognized. What is the own mark luminosity of the view as the school? That we can illumine all things is the wondrous function arising from the substance of the dharmakāya. To illumine things without being turned by them, and to understand that this very capacity to see is our intrinsic nature — thus seeing the nature upon marks, seeing the nature through marks — this is the view as the school. The view as the school is also the wondrous function arising from the dharmakāya, and is also the mark of the dharmakāya's own substance radiating light; this radiating-light mark is the mark of no-mark, and it is called “the own mark luminosity of the view as the school.” This is not seen with the eyes, nor heard with the ears. Earlier we spoke of the insentient preaching the Dharma: “If you listen with the ear, you will never understand; only when you hear sound at the eye will you know it.” That is to say, hear sound with the eyes; and now we are to see luminosity with the ears. How can the eyes hear? How can the ears see? The capacity to illumine all things and hear all sounds is our intrinsic nature. Apart from the intrinsic nature, nothing whatsoever exists; if you can recognize it thus, that is the own mark luminosity of the view as the school. Can this luminosity be seen with the eyes? Hence it is said, see it with the ears. Is this seeing? It is silent accord, direct experience, realization, spiritual understanding.

Toward deluded thoughts and afflictions that well up in circumstances and in function, we do not give rise to the mind that would dispel them, establish them, grasp them or abandon them, because all is like an illusion and a shadow, beyond grasping and rejecting. We must pay them no heed and give rise to no mind at all; only thus do we accord with the wonder of the Way. To dispel is to cover over; to drive out is to chase away. Both dispelling and driving out are suppression. To establish is to follow along with it. For example, you have lost your capital in business and affliction arises. Then you think, “I am a student of Buddhism and should not be afflicted like this; why do I still give rise to affliction? Bad, bad!” The more you think, the more you regret, and the more afflicted you become: this is dispelling and driving out. Again, if you are already able to remain unmoved by the success or failure of affairs, and you consider your concentration-power strong — “the eight winds cannot move me; I sit upright on the purple-gold lotus” — this is a very fine state! That is establishing. We should do the work like this: whether moving or still, favorable or adverse, whether in ease and lightness or in affliction, all is wholly unobtainable and we take nothing at all to heart. Even dispelling, driving out, establishing, setting up, grasping, abandoning — none of it goes to the heart. When deluded thoughts and afflictions come, we neither run after them nor pay them heed, but let them arise and cease as they will; a single sharp awakening is enough. As we said before, if your work reaches the point of “having no mind of love or hate,” then after your death you will no longer turn through the six realms.

One thing “not forgotten” and one thing “not given rise to” are of the greatest importance. Not forgetting “the own mark luminosity of the view as the school,” and not giving rise to the mind of “dispelling, establishing, grasping and abandoning” — this is the most important of all! We must not forget that this capacity to see, to know, to speak and to act is the wondrous function of the intrinsic nature; become familiar with it at every moment. When deluded thoughts and afflictions come, do not suppress them, do not run after them, have no dispelling and no establishing whatsoever, no love or hate, no grasping or rejecting whatsoever; all is wholly unobtainable. Calm and unruffled, plain and ordinary, with a single ordinary mind, quietly vanishing of itself. Let the wind and clouds change as they will; I am neither joyful nor sorrowful. The mind is always empty, the breath always even, the intent always mild. We must do the work thus at every moment and in every place, and this work can be put to use in any school whatsoever.

blocks.text: 4. Repeatedly Dispelling the Powers of Bliss, Clarity and No-Thought

inline.s: When the states of not forgetting and not giving rise to, as described above, are protected and upheld for a long time, states of “emptiness, bliss and clarity” and the like will appear; these are the first stages of entering the Way brought on by the power of practice. Bliss is happiness, clarity is luminosity, and no-thought is the emptiness of mind — the state of “emptiness-bliss-clarity” has appeared. The inner mind is empty and pure, incomparably light and at ease; this body seems to be gone, so relaxed that it is like setting down a heavy burden. Joyful and delighted, incomparably happy — a hundred times happier than “long drought meeting sweet rain, meeting an old friend in a foreign land, the wedding night in the candle-lit chamber, having one's name on the golden roll.” This happiness is beyond comparison with any worldly happiness. (Among the four dhyānas and eight concentrations, cultivation to the third dhyāna brings this bliss; only at the fourth dhyāna does this bliss melt away.) The mind's light is revealed, bright and transparent, like a full moon shining overhead, so that waking and dreaming alike you are bathed in luminosity. Is this “emptiness-bliss-clarity” good? Good it may be, but if you abide upon it and give rise to thoughts, “Fine! I have emptiness and purity, I have bliss, I radiate luminosity,” then you are ruined, for that will cover over the original face of the source. What is the original face of the source? It is the intrinsic nature that we have repeatedly stressed above! If you cling to the mark of “emptiness-bliss-clarity,” it is like wrapping a layer of skin and shell around the intrinsic nature — how then can you still see the intrinsic nature? You should strip off this layer of skin and shell and not abide on this “emptiness-bliss-clarity.”

I have reminded you again and again that in cultivating the Heart Center Dharma you are not permitted to see light and not permitted to see Buddhas. It is not that you are not allowed to see them, but that you are not allowed to cling to marks! The intrinsic nature is neither clear nor dark: to say it is luminous is wrong, and to say it is dark is also wrong. As we said before, when the work is done to the very end it is like “the moon of the thirtieth of the twelfth month” — no light is seen. But this is not darkness, just as a person in the air does not see the air, and a fish in the water does not see the water; “as one who enters a room of irises and orchids, after long smelling it does not notice the fragrance” — neither grasping nor rejecting, wholly transformed and forgotten. To say “not permitted” is to say you are not permitted to abide in marks. To abide in marks is to “establish,” to “grasp,” and these are delusive thoughts and attachments. Only by ridding yourself of these delusive thoughts and attachments can you awaken thoroughly to the original. Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara's “method of perfect penetration through the ear-faculty” is also like this at the later stage of the work: “The perceived and the perceiver are empty; the emptiness and the awareness are perfectly complete; the emptied and the emptying are extinguished.” When the perceiver and the perceived are emptied to the point of perfect completeness, the emptying and the emptied also vanish, and even emptiness is gone; only then does “birth-and-death cease, and still extinction appears before one.” The emptying and the emptied have arising and ceasing; the bliss and the blissed, the clarity and the clarified likewise have arising and ceasing. When all these things that have arising and ceasing have utterly vanished, then the unborn and undying “still extinction,” great nirvāṇa, shines clearly before one. Still means still yet ever illumining, and illumining brings forth the myriad workings of function; extinct means illumining yet ever still, and still means thusness unmoving. Thusness unmoving is called “thus,” and responding to the myriad workings is called “coming” — how could the state of the “Thus-Come” be compared with a shallow “emptiness-bliss-clarity”? Only this is truly becoming Buddha.

You should strip off this layer of skin and shell, “emptiness-bliss-clarity,” and only then can the mark of the intrinsic nature appear nakedly. “This is wisdom shining brightly from within” — this is the light of wisdom emitted from within the mind; this is true luminosity, able to illumine the ten directions with nothing to obstruct it. The light of “emptiness-bliss-clarity” is limited in measure and cannot illumine the ten directions.

Therefore one should repeatedly sweep away this “emptiness-bliss-clarity.” It is the same in Chan cultivation: for example, a monk asked Caoshan, “What about when the bright moon is overhead?” — like a full moon shining overhead, the mind filled with luminosity; look, is my practice up to it? What about this situation? Chan Master Caoshan said, “You are still a fellow below the steps.” When the work reaches this, you are still below the steps, you have not entered the hall and the inner chamber; you are still far from it! The monk said, “Please, Master, take me up the steps.” Please, Master, be so compassionate as to lead me up the steps, so that I may enter the hall and the inner chamber. Caoshan said, “We shall meet when the moon has set.” When the moon has gone down, I will meet you again. (Master Yuanyin asked the assembly, “When the moon has set, how will you meet? Once the moon has gone down, how are you to meet?” The assembly was silent for a long while, and the Master said, “Stop! Stop! Do not think about it. I flick my sleeve and return to the abbot's quarters!”)

The spring water surges, a rushing torrent, wondrous” — the spring water borrows the mountain's slope and races along, its waves surging, the water's force immense, and this rushing torrent is hard to dam. This is a simile for how, when the work reaches a certain degree, wondrous wisdom bursts forth like “the spring water surging, a rushing torrent,” impossible to block. In former days Great Master Hanshan had fine literary talent and was skilled at writing poetry and lyrics, but he did his work until he had forgotten poetry and lyrics completely. When someone asked him to write a poem, he could not produce a single line. Later someone brought a few Tang poems and asked him to chant them, and as soon as he chanted Tang poems the lines came leaping out at once. There was no need to deliberate at all; it was like a mountain torrent bursting forth, impossible to stop, once released beyond all control. Great Master Hanshan knew this was not right — he could not let literary thought cover over the Buddha-nature — so he resolutely cut off this mystery that was like “the spring water surging, a rushing torrent” with a single crack. These are all skin and shell that can cover the “original face of the source”; “if you do not decide when decision is needed, you will instead suffer its disorder” — you should resolutely strip it away.

When the powers of bliss and clarity arise, and when the joys and pleasures of this present life arise, forcefully utter one “Phat!” and send this “Phat” crashing down from above, so as to shatter the skin and shell of clinging to the powers of “emptiness-bliss-clarity,” and let the intrinsic nature shine clearly before you. The Tibetan letter “
P”
is pronounced “pa” and carries the meaning “skillful means that can gather in.” To embrace is to receive and contain; the letter “
P”
has the skillful-means quality of containing all wondrous meanings. The Tibetan letter “
ei”
is pronounced “ei” and carries the meaning “prajñā that can cut off.” To cut off is to sever and remove; the letter “
Pei”
has the prajñā quality of removing all obstructions. “
Pei”
is pronounced “phat”: it can contain all wondrous meanings and remove all obstructions. This “phat” is just that good.

blocks.text: 5. Cultivating “the Great Cultivation That Is No-Cultivation”

inline.s: “Thus at all times one can preserve and sustain the essential point of being free of and cut off from path-experience, and the inexpressible intrinsic nature is thoroughly penetrated; in entering concentration and emerging from concentration one's practice is without difference, and on the cushion and off the cushion one's cultivation is likewise without difference.”

As said above, at all times one can protect and freely sustain this “essential point of being free of and cut off from path-experience, and the inexpressible intrinsic nature.” Path-experience means the verification of cultivating the Way: constantly checking how well one is cultivating, to what degree one has cultivated — has emptiness-bliss-clarity appeared? If a little of it appears, one is beside oneself with joy and the mind sticks there all the time. Others, having no emptiness-bliss-clarity and no superknowledges, keep thinking about these things in their minds and use them to verify themselves: Why have I no news? Why have I no superknowledges? Am I no good? Is this Dharma not efficacious? With such things stuck in the heart, to say nothing of attaining the Way, even the state of emptiness-bliss-clarity is obstructed and will not appear. As we said before, emptiness-bliss-clarity appears in the course of sitting cultivation and of preserving the intrinsic nature; even when it appears, one must “phat” it away. If you do not have it, you have one layer less of obstruction — is that not better! But one who truly works hard at cultivating the Way will naturally unfold emptiness-bliss-clarity in the course of practice. Only, one must not seek it; let it unfold naturally and do not abide on it, and there is no harm. To be free of and cut off from path-experience is to be free of these verifications and to cut them off. Essential point means the key, the crux. To be free of and cut off from using “emptiness-bliss-clarity” and other sensations to verify the attainment of the Way — this is the key to attaining the Way, the crux of practice.

The intrinsic nature is the dharmakāya; the dharmakāya is without marks and yet not without any mark, and it is inexpressible and does not fall within thought. However you may speak of it, it has no appearance to speak of; however you may think of it, it has nothing to think of. Language cannot express it and thought cannot reach it: this is called “the path of language is cut off, the road of mind is extinguished.” The scripture says, “Only this one true reality; the other two are both unreal.” Any thing with marks that can be spoken of or falls within thought is utterly false and unreal, wholly unobtainable. Only this intrinsic nature, of which “the path of language is cut off and the road of mind is extinguished,” is the one thing true and undeceiving; it is called “true mark,” and this is the “one true mark seal” of Mahāyāna Buddhism.

We should never forget “the essential point of being free of and cut off from path-experience,” and never use “emptiness-bliss-clarity” and other sensations to test whether we have attained the Way; at every moment we should freely sustain this “inexpressible intrinsic nature,” neither grasping nor rejecting at any time. Such preserving and sustaining must not be parted from for a single moment. To penetrate thoroughly is to understand clearly and thoroughly. When a practitioner preserves and sustains in this way until the intrinsic nature is clearly and thoroughly understood, so that “the familiar becomes unfamiliar and the unfamiliar becomes familiar,” he is “one who has penetrated thoroughly.” At this time, “in entering concentration and emerging from concentration one's practice is without difference, and on the cushion and off the cushion one's cultivation is likewise without difference.” The great concentration has no entering or emerging. If the mind can settle when entering concentration, but after emerging it runs off after outer objects again, that is not the great concentration, not true concentration. In the true great concentration one is in concentration at every moment: whether the meditation hall is silent or the marketplace is clamorous, whether sitting in concentration or busy with affairs, it is all the same, and in practice there is no difference. True cultivation is no-cultivation; no-cultivation is the great cultivation. In cultivating the Heart Center Dharma we do not merely sit on the cushion forming seals and holding mantras; still more must we, off the cushion, never for a second be apart from contemplative illumination. I told you long ago that contemplation is the primary practice and sitting is the auxiliary practice, yet not a few still neglect contemplation. Here I stress once more: contemplation is the primary practice and must not be neglected! Contemplation is precisely the “preserving and sustaining” just spoken of! On the cushion you form seals and hold mantras, gathering in this mind from left and right; off the cushion you contemplate closely and continuously, also gathering in this mind from left and right. On the cushion and off the cushion there is no difference in cultivation!

“This is the great cultivation that is no-cultivation, the wisdom of self-abiding and universal equality. Like the yoga of a river, without a hair's breadth of correction, yet also without a single instant of distraction.”

The practice of the Ganges Mahāmudrā is “the great cultivation that is no-cultivation.” True practice has no appearance of practicing. You may see such a person as one who does not practice, but in fact he is practicing at every moment; this is his great cultivation that is no-cultivation. For he is contemplating at every moment, protecting his own spirit at every moment.

Having no appearance of practice is called “no-cultivation”; that all is wholly unobtainable, so that even “emptiness-bliss-clarity” is unobtainable, is called “no-attainment”; that one is originally Buddha, and need only extinguish delusive thoughts and attachments without adding anything more, being originally perfect in all wondrous functions, is called “no-realization.” This is what is meant by “no-cultivation, no-attainment, no-realization.” No-cultivation means originally unborn and undying; no-attainment means originally empty and still; no-realization means originally Buddha. This is “the wisdom of self-abiding and universal equality”! Equality means even and equal, universality means all-pervading: to abide naturally and effortlessly on the great wisdom that is perfectly equal and pervades all. Universal equality means that at all times, in all places and among all people all are equal; no one is higher and I lower, nor am I higher and others lower, nor is my Dharma higher and your Dharma lower. People simply love to quarrel, each holding to his own view, thinking that what he says is the truth and slandering others, standing on his own ground to say who is right and who is wrong, who is good and who is bad. To give an example: there is a kind of automatic umbrella that is very convenient to use but not sturdy; it breaks after no great while, and people call it a “short-lived umbrella.” In the eyes of consumers in our country this umbrella is not good, because we like things sturdy and durable. But in the eyes of foreigners this umbrella is very good! For it is handy to use and cheap in price, excellent quality at a low price, and just right for using a while and throwing away. We are not used to throwing things away, so we say this umbrella is bad; they are used to throwing things away, so they say this umbrella is good. In fact an umbrella is just an umbrella; the umbrella itself is neither good nor bad, and to say it is good or bad is only people's deluded mind discriminating — as the saying goes, “all things are originally at leisure; the foolish man troubles himself.” If “the wisdom of self-abiding and universal equality” shines clearly before you and you do not give rise to a mind of discrimination and grasping or rejecting, then you can hear “the short-lived umbrella preaching the Dharma.”

We said before that “the insentient preaches the Dharma” — how does the insentient preach the Dharma? If you cannot hear the insentient preaching the Dharma, it is because ignorance has covered over your true mind and your discriminating mind is still present, and therefore your faculty of awareness can only pervade your own body. Strike your head and your head hurts; strike your foot and your foot hurts too. Strike this chair, and you have no awareness of it at all. But if you break through ignorance, put an end to the habit of “giving rise to mind toward objects,” and sweep away the mind of discrimination and grasping and rejecting, then the awareness-nature can pervade all things, and your mind's measure will be like empty space, with nothing at all outside your mind; then you will stretch across the ten directions and reach through the three times, knowing all and understanding all. Sun, moon and stars, the vast universe, mountains, rivers and the great earth, flowers, birds, fish and insects — all sentient and insentient alike are within your mind. Like the pearls of Indra's net, each light reflecting each light, each pearl perfectly round: it is within your mind, and you are within it; you are in me and I am in you. Pick up any one, and it is the whole. It is like the modern “laser hologram”: any tiny part of it contains the information of the whole picture. This is “universal equality.” If you wish for this, you must take up cultivation. How to cultivate? “Like the yoga of a river, without a hair's breadth of correction, yet also without a single instant of distraction.”

Yoga means correspondence. The yoga of a river is to correspond as a river does. Look at the river water: where the channel bends, it flows bending; where the channel is straight, it flows straight. It corresponds to its surroundings at every point; it is not that it can only go straight and not bend, nor only bend and not go straight. Our true mind is originally like a river, corresponding to every circumstance. Have we not said before, “Deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the intrinsic-awareness wisdom-mark of the dharmakāya”? The dharmakāya is our true mind, our intrinsic nature. It has always been neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; it has always been “without a hair's breadth of correction” and also “without a single instant of distraction” — only this is the root of all things. In doing our work we start from the root, and should likewise be like a river, corresponding to every circumstance, with no success or failure, gain or loss, no love or hate, grasping or rejecting. Do whatever the matter calls for, and do it in perfect order and by the right way; when it is done it is as if not done, and no trace is left in the mind. Working thus, wisdom and skill arise as the hand responds, and though busy one is not disordered, though much is handled it is not cluttered, and the efficiency is high. But if beforehand you hope and fear, carrying a burden of thought, then in doing the work your hand will not respond as your mind would have it. Worse still, afterwards you may be secretly pleased with yourself over success, or dejected and angry over failure — “the wind of joy blows down the bodhi tree, the fire of wrath burns up the forest of merit.” Then you are long since no longer “yoga.”

We should be like a river: bend where it bends, go straight where it is straight, and if the wind comes and raises waves, that does not matter either. Joy and laughter, anger and scolding are all the wondrous function of the Buddha-nature; it is all right to lose your temper once in a while. Why? If you are too yielding toward someone, he thinks you are weak and can be bullied, and his desires flare up higher, and in a moment he may harm many people — how can that be allowed? At such a time you need “a bodhisattva's heart with a rākṣasa's face”: flare up and give him a stern lesson, even give him a beating, so that he turns back quickly — this is education! So we who study Buddhism cannot always be soft and weak either; when we see a bad business, we should flare up when it is time to flare up. Is it real anger? The flare-up is outward, a means of educating people; it is not that the mind has lost control, not that a mind of hatred has arisen. Long ago, under Chan Master Yuanguan of Mount Liang there was a garden head (one who managed the vegetable garden and grew vegetables for the community to eat), and he asked Mount Liang, “When the thief within the house is hard to guard against, what then?” The thief within the house is a simile for deluded thoughts: to run after deluded thoughts is to cover over the luminosity of the intrinsic nature, as if the “thief within the house,” deluded thought, had stolen away the Dharma-wealth. When deluded thoughts come, what is to be done? Mount Liang said, “To recognize him is no injustice.” If you can see it and recognize that it is a deluded thought, and simply do not follow it, then there is no injustice. But if you run after it (clinging to it and suppressing it are both running after it), then you have cultivated in vain — is that not injustice! But the garden head was a man who had awakened; he was not one to hear a few words and let the matter rest. He wanted to “present it face to face,” to hold the vital pass and not let the huatou go. After several questions and answers, he suddenly asked, “What about when the torrents pour and the mountains topple?” — when suddenly a great rage flares up, like a mountain flood bursting and sweeping the mountains over, what then? Chan Master Mount Liang came down from the Dharma seat, seized the garden head with one hand and said, “Ācārya, do not let the old monk's robe-corner get wet!” Even the corner of the robe may not get wet — a simile for the mind's not moving. That is to say, flare up as you will, but the mind must be held steady and must not move in the least!

When you reach this, “without a hair's breadth of correction, yet also without a single instant of distraction.” There is neither concentration nor distraction; concentration and distraction are both unobtainable, equal and one, one and equal. You say, “Here I have entered concentration!” Then you still have “concentration” present, and where there is “concentration” there must be distraction, for “concentration” is spoken in contrast to “distraction” — if there were no distraction, what would concentration be? To speak of the true, there must be the false; to speak of the good, there must be the bad; to speak of the beautiful, there must be the ugly. If there were no “false, evil and ugly,” would there be any need to speak of “true, good and beautiful”? Our mind must be truly equal: neither distraction nor concentration, neither correction nor distraction. The work must be brought to this degree.
“The verse says: Never cultivated and never apart, yet also not apart from the meaning of no-cultivation.”
This verse has three parts: 1. Never cultivated; 2. Never apart; 3. Yet also not apart from the meaning of no-cultivation.

Never cultivated” is the great cultivation that is no-cultivation just spoken of — without a hair's breadth of correction, yet also without a single instant of distraction. This is not to say that no work is done; the work still has to be done, and therefore it says “never apart” — one is also never apart from doing the work. But you must not abide on doing the work: having done it, it is the same as not having done it. This is “yet also not apart from the meaning of no-cultivation.” Do the work as much as you will, but do not give rise to the view that you are doing work; the doing too is unobtainable, the being apart too is unobtainable. Cultivation is like crossing a river by boat: while the boat is still in midstream you cannot leave the boat, for if you left it then, would you not fall into the current (a simile for the stream of birth and death) and drown? But when the boat reaches the far shore you must leave it; if you do not leave the boat, how will you reach the other shore of unborn and undying nirvāṇa? When cultivation is truly brought home, there is neither cultivation nor departure from it; there is neither this shore nor the far shore; there is no six realms into which to fall, and no Buddha-way to attain; there is no birth and death to be ended, and no nirvāṇa to be realized. “No birth and death to be ended” is truly ending birth and death; “no nirvāṇa to be realized” is truly realizing nirvāṇa. This is not something settled by talk; it is known only by realization. As it is said, “like a person drinking water, cold and warm known to oneself.”
“In this intrinsic-nature Dzogchen root-path, there are those who attain the state of the svastika sign

(understanding the perfection Dharma according to its measure), or who are instantly liberated: this is the wondrous function of all dharmakāya manifested by the greatly detached body of form and mind, and there is no cultivating and no cultivated.”

In the Dzogchen teachings there are several methods of cultivation; the most essential are “trekchö” and “tögal.” Trekchö means cutting through: instantly cutting off deluded thoughts, the deluded mind and deluded habits. Tögal means leaping over: leaping over the sea of suffering of birth and death at once. The order is to cultivate trekchö first and tögal afterwards. First one must cut through, that is, first one must see the intrinsic nature; to see the intrinsic nature is to see the root. The Ganges Mahāmudrā is at every moment pointing us to see the intrinsic nature, so the Mahāmudrā is the forerunner of Dzogchen, the root of Dzogchen; one may even say the Mahāmudrā is Dzogchen. Hence it is called “the intrinsic-nature Dzogchen root-path.”

On the Buddha's chest there is a svastika sign. The svastika was originally not read as “wan.” Because it represents ten thousand virtues in majesty, pure and undefiled, people came to read it as “wan.” Ten thousand virtues in majesty, pure and undefiled, is “understanding the perfection Dharma according to its measure.” The svastika turns to the right, as it is written. Some say that a svastika on the chest turning right marks a true Buddha and turning left a false Buddha, and that this is how one tells true Buddhas from false ones. But the demon king can also manifest a Buddha's marks — how then would you tell them apart? Others say that if the svastika on the Buddha's chest radiates light that makes the mind cool, it is a true Buddha, and if the light makes the mind feverish and afflicted, it is a false Buddha. All this makes a fuss over marks and does not reach the root. We say: only the markless is the true Buddha; whatever has marks is a false Buddha. For “the reward-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of Dharma”! The reward-body displays the mark of light; the transformation-body appears in bodily form. The Diamond Sutra says, “If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, that person walks the deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.” The Buddha's transformation-body has the thirty-two marks and eighty subsidiary excellences, but that is a false body; if you recognize and cling to this false body, you cannot see the Tathāgata. Only the dharmakāya is the true Buddha, and the dharmakāya is without marks. The reward-body and transformation-body both have marks, so neither is the true Buddha. But speaking from the ultimate, the false is the true and the true is the false; the wholly false is the true and the wholly true is the false. If there were no dharmakāya, from what would the reward-body and transformation-body appear? Can the reward-body and transformation-body be manifested apart from the dharmakāya? Just as no waves can appear apart from water, and no reflection can appear apart from a mirror, so no reward-body and transformation-body can appear apart from the dharmakāya. Where is the dharmakāya? The dharmakāya is the myriad phenomena before your eyes! Apart from the dharmakāya the myriad phenomena could not appear at all. We see the nature through marks, and the nature is the marks and the marks are the nature. To divide true from false is only our own deluded mind discriminating; the dharmakāya is without marks, and without marks yet not without any mark — the dharmakāya has always been just so. To attain the state of the svastika sign is to accomplish the majesty of ten thousand marks, pure and undefiled: it is “understanding the perfection Dharma according to its measure”!

Or who are instantly liberated”: whether we recite the Buddha-name, investigate Chan, or cultivate tantra, we should be doing the work at every moment and in every place, never parted from it for an instant. Walking is thus, sitting is thus, sleeping is thus, eating is thus, doing business is thus; after long, long practice the work matures, and meeting an occasion and a condition — crack! — it is cut off all at once. The deluded habit of clinging to form and marks has been formed over many lives and kalpas; it is because of it that there is rebirth in the six realms. It binds you like a rope, so that your Buddha-nature cannot shine forth. In practicing the Dharma now you must wear this rope through, finer and finer, finer and finer, until at last it is as fine as a hair, and then — crack! — it snaps apart. This is called “instantly liberated.” If you do not work hard at your practice, you will not be instantly liberated. The instant of instant liberation need not be on the cushion. I have told you again and again that in cultivating the Heart Center Dharma the original may not necessarily be broken open on the cushion; it may be while walking, or in sleep and dreams, or in the midst of work, when suddenly within you see no body and mind and without you see no world, and — crack! — it is opened at once. But you must do the work closely and continuously! If you work today and stop tomorrow, fishing three days and drying nets two, or work on the cushion and let the wild horse run off it, that will not do. For you have not worn the rope of delusive thought and attachment thin, and so it will not break. We should work at every moment, abiding in “the Dzogchen root-path”; when the work matures, we will be “instantly liberated.”

This is the wondrous function of all dharmakāya manifested by the greatly detached body of form and mind.” To attain the state of the svastika sign, or to be instantly liberated, is the wondrous function of the dharmakāya, and this wondrous function is manifested by the greatly detached body of form and mind. “Form” refers to the form-body, this shell of ours; “mind” refers to the deluded mind of delusive thoughts and attachments. Our mind always abides on this shell and clings to it as “I”; this is “the view of the body,” which stands first among the five kinds of “view-delusion.” Delusion means confusion, and so this shell is “the shell of ignorance.” The greatly detached body of form and mind is no longer clinging to this shell as “I.” Once “the shell of ignorance” is broken open, the wondrous function of the dharmakāya appears.

Among us who study Buddhism, not a few seek superknowledges. Seeking superknowledges is the worst thing: once there is something sought, one cannot “understand the perfection Dharma according to its measure” and cannot “be instantly liberated.” That is to say, seeking superknowledges obstructs seeing the nature. Seeing the nature is the root; get the root and do not worry about the branches. If only you abide on the intrinsic nature, doing the work at every moment, day by day reducing your deluded mind and deluded habits, reducing and again reducing, reducing and again reducing… crack! — it breaks apart, and the superknowledges and wondrous functions appear of themselves. These are not sought. Superknowledges that are sought are of no use; whatever is obtained by seeking is a conditioned dharma and cannot be relied on. Some people claim to have superknowledges and to foreknow the future, but in fact this is “dependent superknowledge”: they depend on an “ear-reporting spirit.” What is an ear-reporting spirit? It is the “numinous ghost” we spoke of earlier! Because in past lives it was deeply greedy and committed great evil, it fell into hell and suffered greatly. When the suffering was exhausted and it left hell, because the habit of greed remained it was born in the hungry-ghost realm, and it often attaches itself to people and sucks their essence and blood. If a person's mind is empty and non-abiding, it cannot attach itself; but if a person seeks superknowledges, he is just what it can take advantage of. Ghosts have “ghost-superknowledges,” and if you are taken advantage of by one, it will whisper in your ear: tomorrow such-and-such a person will come, such-and-such a thing will happen — and the next day it is so. If you mistakenly think you have superknowledges, you have fallen for its trick; in fact this has nothing whatever to do with superknowledges. You must not listen to it, must not pay it heed, must not rely on it. If you rely on it, you will be entangled by it and cannot attain the Way.

We must not seek superknowledges; we must work closely and continuously at all times and in all places, paying no heed to any circumstance. Working thus diligently for a long time, suddenly the original will be broken open, subject and object both vanish, faculties and dust fall away, and one is instantly liberated. Faculties and dust falling away is “the greatly detached body of form and mind”; subject and object both vanishing means there is no person who cultivates and no Dharma cultivated. At that time there is “no cultivating and no cultivated.” The Buddha-nature is originally perfect and complete in all things and its wondrous function is boundless, able to manifest all that exists. If only we persist in working hard, one day we will suddenly break open, and the state of “no cultivating and no cultivated” will shine clearly before us; then all superknowledges and wondrous functions come without seeking. We must have firm resolve and persevere, with the mind empty and non-abiding at every moment and all things dissolved back into the intrinsic nature, and only then will we accomplish perfectly.

blocks.text: 6. The Method of Cultivating Concentration for Inferior-Capacity Beings on the Gradual Path

inline.s: “If one has not obtained firmness, one is an inferior-capacity being of the gradual path who gives rise to deluded thoughts and is turned by the power of others. One must still forsake noisy and distracting places and diligently cultivate the fully sufficient concentration of stable gathering. Otherwise, though one cultivates long, no path-experience will arise.”

Not obtaining firmness means having no firm resolve and being unable to persevere. The method of cultivation spoken of above — the great cultivation that is no-cultivation — is addressed to those of superior capacity, whose roots are very good; they can follow the Mahāmudrā's teaching, strive in the upward work, and thus obtain firmness. If one is not such a person and cannot persevere in working hard, that is not obtaining firmness. One who cannot become firm is always indolent and procrastinating, always having excuses for not practicing: perhaps lately the body is unwell, with a cold and a cough; perhaps today there is too much to do and no time; perhaps the surroundings are noisy and too loud… in short, today will not do, let it wait until tomorrow. And so, “tomorrow and then tomorrow, how many tomorrows there are” — when will one ever accomplish cultivation? Such a person will certainly “give rise to deluded thoughts and be turned by the power of others,” running after delusive thoughts and moving with circumstances, and so he is an “inferior-capacity being of the gradual path.” His capacity is of the lowest order, suited to the gradual path of three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas; in this life he merely plants good roots, and it will not be easy for him to attain the Way in this life.
