But one who has not obtained firmness is by no means without any hope of attaining the Way in this life. “One must still forsake noisy and distracting places and diligently cultivate the fully sufficient concentration of stable gathering.” Within, not turned by deluded thoughts; without, not moved by circumstances: one needs fully sufficient concentration-power, and this concentration-power is called “the concentration of stable gathering.” One must forsake bustling and noisy places, because such places stir one's mind into confusion. One must find a peaceful, pure place and diligently cultivate the work of concentration, so as to gain the concentration-power one absolutely must have. If he perseveres in working thus, there is still hope of accomplishing it in this life. Otherwise, “though one cultivates long, no path-experience will arise.” In the marketplace, having no concentration-power, the mind turns with circumstances, and if one is unwilling to leave the marketplace for a pure place to cultivate concentration, then however long one cultivates some Dharma-gate, no “path-experience” will arise. The “path-experience” spoken of here is the “emptiness, bliss and clarity” we discussed earlier. Did we not say that one should eliminate “emptiness, bliss and clarity,” and urgently cry “phat” to strip away the shell of “emptiness, bliss and clarity”? Yes. That is to make you realize the “view as the school” directly, not cling to “emptiness, bliss and clarity,” and still less think that obtaining “emptiness, bliss and clarity” is attaining the Way. It is not said that “emptiness, bliss and clarity” are bad; good they are, but a good thing is not as good as none. If you give rise to a mind of seeking and abiding toward “emptiness, bliss and clarity,” you cannot penetrate thoroughly “the intrinsic-nature Dzogchen root-path”; therefore we do not speak of “emptiness, bliss and clarity” in detail. But since we have now raised the question of “path-experience,” let me speak a little of the gradual stages:

Sitting in meditation and practicing concentration has eight stages: coarse abiding, fine abiding, the concentration of the desire-realm, the concentration of not-yet-reached, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna and the fourth dhyāna. What is called “path-experience” is the verification of which stage one has cultivated to. For example, in reciting the Buddha-name, if one can tie the mind to the Buddha-name without distraction, that is “coarse abiding,” and one has only just subdued coarse delusion. Going further, the mind sticks close and does not move, becoming one piece with the Buddha-name — no Buddha outside the mind, no mind outside the Buddha: that is “fine abiding,” and one has subdued fine delusion as well. Going further still, the mind suddenly opens up, and the body rises into emptiness like a cloud or a shadow, so that one feels one has left the seat: this is “the concentration of the desire-realm.” The so-called “three realms” are the desire-realm, the form-realm and the formless realm. The hells, hungry ghosts, animals and human beings, together with the six heavens, all belong to the desire-realm; above these, the first, second, third and fourth dhyāna, these four heavens, belong to the form-realm; above these again belong to the heavens of the formless realm, divided into four: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothing whatsoever, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Having reached “the concentration of the desire-realm,” if one continues to cultivate and body and world suddenly dissolve into emptiness, this is “the concentration of not-yet-reached”: one has left the desire-realm but has not yet reached the form-realm, and has not yet reached the first dhyāna. With a further step in the work, within one sees no body and mind and without one sees no world, and one reaches the first dhyāna. The first dhyāna possesses the “eight touches and ten virtuous qualities.” The “eight touches” are “movement, itch, lightness, heaviness, cold, warmth, smoothness, roughness.” One feels the body is gone, yet these eight sensations arise. The eight sensations do not necessarily appear at the same time, but they do not go beyond these eight. Movement is moving so buoyantly as to surpass the world's wildest revelry; itch is itching so delightfully as to surpass the world's sensual pleasure… in short, the eight touches are all very comfortable, very happy sensations. Bliss arises from detachment from desire, and so the first dhyāna is called “the ground of bliss born of detachment.” The “ten virtuous qualities” are “emptiness, clarity, concentration, wisdom, a good mind, pliancy, joy, bliss, liberation and correspondence,” and these already include “emptiness, bliss and clarity.” Concentration means not being disordered, wisdom means not being dull, joy means not being sorrowful, and there are also the good mind, pliancy, liberation and correspondence — all of these are excellent states, and so they are called the “ten virtuous qualities.” Only by forsaking the sensations of the first dhyāna's eight touches and ten virtuous qualities can one enter the second dhyāna. The second dhyāna is called “the ground of bliss born of concentration”: bliss arises within concentration. Only by forsaking the “joy” of the second dhyāna can one enter the third dhyāna. The third dhyāna is called “the ground of wondrous bliss apart from joy”: a wondrous happiness surpassing joy is produced. Only by forsaking all sensations can one enter the fourth dhyāna. The fourth dhyāna is called “the ground of pure equanimity of mind.” At this time one is pure and equal, and all sensations such as “emptiness, bliss and clarity” are gone.

What we cultivate is Mahāyāna Chan, the perfect and sudden Chan, not the gradual Chan described above; of course we do not speak of these stage-by-stage workings, but neither are we apart from them. Whatever circumstance we meet, we pay it no heed at all, and these sensations soon pass. We take seeing the nature as our school and pay no attention to these matters. Paying no attention does not mean they do not exist; these processes still occur, only they flash past. The Ganges Mahāmudrā is Mahāyāna Buddhadharma: it regards “emptiness, bliss and clarity” as a shell of skin that must be stripped away before the mark of the intrinsic nature can appear nakedly. But an inferior-capacity being of the gradual path has a mind that is not settled and always runs after circumstances. A lustful person, seeing a young and beautiful woman, has his mind run after her; a greedy eater, seeing fine food before him, has his mind stirred and restless. On the cushion and off it he always lets the wild horse run, so that, not to speak of directly realizing “the view as the school,” even “emptiness, bliss and clarity” will not appear. Therefore of such a person it is said, “though one cultivates long, no path-experience will arise.”

“Therefore one should cultivate in retreat, so as to avoid the defilement of habit in one's conduct and ritual, and thus one can fuse the self-ground path-experience wisdom of the fundamental concentration (that is, the wisdom that verifies the power of the Way) with the subsequently attained wisdom (or the wisdom attained after emerging from concentration).”

To leave noisy and distracting places and find a peaceful, pure place to cultivate in retreat can prevent one's “conduct and ritual” from being defiled by habit. “Conduct and ritual” means practice and rules. For example, in cultivating the Heart Center Dharma, if off the cushion one forgets contemplative illumination and the mind is turned by outer objects, that defiles one's practice; if on the cushion one cannot raise the mantra and the mind flows along with deluded thoughts, that defiles one's ritual. What is called “habit” is “habit become nature,” habit turned into second nature. The greatest habit of ordinary people is to give rise to mind toward objects, always clinging to marks. For example, a person fond of wealth, seeing an opportunity to get rich, has his heart thump and pound, and cannot sleep well at night. In former days Layman Pang said, “Much gold confuses the minds of men” — when money is plentiful the mind is disordered — and so he sank his ten thousand strings of family wealth in the river bottom. He wanted only to understand the mind and see the nature, not these gold and silver treasures that obstruct the Way. This was a true cultivator of the Way, who afterwards attained a great accomplishment. Are there still such people today? Of course one cannot say there is not a single one, but they are truly very few.

An inferior-capacity being of the gradual path easily contracts defilement of habit in conduct and ritual; if he can cultivate in retreat, “then he can fuse the self-ground path-experience wisdom of the fundamental concentration (that is, the wisdom that verifies the power of the Way) with the subsequently attained wisdom (or the wisdom attained after emerging from concentration).” The self-ground path-experience wisdom of the fundamental concentration is the fundamental wisdom. The fusing of fundamental wisdom with subsequently attained wisdom is “the meeting of mother and son luminosity” spoken of earlier. This is to say that an inferior-capacity being of the gradual path, if he can cultivate in retreat, can also accomplish it in this life. After “the self-ground path-experience wisdom of the fundamental concentration,” this passage adds a parenthetical gloss: that is, the wisdom that verifies the power of the Way. To verify is to confirm: confirm what? A cultivator of the Way of course verifies the power of the Way, and this is the wisdom that verifies the power of the Way. With what do you verify the power of the Way? Apart from “the numinous knowing in which not one thought arises yet all is perfectly clear,” what else is there! This is the “nature” of understanding the mind and seeing the nature! This is the fundamental wisdom. “Subsequently attained wisdom” also has a gloss: or the wisdom attained after emerging from concentration. Here “emerging” means “transcending,” transcending concentration and non-concentration. This is wondrous function! Subsequently attained wisdom is wondrous function.
“Cultivating in retreat, though one has protectors, depends on the practice of the fundamental concentration-substance.”

A retreat requires someone to protect and support it. There are two kinds of retreat-protector: one is the outer protector, one is the inner protector. The outer protector takes charge of your food, drink and daily life; you are working hard inside the retreat room and cannot go out to buy groceries, and have no time to cook, so someone must look after you — this is the outer protector. The inner protector guides your practice, keeps you from entering demonic obstructions, and points out to you the realization of the great Way. In cultivating in retreat, though one has protectors, the main thing is still “depending on the practice of the fundamental concentration-substance.” The fundamental concentration-substance is the intrinsic nature. The intrinsic nature is originally unborn and undying, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; only because from beginningless kalpas ignorance has stirred deludedly and mind has arisen toward objects has one fallen into the six realms. The one who tied the bell must untie it; one must still rely on one's own diligent cultivation, break through ignorance, and cannot depend on others. If the retreat-protector could attain the Way on our behalf, then Śākyamuni Buddha and Amitābha Buddha would long ago have saved us all, and how would there still be so many ordinary people! To be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is not so easy either; Amitābha Buddha cannot simply drag you there — you must recite the Buddha-name diligently, cut off the root of love, and only then can you be born in the West. Great Master Yinguang said that to be born in the West one must “have the saṃsāra seal broken and the Pure Land document accomplished.” If your root of love is not cut off, if you cling greedily to gold and silver treasures and are attached to wife and children, then plainly the “saṃsāra seal” is not broken — how then can you be born in the West?

Therefore, even in cultivating in retreat, one cannot depend on the retreat-protector, but must rely on one's own diligent effort to open the fundamental wisdom that we ourselves possess, and then fuse it with subsequently attained wisdom, and only then can one attain the Way.

“But if one does not know how to nurture subsequently attained wisdom and make it accord with conduct and ritual, then one merely uses antidotes and cannot overcome outer conditions, so that one is dragged by the conditions of delusive thought into the obstruction of the ordinary and foolish.”

Subsequently attained wisdom is spoken of in relation to fundamental wisdom. Having obtained fundamental wisdom is “the view as the school” — understanding the mind and seeing the nature; after this one must still be tempered amid circumstances in order to bring forth vast wondrous function. Subsequently attained wisdom is wondrous function. To nurture subsequently attained wisdom is to tend and preserve fundamental wisdom over a long time without interruption, being tempered amid circumstances at every moment, protecting the true mind, so as to bring forth immeasurable wondrous function. Conduct and ritual means practice (rules of behavior) and ritual. For example, in cultivating the Heart Center Dharma, to contemplate at every moment off the cushion, not turning with thoughts and not shifting with circumstances, is practice; to sit in cultivation at least two hours each day, with the hand-seal unbroken and the mantra unceasing on the cushion, is ritual. Antidote refers to what was said before: if the mind of lust is strong, cultivate the contemplation of impurity; if the mind is strongly scattered, cultivate concentration in retreat, and so on.

But if one does not know how to nurture subsequently attained wisdom and make it join with our rules of behavior and cultivation ritual, and merely uses antidote methods in practice, then it will be labor lost, and one will be unable to overcome the invasion of outer conditions. Why is this? Because “if one does not recognize the original mind, studying the Dharma brings no benefit.” Merely using antidotes not only makes one fretful but also makes it very easy to cling to marks; not only can one not overcome the influence of outer factors (circumstances), one will also be dragged along and entangled by inner factors (delusive thoughts), and so fall into the “obstruction of the ordinary and foolish.” The foolishness of ordinary people is the “delusion” of “greed, hatred and delusion,” and it obstructs the attainment of the Way, and so is called the “obstruction of the ordinary and foolish.”

blocks.text: 7. Penetrating the Dharmakāya Thoroughly and Preserving It in Luminous Stillness

inline.s: “Therefore to tend and nourish it long and to penetrate thoroughly the subsequently attained is especially important.”

So to tend and nourish subsequently attained wisdom long and to penetrate it thoroughly, preserving and being tempered by it amid circumstances, is especially important. Then how does one tend and nourish subsequently attained wisdom long and penetrate it thoroughly?

“There is no other method: simply do not depart from the view of the fundamentally stable dharmakāya, be without the discriminations of ‘subject and object, right and wrong,’ and so be naturally free and spontaneous, preserving it in luminous stillness. This is the calm abiding and insight of undiscriminating wisdom, the own mark of the unconditioned, co-arisen, naturally-so, and the heart-essence of all practice.”

Recognize that the dharmakāya is fundamentally stable, never coming or going, without any shaking. This right knowledge and view is called “the view of the fundamentally stable dharmakāya.” Once you accord with this right knowledge and view, there is no “person who cultivates,” no “Dharma cultivated,” no right and wrong, no discrimination; soaring and free, free and soaring, luminous yet never disordered, still yet in the great concentration. The great Way is without form; the intrinsic nature is silent and vast. The dharmakāya is thusness unmoving; it is the substance of the great concentration, and it has nothing to do with whether you believe in it or whether you practice the work of entering concentration.

How does one tend and nourish subsequently attained wisdom long and penetrate it thoroughly? There is no other method: only not forsaking “the view of the fundamentally stable dharmakāya,” abiding on the intrinsic nature at every moment, being tempered amid affairs and circumstances, not clinging to marks, not having the discriminations of “subject and object, right and wrong” and the rest — this is the most important. People's delusive thoughts always fly about, and they discriminate everything: this is good and that is bad, this is right and that is wrong, this is true and that is false… and they discriminate endlessly. If at every moment you can be free of the discriminations of “subject and object, right and wrong” and the rest, not abiding in marks and not sticking to objects, so that all is unobtainable and even unobtainability is unobtainable, then the intrinsic nature shines clearly before you at every moment, and you are never apart from “the view of the fundamentally stable dharmakāya”! “The Buddhadharma is not much”: it is easy to speak of, but this is not something settled by hearing and understanding it once; it must be put into actual practice. Only by doing the work thus at every moment can it be put into actual practice. One must “be naturally free and spontaneous, preserving it in luminous stillness.” Stillness means not one thought arises, and carries the sense of “unmoving”; unmoving is concentration. Luminosity means perfectly clear, and carries the sense of “contemplative illumination”; contemplative illumination is wisdom. To preserve “the numinous knowing in which not one thought arises yet all is perfectly clear” is for concentration and wisdom to fuse: wisdom within concentration, concentration within wisdom. Wisdom without concentration is wild wisdom; concentration without wisdom is dead concentration. Therefore an inferior-capacity being of the gradual path cannot merely cultivate concentration in retreat; after leaving retreat he must still be tempered amid affairs and circumstances, so as to tend and nourish subsequently attained wisdom long and penetrate it thoroughly. “Naturally free and spontaneous” is according with conditions; “preserving it in luminous stillness” is not changing. According with conditions yet unchanging, unchanging yet according with conditions: coming into great wealth does not matter, and being poor as a church mouse does not matter; when there is gruel eat gruel, when there is rice eat rice, giving rise to no mind of discrimination, grasping and rejecting, or climbing after conditions. The ancients said, “Luminous stillness is right; luminosity with delusive thought is wrong. Still luminosity is right; stillness with dull blankness is wrong.” This is the wondrous pith instruction for “tending and nourishing it long and penetrating subsequently attained wisdom thoroughly”: not only does it lodge concentration within wisdom and wisdom within concentration, it also prevents dead concentration and wild wisdom.

This is the calm abiding and insight of undiscriminating wisdom, the own mark of the unconditioned, co-arisen, naturally-so, and the heart-essence of all practice.” The calm abiding and insight spoken of here is not the Tiantai school's “great calm abiding and insight,” nor any other calm-abiding-and-insight Dharma-gate, but the “calm abiding and insight of undiscriminating wisdom” — calm abiding and insight practiced by wisdom that does not discriminate. Stillness is calm abiding, luminosity is insight; calm abiding is concentration, insight is wisdom. “Unconditioned” is vast and without fabrication; “co-arisen” is the myriad phenomena; “naturally-so” is being originally thus. The three words unconditioned, co-arisen and naturally-so vividly set off the markless true mark of the dharmakāya. “The heart-essence of all practice” is the core of every Dharma-gate of cultivation. No Dharma-gate of cultivation is apart from luminous stillness, apart from the mutual support of concentration and wisdom, apart from calm abiding and insight. One who recites the Buddha-name ties the mind to the Buddha-name and so gives rise to no other thoughts: this is calm abiding; hearing the Buddha-name distinctly, word by word, perfectly clearly: this is insight. One who investigates Chan has the mass of doubt covering the whole body, with no leisure to give rise to deluded thoughts: this is calm abiding; raising a huatou, perfectly clear: this is insight. Our cultivation of the Heart Center Dharma is likewise: forming the seal and holding the mantra gathers in body and mind — this is calm abiding; mind reciting and ear hearing, hearing perfectly clearly and distinctly — this is insight. The Mahāmudrā teaches us to “be naturally free and spontaneous, preserving it in luminous stillness”: stillness is calm abiding, luminosity is insight.

In the last years of the Ming dynasty, Chan Master Miyun Yuanwu was abbot of Tiantong Monastery in Ningbo. At that time there were many thatched hermitages around Tiantong Monastery, where monks who pressed forward in Chan investigation lived and cultivated exclusively. In the winter solstice of one year, Chan Master Miyun sent an attendant to deliver cotton-padded clothing to the monks in the hermitages. An old recluse in one hermitage said to the attendant, “The old monk has his own mother-born jacket; he has no need of cold-weather clothing.” The attendant reported these words to Chan Master Miyun. Chan Master Miyun said, “This monk seems to have some place of awakening, but I fear it is not genuine; look further into his words.” So he sent the attendant back to ask, “Before your mother was born, what clothing did you wear?” The old recluse could not answer. Chan Master Miyun then instructed this old recluse to investigate the huatou “Before your mother was born, what clothing did you wear?” Three years later the old recluse passed away, having neither broken through the huatou nor uttered a single turning phrase. After cremation there were countless relics, and many people exclaimed in wonder: so many relics — this old recluse cultivated very well! Chan Master Miyun said, “Ten measures of relics are not worth a single turning phrase. You all try to answer in his place.” Not only could those who praised the relics not answer, but none of the five hundred monks then in Tiantong Monastery could answer either. Chan Master Miyun Yuanwu sighed, “Students of the Way are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and not one awakens.” That they could not answer was because they had not accorded with “the own mark of the unconditioned, co-arisen, naturally-so”; had they accorded with such true mark, they would have answered without deliberation. One might well answer him: “The tender peach and plum have just faded, and fresh chrysanthemum and pear have newly opened.” The tender peach and plum blossoms have just fallen, and fresh chrysanthemums and pear blossoms have opened in turn. What does this mean? It lays out whole and entire “the own mark of the unconditioned, co-arisen, naturally-so.” We said before that the insentient preaches the Dharma, and spoke of “the ten thousand dharmas return to one — where does the one return to?” Where does the one return to? Never at any moment or in any place apart from the dharmakāya, never at any moment or in any place apart from the intrinsic nature. These flowers and plants are all insentient, and the insentient too can preach the Dharma; none of it is apart from my dharmakāya! The intrinsic nature is thusness unmoving yet infinitely changing; thusness unmoving is called the dharmakāya, and infinite change is called the reward-body and transformation-body — the three bodies are originally one body. Some people always think that only when many human bodies are transformed forth is there a transformation-body; they do not know that the myriad phenomena, phenomena myriad, are all our transformation-body. Sun, moon and stars, mountains, rivers and the great earth, chickens, ducks, dogs and cats, tables, chairs and benches, food, drink and daily life, men and women, old and young — all are “the own mark of the unconditioned, co-arisen, naturally-so,” all flowing out from the one true Dharma-realm, all our transformation-body. It is only because of your delusive thoughts and attachments, your deliberate discrimination, that you groundlessly give rise to “the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a life-span,” and so bury one fine, naturally-so Buddha in the six realms, and from the place where there are no six realms illusorily manifest the six realms of rebirth, and from the place where there is no suffering illusorily manifest the boundless sea of suffering. Now, if only you make a firm resolve and cultivate the Dharma diligently, and remove the habitual tendencies of attachment and discrimination formed over beginningless kalpas, then you can accomplish it on the spot and be liberated right where you are.
“One who enters the net of doing with a discriminating mind has no time of liberation.”

Some people take superknowledges as the standard of attaining the Way, thinking that only with superknowledges is there any doing, and they are always there discriminating and guessing: so-and-so has superknowledges, so-and-so has none. Do you yourself have superknowledges? If you have none, how can you tell whether others have them? More importantly, superknowledges cannot be the standard of liberation. Ghosts and spirits all have superknowledges — are they all liberated then? If they were all liberated, why are there Buddhist rites to save them? To seek superknowledges is to fall into the net, to fall into the net of doing. Once you fall into the net with a discriminating mind, there is no time of liberation.

Reciting the Buddha-name is also for the sake of protecting our originally luminous substance, and for the sake of ridding ourselves of the discriminating mind. If you are there discriminating about how many times you have recited the Buddha-name, doubting and hesitating — is three hundred recitations a day too few? I have only recited for a year; can I be born in the West? — all of this is the discriminating mind. Whether Buddha-recitation is done well depends on its quality. Great Master Hanshan said, “Reciting Amitābha with the mouth while the mind is scattered, you may shout your throat hoarse and it is still in vain.” If the quality is poor, no matter how many repetitions, it is of no use. One must rid oneself of the discriminating mind; the discriminating mind is the worst thing, for once there is a discriminating mind one falls into the net of doing and cannot be born in the West. In Buddha-recitation and birth in the West, though one is born, one is not born; though one goes, one does not go. This is the unconditioned Dharma, which does nothing and yet leaves nothing undone: not going, yet going all the same; not being born, yet being born all the same. Therefore the great patriarchs of the Pure Land school said, “Birth is decisively birth; going is truly not going.” To have birth and death, coming and going, is all the discriminating mind. The Buddhadharma is the unconditioned Dharma, and one should rid oneself of the discriminating mind. Buddha-recitation requires deep faith, urgent vows and earnest practice; it does not require a discriminating mind. Still less should one compete for superiority and slander other Dharma-gates — that is an even stronger discriminating mind, and not only does one fall into the net of doing and become unable to be liberated, one also brings on oneself the fault of slandering the Dharma.

“This is the naked wisdom of the dharmakāya's self-abiding, the awareness-nature mind that was originally never deluded; one must decisively protect and sustain it without interruption.” (The above is the second secret meaning.)

The undiscriminating calm abiding and insight spoken of above is the wisdom of the dharmakāya's being originally thus, its abiding that is no-abiding. It does not come from outside, is not obtained from others; it is entirely the intrinsic merit revealed by the intrinsic nature, in no way covered over, originally displayed naked and bare, and so it is called “the naked wisdom of the dharmakāya's self-abiding.” If you earnestly follow this Dharma-gate of undiscriminating calm abiding and insight, cultivating diligently, tending long this “naked wisdom of the dharmakāya's self-abiding,” then all great superknowledges come without seeking; but if there is a mind that seeks superknowledges, you fall into the net of doing, and not only can you not be liberated, you cannot even bring forth superknowledges; and if the discriminating mind that seeks superknowledges is taken advantage of by nature-spirits, ghosts and goblins, so that they possess you, the consequences are beyond imagining.

This “naked wisdom of the dharmakāya's self-abiding” is “the numinous knowing in which not one thought arises yet all is perfectly clear”; it is the awareness-nature mind that was originally without delusion or awakening. “Revealing, awakening, entering and penetrating the ten realms; the myriad phenomena are naturally-so, without delusion or awakening” — sun, moon and stars, mountains, rivers and the great earth, men and women, old and young, each and every thing are all naturally-so, all possessing the Buddha-nature; it is naturally so, neither deluded nor awakened, and so it is called “the awareness-nature mind that was originally never deluded.” The awareness-nature was originally never deluded, and there is no awakening either; it does not increase upon entering the Buddha-realm, nor decrease through passing into the hells. But because ignorance covers it and deluded attachments and deluded grasping arise, the Buddha-nature cannot be revealed, and it is provisionally named “delusion.” If only one cultivates the Way diligently, breaks through ignorance, is tempered amid affairs, and removes the habits of giving rise to mind toward objects and of deluded attachment and deluded grasping, then one can restore the natural-so of the intrinsic nature, and it is provisionally named “awakening.” Delusion and awakening are both provisional names; once we break through ignorance, delusion too is unobtainable and awakening too is unobtainable. The Buddha-nature does not belong to delusion or awakening; even wrapped in ignorance, the luminosity of the intrinsic nature still exists, neither increasing nor decreasing by a single hair. “In pursuit of learning one increases day by day; in pursuit of the Way one decreases day by day.” What the cultivator of the Way must decrease is only the ignorance and habitual tendencies; the naturally-so Buddha-nature was never deluded or awakened, never increased or decreased.

That cultivation does not succeed is because one has not protected this naturally-so Buddha-nature well. Therefore it says, “one must decisively protect and sustain it without interruption” — this is extremely important. “Decisively” means making a great vow with all one's heart and forming a great resolve; “protecting and sustaining” means not turning with thoughts and not shifting with circumstances, never apart from this in walking, standing, sitting and lying down, never for a second apart from the intrinsic nature; “without interruption” means it cannot be broken at any moment. If one cultivates intermittently, fishing three days and drying nets two, advancing one step and retreating two, unable to sustain without interruption, then one cannot attain the Way. For example, in our cultivation of the Heart Center Dharma, if we sit once a day that is only two hours, leaving twenty-two hours. If the twenty-two hours are spent letting the wild horse run, and only two hours are spent cultivating concentration, then the proportion of time is not even one tenth — how can one attain the Way like that? Still more, if one cultivates today and stops tomorrow, then all the less can one attain the Way. So we say that contemplation is the primary practice and sitting is the auxiliary practice. Contemplation is not turning with thoughts and not shifting with circumstances, so that the intrinsic nature is never for a second forsaken — this is precisely for the sake of protecting and sustaining without interruption! Cultivating the Pure Land is the same: Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta taught us the method of Buddha-recitation: “Gather in all six faculties; the pure thought continues in succession.” “In succession” is without interruption. “Pure thought” means that the work of Buddha-recitation has become thoroughly proficient, so that the mind that recites and the Buddha recited fall away at once, with no subject and no object, no purity and no defilement, and the naturally-so Buddha-nature shines clearly before one — only this can be called “pure thought.” Some people get it wrong, thinking that being able to recite “Namo Amitābha Buddha” continuously without break is pure thought continuing in succession; in fact this is far from it. You must know that “reciting Amitābha with the mouth while the mind is scattered, you may shout your throat hoarse and it is still in vain”! The Pure Land school does not set a low standard but a very high one. Nowadays some people are lazy and unwilling to work hard; they recite a few Buddha-names carelessly and not “with all their hearts,” which is as good as not reciting, and yet they dream of being born in the West. And if they are not born there, then it is Amitābha Buddha's fault. They even instruct others that one need not be single-minded and undisturbed. Alas, a fine Pure Land school that reaches through the three times, spans the ten directions, covers all three capacities and gathers in both the sharp and the dull has been misunderstood by them to this degree — how could it not grieve one to the utmost?

To decisively protect and sustain without interruption — this is the second secret essential meaning. Then what is the first secret essential meaning? It is “the view as the school” spoken of earlier. The Mahāmudrā is the one true Dharma-realm, and the one true Dharma-realm is our naturally-so Buddha-nature: it is present at all times and in all places, and the myriad phenomena, phenomena myriad, are all its transformations. First one must see the nature before one can protect and sustain it; if you do not see the naturally-so Buddha-nature, then what are you protecting and sustaining? In brief, the first is understanding the mind and seeing the nature, and the second is close and continuous preserving and sustaining — these are the first and second secret essential meanings.
Not Apart from the Dharmakāya

blocks.text: 1. Recognizing the Importance of the “Liberation-Substance Wisdom”

inline.s: “Concentration is the essence of supreme practice. Without the power of the Way of liberation-wisdom, abiding only in the practice of rest, one still cannot pass beyond the form realm and the formless realm, because one cannot overcome the arising of greed and hatred and the streams of all karmic actions.”

“The essence of supreme practice” means practice of the utmost importance. The “concentration” of “view, concentration, practice” is practice of the utmost importance. Liberation-wisdom is the view as the school and its protection, spoken of earlier. The power of the Way of liberation-wisdom is the power that brings forth immeasurable wondrous function from the view of the substance; this is what the Chan school calls the great mechanism and great function. Here “rest” means resting the mind and ceasing thoughts. The practice of rest is suppressing thoughts so they do not arise — the work of “carrying a stone to press down the grass.” Abiding only in the practice of rest is stopping only at the stage of suppressing thoughts so they do not arise. We mentioned earlier the three realms of “desire realm, form realm and formless realm”; the “form realm and formless realm” here refer to the “four dhyāna heavens” (form realm) and the “four formless heavens” (formless realm). The meaning of this passage is: although cultivating concentration, and even cultivating concentration-power exclusively in retreat, is practice of the utmost importance, if one merely rests the mind and ceases thoughts without the power to realize the substance and bring forth its function, then it is still worldly concentration: though one has passed beyond the desire realm, one has not passed beyond the form realm and formless realm, and one is still within the heavenly paths of the six realms.

Why is this? “Because one cannot overcome the arising of greed and hatred and the streams of all karmic actions.” Such a person can rest the mind and cease thoughts, and “greed and hatred” can be temporarily suppressed, but the conditions for the arising of greed and hatred are still there. “Arising” refers to conditions. “The arising of greed and hatred” is the conditions that give rise to greed and hatred. Why can resting the mind and ceasing thoughts not overcome the arising of greed and hatred? Because he does not recognize the intrinsic nature, and the habit of giving rise to mind toward objects is still present. When a circumstance comes, he has no freedom and is turned by it. For example, when a beautiful woman appears, if you counter your mind of lust by seeing her as a white skeleton or as skin wrapped around pus and blood, that is still an antidote method. Speaking from the root, all marks are false and delusive; every mark is a shadow manifested by the true mind. If the true mind shines clearly before you, no mark of man or woman is to be found at all. When the true mind shines clearly before you and you do not lose it when facing circumstances, that is the power of the Way of liberation-wisdom. Without this power of the Way, one will be deluded by circumstances and turned by them. Because of delusion one creates karma, and because of karma one receives retribution — cause and effect, effect and cause, the six realms of rebirth with no time of escape. This is “the streams of all karmic actions.” Abiding in the “concentration” of resting the mind and ceasing thoughts can only temporarily suppress greed and hatred, but cannot overcome the arising of greed and hatred. In the Chan school this is called “cold water soaking a stone; still water hides no dragon.” Once the concentration-power fades and the habitual tendencies well up, greed and hatred are even stronger — like a stone pressing down grass: remove the stone and the grass grows again. Of course it cannot overcome the streams of all karmic actions.

“Because one has not obtained the power of the Way of the decision-mind, toward delightful and desirable objects and favorable conditions one gives rise to greed and love, and toward adverse conditions and thwarting conditions one gives rise to hatred, as when toward sickness and pain one gives rise to the perception of suffering, and so on.”

Not having obtained the power of the Way of the decision-mind means not recognizing the intrinsic nature. If you recognize the intrinsic nature and know that all things are false, know that all things are shadows of the true mind, with absolutely no doubt, then when facing circumstances your mind will not move and you will not cling to marks. Therefore we must truly realize the intrinsic nature. The Mahāmudrā points us to see the nature and teaches us to be diligent in protecting it, to be tempered amid circumstances, and to truly realize it in that tempering. We must, in that tempering, dissolve body, mind and world into emptiness and truly see the intrinsic nature; only then do we have “the power of the Way of the decision-mind.” If we are not tempered, there will be no power. You hear this teaching here, and at this moment you seem to have great power, but the moment you step out the door you forget it all — what use is that? You must still work steadily and solidly. Here are two methods of doing the work. One is, after hearing the instruction and recognizing the intrinsic nature, to protect it at every moment: “morning here, evening here, in wandering and hardship here” — protect it unmoving at every moment, and as soon as a thought arises turn it around and do not run after it, persisting in this over the long term. The other is to cultivate a concrete Dharma-gate, either Buddha-recitation, or Chan investigation, or the Heart Center Dharma. Not only work on the cushion but also off the cushion, contemplating at every moment and preserving and sustaining closely and continuously; only thus is there any effect. Otherwise, when you see something beautiful you will still be moved, and when you meet an adverse circumstance you will still give rise to anger and resentment. This is “toward delightful and desirable objects and favorable conditions one gives rise to greed and love, and toward adverse conditions and thwarting conditions one gives rise to hatred.”

As when toward sickness and pain one gives rise to the perception of suffering, and so on.” Here are several examples of sickness as a condition appearing before one, to see how the ancients dealt with the condition of sickness. Chan Master Mazu Daoyi was a remarkable great patriarch of the Chan school, known to the world as “Great Master Ma”; he trained more than a hundred disciples who realized the great Way, and sent them out to all regions to teach the world. In his later years Great Master Ma fell ill, and the prior of the monastery came to inquire after him: “How is the Reverend's health these days?” Great Master Ma said, “Sun-face Buddha, moon-face Buddha.” What does this mean? Sun-face is daytime, a simile for times of health; moon-face is nighttime, a simile for times of illness. Buddha means the Awakened One. Awake in the daytime and awake at night too; thus in health and thus in illness. Though only six characters, it simply and clearly sets out Great Master Ma's “power of the Way of the decision-mind.” Chan Master Ciming Chuyuan of the Song dynasty was also a remarkable great patriarch of the Chan school; in his later years he suddenly suffered a stroke and his mouth became twisted. His attendant stamped his feet in alarm: “What is to be done! All your life you scolded the Buddhas and reviled the patriarchs, and now it has come to this.” What is to be done! Usually you scold the Buddhas and revile the patriarchs, and now the retribution has come. Chan Master Ciming said, “Do not worry. I will straighten it for you.” You need not fret; I will straighten it for you. So saying, he used his hand to set his mouth straight, and the twisted mouth immediately became normal. Sickness and pain are also karmic obstructions: “When it is understood, karmic obstruction is originally empty; when it is not understood, one must still repay former debts.” On the body of a great patriarch who has understood the Way, karmic debts are received if he chooses to receive them and not received if he chooses not to. The body is like a house; it must fail in the end, and one lives in it as long as one can, and when one cannot, one simply gives it up. If it is failing and you still cling to it greedily and cannot let go, then suffering comes, and that suffering is of your own making. When Chan Master Chongyun Zhihui was about to pass away, he wrote a verse for everyone to see: “I have a house, built for me by father and mother. I have lived in it eighty years, and lately I feel it wearing out. I meant to move elsewhere, but the matter involves love and hate. When at last it crumbles, neither of us will be hindered.” Having written it, he sat cross-legged and passed away. It is not always like this; here is another example. When Chan Master Cuiyan Kezhen was about to enter nirvāṇa, he manifested an extremely painful appearance of illness, tossing and turning on the mat spread on the ground, rolling over and over without cease. His attendant wept and said, “All your life you scolded the Buddhas and reviled the patriarchs; why has it come to this?” If you had not scolded the Buddhas and reviled the patriarchs all your life, how could it be like this now? Chan Master Cuiyan stared at the attendant for a while and rebuked him: “Do you too hold such a view?” Are you also of this opinion! Then Chan Master Cuiyan sat cross-legged and told the attendant to burn incense. As soon as the incense smoke rose, the Master passed away. You all — since Chan Master Cuiyan had the assurance of passing away sitting or standing, why did he manifest such a painful appearance of illness? He was preaching the Dharma with his own body: suffering is liberation, affliction is bodhi, birth and death are nirvāṇa. When did he ever “give rise to the perception of suffering toward sickness and pain”!

If you “give rise to the perception of suffering toward sickness and pain,” then it is terrible: the sickness-demon will torment you with gusto. But if the mind does not abide on the sickness and pain — “if it hurts, let it hurt; it does not matter, it is nothing” — then on the contrary you do not feel the pain. Again, in cultivating the Heart Center Dharma, when the fingers hurt greatly from forming the hand-seal, do not let the mind think of the hand; concentrate your attention on the mantra, forget the hand, and you will not feel the hand's pain. But as soon as you give rise to a delighted mind — “Oh, the hand does not hurt anymore” — with that one thought the hand hurts again at once. Therefore the sensation of suffering in the end is still a matter of whether the brain accepts it or not. As long as our mind is empty and non-abiding, illness will also be cured, and even if there is pain we will not feel suffering. The Pure Land school puts it this way: “At the time of death, the body is without suffering, the mind is not inverted, the intent is not scattered.” To be without bodily suffering is not to be afflicted by illness; it does not necessarily mean not falling ill at all. If when ill you do not think of the illness but simply recite the Buddha-name, “Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha…,” concentrating your attention on the Buddha-name so that you do not feel the suffering, that is to be without bodily suffering. But if your mind is disordered and you think of the sickness and pain — “Oh, oh!” — then it hurts so much you could die. If you usually work very hard and have deep power of practice, then there is no illness or no-illness, no pain or no-pain. “When the mind can turn things, one is thus-come”; if you truly reach the point of the mind's being empty and non-abiding, illness too can be turned, as with Chan Master Ciming, who with a push of his hand immediately set straight the mouth twisted by his stroke. With somewhat shallower practice, one can still be free of suffering from illness. Therefore we must make the mind empty and pure at every moment. If our mind is not empty and pure, and at the end of life we are pressed by illness, suffering and misery, the mind will be unsettled. I have seen many cultivators of the Pure Land who, when death approached, were told, “You must now work hard at reciting the Buddha-name; this is the critical moment, you are about to be born in the West. The critical moment has come — recite the Buddha-name quickly!” Guess what they said: “Oh! What Buddha-name is there to recite! I am in such pain I could die, so miserable I cannot bear it, I cannot recite.” They simply do not recite, because their minds are scattered. Our working hard at Buddha-recitation now is preparation for use at the single instant of death. If at the time of death one's mind can remain unscattered and one can still recite “Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha…” like this, then birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is absolutely assured. Everyone, work hard! Examples like this are truly too many.
“All that arises is the manifestation of the intrinsic nature's function. Therefore to recognize the liberation-substance wisdom is of the utmost importance.”

We have just said that one must not “give rise to greed and love toward delightful and favorable objects, or hatred toward adverse and thwarting conditions, as when toward sickness and pain one gives rise to the perception of suffering.” Why must one not think this way? Because “all that arises is the manifestation of the intrinsic nature's function.” Do not think that delightful objects and favorable conditions are good and adverse conditions and thwarting conditions are bad, that health is good and illness is bad. Where do these bad adverse conditions and thwarting conditions, and even sickness and pain, come from? They are all manifestations of the intrinsic nature; without the intrinsic nature, where would these conditions come from? We must sharply awaken and understand that these conditions, and even the mind of hatred, are all manifestations of the intrinsic nature — and then naturally we will not hate! The intrinsic nature itself is neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking. Without the bodhi intrinsic nature, even affliction would not exist, just as without water there would be no waves. Precisely because the waves themselves are water, it is said that “affliction is bodhi.” In cultivating the Way we must sharply awaken at every moment: as soon as affliction arises, sharply awaken, and with that sharp awakening we return to the original position, and it naturally shines clearly before us; affliction immediately becomes wholly unobtainable. This is the liberation-substance wisdom.

Therefore to recognize the liberation-substance wisdom is of the utmost importance.” Therefore the recognition of the liberation-substance wisdom is extremely important. Recognize the mind of numinous knowing, not deluded thoughts; recognize the substance of emptiness and stillness, not the form-body. As soon as a deluded thought arises, sharply awaken at once; the mind of numinous knowing appears before you, and the deluded thought instantly melts like ice. One must not recognize the form-body as “I”; cling to this shell of form and you are in trouble. The form-body is like a house: it is not “I,” it is only a temporary dwelling. We must do the work thus at every moment.

blocks.text: 2. The Method of Eliminating Deluded Thoughts: Not Apart from the Dharmakāya

inline.s: “If one has not obtained the essence of arising and ceasing (thoughts), then the deluded thoughts that leak out are all karmic causes of rebirth. Therefore, whether deluded thoughts are coarse or fine, one must let arising and ceasing follow into nothingness while protecting and cultivating well. That is, one neither lets them run so that they blaze up, nor uses a thought to cure a thought. One only does not depart from the natural substance in contemplating them, so that they do not continue, like drawing a picture in water: as one draws, it vanishes.”

The essence of arising and ceasing is the key point of thoughts arising and thoughts ceasing. What then is this key point? “The green mountain is originally unmoving; the white clouds come and go as they please.” The green mountain is a simile for the intrinsic nature, the white clouds a simile for deluded thoughts: the intrinsic nature does not move or shake, while deluded thoughts have arising and ceasing. Though thoughts have arising and ceasing, “to recognize them is no injustice”! To recognize them is to have obtained the essence of arising and ceasing. If one does not recognize them, and a deluded thought has arisen without your knowing it, then you have not obtained the essence of arising and ceasing. “If one has not obtained the essence of arising and ceasing, then the deluded thoughts that leak out are all karmic causes of rebirth.” In cultivating the Heart Center Dharma we stress “contemplation is the primary practice, sitting is the auxiliary practice” precisely in order to highlight the role of contemplation: when a deluded thought comes you must see it, sharply awaken at once, and pay the thought no heed. If you cannot see it, then plainly you have run after the deluded thought — this is “leaking out.” These leaked deluded thoughts are all karmic causes of rebirth in the six realms. To run after thoughts is inevitably to turn with circumstances. After clinging to circumstances one creates karma, and after creating karma one receives retribution, so that there is no time of escape from the six realms of rebirth. It is like a bucket with a hole: the water of the intrinsic nature's wondrous function all leaks away, and one falls to become an ordinary being of the six realms. Falling is the karmic fruit, leaking is the karmic cause. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says, “At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; toward all deluded minds, do not extinguish them either.” The first half teaches us not to leak, not to let deluded thoughts pass, sharply awakening so that deluded thoughts do not arise. And fearing that we might misunderstand and do the work of “dead concentration,” suppressing thoughts so they do not arise, it immediately continues with the second half: “toward all deluded minds, do not extinguish them either.” Do not extinguish deluded thoughts altogether either. Why? In order to bring forth boundless wondrous function and save immeasurable sentient beings! If the true mind can be master, then speech and conversation, raising the hand and moving the foot, the arising of thoughts and the stirring of mind — all are the wondrous function of the intrinsic nature. The five-superknowledge seer asked the Buddha, “What is that one superknowledge?” He had five superknowledges, and the Buddha had six — what was that one superknowledge? The Buddha called his name: “Five-superknowledge seer!” He answered, “Yes?” The Buddha said, “That one superknowledge — you ask me.” With one call and one answer, one question and one reply, the wondrous function of the intrinsic nature is displayed vividly. This is “that one superknowledge” — the superknowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. The exhaustion of outflows means not leaking in the least: the outflows are utterly exhausted. Therefore, though the true mind may seem like that of a fool, great wisdom appearing as foolishness, if no thought arose and no mind stirred, how could boundless wondrous function arise? If all the waves were extinguished, would it not become a stagnant pool? Hence “toward all deluded minds, do not extinguish them either.” Recognize the true mind, let the true mind be master, and deluded thoughts are wondrous function; fail to recognize the true mind, let deluded thoughts be master, and it is leaking, it is the karmic cause of rebirth. This is “the essence of arising and ceasing.” Let me borrow the green mountain and white clouds once more to praise this “essence of arising and ceasing” in a verse: “White clouds drift over the green mountain, the green mountain still is there; the green mountain is its own green mountain, how could white clouds hinder it.”

Therefore, whether deluded thoughts are coarse or fine, one must let arising and ceasing follow into nothingness while protecting and cultivating well.” Deluded thoughts are coarse and fine; what is the difference between coarse delusion and fine delusion? Coarse delusion is giving rise to mind toward objects: delight in favorable circumstances, worry in adverse circumstances, unknowingly running after circumstances. We must first cut off this coarse delusion, understanding that all outer circumstances are false, like flowers in the sky and the moon in the water, wholly unobtainable. The Diamond Sutra says, “All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should one contemplate them.” Here “should” carries the sense of according with and dealing with. Toward all outer circumstances, favorable and adverse, deal with them as you must, and at the same time contemplate them thus, seeing all outer circumstances as a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, morning dew, lightning — wholly unobtainable. Contemplating thus at every moment, after a long time one will no longer be moved by outer circumstances and will have basically cut off coarse delusion. After this, “perfuming habit” still remains. Perfuming habit is the seed of habitual tendency in the field of the eighth consciousness; even if you do not think of it, it will leap up by itself, and this is called “turning up seeds.” Such deluded thoughts are finer than the “coarse delusion” just described, but they are not yet fine delusion. When sitting in meditation one more easily perceives the churning of the seeds, and toward this we still pay no heed, and so enter concentration peacefully. Only what is seen within concentration is fine delusion, like an underwater current, surging and moving. Without entering deeply into concentration one simply cannot see fine delusion at all.

Whether deluded thoughts are coarse or fine, “one must let arising and ceasing follow into nothingness while protecting and cultivating well.” When a deluded thought comes, you must perceive it, then sharply awaken, pay it no heed and not run after it, and it naturally dissolves into formlessness. This is called “arising and ceasing follow into nothingness”: following your awakening, the arising and ceasing of thoughts dissolve into emptiness. But if you cannot perceive it, or do not sharply awaken, the deluded thought will stir without cease, thought following thought without interruption, and then it becomes a karmic cause of rebirth. “Protecting and cultivating well” is protecting and correcting well. Protect what? Correct what? Protect the numinous, luminous, non-abiding true mind; correct the deluded thoughts that flow on without cease. When you perceive a deluded thought, you must sharply awaken at once, at once “let arising and ceasing follow into nothingness”; do not run along for a stretch before sharply awakening. Some people know when a deluded thought has arisen, but they are reluctant to stop; they say, “Let me think it over a little more, let me consider it before I sharply awaken.” Since you already know it is a deluded thought, why go on thinking? Is this not the height of folly? This is plainly flowing along with deluded thoughts! It should not be so; you must sharply awaken at once and let arising and ceasing follow into nothingness. You must protect our true mind at every moment, always clearly knowing, with nothing abided in and nothing stuck to — this is “protecting and cultivating well.”

That is, one neither lets them run so that they blaze up, nor uses a thought to cure a thought.” To let run is to indulge, to let the wild horse go, to run after thoughts. To make blaze is to make thoughts burn without cease, leaping from Zhang San to Li Si, from Li Si to Zhao Wu… flowing on without rest. It is like a great fire burning, ever hotter and fiercer. To indulge thoughts so that they burn on without cease is to “let them run so that they blaze up.” We must not “let them run so that they blaze up”; we must quickly transform them. How to transform? There are two ways. One is to think to yourself: what is the consequence of “letting them run so that they blaze up”? It will be unthinkable! It is the karmic cause of rebirth in the six realms, suffering beyond words! Awaken sharply at once and let the intrinsic nature shine clearly before you. If the deluded thought is too strong and sharp awakening cannot transform it either, then use the second way: quickly recite the Buddha-name or quickly hold a mantra, using the Buddha-thought and the right thought to replace the deluded thought. Both ways are “not letting them run so that they blaze up,” but you must absolutely not “use a thought to cure a thought.” What is using a thought to cure a thought? A deluded thought arises and you bring up another thought to suppress the original deluded thought: “Oh, this thought is a deluded thought, bad, bad, stop it at once.” This is using a thought to cure a thought. Why is using a thought to cure a thought no good? It has two outcomes. One is that it cannot suppress the deluded thought and in fact becomes “the flowing on of deluded thoughts.” The other is that even if you can cure it for a time and suppress the thought to death, it is like “carrying a stone to press down grass: remove the stone and the grass grows again.” After the thought has been pressed to death it becomes like earth, wood, metal or stone — dead. Such “dead concentration” is time-limited: even if you can stay in concentration for several hundred or several thousand years… when the concentration-power fades the deluded thoughts come again, and with even greater force, and the six realms of rebirth are as before; it is still not ultimate. Therefore we do not use a thought to cure a thought and do not press thoughts to death; we transform, sharply awakening and turning them around. When our strength is insufficient, we hold mantras and recite the Buddha-name.

One only does not depart from the natural substance in contemplating them, so that they do not continue, like drawing a picture in water: as one draws, it vanishes.” The natural substance is our naturally-so Buddha-nature. The Buddha-nature is unborn and undying, unmoving and unshaking, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing. To contemplate is the “sharp awakening” just spoken of. If only you sharply awaken and return to the natural substance, that is enough. We must never depart from the natural substance at any moment; when a deluded thought comes, sharply awaken at once, so that the deluded thought cannot continue. If a deluded thought comes and you do not even know it, then it will not do. Therefore “contemplation” has two senses: one is that when a deluded thought comes you must know it, and the other is the sharp awakening. There is a simile, “like a cat catching a mouse,” in which deluded thoughts are compared to mice. You must have a cat's alertness: the moment a mouse pokes its head out, it is discovered at once. In the Chan school this is called “caring for the huatou,” and caring is keeping a good watch on it. This thought of “keeping watch” is right thought, and in doing the work right thought must not be lost. Right thought is like the guard at a government office gate, blocking idlers and strangers and not letting them in. Right thought is the wondrous function of the Buddha-nature. If right thought is lost, either one cannot perceive the profusion of deluded thoughts, or one does the work of dead concentration and turns into earth, wood, metal and stone. These are the two forked roads in doing the work. Therefore the Chan school raises the mass of doubt, the Pure Land school holds fast to the Buddha-name, the tantric school holds mantras and forms seals, and the Mahāmudrā tells us to “not depart from the natural substance in contemplating.”

What is the purpose of contemplation? “So that they do not continue.” That is, not to let deluded thoughts continue, to cut deluded thoughts off. Therefore we say that the function of Buddha-recitation is to cut off deluded thoughts; the Buddha's holy name is a sword of wisdom, “Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha…” — the Buddha-thought appears before you and naturally cuts deluded thoughts off in the midst of formlessness. If you recite the Buddha-name on the one hand while deluded thoughts turn upside down on the other, then that is not Buddha-recitation. In Buddha-recitation there must be “calm abiding and insight”; there must be mind reciting and ear hearing. To recite the Buddha-name in the mind so that deluded thoughts do not arise is calm abiding; to hear the Buddha-name with the ear and be perfectly clear is insight. Whatever the work in Buddhism, its purpose is to make deluded thoughts not continue. “Like drawing a picture in water: as one draws, it vanishes.” Let the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts be like drawing a picture on the surface of water: as you draw, it vanishes with the drawing, leaving not the slightest trace behind — arising and ceasing follow into nothingness.
“But though deluded thoughts cease of themselves, this is not yet purity, because merely knowing deluded thoughts one still cannot cut off the stream of confused karma.”

Even if deluded thoughts do not arise and cease of themselves, that still does not count as purity. Someone is bewildered: if deluded thoughts have ceased, surely that is purity? Why is it said not to count as purity? Because “merely knowing deluded thoughts one still cannot cut off the stream of confused karma.” Merely knowing the state of deluded thoughts, knowing that these are deluded thoughts, without recognizing the true mind — that still will not do. Only after recognizing the true mind can one cut off the stream of confused karma. Confusion means being deluded upon contact with objects, so that the mind becomes disordered. Seeing gold ingots, the mind is stirred and disordered, wanting to get rich; seeing a beautiful woman, the mind is stirred and disordered, the fire of lust burning one's body… these are all confusion. You plainly know that these are all shadows, all false, all unobtainable, and yet you cannot cut them off. Why? Because you only know the state of deluded thoughts and do not recognize the true mind. What the true mind is, you do not know; therefore you have no power, and meeting circumstances your mind is still moved, and so you cannot cut off the stream of confused karma. We ordinary beings, having lost the intrinsic nature, take things as the self, chase after objects, create karma and receive retribution, like a river flowing on without cease. Past karma is like seeds planted in the field of the eighth consciousness — how is it to be cut off? Only by realizing the true mind and cutting off the root can it be cut off. Therefore, to cut off the stream of confused karma one must realize the true mind; merely knowing that deluded thoughts cease of themselves is not enough.
“One must, at the very moment of knowing that deluded thoughts cease of themselves, recognize and clearly see the wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness, and then one naturally abides.”

The wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness” is the fundamental consciousness, the eighth consciousness returning from delusion to awakening, turned around. When the eighth consciousness turns, it becomes “amala-consciousness” (the immaculate consciousness), also called the pure consciousness. This is the so-called “turning consciousness into wisdom,” turning the eighth consciousness into the great perfect mirror wisdom. To “clearly see” the wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness is to see the great perfect mirror wisdom plainly, which is the intrinsic nature shining clearly before one, which is the numinous knowing true mind — in which not one thought arises yet all is perfectly clear — shining clearly before one. Only thus can one cut off the stream of confused karma. To “clearly see the wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness” is not difficult; the difficulty lies in your not understanding and not recognizing it, that is, the difficulty of not “recognizing” it. To “recognize and clearly see the wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness” is called “seizing it in one grab” in the Chan school, “the flower opens and one sees the Buddha and awakens to the unborn” in the Pure Land school, and “entering the accomplishment” in the tantric school.

One must, at the same time as knowing that “deluded thoughts cease of themselves,” “recognize and clearly see the wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness.” When there are no deluded thoughts, one must recognize and take up the true mind, recognize and take up our true Buddha-nature. The Buddha-nature is wisdom-nature — the nature of wisdom — because all work, all superknowledges, all wondrous functions arise from it, and so it is called “wisdom-nature.” Merely knowing that deluded thoughts arise and cease into nothingness, without recognizing and taking up the true mind, still cannot cut off the stream of confused karma. One must recognize and take up the true mind, and understand further that the deluded mind arises from the true mind. When the deluded mind is cut off, what is this that is unborn in not one thought yet always clearly knowing? This is precisely the true mind, precisely the “great perfect mirror wisdom.” At the place where deluded thoughts are cut off, one must recognize the true mind and experience the true mind. If one cannot seize it in one grab, then one has “missed it face to face,” and cannot see the nature. To “see the nature” is to understand. Understand that the deluded mind is unobtainable, understand that the deluded mind is the wondrous function of the true mind. At the place where the deluded mind rests, one “grabs” the true mind on the spot. It is not that you grab some thing with your hand; the true mind is without form or mark, and “to say it resembles a thing misses it at once.” It is not that there exists a thing with marks waiting for you to grab, but that you must experience it, recognize it, affirm it. When the deluded mind has settled down, to recognize and take up the true mind is very, very important. I have reminded everyone again and again: at the time of “the break between before and after,” that is, when the former thought has ceased and the latter thought has not yet arisen, what is this? At this moment you should rouse your spirit to the utmost, recognize the true mind, affirm the true mind, believe in it without doubt, and take it up. After recognizing and taking up the true mind, one no longer clings to marks, and all deluded thoughts are transformed into wondrous function.

The true mind has no form or mark; whatever has form or mark is a false appearance, a shadow, wholly unobtainable. Knowing this, we will not cling to things that have marks. Only then is there power to let go of marks, cast off marks, and not abide in marks. If one does not recognize the true, one is always deluded by the false. “When the false is taken as the true, the true too becomes false.” Because one does not recognize the true, one cannot but take up the false, and so “takes the thief as one's father” and buries the true mind. This is the most, most important question. One must understand where deluded thoughts come from. What are deluded thoughts? Deluded thoughts are not a bad thing; deluded thoughts are the wondrous function arising from our true mind. Do not fear deluded thoughts; only do not run after them, recognize their original face, not stick to objects, not abide in objects, not cling to marks, and at every moment awaken as soon as a thought arises and cut it off as soon as it arises. At the place where one thought is cut off, “the wisdom-nature of one's own consciousness” will shine clearly before one. What is called “no-thought” is not necessarily the absence of even a single thought. If not a single thought arose, one would become earth, wood, metal and stone; that is annihilation, is blankness, not no-thought. No-thought means that thoughts arise but one does not abide in them. A monk asked Zhaozhou, “Does a newborn baby still possess the six consciousnesses?” A baby just born knows nothing at all, and surely cannot give rise to mind toward objects with delusive thoughts flying about! Does a baby possess the six consciousnesses of “eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind”? In fact this is using the baby as a simile to ask what “no-thought” is. Zhaozhou answered, “Hitting a ball on a rushing stream.” The monk then asked Touzi, “Hitting a ball on a rushing stream — what is the meaning?” Touzi answered, “Thought after thought without lingering.” Hitting a ball on a very swift stream, can the ball come to rest? It is swept away at once. “Without lingering” is non-abiding. It is clear that thoughts arising without abiding is no-thought, and it is not that only when there is not a single thought is it called no-thought. We have pointed it out again and again: at the place where one thought is cut off, this perfectly clear knowing is our numinous knowing mind, and this is the true mind, the true-so Buddha-nature. To recite the Buddha-name is to be mindful of this Buddha. Buddha means the Awakened One. To recite the Buddha-name is to be mindful and awake in every thought; this is the true meaning of Buddha-recitation. Not understanding this true meaning and reciting the Buddha-name in a muddled way is as good as not reciting at all. My teacher (Master Wang Xianglu) once said that if one who recites the Buddha-name has recited for many years without gaining wondrous function or power, then he should quickly change to cultivating tantra, and after gaining correspondence and samādhi in tantra, turn back to recite the Buddha-name, and then he will know where Buddha-recitation lands. Therefore we who study Buddhism must recognize where deluded thoughts come from and recognize and take up the true mind at the place where deluded thoughts rest; this is most important.

After recognizing and taking up the true mind, “one naturally abides.” Abiding that is no-abiding is called natural abiding. Naturally, steadily, luminous and still, still and luminous, no longer shaken by circumstances, no longer troubled by deluded thoughts. Studying Buddhism thus is truly gaining power. Otherwise it is all misdirected effort. Some people say: I have already recited such and such a number of sutras, and I must recite such and such a number more; I must fulfill my vows! Doing such things is precisely the great dream not yet awakened, not true effort, not truly studying Buddhism! To truly study Buddhism one must recognize the originally non-abiding wondrous luminous true mind, be awake at every moment, be non-abiding in every place; only then is there hope of becoming Buddha. How many Buddha-names one has recited, how many sutras one has read, dotting little red dots, burning a little, fulfilling a few vows — what use is that? Clinging to marks like this, can one become Buddha? One cannot.
“Where deluded thoughts cease, purity is attained accordingly — this is even more important (merely knowing deluded thoughts, one cannot cut off delusion).”

At the very place where those deluded thoughts cease, the originally pure true mind appears accordingly. When the waves settle, is that not pure water? To recognize and take up this true mind is even more important. (Merely recognizing deluded thoughts, without recognizing and taking up the true mind, one cannot cut off the stream of confused karma.) We have already said a great deal about this just now.

“The arising and ceasing of a thought are simultaneous, like drawing on water: as one draws, it vanishes, and all is originally pure. Arising of themselves and ceasing of themselves, closely and continuously, continuing without cease, one attains free spontaneity.”

A thought has only just arisen when it does not stick in the mind but ceases of itself at once, leaving no trace; this is called “the arising and ceasing of a thought are simultaneous.” It is much like drawing a picture on water: a thought has just arisen, which is like our drawing one stroke across the water (the water of the mind); the thought ceases of itself, which is like the picture drawn on the water whose trace is gone. Hence it is said, “as one draws, it vanishes, and all is originally pure.” The Buddha said, “I dwelt in the world forty-nine years and did not speak a single word.” This is vanishing with the drawing, speaking and it being as if not spoken. The Chan school says, “Eating all day, one has not bitten a single grain of rice; wearing clothes all year, one has not hung a single thread of silk on oneself.” It is not that he does not eat or does not wear clothes; having eaten and worn them, it is finished, and he does not discriminate or fuss about it. The mind must be empty and pure like this to attain the Way.

Arising of themselves and ceasing of themselves, closely and continuously, continuing without cease, one attains free spontaneity.” A deluded thought has just arisen when it naturally ceases; this is the “the green mountain is originally unmoving, the white clouds come and go as they please” spoken of earlier. My green mountain (the true mind) does not move, and I let your white clouds (deluded thoughts) come and go. Though they come and go, once they have come and gone they are gone; this is called “arising of themselves and ceasing of themselves.”

Closely and continuously, continuing without cease” speaks of doing the work. The difficulty of doing the work lies precisely in this. “Continuous” means drawn out, and continuity means persisting long; “close” means not sparse, and closeness means without interruption. Closely and continuously is to go on thus over a long time without interruption. Continuing without cease is to succeed one another without stopping. The work must be done thus to do at all. If we can truly work thus, in three or five years we will certainly succeed. To say three or five years is already to speak generously. My teacher (Master Wang Xianglu) once said: a year and a half guarantees accomplishment — if you do not accomplish it, come and ask me. This is true! If we can “be closely and continuously, continuing without cease,” how could we fail to accomplish it? We will certainly accomplish it! The trouble is precisely that we cannot “be closely and continuously, continuing without cease”; we all cultivate and stop, fishing three days and drying nets two.

This passage is very important; let me repeat it once more: when deluded thoughts have stopped, that clean and pure, perfectly clear knowing is the true-so intrinsic nature, and apart from this nothing else is it. Do not be there doubting, “This is not it, is it? If this were it, why do I not bring forth superknowledges?” If you think that way, you are ruined, for you have clung to the demon of superknowledges. Do you want to see superknowledges? Then I will show them to you right now: that I am speaking here — is that not a superknowledge? That you are here listening to this teaching — is that not a superknowledge? That you walked here — is that not a superknowledge? All of these are superknowledges, all are the wondrous function of the true-so intrinsic nature. The true-so intrinsic nature is the spirit, and having no obstruction is the penetrating. When the mind abides nowhere, it is naturally penetrating. But our present superknowledges are small superknowledges. As long as we “closely and continuously, continuing without cease” protect the true-so intrinsic nature, after a long time great superknowledges will come forth. When great superknowledges appear in the future, they will depend on this little bit of today, on this “recognizing and taking up the true mind.” When we now recognize and take up the true mind, it is like a newborn babe (an infant) just born, which cannot yet function as an adult does; therefore one must protect it.
